  • profile_face (optional, mitcad#535): {"body": "F2.b0", "face": "F2:end(r{…})"}, a planar face of a body as the profile instead of profiles: its bounded area, holes kept, swept along its outward normal (against it with flip or a negative distance) by Kernel::extrude_face (geometry/src/face_extrude.cpp). The face is a topological name found on its body at the feature’s point of the timeline on every recompute (a face a sketch change renamed is found again, with the warning of renamed faces), so an upstream edit moves or resizes the extrusion with the face; the body is read in the feature’s component, and the feature depends on it and on the features the name refers to. It takes every extent of profiles (mitcad#2033): distance, symmetric, to_object, through_all (one way or both_sides) and two_sides of any of their sides, each side with its taper as for profiles (mitcad#541: the outside grows away from the face and its holes shrink with a positive taper; up to an object only along the face’s normal). Up to an object: a plane, a face (its surface continued, or chained with the faces next to it), a body (its first face reached, or through it), a point or a line (the plane through it parallel to the face), of the face’s own body or another one, moved by the side’s offset; the face’s prism past it, trimmed where it reaches it (the caps there named as the side’s far cap). The stepped block’s lower top extruded to_object the higher top’s face with join fills the step: one level body. Through all: past every participant body (all bodies when none are listed) from the face, as for profiles (there are no bodies in the extrude direction when none lies that way). From the face (profile_plane) or an offset along its outward normal, and a direction of its own (mitcad#541, not in the face’s plane; the distances along it, a taper growing the face in its plane by d tan(taper) at distance d); no profiles, thin, surface, curves, wrap, cut_scope or start object (refused: an extrusion of a body face starts at the face or offset from it, … takes no sketch profiles, … has no thin walls, surface, curves or wrap, … works on the bodies of its own component, without cut_scope). Two sides built apart (a taper or a target) leave no face between them (mid(<face>) only where their shapes differ). A face that is gone, not planar without a direction (face F3:side0 is not planar: an extrusion takes a planar face …; a curved face goes along a direction only, as its prism, without a taper or offset), a mesh body’s, or names several faces fails the feature; no other profile is ever taken instead. Operations and participants as above (automatic operation too). Faces: side(<edge>) from each edge of the face, by the edge’s name in the body (a surface body’s free edge, which has none, by its index among the face’s edges: side(2)), start(<face>) and end(<face>) keyed by the stored face reference, the caps as for profiles below: F5:side(E{F2:end(r{…})|F2:side(c1[c4,c2])}), F5:end(F2:end(r{…})).

Faces: side(<segment>); outer(<segment>) and inner(<segment>) for thin walls (side 1 and side 2); start(<region>) and end(<region>). Walls along curves: outer(<curve>) and inner(<curve>) along each curve, tip0(<curve>) and tip1(<curve>) at an open chain’s start (on its first curve) and end (its last), and the caps keyed by the chain’s curves (start(r{c1,c4})). With one side the start is the cap at the start and the end the far cap; with two sides (and symmetric) the start is the far cap of side one and the end the far cap of side two (startFaces and endFaces in .f3d designs). The faces of an object where the extrusion ends get the cap’s name. A side face that a two-sided taper bends at the start is two pieces (#0, #1); mid(<region>) is what remains of the start between two sides of different walls.

Operations: new body makes a body per solid (<extrude>.b0, .b1, …). Join fuses the tool with every participant it touches; joined bodies merge into the first of them, and a tool solid that touches nothing becomes a new body. A tool solid that merges with no body (one that touches a body only along an edge or at a point, which cannot make one solid with it, or a profile of several that lies away from the bodies) is a new body too, and the feature warns: “a part of the joined shape touches the bodies at most along an edge or at a point, so it became a body of its own”, with the box of each such solid as the warning’s place (mitcad#2127); the preview’s warnings carry it while the command panel is open. The same holds for the joins of primitives, forms, patterns and the other features that apply a tool to bodies. Cut and intersect work on each participant they reach; a cut through all of a body removes it, and a cut that splits a body keeps the body for the first piece in geometric order and makes the others new bodies of the cut (after an upstream edit the pieces keep their ids: Body ids of a split’s pieces); a piece with less than a millionth of the volume of the largest piece (a needle left where the tool’s wall lies almost on a wall of the body) stays in that piece’s body as a lump. A body of several lumps (disjoint solids, as a combine of bodies apart makes it) is cut lump by lump (mitcad#658): it keeps the first piece of each lump and the lumps the cut does not reach (an intersection leaves nothing of those), and only the other pieces of a lump the cut splits are new bodies; before, every piece of such a body was a body of its own. A join, cut or intersection that reaches no participant fails. A participant (or lump) lying wholly inside the tool of an intersection is kept whole, with its names (mitcad#1534).

A join works on a body of several lumps lump by lump as well (mitcad#1003): the lumps it reaches are fused with the tool, the lumps it does not reach stay in the body, and a body left with several solids holds them together; a body merged into another brings all its lumps. The same holds for the joins of primitives, patterns, mirrors and the other features that combine a tool with bodies. Before, the body kept only one of the solids the kernel gave back for it and the others were dropped.

Assembly scope for Extrude Cut

An optional cut_scope enables a single cut across component definitions:

{"context": {"component": "C1", "occurrence": "O1"},
 "targets": {"type": "automatic",
 "excluded": [{"component": "C2", "occurrence": "O2"}],
 "excluded_bodies": [{"component": "C1", "occurrence": "O1", "body": "F2.b0"}]}}

context names the sketch/feature’s owning component and the exact absolute occurrence path in which the tool is displayed. Root uses C0 and "". Target identities use the same absolute-path convention, including nested paths such as O3/O4. Missing paths fail; there is no first-occurrence fallback.

automatic considers the bodies available before the cut across the assembly, then cuts eligible actual intersections except the persistent component and body exclusions and the components that move against the context through joints (Parts that move through joints below). New intersections join the scope; changing an extent never removes an exclusion. Alternatively, {"type":"explicit","included":[...]} limits it to the listed component/path pairs; included: [] means no targets. Both modes accept excluded_bodies for finer selection. A missing included target fails the cut, instead of broadening its scope; so does an exclusion whose path does not exist in the design or places another component, and an excluded body that is in another component. The creators of the context and of included components must precede the feature. Automatic discovery reads only the preceding timeline state, and of later features only the definitions of joints, so later features cannot form a dependency cycle. Deleting a component definition follows normal dependent-feature deletion, including cuts that explicitly include it; Undo restores the cut and its scope. Missing occurrence paths after other edits remain repairable failures.

Exclusions are no references (mitcad#1236). An occurrence in excluded or a body in excluded_bodies names what the cut leaves alone, so it makes the cut a dependent of no feature that builds that occurrence’s bodies or that body: the dependents query does not list the cut for them, delete_feature deletes them without refusing, delete_feature with "dependents": true does not take the cut along, and they may be suppressed or moved after the cut. An exclusion of an occurrence that is not placed yet at the cut, or of a body that is not there at the cut, leaves nothing alone there and does not fail it. When a delete (delete_feature, delete_occurrence, build_remove) takes the excluded occurrence or body out of the design, or the feature that made the body, the exclusion is dropped from the scope: the cut keeps working, and the command’s result has an info notice about the cut (target: its uid) for each exclusion dropped. Undo restores it. The real references keep their dependencies: an explicit scope’s included components, participants, object_links, the profile’s sketch and its projections, and planes on another component’s geometry. The cut scope is the only stored list of what something leaves out: combine (its tools and tool_links), split_body (its tools and tool_links), the moves (the bodies and occurrences they move), the patterns (their objects) and Section Analysis (its plane’s and axis’ occurrences) name only what they use, so what they name stays a reference; the interference query’s bodies are a query’s input, not stored in the design.

Only Cut activates cut_scope, and an active scope cannot be combined with nonempty legacy participants. Other solid operations may retain a dormant scope so that changing back to Cut restores the chosen targets and exclusions. For a modern non-Cut that has never chosen targets, the scope may contain "initialize_on_cut": true (default false, omitted when false). The editor then initializes automatic targets and samples current visibility when Cut is chosen, removing this flag before submission. Cut rejects a scope whose flag is still true. Automatic Join participants remain Join bookkeeping; explicitly selected local participants keep local behavior without a scope. A dormant scope affects no geometry, references, target discovery or feature replay; it is checked when Cut activates it again. Surface, face-profile and wrapped extrusions continue to reject scopes. Omitting cut_scope preserves existing local-component behavior and the meaning of an empty participants list. Through All uses all discovered bodies, including excluded or disabled ones, to define the tool length; toggling a target does not shorten the tool. Every Boolean uses the target’s local frame.

A scoped cut that reaches no body it may take fails with No eligible components intersect the cut. When the same cut with flip reversed would cut such a body (a checked, eligible component’s body that is neither excluded nor a mesh), the failure says so instead: No eligible components intersect the cut. Try Flip: the other direction cuts a component (mitcad#1676; a cut drawn out of the body’s face is the usual case). A symmetric extent and Through All to both sides, which Flip does not change, never give the hint. The preview’s cut_targets report then has "flip_would_cut": true and is otherwise the miss’s own. The first surviving piece keeps its body ID; additional pieces receive IDs of the cut and all pieces retain the target component’s ownership (ids kept after upstream edits as in Body ids of a split’s pieces). Results publish atomically, so a target failure leaves all preceding bodies unchanged.

A definition with multiple available root-to-component paths is disabled, including hidden occurrences and repetitions through shared parent assemblies. Linked definitions and their descendants are also disabled. Automatic mode skips these targets and reports why; explicitly including one fails. This version does not create per-occurrence replacement geometry.

The extrusion’s own component (context.component) is the exception (mitcad#769): a cut made inside it changes its definition, as any of its features does, so however many occurrences place it, its bodies are one target, at the context occurrence, and every occurrence shows the result. Its row is eligible and, with more than one occurrence, carries a note (Component being edited; the cut changes all 2 occurrences.); its other occurrences get no rows. Explicitly including it at another occurrence fails; exclusions stored for its other occurrences are ignored. Other components below it that are placed more than once stay disabled. A mirror or a pattern repeats a scoped cut only in its own component (Mirrors and patterns of a scoped cut).

Parts that move through joints (mitcad#1667). An automatic scope leaves alone a component that moves against the context through joints, so that a link’s holes and recesses never cut the link it turns on and no body changes with the mechanism’s pose (a joint drag, drive_joint, an animation). Its row is unchecked and not eligible in the automatic scope, with the reason Moves against this component through joints, so it is left out; check it to cut it as well. and "joint_motion": true (left out when false; mitcad#1789), which tells it from the rows unavailable for other reasons (linked, placed more than once): the Affected components list lets the user check it, and an explicit scope that includes it cuts it as any other target (the list’s step from one scope to the other: app/COMMANDS.md, “Extrude, Affected components”). An explicit scope marks no row. What moves is read from the joints, as-built joints and rigid groups of the whole design that are not suppressed, wherever they are in the timeline (adding, suppressing or editing one evaluates the cut again): the joint solver’s units, an occurrence placed in a joint’s component with those its rigid joints and rigid groups join to it, move when a joint with free motions connects them and no member is grounded or joined rigidly to its component’s own geometry. Below the occurrences the context’s path and a target’s path share, the target moves against the context when their first occurrences are different units of which one moves, or an occurrence further down either path moves. The context’s own component is always cut (mitcad#769). Assembly constraint sets do not count. Occurrences no joint names do not move: an automatic cut still reaches them, and a designer moving one by hand changes what it cuts, as before.

Inserted designs (mitcad#1667). An automatic scope found its targets in the design the cut was made in. insert_component with "link": false and a library part inserted as a copy turn it into an explicit scope: the context, then the other copied components (the inserted design’s root among them) that are placed once, not linked, made before the cut and not excluded, at their paths in the new design; excluded bodies stay. The cut then reaches nothing of the design it is inserted into, wherever the copy is placed; the Affected components list shows the new design’s components it intersects unchecked, to be chosen. Paste New and other copies within one design keep an automatic scope automatic. Before this, an inserted part’s cuts also cut every body of the new design they overlapped, and a design saved so keeps automatic scopes: its parts that move through joints are left alone by the rule above.

The normal feature preview adds cut_targets:

{"mode":"automatic", "selected_components":2, "selected_bodies":3,
 "can_commit":true,
 "rows":[{"component":"C1", "occurrence":"O1", "name":"Bracket",
 "path_name":"Root / Bracket:1", "intersects":true,
 "eligible":true, "checked":true, "partial":false, "reason":null,
 "bodies":[{"body":"F2.b0", "name":"Body1", "checked":true}]}]}

Rows contain intersecting bodies, plus stored component/body exclusions or explicit inclusions even when they no longer intersect. partial identifies a component with only some intersecting bodies checked. Boolean intersection, not bounding-box overlap alone, determines membership. The report is retained for no-target and unsupported-target evaluation errors; the ordinary preview status/error and can_commit control acceptance. A missing report means the tool or context could not be evaluated and the previous list must not be used. "flip_would_cut": true (left out when false; mitcad#1676) marks a cut that reaches no body but would cut one with flip reversed (the Flip hint above); the rest of the report is the miss’s own, and the Cut targets panel’s status line then suggests Flip.

Mirrors and patterns of a scoped cut (mitcad#2126)

A mirror or a pattern of features (any pattern type) repeats a cut with a cut_scope in the cut’s own component: its copies cut the bodies of that component that the scope does not exclude, and nothing else. Other components do not refuse it as long as neither the cut nor a copy reaches them; the cut’s own result says what it reached (the cut_targets of its evaluation, a row of another component with a body cut). It is refused, in words with the cut’s and that component’s names and the component’s occurrence as the failure’s place (no ids), when:

  • the cut also cuts another component (its result changed a body there, or its explicit scope includes one): Could not mirror Extrude2: it also cuts Component1, and a mirrored or patterned cut changes only the bodies of its own component. Leave that component out in the cut's Affected components. (Could not repeat Extrude2 in the pattern: … for a pattern);
  • one of its copies would cut a body of another component that the scope takes (checked, eligible, not excluded, not a mesh), so that it is never left uncut there silently: Could not mirror Extrude2: its mirrored copy would also cut Component1, and a mirrored or patterned cut changes only the bodies of its own component. (Could not repeat Extrude2 in the pattern: a copy of it would also cut Component1, …). With "compute": "optimized" and a fillet or chamfer among the features, whose faces are copied instead of the features (mitcad#2171), each copy of the cut is checked the same way first; a pattern none of whose copies reaches another component keeps the face copy;
  • its own component is not eligible (Could not mirror Extrude2: and the row’s reason), or no body of it is left to cut (Could not mirror Extrude2: it cuts no body of its own component, and a mirrored or patterned cut changes only the bodies of its own component.).

An explicit scope that includes another component is refused where the mirror or the pattern is evaluated, as the others: the feature is added and fails with the message (before, adding it was refused without names). Cuts without a stored scope (a cut from a body face, an older design, a Hole) are repeated as before.

A direction of its own (mitcad#539)

"direction": [x, y, z] (any length but zero; left out by default) extrudes the profiles along that fixed direction instead of the sketch normal; flip and a negative one-sided distance reverse it, and it turns with the profile in patterns and with Reorient Design. Distances are measured along it (a prism of the profile slanted by the direction), a start offset still along the sketch normal. A taper grows the profile in its plane: every loop moves outwards from the material by t tan(taper) at the distance t along the direction, each side face ruled from its edge to that edge’s offset moved along the direction (as the FreeCAD import’s pads along a custom direction are; along the normal it is the usual taper). The geometry builds it as the taper along the normal to the same height (the distance times the cosine c of the direction’s angle to the normal, the taper’s tangent over c) sheared along the direction, which keeps the planes parallel to the sketch, and gives the side faces back their planes; a circle’s side is the oblique cone through the grown circles (geometry/tests/test_extrude_feature.cpp, test_oblique). A direction in the sketch plane fails the extrusion (the extrusion direction lies in the sketch plane); it is refused with a start object or a wrap, and a tapered side up to an object along it is unsupported. A body face as the profile (profile_face, mitcad#541) goes along it too, tapered alike (the extrusion direction lies in the plane of face … for one in the face’s plane); a curved face goes only along a direction.

Profile selections

The profiles of extrude, revolve, sweep and helix select an area of their sketch (mitcad#199), the same in a preview and in the feature:

  • A selectable area is one profile region: a face of the planar arrangement of the sketch’s curves with its holes, as the application shows and highlights it. Nested and overlapping shapes are separate regions: squares A, B and C, each inside the one before, make the ring between A and B (B its hole), the ring between B and C and the square C; two overlapping shapes make each one’s own part and their overlap.
  • A sketch whose plane is a planar body face also uses that face’s named boundary edges in the arrangement (mitcad#1138). They are transient profile geometry, not sketch entities or projections. A line across the face splits it; an octagon inside a circular face adds the region between them. Construction curves do not split profiles, face holes stay holes, and closed sketch regions outside the face remain selectable. Such regions carry "face_bounded": true in profiles and the sketch query’s regions. Their keys use b{<edge>} for a boundary curve, for example r{b{E{F2:end(r{c2})|F2:side(c2)}}}. A one-sided open edge constructed from a sketch profile instead uses b{O{<source profile face>|<source segment>}}, for example b{O{F2:patch(r{c1[c4,c2],c2[c1,c3],c3[c2,c4],c4[c3,c1]})|c1[c4,c2]}} (mitcad#1142). This names the actual source profile segment in its creating face’s namespace; a profile Patch accepts regions of one sketch only. It is not an edge index, a coordinate-derived identity or a fictitious pair of adjacent faces. Existing b{E{...}} names do not change. Intersection ends use the same curve names; face edges in a hole also participate in the region’s key. These are ordinary profile references accepted by Extrude, Revolve and the other profile consumers, including previews and joins or cuts. Boundaries follow the supporting body on recompute. Redefining the sketch onto another plane, or offsetting it off its face, removes them; a feature using one then reports has no profile, rather than falling back to a remaining region sharing only a sketch curve. Source-profile boundary provenance follows explicit operation history and survives stored results and save/reopen. Ordinary face and edge selections keep their existing names; O{...} is a profile-boundary reference only. A boundary without a usable named edge or unambiguous source-profile provenance retains the sketch’s own regions and reports a warning that face-bounded profiles are unavailable. History that merges distinct provenance references or splits one into ambiguous boundary pieces is diagnosed rather than numbered by geometry. A reference whose key has no boundary curve and is not one of these regions (a region of the sketch’s own curves that the face’s edges cut: a design saved before they bounded profiles, or a face that changed under the sketch) means the region the sketch’s curves bound by themselves: it is found exactly, without a warning, not as the face-bounded piece most like it (mitcad#1182).
  • The face’s edges and the outline a sketch got when it was made (sketch.create with project_face, a projection with "automatic": true) are automatic boundaries: geometry the user neither drew nor chose, which does not split what the user drew (mitcad#2197). The sketch’s other profile curves (drawn curves, texts, projections the user made) are its own curves, and an own area is a region of the own curves alone, with its holes. An own area is one profile region whatever automatic boundaries cross it, keyed as without them: a circle across the face’s edge is one disc (r{c5}), a rectangle reaching past the face is one region with its holes, and a hole of the face inside it makes no hole in it. Outside every own area the automatic boundaries bound regions as above: the face’s leftover around the shapes, a region closed by drawn lines and the face’s edge, the face alone. A line across the face still splits it (a line closes no area), and so does an edge the user projected: a projection the user made is a choice. A 3D sketch on a face follows the same rule. There is no preference for it: the regions are part of the design. A reference to a piece the rule before made (a key with an automatic boundary inside an own area, as designs saved before mitcad#2197 have) still means that piece, found exactly and without a warning, so that saved designs keep their bodies; new picks take the own area. A face outline projected by hand, and the outline of a design saved before the flag existed (it cannot be told from a Project of the face as the sketch’s first step), count as the user’s.
  • The selected area is the odd/even (XOR) composition of the selected regions: covered by an odd number of them, it is extruded. Regions of one sketch never overlap, so that is each selected region once: the outer ring alone is A minus B (its hole stays a hole, it is neither filled nor taken away twice), the outer ring and C are A minus B plus C (A xor B xor C), all three regions are A; the two own parts of overlapping shapes leave their overlap out (their xor). The order of the list does not matter for the area.
  • The list is a set: a reference listed twice is read once (a definition keeps it once), and references that find the same region (a key that changed with the sketch and the current key) use it once. Neither is an error; an empty list is (no profiles selected).
  • Toggling is the application’s: a click on a selected region takes its entry out (every entry that finds that region; a click on one piece of a region a sketch edit split takes out that piece, the reference’s other pieces staying listed under their own keys, mitcad#410), a click on another one adds it (app/COMMANDS.md, “Selection inputs”).
  • The profile query (sketch, region) gives the region a reference means now: sketch, region (its current key: the same key, or the main region found when the sketch changed), regions (the current keys of every region it means, the main one first: more than one when a change split it), exact (the key is the region’s own); null when no region shares a curve with it. profile_shape (the bridge) draws all of them.

Profile references after a sketch change

A sketch edit can rename the regions later features use: their keys are made of curve ids, and a curve that now crosses, touches or leaves a region’s boundary changes the key (mitcad#407). A reference whose key is no longer a region’s own is found again:

  1. Each segment c3[c2,c4] of the key is traced on the current curves: the pieces of c3 from where it meets c2 to where it meets c4 (both may meet it there with other curves now). When the traced segments close one loop, the regions inside it are what the reference selects: the region renamed, or all pieces of a region the edit split (a bar lengthened across another curve keeps both of its parts selected, so the area that was selected stays selected). Regions in a hole of those pieces (islands inside) stay out, as the old region’s holes did. A hole that the change took across the outline stays out too (mitcad#1740): a 40 x 20 plate less a hole whose diameter grows to 24 is found as its left and right pieces, not the piece of the plate inside the circle. The key names only the outline, so the holes are read from the curves: an area that curves outside the key bound alone (the key’s curves crossed freely) stays out when it holds none of the outline’s corners, does not reach the outside of every region, and lies more inside the outline than outside it. A line across the region (it bounds no area), a region lengthened across another curve (its pieces hold corners) and a region grown into an outline lying mostly outside it keep every piece.
  2. When the key’s segments trace no loop (a curve of it is gone, or no longer meets the curve at its end), the reference means the region with the most curves in common, then the most identical segments, then the fewest other curves, then the largest. Every other region as like it by the first three is selected too, as the pieces of a split region are (mitcad#1993): a region between two outlines that a change moved apart (two letters of a text on a tight arc, overlapping until the text was flipped to the arc’s other side) names pieces of both, and both letters’ regions are what it selected, not the larger alone.
  3. A key that shares no curve with any region fails the feature: Sketch1 has no profile r{…}.

The main region (the piece with the most curves in common, by rule 2’s order) carries the referenced key, so that the faces made from it keep their names (F2:end(r{…})); the other pieces carry their own keys. The feature keeps its definition and succeeds with a warning, shown in the timeline (status warning) and the feature query’s warnings, as renamed faces do (Faces, edges and vertices a sketch change renamed): region r{c5[c11,c13],c11[c5,c12],…} found as r{c3[c11,c13],…} + r{c3[c11,c13],…} after a change in Sketch1 (the current keys, the main one first); its notice reads “a region found again after a change in Sketch1” (“a region found as 2 regions …” for a split one), the keys its places of kind region with the sketch’s uid (Notices, mitcad#1334). A loft section, one region, lofts the main piece and warns that the section was split. Reverting the edit restores the keys and removes the warning.

revolve 

{"type": "revolve",
 "profiles": [{"sketch": "F1", "region": "r{c1[c4,c2],c2[c1,c3],c3[c2,c4],c4[c3,c1]}"}],
 "axis": "y",
 "extent": {"type": "angle", "angle": 1.5708},
 "operation": "new_body"}
  • surface, curves: a surface revolution, walls without caps (Surface modelling, mitcad#455).
  • axis: a line reference: a sketch line {"sketch": uid, "curve": "c4"} (from its start to its end; any line, also a construction or centre line), an origin axis, a construction axis "F7", a straight edge {"body": b, "edge": e} or a fixed axis. project_axis: true projects it into the sketch plane (isProjectAxis in .f3d designs).
  • extent (positive by the right hand rule about the axis direction): {"type": "angle", "angle": a} (one side; negative turns the other way), {"type": "full"}, {"type": "symmetric", "angle": a} (a to each side, as .f3d designs measure it), {"type": "two_sides", "angle1": a1, "angle2": a2} (a1 not negative; a negative a2, mitcad#955, ends side two past the profile: the turn runs from -a2 to a1, so a1 + a2 must be more than zero; not for a body face) or {"type": "to_object", "object": <object>} (the positive way to the first face of the object reached; with a body’s "through": true, mitcad#539, through the body to its last face, where the turn leaves it for the last time: the pieces of the turn are taken in the order of their angles about the axis up to the last one inside the body; geometry/tests/test_revolve.cpp, test_to_object).
  • object_links (mitcad#762): the body of another component that the to_object object is or is a face of, with where it is seen, {"F2.b0": {"source": "O1", "target": "O2"}}, as an extrusion’s object_links: the body is read in its component and moved into the revolution’s coordinates by the occurrences’ placements at its point of the timeline. Without a link another component’s body fails the revolution; a link for a body that is not the object’s is refused.
  • operation, participants: as for extrude.
  • profile_face (optional, mitcad#539): {"body": "F2.b0", "face": "F2:side(c1[c4,c2])"}, a planar face of a body as the profile instead of profiles, as an extrusion’s profile_face: its bounded area, holes kept, turned about the axis by Kernel::revolve_face (geometry/src/face_revolve.cpp). The face is found by its topological name on every recompute; the feature depends on its body and on the features the name refers to. Extents angle, full, symmetric and two_sides (as for profiles: a negative single angle turns the other way, a side of nothing leaves one side); no profiles, surface, curves, project_axis or to_object (refused: a revolution of a body face …). A face that is gone, not planar, a mesh body’s, names several faces, crosses the axis or has the axis through it fails the feature; no other profile is taken instead. Faces: side(<edge>) from each edge of the face off the axis (by the edge’s name in the body, an edge without one by its index among the face’s edges), start(<face>) and end(<face>) keyed by the stored face reference, as for profiles below; a full turn has no caps.

The profile may touch the axis. Regions that touch are united into one face before the turn (turned apart and fused, two parts of one surface that their shared edge cut in two were merged back into a face built wrong). A profile that straddles the axis line (an imported one: an edge on the axis with a part beyond it) is parted at the line and each part turns on its own side. An axis that passes through a profile is refused. Faces are named as an extrusion’s (a face across two regions carries both their segments’ names); a full turn has no caps.

hole 

{"type": "hole",
 "placement": {"type": "face", "body": "F2.b0", "face": "F2:end(r{…})", "points": [[30, 20, 20]]},
 "diameter": 10,
 "kind": {"type": "counterbore", "diameter": 16, "depth": 5},
 "tip_angle": 2.0595,
 "extent": {"type": "distance", "depth": 10},
 "thread": {"designation": "M10x1.5", "class": "6H", "modeled": false}}

  • placement: {"type": "face", "body": b, "face": f, "points": [[x, y, z], …]} (points put onto a planar face’s plane, one hole each; on a cylindrical face each point moved across its axis onto the cylinder, the hole along the radius into the material, mitcad#719), {"type": "face_offsets", "body": b, "face": f, "edge1": e1, "offset1": o1, "edge2": e2, "offset2": o2} (one hole at those distances from the lines of two edges, on the face’s side of both) or {"type": "sketch_points", "sketch": uid, "points": [[u, v], "c5", "p3", …]} (sketch coordinates, the centres of the sketch’s circles, arcs and ellipses, or its points; setPositionBySketchPoints in .f3d designs) or {"type": "plane", "plane": g, "points": [[x, y, z], …]} (points put onto an origin plane, a construction plane or a planar face’s plane: the holes start on it, also inside a body, and cut the participants they reach; setPositionByPoint on a plane in .f3d designs) or {"type": "cylinder_offset", "body": b, "face": f, "plane": g, "offset": o, "toward": [x, y, z]} (one hole on a cylindrical face, at the point of its axis o from the plane g the axis crosses, measured along the plane’s normal on the face’s side of it (along the axis for a plane square to it), on the side of the axis where the point lies, along the radius into the material; setPositionByPlaneAndOffsets on a shaft’s side in .f3d designs, mitcad#719). Holes go against the face, plane or sketch normal, into the material; flip turns them round (isDefaultDirection false). The Hole panel edits face_offsets, plane and cylinder_offset placements as they are (Placement From Two Edges, On a Plane, Along a Shaft), the distances as Edge Offset 1 and 2 or Offset (mitcad#733).

  • kind: {"type": "simple"} (default), {"type": "counterbore", "diameter": D, "depth": d}, {"type": "countersink", "diameter": D, "angle": a} (the cone’s full angle), {"type": "counterdrill", "diameter": D, "depth": d, "angle": a} (a counterbore whose floor is a cone of the full angle narrowing to the hole), {"type": "nut_pocket", "across_flats": s, "depth": d} (mitcad#1518, below).

  • A nut pocket (kind nut_pocket, mitcad#1518) is a hex pocket for a nut about the round hole, for printed parts: a regular hexagon across_flats wide, depth deep. The hole_sizes query’s nut_pocket gives both for a screw size: ISO 4032’s nut with a clearance (M3: 5.5 + 0.3 across the flats, 2.4 + 0.3 deep); the hole stores them as plain values. Place the hole on the face where the screw comes out: the pocket lies at the hole’s start. Optional:

    • offset: the pocket’s top that far below the hole’s start (0 when left out); a pocket below the start with no slot is a closed cavity, for a nut put in at a print pause;
    • angle: the hexagon turned about the axis from where its first flat’s normal lies along the x axis projected onto the start plane (the y axis for a hole along x), counterclockwise about the hole’s direction, as a press fit’s section;
    • slot: a side slot to slide the nut in, the pocket run out sideways to that distance from the axis (more than the corners’ across_flats / √3, usually out of the body), along the first flat (a quarter turn on from its normal), as wide as across the flats and as deep.

    The pocket must be wider than the hole and, with a distance extent, end before the hole’s depth. A nut pocket’s hole has no thread (the nut has it), taper, print_shape or press_fit; a clearance names the screw size as for a counterbore. Faces besides the round hole’s: hole<i>.pocket<k> (the flats, k from 0 counterclockwise about the hole’s direction; a slot takes the second and the third away and carries the first and the fourth on as its sides), hole<i>.pocket_floor, hole<i>.pocket_roof (a pocket below the start: its top and its slot’s) and hole<i>.slot_end; the wall of a hole through a pocket below the start is in two pieces. The hole’s callout gives the bore. Tests: nut_pocket_insert_tests (core/model-tests/features-profile), features::hole::tests::nut_pockets_and_insert_holes_keep_their_values, test_nut_pockets (geometry/tests/test_hole.cpp).

  • taper (optional): the wall’s angle to the axis, positive narrowing the hole from its diameter at the start as it goes deeper (a counterbore’s floor and a countersink’s or counterdrill’s cone meet the leaning wall; the drill point starts from the wall’s end). Not with a thread.

  • tip_angle: the drill point’s full angle, 118° when left out; flat: true for a flat bottom.

  • extent: {"type": "distance", "depth": d} (to the shoulder, from the start; the point is extra), {"type": "through_all"} (past every participant, flat) or {"type": "to_object", "object": <object>, "offset": o} (the cylinder ends where each axis first meets the object, the point beyond; a point or line object is the plane through it at right angles to the axis, mitcad#1329).

  • thread (a tapped hole): standard (iso_metric default, unified, whitworth, npt, tyre_valve, forming_screw, trapezoidal, iso_taper, custom), designation, class, right_handed (default true), modeled (ISO metric, Unified, tyre valve, forming screw, trapezoidal, custom and NPT only), and length, offset from the hole’s start (the whole wall when left out), and for a modelled thread radial_clearance and flank_clearance; a custom thread’s custom size and a modelled thread’s starts (Custom and multi-start threads); as for the thread feature. A modelled thread’s ends (mitcad#1307) as the thread feature’s: run_out runs the grooves out into a countersink’s or counterdrill’s cone that opens away from the thread, flat stops them flat with a lip at the cone’s root. An add_feature or edit_feature without it gives run_out, and the design file stores it with every modelled thread; a hole’s modelled thread in a design file written before it existed is read as flat, so that the hole keeps its shape and the names at its thread’s ends (saving writes flat). Ignored on a cosmetic thread. The bore is the size’s basic minor diameter (a custom thread’s D − 5H/4, a trapezoidal thread’s D1 = d − P); diameter is then ignored. A taper pipe thread (npt, iso_taper Rc …; mitcad#733) with "taper": true keeps diameter, the tap drill (the thread_sizes query’s tap_drill, the Hole panel’s default), and tapers the bore from the hole’s start: 1:16 on the diameter from its minor diameter at the opening, down to where it meets the drilled bore, cosmetic or modelled (see thread); diameter must then be greater than zero. Without taper (holes saved before) its bore is the size’s minor diameter and nothing tapers, as it was, and NPT cannot be modelled. Patterns and mirrors of a tapering hole (or of one with a modelled thread) copy the hole feature, not only its tool.

  • clearance (optional, mitcad#903): a clearance hole’s screw size and fit, {"size": "M6", "fit": "normal"} (fine, normal, coarse; normal when left out), a size of the hole_sizes query; not with a thread. It only names where the hole’s values came from: the hole is cut at its own diameter and kind, plain values as any hole’s. Holes saved before have none.

  • insert (optional, mitcad#1518): a heat-set insert’s hole for printed parts, {"size": "M3"}, a size of the hole_sizes query’s insert series, whose insert gives the hole’s diameter and depth (M3: 4.0, 6.7 deep). As clearance, it only names where the values came from: the hole is cut at its own diameter and extent. A simple hole with no thread, clearance or press_fit.

  • press_fit (optional, mitcad#1517): a press-fit hole for printed parts, {"shape": "hex", "interference": "press_fit_interference"}. diameter is then the nominal diameter of the pin or bearing that goes in, and the hole’s section runs along the whole hole, which has a flat bottom (tip_angle and flat are not used):

    • shape: hex or square (a regular hexagon or square whose flats touch a circle of diameter − interference: flats that grip a pin), or crush_ribs (a round bore with small triangular ribs evenly spaced round it, their tips on a circle of diameter − interference, each rib’s base on the bore twice its height wide; the pin or bearing crushes them as it goes in, for parts assembled once);
    • interference: on the diameter, usually the printed fit parameter press_fit_interference (0.1 mm, created when a field names it); a negative one leaves a clearance;
    • ribs (crush ribs only, 3 to 64, 3 when left out) and rib_height (crush ribs only, 0.3 mm when left out): how far each rib stands out of the bore, more than half the interference so that the pin touches only the ribs; the bore is diameter − interference + 2 rib_height;
    • angle (optional): the section turned about the hole’s axis, from where the first flat’s normal or the first rib lies along the x axis projected onto the start plane (the y axis for a hole along x), counterclockwise about the hole’s direction.

    A press-fit hole is a simple hole: no kind other than simple, no taper, thread or clearance. Its faces are hole<i>.flat<k> (a hex’s or square’s flats, k from 0 counterclockwise), or per rib k hole<i>.rib<k>.side0 and hole<i>.rib<k>.side1 (its flanks before and after its tip) and hole<i>.wall<k> (the bore after it), with hole<i>.tip (the flat bottom) and hole<i>.top. It is not round, so it has no hole callout. Tests: features::hole::tests, press_fit_hole_tests (core/model-tests/features-profile), test_press_fits (geometry/tests/test_hole.cpp), tools/cli/tests/press_fit_holes.json.

  • print_shape (optional, mitcad#1515): how a hole printed lying is shaped, for FDM printing: round (the default), teardrop or flat_roof. A round hole whose axis lies parallel to the print bed prints with an unsupported roof that sags, out-of-round and undersized. Over the hole’s cylindrical part (and a counterbore’s or counterdrill’s wider one) its upper arc then gives way to two sides at 45° to the bed’s normal, tangent to the circle: a teardrop meets them at a point the radius × √2 above the axis; a flat_roof cuts them short with a flat roof that bridges, roof_sag above the circle so that the bridge sags onto it (a roof above the point leaves the point). The lower arc keeps the diameter.

    • The bed is the participant bodies’ print bed faces (set_print_bed_face): the first participant that has one, as it is found before the hole, its outward normal down; the design’s −Z is down when none has one (as the 3D print export and Print Analysis take it). Each hole whose axis lies parallel to the bed gets its roof pointing away from it; a hole whose axis does not stays round (all of them round: an information on the feature). A bed face the participants have that is not found before the hole leaves the holes round, with a warning. Setting or clearing a print bed face evaluates print-shaped holes again.
    • roof_sag (flat_roof only, greater than zero, 0.4 mm when left out): usually the printed fit parameter hole_roof_sag (0.4 mm, created when a field names it).
    • Only the solid is shaped: the hole keeps its diameter, its callout and the drawing’s size (hole_callouts). Not with a press_fit, a taper, or a modelled or tapering thread (a cosmetic thread is fine: its bore takes the roof).
    • Faces besides the round hole’s: hole<i>.roof0 and hole<i>.roof1 (the sides, counterclockwise about the hole’s direction after the wall), hole<i>.roof (the flat roof), hole<i>.roof_end (the roof’s end where the cylindrical part ends; on a flat bottom the bottom, also hole<i>.tip), and a counterbore’s hole<i>.cbore_roof0, cbore_roof1, cbore_roof and cbore_roof_end.
    • Tests: print_shape_hole_tests (core/model-tests/features-profile), test_print_shapes (geometry/tests/test_hole.cpp).

  • print_bridging (optional, mitcad#1516): how a counterbore, or a nut pocket at the hole’s start without a slot, that opens toward the print bed is bridged for printing: none (the default), sacrificial or stepped. A hole going up from the bed leaves the bore’s ring over the recess’s floor in the air, so the layers above the floor bridge it, each as thick as the design’s layer height: its own Print Process layer_height, else that of the process profile it uses, else 0.2 mm (the standard printer of mitcad#1498 D5).

    • sacrificial: one layer closes the bore over the floor, a membrane drilled out after printing; the bore starts again a layer above the floor.
    • stepped: the first layer above the floor leaves open only a strip as wide as the hole across the recess, so that bridges span the recess on both sides of it; the second leaves open only the square of the hole’s diameter on the strip, bridged across it; the round hole goes on above. The strip runs along the x axis projected onto the start plane (the y axis for a hole along x), along a nut pocket’s first flat’s normal.
    • It applies to the holes whose axis points straight away from the print bed, as print_shape finds the bed: the participants’ print bed face, else the design’s −Z down. A hole whose recess opens away from the bed is cut as it is (an information on the feature when none is bridged); a bed face that is not found before the hole leaves them all unbridged, with a warning. Setting or clearing a print bed face, or a change of the design’s layer height, evaluates bridged holes again.
    • Not with another kind, a nut pocket’s offset or slot, a taper, a print_shape or a modelled or tapering thread (a cosmetic one is fine). The bridge layers must end before the hole’s depth.
    • Faces besides the hole’s: hole<i>.bridge0 (the first layer’s top: a sacrificial membrane’s, where the bore starts again; the stepped bridges’ tops, two pieces beside the square: bridge0#0 and bridge0#1), hole<i>.bridge0.side0 and .side1 (the strip’s sides), hole<i>.bridge0.end (where the strip ends against the recess’s wall), hole<i>.bridge1 (the square’s top: four corners round the bore, bridge1#0 to #3) and hole<i>.bridge1.side0 to .side3 (the square’s sides, counterclockwise about the hole’s direction from the strip’s first side).
    • Tests: print_bridging_tests (core/model-tests/features-profile), features::hole::tests::print_bridging_keeps_its_mode, test_print_bridging (geometry/tests/test_hole.cpp).

  • participants: the bodies to cut, all when left out.

A simple hole (no taper, no thread) into one sheet-metal body, every axis starting on the front or back surface of one planar panel, normal to it and into the material, through all or at least as deep as the sheet, cuts the sheet’s material domain as sheet_cut does (mitcad#211): the body stays a valid sheet for later sheet features, and the walls are named as a cut’s (<sheet>:sheet_side…(<hole>:sheet_curve(<i>))). The hole’s tool is the same, so patterns and mirrors of it repeat it. A hole the domains cannot take (one reaching a bend) is an ordinary cut.

Faces: hole<i>.wall, hole<i>.tip (point or flat bottom), hole<i>.cbore_wall (a counterbore’s or counterdrill’s), hole<i>.cbore_floor, hole<i>.csink, hole<i>.cdrill (a counterdrill’s cone), hole<i>.top (at the start, gone after the cut); i numbers the positions from 0.

thread 

{"type": "thread", "faces": [{"body": "F2.b0", "face": "F2:side(c1)"}],
 "thread": {"designation": "M10x1.5", "class": "6g"},
 "modeled": false, "length": 12, "offset": 2, "location": "high_end"}

  • faces: cylindrical faces, all internal (hole walls) or all external.

  • thread: standard (iso_metric default, unified, whitworth, npt, tyre_valve, forming_screw, trapezoidal, iso_taper, custom: a size of one’s own, see Custom and multi-start threads), designation (M10x1.5, M10 for the coarse pitch, 1/4-20 UNC; Whitworth 1/4-20 BSW, 1/4-26 BSF, the parallel pipe threads G 1/4; NPT 1/4-18 NPT (also 1/2 - 14 NPT); the taper pipe threads of ISO 7-1 R 1/2 on a shaft and Rc 1/2 in a hole (the other side’s fails: “Rc 1/2 is an internal thread; use R 1/2 for a shaft”), mitcad#733; the tyre valve threads of ISO 4570 5V1, 8V1, … on the 60-degree profile, mitcad#59; the forming screw threads of ISO 1478 ST3.5x1.3, the ST may be left out; the trapezoidal threads of ISO 2904 Tr8x1.5, a multi-start one by its lead and pitch Tr10x4(P2), mitcad#449), class (6g external, 6H internal; trapezoidal 7e, 8e, 8c, 9c external, 7H, 8H, 9H internal; Whitworth Close, Medium, Free, A, B external, Medium, Normal, A internal (a pipe thread’s A is on the internal threads of the stored designs); NPT, ISO 7-1 and tyre valve Standard; checked against the face: a class of the other side fails with the class to use, “class 6g is for external threads; use 6H for a hole”), right_handed. Sizes: core/model/data/threads.json (the thread_sizes query). An NPT size is listed at its pipe’s outside diameter, an ISO 7-1 size at its gauge diameter.

  • modeled: build the 60° profile on the faces (ISO metric, Unified, tyre valve, forming screw, custom, and NPT with taper), or the trapezoidal 30° one (trapezoidal, mitcad#893; the others, Whitworth and ISO 7-1, are cosmetic only); otherwise cosmetic: no geometry, listed by the threads query (a cosmetic thread’s end chamfers, below, and a tapering taper pipe thread’s cone are cut into the geometry). The profile is ISO 68-1’s: flanks at 30° to the radius, half a pitch wide at the pitch diameter, flat crests and roots on the major and minor diameters. Along the threaded part the material becomes the thread: removed beyond the profile, and added up to the crest where the face lies inside it (a shaft thinner than the major diameter, a bore wider than the minor one). The part ends in planes across the axis, and runs out through ends of the face with no material beyond them (a shaft’s free end, a hole’s mouth). A straight one’s grooves also run out by a pitch through an end of the face beyond which material lies only on the material’s side of the crest (mitcad#1300): a cone or a countersink that opens away from a hole’s thread, a shaft’s end chamfer or a neck narrowing away from its thread. They cut into that face as far as they reach it and fade out of it, with no flat, unthreaded lip at the face’s end. Material past the end on the crest’s other side (a hole’s floor, a hole or shaft going on, a shoulder) stops them flat at the end, as does ends flat. A partial thread’s ends inside the face run out along a chamfer’s cone where chamfer asks for them (below). Threads of designs saved before keep their flat ends (ends, below).

  • diameters (modelled, or a tapering taper pipe thread): {"major": D, "minor": D1, "pitch": D2}, the profile’s diameters, e.g. a tolerance class’s (the middles of its tolerances, as .f3d designs store them: M10x1.5 6g is 9.85, 8.141, 8.928); the size’s basic diameters (D, D1 = D − 5H/4, D2 = D − 3H/4) when left out, a trapezoidal thread’s with its crest clearance (below). A taper pipe thread’s are those where it starts (below).

  • taper (true; taper pipe threads npt and iso_taper only, mitcad#733): the thread is tapered 1:16 on the diameter. Without it (a thread saved before) a taper pipe thread is straight, as it was: cosmetic only, its size’s diameters, no cone, its end chamfers cut. The Thread panel sets it for new NPT and ISO 7-1 threads (Tapered). A tapering thread’s diameters shrink by 1/16 of the length into an internal thread from where it starts and grows along an external one. It starts at the face’s free end (nothing of the body beyond it: a hole’s mouth, a shaft’s end) where only one end is free, else at the end location names (high_end by default; a part measured from it starts there). Its diameters there are the size’s unless given: NPT (ASME B1.20.1) the pitch diameter E1 = E0 + L1/16 at an internal thread’s opening (the hand-tight plane) and E0 = D − (0.05 D + 1.1) P at an external thread’s end, the major and minor diameters h = 0.8 P above and below it; ISO 7-1 the gauge diameter (the major diameter) at an Rc thread’s opening and the gauge length before it at an R thread’s end, h = 0.640327 P. Even cosmetic it changes the geometry: it cuts the cone of its minor diameter out of a bore (the tapered bore of a tapped pipe hole) or what lies outside the cone of its major diameter off a shaft, over its part, where the cone lies off the face; the cone’s faces are named <feature>:thread_taper(<face>). A modelled NPT thread sweeps its profile, flanks square to the axis, along the tapered helix (no teeth are added where the face lies inside the crest: they stay short, as a tap leaves them). It has no end chamfers: chamfer is left out with a warning (not refused); the threads query gives its taper (0.0625).

  • angle (modelled only): the thread turned about its axis (right-hand rule), 0 when left out. At angle 0, with the axis pointing up (+Z; axes across Z towards +Y, the X axis towards +X), from the face’s end at the low end of that axis and at the reference direction (the X axis projected across the axis; Y for axes within about 25° of X), an external thread’s groove spans the first half pitch at the pitch diameter, an internal thread’s tooth the same half pitch (a bolt and a nut threaded from the same plane mate).

  • length and offset: part of each face, from the end its cylinder’s axis points to (location: high_end, default) or from the other (low_end); the whole face when left out.

  • radial_clearance and flank_clearance (modelled only, lengths of 0 or more, 0 when left out; mitcad#195): extra clearance for a looser fit, e.g. for 3D printing, on top of the profile’s diameters (the size, class, pitch, hand and extent stay). radial_clearance moves the whole profile (crests, roots, flanks and the pitch diameter) along the radius away from the material, per side: an internal thread’s diameters grow by twice it, an external thread’s shrink (0.2 changes each diameter by 0.4). Then flank_clearance moves each flank that far perpendicular to itself into the tooth (not along the axis, not a scale factor): an external thread’s teeth get thinner, an internal thread’s grooves wider; the flank angle, the pitch and the crest and root radii stay, so each flank moves flank_clearance / cos 30° along the axis and the crests narrow by twice that. Clearance on both mating parts adds up. A negative or non-finite value is refused; a flank clearance that leaves the crest narrower than P/50, or a radial clearance that leaves an external thread no core, fails the feature. The largest flank clearance a thread takes is (crest - P/50) cos 30° / 2, the crest without clearance being P/4 inside and P/8 outside for the basic profile: 0.0996 mm on an internal M6x1, 0.0455 mm on an external one. The failure names it, rounded down (“this thread takes a flank clearance of at most 0.0995 mm”).

    • The printed-fit parameter thread_flank_clearance itself as the flank_clearance (the panels’ default, Printed fit parameters; mitcad#691) is a printer’s fit shared by threads of every size: on a pitch too fine for it, the thread uses the largest flank clearance it takes instead (a micrometre below the limit), so a new M6x1 in a 5 mm bore is made with the default 0.1 mm. The parameter keeps its value; a value that fits is used as it is. A number or any other expression is used as given and fails as above when it is too large.

  • chamfer (mitcad#304): "start", "end" or "both", none when left out: a cone cut at those ends of each face, before the profile, so that the first turn starts on the cone and leaves no knife edge. The start is the end location names (high_end by default, also for a thread over the whole face), the end the other one. Only free ends get one: ends the thread reaches with nothing of the body beyond them (a shaft’s free end, a hole’s mouth; not the shoulder under a bolt’s head, nor a cone or countersink the grooves run out into: it is the chamfer already). An external thread’s cone widens from chamfer_diameter at the end into the material at chamfer_angle to the axis, cutting off what lies outside it; an internal thread’s (a countersink) narrows from chamfer_diameter, cutting off what lies inside it. A cosmetic thread gets the same cones (its only geometry), and the threads query starts its rings where a cone meets the cylinder.

    • At a modelled straight thread’s end inside the face (a partial thread’s; mitcad#1300) the chamfer is the thread’s run-out: the grooves, and the cut of the face to the crest, go on past the end inside a cone at chamfer_angle, for an internal thread narrowing from the major diameter (the root, moved by a radial clearance) at the end to the face’s diameter, for an external one widening from the minor diameter to the face’s, so that they fade out of the face with no flat wall; chamfer_diameter does not apply there. The run-out ends at the face’s end. Without a chamfer at that end, the end stays flat. A cosmetic thread’s end inside the face gets nothing.

  • ends (modelled only, mitcad#1300): run_out (the run-outs above) or flat, the ends as they were cut before: the grooves stop flat at every end that is not free (a cone or countersink that opens away from the thread too), and no run-out along a chamfer at an end inside the face. An add_feature or edit_feature of a modelled thread without it gives run_out, and the design file stores it with every modelled thread. A modelled thread in a design file written before it existed (no ends) is read as flat, so that a saved design keeps its shape and what refers to its threads’ ends (a chamfer or fillet on an edge of an end, its pieces’ names) keeps working; saving writes flat, and an edit of the thread without ends gives it the run-outs. An import sets it to what the source program does (mitcad#1302): the .f3d import flat (the file’s threads end at their faces’ ends and leave a cone’s lip), the FreeCAD and .solidcraft imports run_out (their grooves run on through a countersink or cone at a face’s end). Ignored on a cosmetic thread. Versions before mitcad#1300 do not read a design with ends.

  • chamfer_angle: the cone’s angle to the axis, between 0 and 90°; 45° when left out (inside: a 90° countersink).

  • chamfer_diameter: the cone’s diameter at the end. When left out it follows the size (a size change changes it; the thread_chamfer query gives it): an external thread’s minor diameter less P/10, an internal thread’s major diameter plus P/10 (from the size table), and further in (out) when a modelled thread’s root lies beyond that (a class’s minor diameter, a radial clearance), so that no groove reaches the end’s plane. A diameter that leaves the cone outside the thread (an external one not smaller than the face and the crest, an internal one not larger than the bore and the crest), or chamfers deeper than the thread is long, fail the feature. Only with chamfer.

A modelled thread’s new faces (flanks, crests and roots) are thread(<face>), the chamfers’ cones thread_chamfer_low(<face>) and thread_chamfer_high(<face>) (the low and high end along the axis of the face’s cylinder). The thread’s pieces, a crest, two flanks and a root a turn, and the threaded face’s pieces are numbered by their place along the axis (their centres of mass along it, then from it, then their areas), the same on every platform; the numbers start at the pieces' count, thread(<face>)#57 to #113 for 57 pieces (mitcad#490). A piece also keeps the number it had before that, where that number was the same on every platform (pieces at the thread’s ends); references saved to the pieces of whole turns before then no longer find a face and are reported, to be picked again. The work is local: only the body’s faces near the thread take part, so a large body does not slow it down. Imported threads have no end chamfers: the thread properties the imports read (core/import/SCHEMA.md, ThreadFeature) include none; a chamfer in those designs is a feature of its own.

A modelled thread’s end pieces

(mitcad#1231) The numbers along the thread change with the pieces' count: more or fewer turns (a length, an offset, a pitch or a profile change) renumber every piece, the pieces at the thread’s ends too. So each piece of a modelled thread is also named by its place from the nearer end of the face, from 0 at the end: low_thread(<face>)#k from the face’s low end and high_thread(<face>)#k from its high end (the ends along the face’s cylinder’s axis, as the chamfers’ cones name them). A piece has one of them, from the end it lies nearer to, besides its number along the thread. These names come first, so the piece’s edges are named after them: the edge where the thread meets the plain rest of its face, a chamfer’s cone or the body’s end face keeps its name, E{F3:side(c51[c57,c61])|F26:high_thread(F3:side(c51[c57,c61]))#0}, when turns come or go at the other end. Pieces of whole turns in the middle may change their end and place.

A design saved before that names the end’s edge by the piece’s number along the thread (E{F26:thread(F3:side(c51[c57,c61]))#22|F3:side(c51[c57,c61])}#0) finds it again after a change of the pieces’ count (Faces, edges and vertices a sketch change renamed).

Custom and multi-start threads, modelled trapezoidal threads

(mitcad#893)

{"type": "thread", "faces": [{"body": "F2.b0", "face": "F2:side(c1)"}],
 "thread": {"standard": "custom", "right_handed": true},
 "custom": {"major": "12 mm", "pitch": "3 mm"}, "starts": 2, "modeled": true}
  • A custom thread ("standard": "custom") takes its size from custom: major (the major diameter D) and pitch (P), expressions, so it follows parameter changes. It has no designation and no class (one fails: “a custom thread has no tolerance class”), and is the 60-degree profile of ISO 68-1 at that size: D1 = D − 5H/4, D2 = D − 3H/4, H = 0.866025 P. The pitch must leave a core (P < 0.9238 D; “too coarse” otherwise). Cosmetic or modelled like a size of the table, with the same diameters, clearances, angle, part and end chamfers (their default diameter from its minor or major diameter). Without custom the feature fails (“a custom thread needs its size”), and custom on a standard size fails. The threads query lists it with standard custom and designation <D>x<P> (12x3). A tapped hole takes the same custom in its thread (its bore D1).
  • starts (an expression, a whole number from 1 to 64; 1 when left out): a modelled thread’s number of starts. Its grooves are evenly spaced round the axis, a pitch apart along it, each on a helix of lead starts × P: the first is placed as angle says, rising a lead a turn, the others are it turned by 360°/starts. In every section through the axis its profile is a single-start thread’s of the same pitch. A designation with a lead gives its own starts (Tr10x4(P2): 2, lead 4); starts may only repeat it (“Tr10x4(P2) has 2 starts …”). Any size takes starts; the Thread and Hole panels offer it for Custom. The threads query gives a multi-start thread’s starts and lead.
  • A trapezoidal thread is modelled with the profile of ISO 2901: flanks at 15° to the radius (a 30° included angle), half a pitch wide at the pitch diameter d2 = d − P/2, flat crests and roots, and the standard’s crest clearance ac (0.15 mm for P 1.5, 0.25 mm for P 2 to 5, 0.5 mm for P 6 to 12, 1 mm from P 14): an external thread’s root d3 = d − 2 (P/2 + ac), an internal thread’s D4 = d + 2 ac, its crest D1 = d − P (Tr10x2: 10, 7.5, 9 outside; 10.5, 8, 9 inside). Extra flank clearance moves the 15° flanks: flank_clearance / cos 15° along the axis, at most (crest − P/50) cos 15° / 2 (0.3342 mm on an external Tr10x2, whose crest is 0.366 P).
  • The kernel gets them as ThreadSpec::starts and ThreadSpec::flank_angle (geometry/include/mitcad/geometry/thread.hpp).

A thread’s fit to its face: warnings

(mitcad#1262) A thread whose size does not suit its face, or a modelled thread that cut through the material behind its face, is made all the same, with a warning that says what happened (the feature’s warnings, yellow in the timeline, and the Thread panel’s message while it previews). Neither is a refusal. Lengths are shown in the design’s length unit, the face by its reference:

  • The size far from the face’s diameter (cosmetic or modelled; not a tapering taper pipe thread, whose faces are cut to its cone): an external thread’s major diameter, or an internal thread’s minor one (the bore of a tapped hole), further from the face’s diameter than the classes’ tolerance (taken as a quarter of a pitch) plus 0.5 mm plus twice a radial_clearance. The profile’s diameters are the given diameters or the size’s. “M80x2 (Ø80 mm) on face F45:side(c21) (Ø87.1 mm): the face’s diameter is 7.1 mm larger than the thread’s major diameter”; inside, “M8x1.25 (Ø8 mm, minor Ø6.647 mm) on face F6:side(c1) (Ø5 mm): the hole’s diameter is 1.647 mm smaller than the thread’s minor diameter”.
  • The thread cut through the wall behind the face (modelled, not tapering): the material behind the face, measured on the body before the thread along the radius (segment_crossings) at the middle, a quarter and three quarters of the thread’s part, in four directions round the axis, from the face to where the material ends, is no thicker than the thread’s cut (from the face to the profile’s root: an external thread’s minor diameter, an internal thread’s major one, each moved by radial_clearance) at every direction that finds the face at one of those places (a cross hole under the thread thins the wall at some directions only and does not warn). The thickest of those walls is named: “M80x2 (Ø80 mm) on face F45:side(c21) (Ø87.1 mm): the thread cut through the 3.5 mm wall behind the face” (a ring threaded down to a root inside its bore is gone along the thread). A body the thread left in more solids than it was, or none, is named where no wall told why: “M10x1.5: the thread cut body F2.b0 into 2 pieces”, “M10x1.5: the thread left nothing of body F2.b0”.

Fitting the face to the thread (mitcad#1632)

A face whose diameter is too far from the thread’s (the first warning above) is fitted by changing what sets its diameter to the thread’s crest diameter: the minor diameter on a hole, the major diameter on a shaft. The thread’s evaluation finds what sets it (core/model/src/features/thread/fit.rs) and keeps it with the result (thread_fits, also in the result store); auto_fix and add_feature with fit_faces change it (core/model/src/document/thread_fit.rs).

  • What sets the diameter: a Hole’s wall, the hole’s diameter (a simple hole: not tapped, tapered, a clearance or a press-fit hole); a Cylinder’s round side, its diameter; the side an Extrude or a Cut makes of a sketch circle or arc, or a Revolve of a sketch line along its axis, the one driving dimension of the sketch that moves the curve’s radius or its distance from the axis (each active driving dimension is tried with its value moved a little and the sketch solved again: a diameter or a radius dimension, a distance from a point or a line on the axis, a linear diameter, …), whose value is then solved for. The sketch’s other geometry follows as its constraints and dimensions say: a wall dimensioned 3 mm from the bore’s line moves out with it.
  • No source: a face of an imported body, one a fillet or a boolean made, a face whose diameter comes from several dimensions or from none, or one moved after it was made: the warning ends ; the hole has to be changed by hand (<why>) (the shaft on a shaft), and Auto Fix is not offered for it. A face of a projected curve (a reference curve of the sketch, which follows the model geometry it was projected from) says so (mitcad#1780): the face follows an edge projected into Sketch50: draw and dimension the curve instead, or change the geometry it was projected from.
  • The expression keeps its form: one number of the dimension’s expression is solved for, the one that carries most of its value, in its own unit and with as few decimals as give the value within half a micrometre (M76x2’s minor diameter 73.8349 mm: 72/2 becomes 73.835/2; 1 in becomes 1.25 in); an expression no number of which can give it becomes the plain value. The value is worked out from the face’s diameter as the geometry measured it and the dimension’s slope (a diameter 1, a radius or a distance from the axis 2), so that the sketch solver’s last digits do not reach it.
  • A named parameter: a dimension whose value is a parameter’s name (bore) or whose expression uses one (bore/2, the parameter that carries most of it): when nothing else uses the parameter it is changed, its own expression keeping its form. When other places use it (other slots of the definitions, other parameters’ expressions), the fit is not silent: shared parameter changes the parameter (the result says in how many other places it is used), shared own gives the dimension a value of its own in its place (a new dimension parameter where the slot named the parameter); without shared the fit is left, and auto_fix’s choices names the parameter.
  • Checked before it is taken, as Auto Fix’s reference fixes: a fit that would make a feature that built fail, or after which the face still does not fit, is not taken, with the reason.
  • add_feature of a thread with "fit_faces": true (and shared) adds the thread and fits its faces in one undo step (Add Thread1); its result has fitted (as auto_fix’s) and fit_left (face and its reason or choice). The same in a preview (fit_faces, shared): it shows what moves with the face. A preview of a thread whose faces do not fit has thread_fits: each face (its name, for agents), body, diameter, needed (mm), internal, fixable, and reason (why not), source (the feature that sets it) or choice (parameter, others).

Tests: core/model-tests/features-profile/src/thread_autofix_tests.rs (a Hole, an extruded circle, a revolved line and its wall, a Cylinder; a named parameter used elsewhere, both choices, and one used only there; a face no dimension sets; fit_faces and its undo; the previews), features::thread::fit::tests, document::thread_fit::tests (the expressions), and cli.thread_fit_reported on a reported design (tools/cli/thread-fit-reported-test.cmake, under MITCAD_MITCAD_REPORTED: a revolved bore of 72/2 under an M76x2 thread; as saved the fit is refused because a chamfer on the step between the bore and the thread’s crest would fail; without that chamfer the bore becomes 73.835/2, nothing newly fails, the 3 mm wall stays).

fillet 

{"type": "fillet", "body": "F2.b0", "edges": ["E{F2:side(c1[c4,c2])|F2:side(c2[c1,c3])}"], "radius": 2}

The short form is one set of edges with a constant radius. The general form lists edge sets:

{"type": "fillet", "body": "F2.b0", "sets": [
 {"edges": ["E{…}"], "size": {"type": "constant", "radius": 5}, "tangent_chain": false},
 {"faces": ["F2:end(r{…})"], "size": {"type": "chord_length", "length": 3}},
 {"edges": ["E{…}"], "size": {"type": "variable", "start": 2, "end": 4, "start_vertex": "V{…}",
 "mid": [{"position": 0.25, "radius": 3}]}, "continuity": "tangent"},
 {"edges": ["E{…}"], "size": {"type": "constant", "radius": 2}, "continuity": "curvature",
 "tangency_weight": 1.5},
 {"edges": ["E{…}"], "size": {"type": "asymmetric", "distance1": 2, "distance2": 4, "flip": false},
 "reference_face": "F2:side(c1[c4,c2])"}],
 "rolling_ball_corners": true}
  • A set rounds its edges and every edge of its faces; an edge may be in one set only. Any number of fillets per body.
  • all_edges (default false, mitcad#793): the set rounds every edge of the body as it is when the fillet is computed (the FreeCAD import’s “use all edges”), so that the edges an edit upstream adds are rounded too and those it takes away are no error. Such a set lists no edges or faces, has no start_vertex and is the fillet’s only set: {"type": "fillet", "body": "F2.b0", "sets": [{"all_edges": true, "size": {"type": "constant", "radius": 1}}]}. Patterns that copy fillets onto their copies leave such a set out.
  • size: constant (radius), chord_length (length, the width across the rounding; the faces must meet at a constant angle along the chain), variable, asymmetric or spline.
  • variable: start at start_vertex (an end of the chain, or the kernel’s start when left out) to end at the chain’s other end, through the mid radii at their positions along the chain (0 to 1 from the start, increasing). The radius follows OCCT’s smooth interpolation of all the radii, level at both ends, along the whole tangent chain (not confirmed to be the law of .f3d variable fillets). Mid radii around a closed chain are unsupported.
  • spline (mitcad#464): {"type": "spline", "knots": [0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1], "radii": [2, 6, 3, 4], "start_vertex": "V{…}"}, the radius a clamped B-spline of the position along the chain (0 at start_vertex, an end of the chain or the kernel’s start when left out, 1 at the other end; by arc length): radii its control radii (2 to 100, each greater than zero) and knots its full knot vector, as many as the radii and the degree and one more (degree 1 to 3), from 0 to 1, each end repeated degree + 1 times and an inner knot at most degree times. The radius keeps within its control radii, passes through the first and the last, and runs exactly as the spline does (the law goes to OCCT’s fillet as it is, port patch 0920; geometry/tests/test_dressup.cpp, test_fillet_spline_radius). Slots radii[k]. Not around a closed chain and not with curvature continuity (unsupported); the kernel’s chain, as for variable.
  • asymmetric: distance1 from the edge along the set’s reference_face (or along the first face of each edge’s name), and distance2 along the other face; flip swaps the faces. The cross-section is a conic, the affine image of the circular arc, tangent to both faces (MitCad’s own convention).
  • tangent_chain (default true): the edges that continue an edge smoothly are rounded too: every edge that meets an edge of the set end to end in the same direction (within 0.01 rad) and lies between two faces at an angle, convex where the edge is convex and concave where it is concave (a rounding vanishes where a concave edge runs on into a convex one, mitcad#439), and so on from those (MitCad’s own chain, mitcad#224; constant and chord length sets and chamfers; variable, asymmetric and G2 sets keep the kernel’s chain), besides the edges the kernel follows itself where the faces at a vertex go on tangentially. The kernel stops where a third sharp edge meets the vertex (a ring that two chamfers split into two arcs); MitCad’s chain does not. Where the kernel cannot build MitCad’s chain, the set takes the kernel’s chain alone, with a warning only where the result leaves edges of MitCad’s chain sharp, a remark, not a warning (mitcad#1914: The fillet's tangent chain stops where other sharp edges meet: 2 edges that continue it are left sharp., the edges its places; mitcad#1327): the panel points it out as information while it is open, and nothing marks the feature once it is accepted (the chamfer’s The chamfer's … the same). The kernel chain of a fillet or a chamfer also stops where its edges turn (by 0.01 rad or more) although the faces go on tangentially across a shallow crease there (a wall drafted by a few degrees above a vertical one), unless the next edge is bevelled too (OCCT port patches 0180, mitcad#241, and 0531, mitcad#263): a rounding ends at that vertex, cut by the face beyond the crease, where the crease is concave (at a convex crease that end is not built and the fillet fails); a chamfer’s analytic blend (a cone along an arc) runs on past the vertex, cut by the face beyond the crease, up to where its other contact reaches that face. Elsewhere the kernel follows its own chains, and edges the kernel chains beyond MitCad’s chain stay bevelled.
  • Without tangent_chain, only the selected edges are rounded or bevelled, also where the kernel’s chain runs on into an edge no set selects (a straight edge into a rounded corner; mitcad#2037): the dressup is built over the kernel’s whole chain and kept over the selected edges. Where a selected edge meets the next edge, the rounding or bevel runs out over that edge: in each section its profile (the bevel’s line, the rounding’s arc) lies closer to the edge by a depth that grows linearly with the length along it, from the full section at the vertex to nothing just before the edge’s far vertex (2 % of its length). The edges beyond stay sharp. Where the next edge is shorter than the dressup is wide, or the run-out does not build, the dressup ends flat at the vertex, in the plane normal to the edge there. The run-out’s face is <feature>:runout(<edge>) (the edge it runs over), the flat end’s <feature>:runout_end(<vertex>); the other faces keep the dressup’s names. Constant and chord length fillets and every chamfer do this; variable, asymmetric, spline and curvature continuous (G2) fillets are refused there, in words ("… need Tangent Chain on where a selected edge continues smoothly into an edge not selected"), as is a set where neither the run-out nor the flat end builds.
  • A rolling ball rounding of constant radius whose chain ends at a small notch in the rim it rounds (edges not rounded, each within the rounding’s contact on the face the notch breaks and within the ball’s diameter of the chain’s end) carries on across the notch onto the next edge of the rim, when that edge lies on the same line or circle between faces of the same two surfaces, whether or not the set selects it or follows tangent chains (OCCT port patch 0260, mitcad#307): the rounding is one surface over both edges, cut by the notch’s faces, as in the .f3d files' roundings. A wider notch ends the rounding.
  • continuity: tangent (G1, default) or curvature (G2). A G2 set touches the faces where the G1 rounding of its radius would (the asymmetric one at its distances) and its quintic cross-section follows the faces’ curvature there; tangency_weight (0.1 to 2, default 1) pulls it closer to the edge’s corner (larger) or to the chord (smaller). MitCad’s own shape; variable radius G2 sets are unsupported.
