{"type": "web", "curves": {"sketch": "F9", "curves": ["c1", "c4"]}, "thickness": 2,
 "extent": {"type": "depth", "depth": 10}, "extend_ends": true, "draft_angle": "1.5 deg"}
  • A rib grows from one open chain of sketch curves in the sketch plane, at right angles to the chain’s chord, to its left (the sketch normal up) or with flip to its right; its thickness is across the sketch plane, symmetric, side1 (along the sketch normal) or side2.
  • A web grows from each curve (lines and arcs) along the sketch normal (against it with flip); its thickness is in the sketch plane, side 1 to the left of the curve. Its walls are joined where the curves’ ends meet (mitcad#1968): two walls whose curves share an end meet in a mitre with no notch, at any angle and for every thickness_location; at an angle so sharp that the mitre would reach more than half the thickness and a thickness past the corner (a thickness past the wall for side1/side2) it is cut off there, square to the corner’s bisector. A run of curves joined end to end keeps its walls on one side, the side its first curve (in curves) gives: a curve drawn the other way round has its side1 and side2 turned. Where three or more ends meet at one point (a Y, or a T whose bar is two curves) the walls end square there and are joined by the convex hull of those ends. A curve whose end touches another curve between its ends (a T’s stem on its bar) ends square on it, as drawn.
  • extent: to_next (up to the faces of the participant bodies it reaches first, which must close it off; otherwise it fails) or {"type": "depth", "depth": d}. The result joins the participants (all bodies when left out); one that reaches none fails (“the rib does not touch any participant body”).
  • curves may instead be the curve of an Intersection Curve before it (mitcad#1417): {"feature": "F5"}. It must lie in one plane, which is then the sketch plane: its normal points the way of the curve’s sketch normal it is most nearly parallel to. Its pieces are the curves c1, c2, … in order along it (faces side(c1), wall1(c2), …). A straight curve, or one with a point off the plane by more than the joining tolerance (1e-6 of its size), is refused with where; a web takes lines and circular arcs, as from a sketch.
  • extend_ends (a rib’s, mitcad#1746; a web’s, mitcad#1968; absent: false, so ribs and webs saved before it keep their ends as drawn; the Rib and Web panels turn it on for a new one). A web’s free ends take it: an end that touches no other curve of the web (a T’s stem is not free at its bar, a corner’s ends are not free); for a rib, the chain’s two ends. Each such end lying past a wall the curves cross (its tangent out of the curves meets no face of the participants, and a wall lies between it and the curves’ middle) is cut back to that wall: the piece beyond is dropped and the end is not continued (a copy of a pattern where the room is narrower is so cut back to its walls). Any other such end is continued straight along its end tangent (a line straight on, an arc or spline by its tangent there) until the rib or the wall, across its whole thickness and depth, meets the participants’ faces: the continuation fills from the end’s tip up to a curved or slanted face with no gap, whatever the extent. An end that the faces close off over only part of the rib (mitcad#1857: a line starting on a boss’s top rim, whose continuation passes over the top while the wall below closes it off) fills that part: the material from the tip up to the faces its points reach along the tangent, and nothing of the continuation that passes over or beside the participants; it says nothing. Where it passes over is found from the faces’ edges and their outlines seen along the tangent, on any kind of face: planes, cylinders, cones, spheres, tori (a rounded rim) and freeform faces (mitcad#1865). At a sharp rim between a face the tangent runs into (the wall) and a plane face it runs away from (the top face), the fill goes up to the top face’s level, its plane extended past the rim (mitcad#1888): the fill’s top lies in the top face and meets it along the rim, with no step under the rim and nothing above the top face. Past a curved face it runs away from, the fill ends at the line along the tangent through the rim. end_offset moves those faces as for a whole end, but not the line where the participants stop closing it off: a positive offset fills further into the wall below a top edge, never over the top face. An end that meets no face at all within the participants’ bounds (or, up to the next faces, is closed off by none of them) stays as drawn, and the rib warns in words: “the start of the rib’s curves meets no face of the bodies when continued along its curve; it stays where it is drawn”, the end’s point as the warning’s place (a web’s: “an end of the web’s curves meets no face of the bodies …”). An end already in the material adds nothing.
  • end_offset (a length, absent: 0; with extend_ends only; a rib’s and a web’s): the faces each continued end stops at are moved this much along its tangent, positive further into them (a rib sunk into a thin wall), negative short of them. It never shortens the drawn curves.
  • direction (a rib’s, mitcad#1746; absent or "perpendicular": at right angles to the chain’s chord, as before): "sketch_x" or "sketch_y" (the sketch plane’s axes) or {"along": <reference>}, a straight line, edge or axis ("z", {"sketch": "F3", "curves": ["c2"]}, an edge) in or parallel to the sketch plane; flip turns it. A slanted line between two bosses with "direction": "sketch_y" on a plane whose sketch y points down grows straight down to the base, and with extend_ends its ends fill up to both bosses’ faces. Refused: a direction across the sketch plane (“the rib’s direction must lie in or parallel to its sketch plane”), one along a straight chain’s chord, and any on a web.
  • draft_angle (mitcad#2102, GitHub mitcad/Mitcad#488; radians or an angle expression such as "2 deg"; absent: 0, no draft, as ribs and webs saved before it; the panels write it only when it is not 0): both sides of the wall lean by this angle so that it is thicker where it meets the body, the draft of a moulded part. The thickness is measured at the curves (Thickness Side places the wall there as without a draft); at a distance u from them, the way the wall grows, each side lies u tan(draft_angle) further out, so the wall is thickness + 2 u tan(draft_angle) thick. A rib grows from its curves towards the faces it reaches, so it is narrowest at its curves and widens towards them; its sides are the curves swept along the leaned directions (planes for a straight chain). A web follows the same rule: one whose curves lie on a face of the participants (the material just behind the sketch plane at a curve’s middle: drawn on the plate it stands on) is thickest at its sketch plane and narrows the way it grows; any other (drawn off the body and grown, To Next or by a depth, onto faces) is thickest at its far end and narrowest at its curves. A negative angle does the opposite. Each wall’s free ends stay square to their curve, their sides leaning with the wall’s; mitred corners and the pieces joining three or more walls lean with the walls and stay joined (a mitre cut off at a sharp corner is cut at the same share of its length at both ends of the wall). The draft is built into the tool before it joins, so To Next, extend_ends and end_offset are solved for the drafted wall (a continued end leans as the wall does) and the result does not depend on the faces it meets; a pattern’s copies are drafted as the original. An angle that makes the sides meet before the wall’s depth fails: “the draft angle closes the rib before its depth” (a web’s: “… the web …”), the place where they meet painted on hover; up to the next faces the wall runs no further than where its sides are a tenth of the thickness apart, and fails with “the draft angle closes the rib before it reaches the faces of the bodies” where no face closes it off by then. An angle of 90 degrees or more either way is refused (“the rib’s draft angle must lie between -90 and 90 degrees”). The faces keep their names (a drafted rib’s wall1, wall2 and end are one face per curve of the chain, as end was), so references to them keep working.

Faces of a rib: side(<curve>) along the curves, wall1 and wall2 (its sides along and against the sketch normal), tip0 and tip1 at the chain’s start and end, end at the depth; a continued end adds extend0 or extend1 along its continuation, its tip tip0 or tip1. Of a web, per curve: wall1(<curve>), wall2(<curve>), tip0(<curve>), tip1(<curve>) (also at a mitred or joined end, and on the piece joining three or more walls, named after the first curve’s end there), start(<curve>) in the sketch plane and end(<curve>) at the depth; a continued free end adds extend0(<curve>) or extend1(<curve>) where its continuation is divided.

In a pattern (mitcad#1968) with Adjust (the default), each copy of a rib or a web whose extent is to_next or which has extend_ends is built again where it lands, its curves and sketch plane moved: it runs to the faces there and its ends are continued or cut back to the walls there, as the original’s. A web or rib by a depth without extend_ends is the tool moved.

emboss 

{"type": "emboss", "profiles": [{"sketch": "F3", "region": "r{t1.g0.c0}"}],
 "face": {"body": "F2.b0", "face": "F2:side(c1)"}, "depth": 1, "mode": "raise",
 "participants": []}

Profiles of one sketch (a set, as an extrusion’s; the glyphs of its texts bound regions too) raised from a face by depth (> 0) and joined, or with "mode": "sink" sunk into it and cut (mitcad#458, core/model/src/features/emboss.rs).

  • face a planar face: the profiles are extruded along the sketch normal from the face’s plane (projected onto it when the planes are not parallel), out of the material or into it.
  • face a cylindrical face: the profiles are wrapped onto the cylinder (Kernel::wrapped_emboss, geometry/src/emboss.cpp). The sketch plane must be parallel to the axis. A sketch point at distance s across the axis (from the line where the axis lies under the sketch) and z along it goes to the angle s / r about the axis, at z, from the radial direction towards the sketch plane (the sketch normal for a plane through the axis): lengths around the face are the sketch’s, not projected ones. The profiles grow radially by depth: outwards on an outer face when raised, inwards when sunk; on a bore’s wall the other way. A sink that reaches the axis, profiles wider than the circumference and a sketch across the axis fail.
  • face a conical face (mitcad#473, Kernel::face_cone): the profiles are laid onto the cone by its development, the sketch laid against the cone along the generator under the sketch’s origin. With the sketch plane parallel to the axis, a sketch point at s across the axis and t along it (from the origin’s height, towards where the cone widens) goes to the distance hypot(s, t + ρ0) from the apex along the generator turned atan2(s, t + ρ0) / sin α about the axis (α the half angle, ρ0 the slant distance of the origin’s height): lengths, angles and areas on the cone are the sketch’s. The profiles grow along the cone’s normals by depth (the top a cone of the same angle), out of the material when raised; on a countersink’s wall the other way. A sketch origin past the apex, profiles past the apex or around the cone, and a sink that reaches the axis fail.
  • Wrap offsets (mitcad#1259): on a cylindrical or conical face, wrapped, along_axis (a length), around_angle and rotation_angle (angles: numbers in radians, or expressions such as "90 deg" or a parameter’s name) move the profiles from where the sketch puts them, before they are wrapped (features::emboss::WrapOffsets, in Rust; the kernel gets the moved frame and regions). along_axis moves the sketch along the face’s axis, counted towards +Z of the component, or towards +Y for an axis across Z, else +X (counted: the face’s own axis may point either way; an extruded rod’s cylinder has its axis against the extrusion); around_angle turns it about the axis, right-handed about that direction; rotation_angle turns the profiles in the sketch, counter-clockwise about the middle of their bounds, so that on the face they turn about their middle and keep their shape. On a cylinder the wrapped profiles move rigidly; on a cone the moved sketch’s origin is where the development is laid against it, so Along Axis lays them at the new height. Each is left out when absent (0: the sketch’s wrap; older files read as before) and written when given, 0 too. Values that are not numbers fail the feature, and given values that are not 0 fail it when the profiles are not wrapped (a planar face, a projection, no face): Along Axis, Around and Rotation move only profiles wrapped onto a cylindrical or conical face. around_angle and rotation_angle warn beyond one turn as other one-turn angles do (parameters::one_turn_slot).
{"type": "emboss", "profiles": [{"sketch": "F3", "region": "r{c1[c4,c2],c2[c1,c3],c3[c2,c4],c4[c3,c1]}"}],
 "face": {"body": "F2.b0", "face": "F2:side(c1)"}, "depth": 1,
 "along_axis": "lift", "around_angle": "90 deg", "rotation_angle": "90 deg"}
  • face any other face (a sphere, a torus, a B-spline or other free-form face), or any face with "projection": true or a direction (mitcad#1091, Kernel::projected_emboss, geometry/src/emboss_projection.cpp): the profiles are projected onto the face along the sketch normal, or along direction (a reference: an axis, a straight or circular edge, a sketch line, a face of revolution’s axis, or a plane or planar face’s normal; it must cross the sketch plane). Each projected region is raised from the face by depth along the face’s normals (or sunk into it): its top is the region offset from the face, so it follows the face’s curvature, and its walls stand along the normals on the region’s boundary. The line through a sketch point along the direction may meet the face more than once (a sphere twice): each profile takes the part of the face nearest ahead of the sketch plane along the direction, else the nearest behind it. A profile that misses the face, falls partly off it or reaches past where the face turns away from the direction (a sphere’s rim) fails the feature with an error that names its region (the profile r{…} falls partly off face F1:side0 along the projection …). The body’s face is not changed in place: the tool is a new solid joined or cut as the other kinds are.
{"type": "emboss", "profiles": [{"sketch": "F4", "region": "r{t1.g0.c0}"}],
 "face": {"body": "F1.b0", "face": "F1:side0"}, "depth": 1,
 "projection": true, "direction": {"body": "F1.b0", "edge": "E{…|…}"}}

projection is written only when true; a face that is neither planar, cylindrical nor conical needs neither it nor direction. Wrap (projection false) stays the default on a cylinder or cone: a projection there keeps the profiles’ shape as seen along the direction, a wrap their lengths around the face.

  • No face: from the sketch plane along its normal (raise) or against it (sink). projection and direction need a face.
  • participants: the bodies joined or cut; empty for the face’s body, or all bodies without a face. A raise that touches none, or a sink that cuts into none, fails.
  • taper_angle (mitcad#1547): the walls tilted from where they stand without it (along the face’s normals), an angle (a number in radians, or an expression such as "10 deg" or a parameter’s name) strictly between -90 and 90 degrees, signed as an extrusion’s taper: positive widens the profiles away from the face (the top, or a sink’s floor, larger than the foot), negative narrows them. Left out when absent (0: walls along the normals; older files read as before) and written when given. Every kind of emboss takes it:
    • a planar face or no face: the extrusion’s taper (ExtrudeSide::taper; a sketch plane not parallel to the face takes none, as an extrusion’s start plane);
    • wrapped onto a cylinder or a cone (EmbossWrapSpec::taper): the top’s boundary is the foot’s moved within the top surface by depth tan(taper) along its normal there. On the top surface’s development (its lengths the surface’s) each edge’s curve is offset by OCCT, the corners where neighbouring offsets meet (continued past their ends as far as needed), and an edge whose corners pass each other drops out, its neighbours meeting instead (short edges of letters). Each wall is ruled between its edge on the foot and its moved edge (or that corner) on the top. A 10 x 10 square on a cylinder of radius 25 raised 45 is 28 around the axis and 10 along it at the top; at 10 degrees 28 + 2 * 45 tan(10 deg) and 10 + 2 * 45 tan(10 deg);
    • projected (EmbossProjectSpec::taper): measured as the projection sees the profiles, the region moved so in the sketch plane by depth tan(taper), projected onto the face and grown along its normals, the top that solid’s far faces; the walls ruled between foot and top. A wrapped taper whose walls meet or vanish on the way (the top’s moved loops collapse: a slot it closes, a narrow part it eats away; mitcad#1854) is built as an extrusion’s taper of the profile laid out on the top’s development, its topology events resolved as an extrusion’s (a slot fills from where its walls meet), bent onto the surfaces: a point h up goes h / depth of the way from the foot to the top at its parameters. The foot and the top lie on the cylinders or cones; the walls keep their side(<curve>) names. One that closes the whole profile before the top keeps the emboss’s own refusal, naming the region: the taper collapses the profile r{…}: neighbouring edges of its top do not meet (the square above at -10 degrees: 10 - 2 * 45 tan(10 deg) < 0 along the axis); one that cannot be built so fails with the taper closes part of the profile on its way, and the geometry kernel could not build that; make the angle smaller, the collapse in the error’s detail, the foot’s edges as its places. A projected taper on a curved face whose top collapses fails as before (on a plane it is an extrusion’s taper, mitcad#1851).
{"type": "emboss", "profiles": [{"sketch": "F3", "region": "r{c1[c4,c2],c2[c1,c3],c3[c2,c4],c4[c3,c1]}"}],
 "face": {"body": "F2.b0", "face": "F2:side(c1)"}, "depth": 45, "taper_angle": "10 deg"}

Faces are named as an extrusion’s: side(<segment>) the walls, end(<region>) the top of a raised profile or the floor of a sunk one, start(<region>) its foot on the face (inside the body after a raise). Tests: core.model (emboss_tests), geometry.emboss (test_emboss.cpp: a square projected onto a sphere and onto a B-spline face, its top 1 mm off them within 1e-6 mm; a slanted direction; the refusals), cli.emboss, cli.emboss_projection (a square and a text on a ball, a square on a scaled ball’s B-spline face and one partly off it, a direction onto a box’s top), cli.emboss_wrap_offsets (mitcad#1259: a rectangle on a rod moved along the axis by a parameter, around it and turned, its volume kept and its centre of mass where the offsets put it; refused on a planar face), core.model’s a_wrap_moves_along_the_axis_around_it_and_turns_on_the_face and features::emboss::tests (the moved frame and regions). The taper (mitcad#1547): cli.emboss_taper (the square above at 0, 10 and -5 degrees, its top’s edge lengths and the volumes, -10 degrees refused, and on a block’s top 5 degrees as an extrusion of the square with that taper), geometry.emboss (test_emboss.cpp: the square’s top within 1e-6 mm and its volume by the divergence theorem over its faces, sunk too; a cone; a circle, a holed rectangle and letters; a square projected onto a plane as the frustum and onto a ball; letters projected; the refusals) and core.model’s a_taper_reaches_every_kind_of_emboss. The .solidcraft import maps SolidCraft’s emboss onto it (a deboss sinks), and the .f3d import the file’s embosses (a negative depth sinks; core/import/docs/f3d-components.md).

Patterns 

{"type": "rectangular_pattern",
 "objects": {"type": "features", "features": ["F4"]},
 "direction1": {"axis": "x", "quantity": 3, "distance": 20},
 "direction2": {"axis": "y", "quantity": 2, "distance": 20, "symmetric": false},
 "distance_type": "spacing", "compute": "adjust", "suppressed_elements": [4]}
{"type": "circular_pattern", "objects": {"type": "bodies", "bodies": ["F2.b0"]},
 "axis": "z", "quantity": 4, "angle": 6.283185307179586, "symmetric": false,
 "axis2": {"axis": "x", "quantity": 3, "angle": 3.141592653589793, "symmetric": true}}
{"type": "path_pattern", "objects": {"type": "faces", "body": "F2.b0", "faces": ["F4:side(c1)"]},
 "path": {"sketch": "F9", "curve": "c1"}, "quantity": 4, "distance": 15,
 "distance_type": "spacing", "start": 0, "flip": false, "along_path": false, "symmetric": false}

Patterns, mirrors, combine, moves and primitives: modules pattern.rs, mirror.rs, combine.rs, moves.rs, align.rs, scale.rs, primitive.rs. Examples: tools/cli/tests/f4_*.json.

  • objects: bodies (each copy a new body), features (their tool bodies combined with the bodies again by the feature’s operation; only features that leave a tool, see Adding to the API, and fillets and chamfers, below) or faces of one body (with planar caps where they meet the body they bound a boss, joined, or a pocket, cut). A pattern or mirror of features among the features (a pattern of patterns) stands for its originals at each of its elements (the original’s too, not the suppressed ones): the copies go to every product of the inner and the outer elements, the inner one applied first. A feature that the features reach at the same place more than once (a mirror of a feature and of a mirror or pattern whose original it is) is copied once there. A pattern or mirror of bodies among the features (mitcad#547) stands for its bodies as they were before it, at each of its elements: the copies of those bodies go to every product of the elements, new bodies <pattern>.b<k> (k counting them in order) or, with combine, joined to the body (as the patterns before left it) where they touch — FreeCAD’s MultiTransform of the whole body, each copy of the body scaled and skipped on its own. Such patterns cannot be mixed with features. Patterns of faces cannot be patterned again.
  • direction3 (optional, rectangular patterns; mitcad#1446): a third direction as direction2 (axis, quantity, distance, symmetric), for a 3D grid of copies in one feature: the elements are the product of the three quantities, numbered along direction 1 first, then 2, then 3 (Elements below), and scale, scale_groups, scale_copies, scales, combine, skipped_copies and suppressed_elements count them as they count the elements of two directions. Without it a pattern reads and saves as before (the key is left out). The Rectangular Pattern panel’s Direction 3 sets it (app/COMMANDS/). Tests: core.model.features-solid’s a_third_direction_makes_a_grid_of_bodies, a_third_direction_makes_a_grid_of_features, a_third_direction_counts_in_the_scale_runs and an_old_document_without_a_third_direction_loads_unchanged.
  • axis2 (optional, circular patterns; mitcad#1588): a second axis, {"axis": …, "quantity": …, "angle": …, "symmetric": false} (any axis axis takes; quantity, angle and symmetric as the first axis’s, the slots axis2.quantity and axis2.angle). Every copy about axis is turned again about axis2: the elements are every product of the two turns, numbered about axis first (element = k1 + n1 · k2, the turn about the first axis applied first, as an inner pattern of a pattern of patterns), and scale, scale_groups, scale_copies, scales, combine, skipped_copies and suppressed_elements count them as a rectangular pattern’s two directions. Without it a pattern reads and saves as before (the key is left out). The Circular Pattern panel’s Axis 2 sets it (app/COMMANDS/). Tests: core.model.features-solid’s a_second_axis_turns_every_copy_about_it_again and an_old_circular_pattern_without_a_second_axis_loads_unchanged, cli.f4_pattern_two_axes, cli.f4_pattern_lattice.
  • Copies that add nothing (rectangular, circular and path patterns; mitcad#1588): a copy that is the same solid at the same place as its original, or as a copy made before it at the same place of the pattern’s originals (a body of revolution turned about its own axis; two products of a two-axis pattern on one place), is left out instead of joined, so that no boolean meets the faces both have: the copies of the features with a tool at each place (not fillets, chamfers, sheet features or scoped cuts), every compute option, and the copies of bodies with combine (and combine_any, and patterns of bodies among the features with them). Only a copy that turns or mirrors its object can land there: its centre of mass must land within 1e-5 mm of the other’s, their tight boxes agree (Kernel::bounding_box), then the points the kernel spreads over the faces of each (Kernel::face_points) must lie within 1e-5 mm of the faces of the other (Kernel::boundary_distances), whatever their surfaces' parametrizations. A left-out copy has no faces (<pattern>:inst<e>(…) names nothing); copies that overlap only partly are joined as before. Mirrors, scale patterns and Pattern at Points keep every copy. Tests: copies_that_land_on_the_original_or_on_each_other_are_left_out, joined_copies_of_bodies_that_add_nothing_are_left_out, cli.f4_pattern_two_axes (a ball’s rod turned about X and Z) and cli.f4_pattern_lattice (a cubic lattice of one revolve with its centre ball, one pipe and one pattern about two axes, filleted at all 40 joints).
  • Quantities include the original. distance_type: spacing between neighbours or extent from the first element to the last. A negative distance or angle goes the other way. A full turn spaces a circular pattern by angle / quantity, a partial angle by angle / (quantity − 1). symmetric: the quantity’s elements lie on both sides of the original (⌊quantity / 2⌋ before it, the rest after; the spacing as without; a full turn is not affected). Path distances are arc lengths along the path; start (0…1) is where the original sits on the path; along_path turns the copies with the path. start_point (optional, [x, y, z] mm; mitcad#673) gives that place as a point instead of start: the path’s point nearest to it (the .f3d import passes the patterned objects’ centre, which the file keeps).
  • A path pattern along a chain of sketch lines and arcs (mitcad#464, "path": {"sketch": "F9", "curves": ["c1", "c2"]}): the curves joined end to end as for a sweep’s path (Paths: from the free end of the first listed curve), the distances arc lengths along the whole chain. Each copy moves from the original’s place on the chain to its own; with along_path it also turns about the sketch’s normal through the original’s place by the angle the chain’s tangent turns between the two (at a vertex between two curves the first curve’s tangent). Before the start and past the end the first and the last curve go on (straight, or around their circle); a closed chain (its last curve ends where the first starts, from the first listed curve’s start) goes round again instead (mitcad#673). Ellipses and splines in the chain are refused.
  • A path pattern along a body’s edges (mitcad#2105, "path": {"body": "F2.b0", "edges": ["E{…}", …]}): the edges, in any order, joined end to end as a sweep’s path of edges is (open, or closed when the last ends where the first starts), measured along their exact curves as an Intersection Curve is; along_path turns the copies as the tangent turns. tangent_chain (default true; saved only when false) also takes the edges joined to each listed one through smooth joints, the edges a fillet with a tangent chain rounds together (the tangent_chains query’s chains): one bottom edge of a box with rounded vertical edges brings its whole bottom outline, and the chain stops at sharp corners, past which further edges are listed one by one. The edges keep their topological names, so the pattern follows the body’s edits; an edge that is gone is an error placed at the edge (“an edge no longer exists after …”). Tests: cli.f4_pattern_edge_path (a box’s bottom edges with sharp corners listed one by one, open and closed; a filleted box’s bottom outline from one edge, with and without the chain; the edit of the box’s size).
  • A path pattern’s combine (mitcad#673) also takes features: the bodies its copies make (copies of a feature that made a new body, with the fillets and chamfers patterned with it) join, in one operation, the one body the patterned features made or changed, where they touch it; other patterns refuse combine with features.
  • Signed distances (mitcad#447): a rectangular pattern’s direction keeps one signed distance (spacing or extent); a negative one puts the copies against its axis, and a symmetric direction then has the copies of the positive distance (an even quantity’s extra element on the other side). Zero is refused when there are copies. The panel’s Flip of a direction negates the distance it builds (-(expression) for an expression); an edited pattern shows its stored signed distance with Flip off. The arrows in the view follow the sign. A direction the panel makes Symmetric hides its Flip (mitcad#545, app/COMMANDS.md Pattern options).
  • scale (optional, a factor; mitcad#59): the copies grow (or shrink) element by element up to that factor: element e of n is scaled by 1 + (scale − 1) · e / (n − 1) about the centre of mass of the first object (a feature’s tool, the first body; not for faces) carried to the copy (FreeCAD’s Scaled transformation after a pattern). In a pattern of patterns each copy of an inner pattern’s copy is scaled about its own centre: the first original’s centre carried through the inner elements too (mitcad#539). Not with fillets, chamfers or sheet features among the features.
  • scale_groups (optional, with scale; mitcad#539): the copies of the originals, numbered j = p + P · e (p the copy’s number among the P copies the patterns among the features make, the innermost pattern’s element turning fastest; e the element), fall into this many runs of equal length: run g = ⌊j · groups / (P · n)⌋ is scaled by 1 + (scale − 1) · g / (groups − 1) (FreeCAD’s Scaled transformation of fewer occurrences than the copies before it). From 2 to n; the runs must divide the P · n copies. Default n: each element a run.
  • combine (bodies, and patterns of bodies among the features, mitcad#547; mitcad#539): each copy that touches its original is joined to it, one after another (a copy that touches the original joined with the copies before), as a mirror’s combine; the body keeps its id, a copy that touches nothing stays a body of its own. A pattern of that body then copies it with the copies joined to it (FreeCAD’s MultiTransform of the whole body).
  • combine_any (optional, with combine; bodies and patterns of bodies, as combine; rectangular, circular, path and scale patterns and mirrors; mitcad#1006): a copy joins every body of the pattern it touches, not only the body it is a copy of: the patterned bodies as the copies before left them (of a pattern of patterns of bodies, those of the inner patterns’ bodies still there) and the copies before it that stayed bodies of their own. The copies are made of the bodies as they were before the pattern, the bodies in their order, each at every element. The bodies a copy reaches are found by their boxes and, where the boxes of several meet, by the kernel’s contact test (Kernel::tool_contacts). A copy that touches one body is joined with it as combine joins it (a mirror image’s near-copy join too); one that touches several joins them in one join (of their lumps, as a join of a body of several solids), into the first of them, the patterned bodies first: the bodies merged into it are removed. A copy that touches none is the body it is without combine (<pattern>.b<k>, k = (element − 1) · (number of bodies) + (body’s position); of a pattern of patterns, k counting such bodies in order); solids of a copy that touch nothing while the rest of it joins are new bodies after those. The FreeCAD import sets it on the transformations of the whole shape of a Body of several solids, as FreeCAD fuses a copy with whichever solid it reaches. combine_any without combine is refused (combine_any needs combine).
  • scale_copies (optional, with scale; mitcad#542): the N copies the runs are counted over, run g = ⌊j · groups / N⌋ (default P · n, the pattern’s own copies; at least those): a pattern inside a pattern of patterns whose runs an outer pattern’s scale continues, so that runs may split the copies of the patterns among the features (groups up to N). Each copy of an inner copy is scaled relative to that copy: to the factor of its run over the factor of the inner copy’s run, so that it ends up at its own run’s factor whatever the inner pattern scaled it by (with the default N and at most n groups the inner copies are the first run, factor 1, and nothing changes).
  • scales (optional; mitcad#542): more scales, [{"scale": f, "groups": m, "copies": N}] (groups and copies optional, as scale_groups and scale_copies); the factors of all scales multiply (FreeCAD’s MultiTransform with several Scaled transformations).
  • scale_center (optional, a point reference; mitcad#542): the copies are scaled about this point carried to each copy instead of the first object’s centre of mass (FreeCAD scales a whole body’s copies about the Body’s origin).
  • skipped_copies (features and bodies, not faces; mitcad#542, bodies mitcad#547: the body of a skipped element is not made, the others keep their ids): copies the pattern does not make, by their numbers j = p + P · e (as for scale_groups; never 0, the original). Unlike suppressed_elements a pattern of the pattern still places the originals there: the inner pattern’s copy left out at its own element and copied at the outer ones (FreeCAD 1.0 and 1.1 leave out the copies a Scaled transformation does not change).
  • Elements: element 0 is the original. Along a direction the positions are 0, 1, …, q − 1; when symmetric 0, 1, …, q − 1 − ⌊q / 2⌋, then −1, …, −⌊q / 2⌋ (q elements again); a rectangular pattern numbers direction 1 first, element = k1 + n1 · k2 (+ n1 · n2 · k3 with a third direction). suppressed_elements leaves elements out (not 0).
  • compute (features and faces): adjust (default) applies the elements one after another, rebuilding a feature’s tool in place where the feature can (a primitive; an extrusion up to an object or through all bodies: its profile moved, its end found again; a face the feature itself took away, as a join up to a face of the body it joins does, is found in the body as it was before the feature), and skips elements that reach no body (a cut or join applies them in one boolean when that gives the same bodies: nothing split apart); identical and optimized move the feature’s tool to every element and combine all at once; optimized with fillets or chamfers among the features copies the faces the features made instead (Optimized: copying the faces). The pattern fails if no copy reaches a body. Consecutive features whose copies all join, or all cut, the same one body, with the copies of different features more than 0.1 mm apart (their boxes), are applied in one boolean (mitcad#855) when that gives the bodies and face names the features give one after another: no body split apart or new, each feature’s copies in the result, and a face split into pieces near the copies of one feature only; otherwise one after another. MITCAD_NO_PATTERN_RUNS=1 turns it off, for comparisons.
  • original_bodies (features; default false, mitcad#74): the copies of a feature without participants of its own act only on the bodies that feature changed (still there), as in .f3d designs, where a pattern of a hole leaves another body its copies reach alone; by default they act on the feature’s participants, every body without them. The .f3d import sets it for patterns and mirrors of features.
  • Participants the feature itself consumed (mitcad#406): the copies act on the bodies there are at the pattern. A join that touched several of its participants merged them into the first of them it touched (the others are removed), and its copies join that body instead of the removed ones (a post joined to two rings of one revolve, participants: ["F2.b0", "F2.b1"], leaves F2.b0, and a circular pattern of the post joins its copies to F2.b0). When the join made several merged bodies, a removed participant went into the one (of the participants before it) whose box after the join holds its box before it, the smallest such. A participant the feature removed otherwise (a cut that left nothing of it) fails the pattern with participant F4.b0 of Extrude3 was consumed by Extrude3 itself; one that a later feature removed with body … does not exist at this point of the timeline.
  • Names: copied faces are <pattern>:inst<element>(<original face>), e.g. F5:inst4(F4:side(c1)); their edges follow. A pattern of a pattern names its copies of the inner copies around the inner names (F6:inst1(F5:inst2(F4:side(c1)))). Copies of bodies are bodies <pattern>.b<k>, k = (element − 1) · (number of bodies) + (position of the body), so suppressing an element keeps the other ids.
  • The preview of a pattern lists elements (see Preview).

Fillets and chamfers among the features

A fillet or chamfer may be among the features of a pattern or mirror, usually with the features whose edges it rounds (mitcad#105):

{"type": "rectangular_pattern",
 "objects": {"type": "features", "features": ["F4", "F5", "F6"]},
 "direction1": {"axis": "x", "quantity": 3, "distance": 20}, "distance_type": "spacing"}
  • It leaves no tool body, so it is not copied but applied again at each element, on the copies of its edges, with its own sizes (parameters) and options. The features go in timeline order then: a fillet after the copies of the features before it, whatever the order of features.
  • The copies’ edges are found by their names: in an edge name, a face that a copied feature made becomes that face’s copy at the element (<pattern>:inst<element>(…), inner instances of a pattern of patterns inside), a face of another feature stays. A chamfer between a copied boss F4 and the plate F2 it stands on, E{F2:end(r{…})|F4:side(c1)}, is repeated on E{F2:end(r{…})|F7:inst1(F4:side(c1))}.
  • An edge whose copy no body has by that name (none of its faces copied, as for a fillet patterned alone over holes an earlier pattern made, or its other face is another face at the copy’s place) is found by its place: the edge whose middle (within 1e-4 mm), direction and length are those of the original edge, on the body before the fillet, moved by the element’s transform. An edge found neither way (a copy that reaches no body) is left out with the warning <fillet> is not repeated where the copies lack its edges (elements …); faces (faces sets) are found by name only.
  • The copies’ new faces are the pattern’s: <pattern>:fillet(<the copy's edge>), <pattern>:chamfer(…), <pattern>:corner(…) (e.g. F7:chamfer(E{F7:inst1(F4:end(r{c1}))|F7:inst1(F4:side(c1))})). A fillet among the objects that rounds a copied chamfer’s edges is repeated on the copy of that chamfer’s face the same way.
  • A two-distance or distance-angle chamfer or an asymmetric fillet without a reference face measures its first distance on the first face of each edge’s name; where the copy’s name puts the other face first, the copy takes it with flip swapped, so that the distances stay on the faces the original measured them on (also with a mirror). Sets by faces, and edges found by their place, keep the sorted order of the copies’ names.
  • The copies go on the body that has their edges (the fillet’s own body first), all elements in one operation; when that fails, one element after another. When that fails too, the pattern starts again with the features of one element after another (each element’s copies of all the objects, then the next element’s): where copies overlap (pockets around a hub), the rounding of one copy otherwise ends at the edges of the next. A fillet whose copies fail even so fails the pattern (Fillet1 at element 2: …), as does one whose copies find no edge at all (no copy of the edges of Fillet1 is on a body) and one that failed itself. scale with fillets or chamfers is unsupported.
  • A thread among the features (mitcad#719: a tapped hole’s thread on its wall) is repeated alike on the copies of the faces it threads. Its faces’ copies are found by name; where none was copied (a pattern of the thread alone, mitcad#733), on the cylindrical faces at their places: the same radius, the moved axis and ends (within 1e-4 mm). A modelled copy is turned as the original moved there (its helix where the moved helix lies, not the original’s angle about the copy’s own axis), and a mirror’s modelled image is left-handed. A cosmetic copy keeps the designation, also in a mirror (a tapped size; mitcad#733).

Optimized: copying the faces

With "compute": "optimized" a pattern or mirror of features that has fillets or chamfers among them does not work them out on each copy (above): it copies the faces the features made, as the .f3d option of the same name does. Without a fillet or chamfer the features’ tools are the faces they made, and optimized is identical.

  • What the features did to a body is what lies between the body before the first of them and the body after the last: the material they added (a boss with the roundings at its foot and on its top) and the material they removed (a pocket with its chamfer), each a closed solid bounded by the faces the features made (Kernel::feature_changes). The solids are moved to every element, as a feature’s tool is, the removed ones are cut from the body and the added ones joined to it, each in one operation: no fillet or chamfer is evaluated at an element, so one that the geometry kernel fails on at some copy (the roundings of a thousand pins on a large body) does not fail the pattern.
  • The features are taken in runs of consecutive features of the timeline (no other body-changing feature between them), one pair of bodies per body a run changes. Features that make or remove bodies, or that do not stand at the same places (a pattern of patterns that copies only some of them), are repeated as the other options do.
  • A copy of added material stands on the faces under its seam (the planar faces of the solid that lay on the body, such as the disc a boss’s foot rounding ends on): the material over the part of a seam face that no planar face of the body lies under (coplanar, facing it) is cut off along the seam’s normal, a copy with nothing under its seam is left out (Kernel::supported_copies). A seam on a curved face is not clipped.
  • The copies’ faces are named <pattern>:inst<element>(<original face>) (the chamfers’ and fillets’ faces too, not <pattern>:fillet(…)). A failure of the kernel is the pattern’s: the roundings are not tried copy by copy. original_bodies and the features’ own participants do not apply: the copies act on the bodies the features changed.

pattern_at_points 

{"type":"pattern_at_points",
 "objects":{"type":"features","features":["F3","F4"]},
 "targets":[{"point":{"sketch":"F5","point":"p1"}},
 {"point":"F6","occurrence":"O1/O2"}],
 "context":"", "compute":"adjust"}

Repeats bodies (objects.type:"bodies", bodies:[BodyUid]), features (features:[FeatureUid]), or shared component occurrences (objects.type:"components", occurrences:["O1/O2",…]). Body and feature sources belong to the feature’s component; component sources may be elsewhere in the assembly, provided the new occurrence does not create a component cycle. Originals remain. Each target adds one translated copy of the entire source group, preserving relative positions and orientation. Features replay their tools and operations, including grouped fillets/chamfers, rather than duplicating the resulting cut body. An unreachable feature copy fails with its target number.

The anchor is automatic unless anchor:{point:GeomRef, occurrence?:"O1"} is given. Remove anchor to restore Automatic. The deterministic policies are:

  • Components: centre of the axis-aligned bounds of the selected occurrence origins; one component uses its local origin at its current placement.
  • Feature groups containing holes: centre of the bounds of all selected holes' placement/start points. Other selected features, including fillets and chamfers, do not move this anchor. Hole depth never substitutes a tool midpoint.
  • Feature groups of threads only (mitcad#733): centre of the bounds of the middles of the faces they thread (thread_faces); the copies go on the faces at those faces’ places moved to each target, as a pattern or mirror of a thread alone does.
  • Other bodies/features: centre of the union of source body/tool bounds. A group consisting only of finishing features uses the bodies those features changed.

point is the normal geometry reference: a sketch point, construction point, vertex, origin, fixed point, or a resolvable edge centre/midpoint. Keep references to retain associativity. occurrence names the point’s frame by an absolute path from the root; an explicit empty path means the root. If omitted, coordinates belong to the feature’s component. context identifies the feature component’s displayed occurrence; if omitted, its first occurrence is used. Invalid explicit paths never fall back to the origin. Point and source edits recompute placements; missing or unavailable references produce a failed feature without stale copies.

Duplicate references are rejected. Distinct references resolving to the same position, or to the source anchor, fail explicitly (distance below 1e-7 mm). Other geometric overlap follows normal pattern semantics: separate body or component instances remain separate; feature tools use their normal booleans. One to 10000 targets are supported. Reordering component targets preserves each instance’s UID; removing a target removes its occurrence. Suppression, rollback and failure make generated occurrences unavailable, including to downstream moves and joints. Undo and design files preserve ownership and shared definitions.

Preview adds anchor:{point:[x,y,z],world:[x,y,z],mode,policy} and the normal pattern elements (identity first). mode is automatic or selected; policy is component_origins, hole_placements, thread_faces, source_bounds or selected_point. instances:[{body,occurrence,transform,visible}] lists added occurrence/body pairs with 4×4 world-transform rows. removed_instances:[{body,occurrence}] removes existing pairs during an edit preview; unchanged shared body IDs stay in bodies.

mirror 

{"type": "mirror", "objects": {"type": "bodies", "bodies": ["F2.b0"]},
 "plane": "yz", "combine": false, "compute": "adjust"}

A pattern of one copy, element 1 (<mirror>:inst1(<face>)). Mirrored bodies are new bodies; combine joins each to its original when they touch, and with combine_any (mitcad#1006, as for patterns) to every mirrored body or image before it that it touches. Mirrored features reflect their finished tool (never a rebuilt one); original_bodies, and fillets and chamfers among the features, as for patterns. scale and scale_groups (mitcad#539) as for patterns with two elements: the image scaled by the factor about its own centre (FreeCAD’s Scaled transformation after a mirror).

The mirror image of a nearly symmetric body lies on the body almost everywhere, nearly but not exactly, and a boolean of the whole shapes intersects every such pair of faces (minutes for free-form faces, often with a wrong result). combine therefore joins an image that differs from its body in at most half of the faces of each only where they differ by more than 0.1 mm (Kernel::join_near_copy, mitcad#88): material of the image within 0.1 mm of the body’s faces is left out, and an image that differs nowhere by more gives the body unchanged. Any other image is joined whole. MITCAD_NO_NEAR_COPIES=1 joins every image whole (for comparisons).

combine 

{"type": "combine", "target": "F2.b0", "tools": ["F4.b0"], "operation": "join",
 "keep_tools": false, "new_component": false}

join gives the target one body of the union (several solids when they do not touch); cut removes the tools’ union, the first piece in geometric order keeping the target’s id and the others becoming bodies of the combine (a piece with less than a millionth of the volume of the largest stays in that piece’s body as a lump, as with an extrusion’s cut; after an upstream edit the pieces keep their ids: Body ids of a split’s pieces); intersect keeps the common volume as the target (fails when empty: “the target and the tool bodies do not intersect”, also for bodies that only touch; a target lying wholly inside the tools is the intersection as it is, with its face names, mitcad#1534). A join, cut or intersection of bodies with material whose result (or the union of its tools) holds no solid fails (the join of 257 bodies gave an empty result), keeping the target and the tools (Unions of many bodies). Tools are removed unless kept; faces keep their names through the boolean. With new_component the target goes into a new component. A join whose target and tools (of its own component) are all valid sheet metal bodies merges them into one sheet where they meet as a sheet and its mirror image or copy (Mirrors and patterns of sheet metal bodies, mitcad#1558).

The target is a body of the combine’s component; a tool may be a body of another component where an occurrence shows it (mitcad#104, mitcad#544): a tool entry {"body": …, "occurrence": …} instead of an id:

{"type": "combine", "target": "F7.b0", "operation": "cut", "keep_tools": true,
 "tools": [{"body": "F2.b0", "occurrence": "O1", "context": "O2"},
 {"body": "F2.b0", "occurrence": "O3", "context": "O2"}]}

occurrence is the occurrence path to the tool’s component, context the one to the combine’s (default: its first path); the model keeps them as an OccurrenceLink (Geometry of other components), source and target. The tool is read there and moved into the combine’s coordinates by the occurrences’ placements at the combine’s point of the timeline, so the combine follows when either occurrence moves. A body is a tool once per occurrence: two occurrences of one component (two screws of one part) are two tools, each cutting (joining, intersecting) where it is and each following its own occurrence; the occurrences not listed do nothing. The same body in the same occurrence twice is refused (body F2.b0 in O1 is listed more than once). A consumed tool (without keep_tools) leaves its own component, once however many occurrences it was a tool in. The target stays a body of the combine’s component: a cut changes that component’s definition, so every occurrence of it shows the cut.

A plain id is a body of the combine’s own component, or, as files of earlier versions and imports write it, a body of another component whose link tool_links holds (saved and read as it was written):

{"type": "combine", "target": "F7.b0", "tools": ["F2.b0"], "operation": "cut",
 "keep_tools": true, "tool_links": {"F2.b0": {"source": "O1", "target": "O2"}}}

A tool_links entry for a body that is not a plain-id tool is refused (linked but not a tool); a tool of another component without an occurrence or a link fails the combine (body F2.b0 (from Extrude1) belongs to A; …). Paste New, moves into components and occurrences moved into others carry both forms’ links. Tests: core/model-tests/links/src/link_tests.rs (a_combine_cuts_with_a_body_in_two_occurrences_each_where_it_is, a_combine_joins_a_body_in_two_occurrences, a_combine_of_an_earlier_version_with_tool_links_loads_and_recomputes_as_before, paste_new_keeps_a_combines_tools_in_occurrences).

move, align, scale 

{"type": "move", "bodies": ["F2.b0"], "copy": false,
 "transform": {"type": "translate_xyz", "x": 10, "y": 5, "z": 0}}

transform: {"type": "free", "matrix": [[r00, r01, r02, tx], [r10, …], [r20, …]]} (a rotation and a translation), translate_xyz (x, y, z), translate_along (axis, distance), rotate (axis, angle, right-handed), point_to_point (from, to), point_to_position (point, x, y, z). A moved body keeps its id and face names; with copy the moved copies are new bodies <move>.b<j> with faces <move>:inst1(<face>) (a copy that does not move is a copy and paste). A rotation and a translation (a move or an align) place the body as a location on its own shape (mitcad#838, Kernel::move_shape): its faces keep their geometry and the display meshes they have, so the view meshes nothing again; the body before the move is not changed. A mirror or a scale makes a transformed copy.

A point or an axis may be geometry of another component, picked where an occurrence shows it (mitcad#699): from_occurrence, to_occurrence, point_occurrence or axis_occurrence beside the reference is that occurrence’s absolute path from the root ("O1/O4"; "" the root), as pattern_at_points gives its points’ occurrences. move, move_occurrence and move_face take them alike:

{"type": "move_occurrence", "occurrences": ["O2"],
 "transform": {"type": "point_to_point",
 "from": {"body": "F2.b0", "vertex": "V{…}"}, "from_occurrence": "O2",
 "to": {"body": "F2.b0", "vertex": "V{…}"}, "to_occurrence": "O1"}}

The reference is resolved in the component the path ends in (a vertex of its body, a sketch point or construction point of it), placed where the occurrence puts it at the feature’s point of the timeline, and taken into the coordinates of the feature’s component (its first occurrence). So two copies of one component are told apart, and the move follows when either occurrence moves later. A point on an occurrence the feature itself moves is where it was before this motion. Sketches and construction geometry must be in the component the path ends in (Sketch1 is in B, not in Root); a path that leads nowhere fails the feature. Without an occurrence a reference is in the feature’s component’s coordinates, as in earlier versions (and a body of another component fails the feature: body F2.b0 (from Extrude1) belongs to Part; …); definitions are written back without the fields they did not have. Moving an occurrence a path runs through to another parent is refused. Tests: core/model-tests/assembly/src/component_tests.rs (a_move_of_an_occurrence_takes_points_where_their_occurrences_place_them, a_move_of_an_occurrence_tells_the_copies_of_a_component_apart, a_move_takes_a_sketch_point_of_another_component_by_its_occurrence, a_move_without_occurrences_takes_its_points_in_its_component_as_before).

{"type": "align", "bodies": ["F2.b0"],
 "from": {"type": "plane", "plane": {"body": "F2.b0", "face": "F2:start(…)"}},
 "to": {"type": "plane", "plane": "xy"}, "flip": false, "angle": 0}

from and to are {"type": "point", "point": …}, {"type": "axis", "axis": …} or {"type": "plane", "plane": …}: a point goes onto a point, line or plane; an axis onto an axis (direction and line; circle centres meet); a plane onto a plane with the normals opposite (faces against each other) and origins together (a face’s middle). flip turns the moved geometry over; angle turns about the target axis or normal.

{"type": "scale", "bodies": ["F2.b0"], "point": "origin",
 "scale": {"type": "uniform", "factor": 2}}

scale: {"type": "uniform", "factor"} or {"type": "non_uniform", "x", "y", "z"} along the model axes; factors greater than zero. A non-uniform scale turns faces into B-splines (names stay).

box, cylinder, cone, sphere, torus 

{"type": "box", "plane": "xy", "corner": [0, 0],
 "length": 30, "width": 20, "height": 10, "symmetric": false, "operation": "new_body", "participants": []}
{"type": "cylinder", "plane": …, "center": [u, v], "diameter": 20, "height": 30, "symmetric": false, "operation": …}
{"type": "cone", "plane": …, "center": [u, v], "radius": 10, "top_radius": 4, "height": 30, "symmetric": false, "operation": …}
{"type": "sphere", "plane": …, "center": [u, v], "diameter": 30, "operation": …}
{"type": "torus", "plane": …, "center": [u, v], "diameter": 40, "section_diameter": 10,
 "position": "on_center" | "inside" | "outside", "operation": …}

Placed on the plane at plane coordinates (the frame a sketch on the plane has), height or axis along the plane’s normal (negative height: against it). Each coordinate of corner and center is a number or, like the sizes, a value (mitcad#689): an expression or a parameter, such as "corner": ["-L/2", "-W/2"], which becomes a dimension of the feature (slots corner.x, corner.y, center.x, center.y) and moves the primitive when the parameters it uses change. A plain number stays a number, without a parameter, as documents and imports have always written it, so stored documents load unchanged; the feature query gives a value’s parameter name. operation and participants as for extrude. Faces: <feature>:bottom, top, side0..side3 for a box (side0 at the corner’s y, side1 at x + length, counter-clockwise) and side0 for curved faces.

Cone (mitcad#2239): a cone or a frustum, placed as a cylinder (plane and center, or at). radius is the base’s, on the plane; top_radius the radius at the height, left out or 0 for a full cone ending in an apex. A negative height goes against the plane’s normal with the base still on the plane (the cone turned over, not moved); symmetric puts the base half the height below the plane (above it for a negative height). Its faces keep their names when the values change, so a fillet on the base edge E{<feature>:bottom|<feature>:side0} follows a new radius: bottom the base disc (none when radius is 0), top the top disc (a frustum only) and side0 the conical face. Refused in words: a negative radius, both radii 0, a zero height, and equal radii (that is a cylinder, use Cylinder); a parameter changed into one of them fails the feature with the same words. The kernel builds it with Kernel::primitive (PrimitiveShape::Cone; OCCT’s BRepPrimAPI_MakeCone; test_primitives_name_their_faces of the geometry suite, geometry/tests/test_transform.cpp). Tests: core.model.features-solid (cone_tests) and core.model (features::primitive), both with the mock kernel, cli.primitive_cone (OCCT: the volumes pi r^2 h / 3 and pi h (R^2 + R r + r^2) / 3, a fillet on the base edge through a radius change, a cone cut from a box), the .solidcraft import’s format-50-cone test design and the UI test primitive-cone.

bounding_solid 

{"type": "bounding_solid", "bodies": ["F2.b0", "F4.b0"], "margin": 5}
{"type": "bounding_solid", "margin": 0}

A new body (BoundingSolid<n>, mitcad#460): the box around the bodies, grown by margin on every side (a negative margin shrinks it; one that leaves no box fails the feature). bodies empty or left out: every body of the feature’s component at its point of the timeline (an earlier bounding solid too). The box is aligned with the component’s axes and holds the bodies’ exact geometry (Kernel::bounding_box, the tight box of their faces, not of a display mesh); it is built with the box primitive (Kernel::primitive), so its faces are named as a box’s: <feature>:bottom at the lowest z, top at the highest, side0 at the lowest y, side1 at the highest x, side2 at the highest y and side3 at the lowest x. The bodies are only read: the box is built again from them on every recompute and follows their edits and the margin’s. A body is listed once and must be of the feature’s component; no bodies at all fails the feature. Patterns and mirrors cannot repeat it as a feature (it has no tool); its body is patterned, mirrored or moved like any other.

Tests: core.model (features::bounding_solid, mock kernel), cli.bounding_solid (OCCT) and the .solidcraft import’s bounding-solid test design.

construction_plane, construction_axis, construction_point 

{"type": "construction_plane", "definition": {"type": "offset", "plane": "xy", "distance": 10}}

Named Plane1, Axis1, Point1; they make no bodies. Their result is a datum, which follows parameter edits and is cached like a body.

A construction plane may take the faces, edges and vertices its definition names from bodies of other components (mitcad#196): "links": {"F2.b0": {"source": "O1", "target": ""}} (an OccurrenceLink per body, as an extrusion’s object_links, Geometry of other components) reads the body in its component and moves it into the plane’s coordinates by the occurrences' placements at the plane’s point of the timeline, so that a midplane between faces of two components lies where the design places them and follows when they move. Without a link another component’s body is out of reach and the plane fails.

Construction axes and points take the same links (mitcad#1029): an axis through an edge of another component, a point at its vertex, an axis or point on its face are read in that component and moved into the axis’s or point’s coordinates by the placements, so that they lie where the design shows the geometry and follow when its occurrence moves. The application’s Construct commands send a link for each face, edge or vertex picked in an occurrence of another component than the one the datum is made in (the active one, or an edited datum’s own), with target the occurrence the view shows that component at, so the other component does not have to be activated.

A construction plane, axis or point of another component is made in that component’s coordinates, so without a link a construction feature that names one in its definition ("plane": "F5") is refused, as any feature using another component’s sketch or construction geometry (F6: “Plane1 is in Motor; a feature of Frame cannot use it”). "datum_links": {"F5": {"source": "O1", "target": "O2"}} (an OccurrenceLink per datum feature, mitcad#1035) lets it through and moves the datum into the plane’s, axis’s or point’s coordinates by the placements, as links moves a body, so that an offset plane from another component’s plane or an axis through its axis lies where the design shows it and follows when its occurrence moves. A link whose source occurrence shows another component than the datum’s is refused (“Plane1 is in Motor, not in Frame, where the link O2 leads”; at recompute, after later edits, the feature fails). The application’s Construct commands send a link for each construction datum of another component than the one the new datum is made in. The links follow reparenting, copies and moves as links do and count as references for the design policy.

A sketch of another component named in the definition (a sketch line, point or path, {"sketch": "F3", "curve": "c1"}) is likewise made in its own component’s coordinates and refused without a link (F6). datum_links takes a link keyed by the sketch too ("datum_links": {"F3": {"source": "O1", "target": "O2"}}, mitcad#1039): it lets the sketch through, and the sketch’s frame is moved by the placements, its curves and points with it, so an axis along another component’s sketch line, a point at its sketch point or a plane along its sketch curve lies where the design shows that sketch. A link whose source shows another component than the sketch’s is refused as for a datum. The Construct commands send a link for each sketch of another component.

An edge is a line where it runs straight, whatever curve the kernel stores it as (mitcad#1537): a B-spline or Bezier edge whose poles lie within 1e-6 mm of the segment between its ends is a line to line, line1, line2 and edge (the kernel’s edge_geometry), as a planar spline face is a plane to plane. The straight edges and planar walls of a sheet body with a bend (a Fold, a Convert to Sheet Metal with bends) are such splines, so datums on them work as on a solid’s and follow the sheet when it changes (tools/cli/tests/sheet_datums.json: each datum on a converted plate, a converted channel and a folded sheet, within 1e-6 mm, after the plate’s length and the fold’s angle change too).

Every reference that takes a plane reads a flat face alike, whatever surface the kernel stores (mitcad#1554): a face within 1e-6 mm of a plane is that plane (its normal out of the material) as Mirror’s plane, a construction feature’s plane, a sketch plane (with the face’s edges as the sketch’s references), Split Body’s and Split Face’s tool (extended along its plane), Draft’s fixed plane, Align’s plane, an extrusion’s start or to_object face, a hole’s end face and the faces whose middle Kernel::face_plane gives (holes and joints on a face) (face_geometry, and detail::reference_plane in geometry/src/face_select.cpp). A face that is not flat (a bend’s surfaces, the side of a bend whose boundary is not square to the bend line) stays refused: face … is not planar (bspline). tools/cli/tests/sheet_face_planes.json mirrors a block about the flat faces of a converted plate, a converted channel and a folded sheet (its B-spline walls among them), splits, aligns, sketches and extrudes on a wall, and checks that the images follow the sheets when the channel’s height and the fold’s angle change, within 1e-6 mm.

A face is round where it is round, whatever surface the kernel stores it as (mitcad#1855): a face whose stored surface (an extrusion of a circle, a revolution, a B-spline or Bezier surface) lies within 1e-6 mm of a cylinder, cone, sphere or torus all over the face is that one to every reference that reads a face’s surface through Kernel::face_geometry (Axis Through Cylinder/Cone/Torus’ face, a point’s center on a sphere or torus, joint and mount frames, section picks, helix and coordinate system references) and to Kernel::face_cylinder (Bearing, thread fits, hole callouts); an edge within 1e-6 mm of a circle is that circle to Kernel::edge_geometry (a point’s center, joint frames on a circular edge). The walls of holes in a sheet body with a bend are such B-spline cylinders and their rims B-spline circles once a sheet feature (a Hole, a Flange) has rebuilt the body, also where the hole was cut by Sketch + Extrude Cut. The recognition is OCCT’s (GeomConvert_SurfToAnaSurf, GeomConvert_CurveToAnaCurve), checked again over the face or edge (geometry::analytic_surface and geometry::is_circular in geometry/src/datum.cpp). The faces and edges queries read such items the same way since mitcad#1863 (Faces and edges with geometry); Kernel::face_geometries and Kernel::edge_geometries, which the imports and sheet features read large bodies with in one pass, still give them their stored type. tools/cli/tests/round_faces_recognised.json takes the walls of a cut and a Hole in a plate and in a sheet’s flange as axes, the flange wall’s rim as a centre point, and a cut wall in each as a Cylindrical joint’s origin.

Fractions and lengths beyond a path’s ends continue straight along the end tangent. A plane’s frame (x_axis, y_axis) is what a sketch on it uses: offsets and angles move the reference frame; other planes take the model X axis projected onto them (Y when X is along the normal). Inputs that do not fit (parallel lines, collinear points, lines that pass each other) fail the feature with a message. The preview of a construction feature adds its datum.

base 

{"type": "base", "source": "bracket.step",
 "bodies": [{"name": "Bracket", "color": [0.8, 0.8, 0.8],
 "brep": {"format": "occt", "compression": "zlib", "size": 6146, "data": "eJy1V..."}},
 {"name": "Scan", "mesh": true, "brep": {…}}],
 "operation": "new_body", "participants": []}

Bodies without history: imported files, the bodies of .f3d files and the .f3d importer’s fallback (features/base.rs). Normally created with import_file or the shape API, not written by hand.

  • bodies: B-rep data (OCCT’s binary format, zlib-compressed, base64; compression may be "none") with an optional name and color (sRGB, 0..1); mesh marks a mesh body (triangles only, from STL or OBJ). In a project the data is a reference into the project’s store (sha256 instead of data, see Design files). A linked design’s body records the material and appearance (ids in this design) its source design gives it (Materials of inserted components); they do not change the body.
  • operation: new_body (default; body i is <feature>.b<i>, named after its name, made unique with (2), …), or join, cut, intersect with participants (all bodies when empty), with the same results as an extrusion’s. Mesh bodies can only be new bodies; placed by a moved or turned occurrence they are measured and reported where the design shows them, like other bodies.
  • replaces: ["F2.b0", …] (new bodies only): body i takes the id and display name of the i-th listed body, so later features that use that body continue on the new one; listed bodies beyond the new ones are removed. The importers’ fallbacks use it.
  • Faces are <feature>:import(<j>), j counting the faces of all bodies in order (body 0’s first) in the kernel’s face order, so the names stay as long as the data does. Edges and vertices follow: E{F4:import(0)|F4:import(3)}.
  • cage (optional, per body): the control cage an imported Form body was made from, kept as data (Control cages of imported Form bodies).

Component features 

{"type": "component_from_bodies", "bodies": ["F2.b0"]}
{"type": "move_occurrence", "occurrences": ["O2"],
 "transform": {"type": "translate_xyz", "x": 0, "y": 0, "z": 30}}
{"type": "capture_position", "positions": [{"occurrence": "O2",
 "transform": [[1, 0, 0, 0], [0, 1, 0, -50], [0, 0, 1, 0]]}]}

move_occurrence takes the motions of move (rigid ones only) and is named Move<n> like moves of bodies; its points and axes may be on other components with the occurrence they were picked in (from_occurrence …, move, align, scale, mitcad#699), a point on a moved occurrence where it was before the move; capture_position is Position<n>. See Components and occurrences.

Mesh bodies in surface operations

A mesh body (triangles without surfaces: STL and OBJ files, the face sets of IFC files and the meshes of other imported models; kind mesh in the bodies query) has no surfaces for the operations that intersect, offset or round faces (mitcad#399; OCCT’s boolean read a face’s null surface and crashed on Windows, mitcad#392). The features refuse one before the geometry kernel gets it (features/surface_bodies.rs), with an error naming the body: body F5.b0 (from Base1) is a mesh body (triangles without surfaces), which Combine cannot use; it works on solid and surface bodies.

  • Refused where a feature names it: combine’s target and tools; the participants of extrude, revolve, sweep, loft, pipe, coil, helix, rib, web, hole, emboss (its face’s body too), base and the patterns’ features; an extent up to its face or the body; the body of fillet, chamfer, the face features (shell, draft, offset_face, delete_face, replace_face, split_face), split_body and thread; a face of it as a hole’s face, a loft section, a sweep’s guide surface, a draft’s fixed plane, a replace target or a splitting tool; a pattern of its faces; and a mirror or pattern of bodies with combine.
  • Left out where an operation takes all bodies (Join, Cut or Intersect without participants, a cut’s cut_scope targets, Extrude’s automatic operation): mesh bodies are not cut or joined, the others are.
  • Taken as they are: moves, copies, patterns and mirrors of bodies without combine, scales, remove_body, components, appearances, measurements, physical properties, interference (which skips them), Section Analysis (which cuts their triangles, mitcad#392) and export.

The geometry facade refuses faces without surfaces too (detail::require_surfaces: booleans, unions, fillets, chamfers, face operations, splits, removed material and joins of near copies, for every other caller such as the importers): join: a mesh body (faces without surfaces) cannot be used; the operation works on solid and surface bodies. A tool’s contacts take a mesh body as apart, a mesh face’s face_geometry is mesh (not planar), and a sketch’s section of a mesh face is an error (mesh_section cuts a mesh body into sketches instead: Mesh tools for reverse engineering).

Body ids of a split’s pieces

A feature that leaves a body in several pieces (a Cut or Intersect of extrude, revolve and the other profile features, of box and the other primitives and of the copies of patterns and mirrors; a combine cut; split_body; a cut’s cut_scope) gives the body’s id to one piece and new ids of the feature (F4.b0, F4.b1, …) to the others. The first time, the pieces come in geometric order (along a planar splitting tool’s normal for split_body) and the first keeps the body. The feature then remembers each piece’s volume and centre of mass, and later evaluations give the ids by matching the new pieces with the remembered ones (mitcad#408, core/model/src/features/pieces.rs), so an upstream edit that changes the order or the number of the pieces does not hand a later feature’s body (a remove_body’s, a fillet’s, a combine’s) to another piece:

  • A piece matches a remembered one when its volume is within a factor of two of it and its centre moved less than a quarter of the size of the pieces (the diagonal of their bounding box). The closest pairs are taken first (volume change and shift, each 1 at the limit, added); ties go to the remembered piece listed first, then to the piece first in geometric order.
  • The body that was split keeps its id for the piece that matches it. Without one it takes the piece left that comes closest to it, and every later feature that names the body warns (timeline status warning): body F2.b0 is now another piece of what Extrude2 split it into (volume 40000 → 8000 mm³, centre moved 0 mm). The warning lasts while that result stands (until the split is evaluated again). When every piece matches another remembered piece, the body is gone.
  • A remembered piece that no piece matches is no longer made: its id goes to no other piece, and new pieces get new ids. remove_body passes such a body by with a warning (body F4.b1 is a piece Extrude2 no longer makes (its pieces changed): nothing to remove); any other feature that names it fails with the same words. A piece like it that comes back gets the id again.
  • A body left whole that never was in pieces is not remembered: when a later edit splits it, its pieces come in geometric order as the first time. Pieces the geometry kernel cannot measure (no volume) also come in geometric order.

What a feature remembers is saved with it in the design file, so a design opens with the ids it was saved with:

{"uid": "F4", "name": "Extrude2", "type": "extrude", …,
 "split_pieces": [{"body": "F2.b0", "size": 70.71,
 "pieces": [{"body": "F2.b0", "volume": 40000, "centre": [25, 20, 10]},
 {"body": "F4.b0", "volume": 20, "centre": [54.5, 0.5, 10], "gone": true}]}]}

body is the body split (pass numbers the splits of one body when the feature splits it more than once, as a pattern’s copies do), size the diagonal of the pieces’ bounding box (mm), each piece’s volume (mm³) and centre (mm, in its component’s coordinates), and gone for a piece the last evaluation did not make. A file without split_pieces (saved before mitcad#408) opens in geometric order and takes it on its first recompute. The document takes what each evaluation remembers without an undo step; it is an input of the feature’s evaluation like a parameter, and a result fits both what it was evaluated with and what it leaves, so the recompute cache and the result store reuse results as before. Sheet-metal cuts (sheet_cut) keep the geometric order. Tests: core.model (piece_ids_tests.rs, features::pieces).

A remove_body of every piece below a volume ({"smaller_than": …}) is not offered: a definition’s values are lengths, angles or unitless numbers, and a size filter over a component’s bodies would take small bodies that are no fragments as well; with the ids kept, the named pieces stay right.

The extended tool of a split or trim (mitcad#712)

A preview of split_body, split_face or trim_surface with extend (the default) and a plane or face tool shows the tool as the feature extends it: the preview reports "tool": true and preview_tool_shape() returns it (with tool_instances), so that a display can show where the cut runs. It is the faces the operation itself cuts with (a plane as a face across the box, a face grown along its surface: the same construction, Kernel::extended_tool, the OCCT kernel’s geometry::extended_tool), clipped to the box of the bodies split (of every body of a split_body together) grown on every side by 5 % of its diagonal, at least 1 mm. A split_body with further tools (more_tools) shows every plane or face tool, in one compound. Without extend, with a body or sketch curves as the tool, or where the kernel cannot make it (a tool that does not reach the box), there is none; the split itself is not affected.

Only a preview makes it (Evaluate::preview_tool, for the feature Cache::preview names while Document::preview_state computes): it is made again for every preview of the feature, also when the split’s result comes from the cache, and is kept in the preview’s result (Recomputed::preview_tool), never in the feature’s output, the cache or the result store. Recomputes, commits (which reuse the preview’s result) and imports do not make it. Tests: core.model (f2_tests.rs, surface_modelling_tests.rs), geometry (test_split.cpp).

Commands

command takes one command object ({"cmd": "<name>", …}) or an array of them. An array runs in order, each command its own undo step, and stops at the first failure (commands[2]: …); the result is the array of results.

Every result has "recomputed": the number of features the command evaluated (results from the cache, including a preview’s, are not counted), and "error": the first failed feature ("Fillet1: …") or null. A command that took results from the result store has "restored", their number. A failed feature does not reject the command: it is skipped, and the timeline query shows its error. When any feature fails, the result also has "failed_features": each one and whether this command added or edited it (Failed features in command results).

A command that brings a warning to a feature that was there before it says so in its result (mitcad#1729): "warnings" lists each warning such a feature has now and did not have before the command, as "<feature's name>: <warning>" in timeline order, the text the feature query gives (with the names, for agents), and "warning_messages" says the same in plain words. So set_parameter, suppress_feature, set_marker, undo and the others tell, for example, that a driven dimension split an extruded profile and the extrude kept its region as the pieces ("Extrude1: region r{…} found as r{…} + r{…} after a change in Sketch1"), without a look at the timeline; a warning that stays as it was is not repeated, and one that goes brings nothing. In add_feature and edit_feature they come after the feature’s own warnings (which are without its name; no "warning_messages" there); in a sketch command after its own, in both lists. A feature the command added is left out (add_feature gives its own, an import reports its items). A command whose "warnings" say something else (an export’s, a count) keeps them as they are. In every case each is also a warning among the result’s "notices", with the feature’s uid as its target and its places. Tests: core.model.sketch-refs (profile_selection_tests.rs), cli.mcp (mcp-test.py, with "timeline": "none").
