  • A command’s answer with "restored" also has "restored_packed": of those results, the ones whose shapes were never unpacked.
  • The cache query’s store adds deferred (hits kept packed), unpacked (of them, unpacked since) and unpack_ms, and display_meshes: lookups, hits, faces, read_bytes, read_ms, writes, write_bytes, write_ms; its disk adds display_meshes {files, bytes}; last_recompute adds restored_packed.

Display meshes. The application keeps each shown body’s display triangulations (the final tier’s, app/framework/DisplayMeshes) in the store beside the results, under the body’s version and the meshing options (.mms files, store.rs). gc, clear and the store’s size count them.

Rust / C++ Meaning
ResultStore::write_display_mesh(kernel, version, options, shape) writes Kernel::display_mesh_bytes of a shape meshed for display to the end; the file’s bytes
ResultStore::restore_display_mesh(kernel, version, options, shape) Kernel::restore_display_mesh of what is stored for that version and those options: the faces given a triangulation, None when there is none (another build, other options, another shape: nothing written)
Document::restore_display_meshes(request) (bridge) {"bodies": [uids], "options": "…"}: each body at the marker takes what the store keeps for its version; JSON {"restored": [uids], "faces", "bytes", "ms"}
Document::persist_display_meshes(request) (bridge) the same request: writes the bodies’ display meshes; JSON {"stored", "bytes", "failed", "errors", "ms"}

OCCT: io::triangulation_bytes and io::restore_triangulations (geometry/io/include/mitcad/io/mesh_store.hpp): each face’s nodes, parameters, triangles, deviation and meshing parameters and its edges' polygons, checked against the face (its surface’s kind, its edges and their end points) before anything is written. Tests: store_tests.rs (a_state_replaced_before_anything_reads_it_is_not_unpacked, an_evaluation_reads_the_restored_shapes_unpacked, display_meshes_are_kept_for_the_body_s_shape), ctest geometry.io (test_display_mesh_bytes), app.preview_meshing (testWarmOpen).

Memory cache and diagnostics

Document::set_memory_budget(Some(bytes)) (the bridge’s set_memory_cache_budget(megabytes), 0 for none) limits the estimated size of the memory cache’s results: Kernel::shape_memory of each result’s shapes (OCCT: geometry::memory_estimate; parts shared with other results are counted with each), a sketch’s regions and what it read. Beyond it the results used longest ago go, except those the document’s results and its preview hold; with a result store they come back from there. Each feature keeps at most eight results whatever the budget; without a budget (the default) nothing else goes.

Command / query Fields Result
clear_cache drops the cached results the document’s results and preview do not hold: results, bytes. No undo step, the revision stays
cache query disk (default false: also read what the store’s files hold) memory: bytes, budget (null for none), used (bytes / budget), results, features, lookups, hits, misses, restored (from the store), evicted, evicted_bytes, by_feature (uid, name, type, results, bytes; the largest first), by_type (type, features, results, bytes); store (null without one): dir, build_id and what the stores of this process did: lookups, hits, misses, damaged, other_build, read_bytes, read_ms, writes, write_bytes, write_ms, write_errors, and with disk its disk: files, bytes, other_builds {files, bytes}, damaged, by_document (document, features, results, bytes), by_feature (document, uid, name, type, results, bytes), by_type, the largest first; last_recompute: evaluated, restored, cached, evaluate_ms, restore_ms, features in timeline order (uid, name, type, source: evaluated, store, cache, suppressed or rolled_back; ms: how long it took now; evaluated_ms: how long its evaluation took)

The bridge’s query adds to the cache answer process: resident, peak_resident and heap bytes (geometry::process_memory, OCCT’s OSD_MemInfo). mitcad-cli info <file> --diagnostics prints it (Cache: {...}, with disk). Tests: core/model-tests/api/src/cache_tests.rs, ctest cli.store_diagnostics.

Geometry of other components

A sketch belongs to its component and lies in that component’s coordinates, but its plane and its projections may be geometry of another component (mitcad#100, core/model/src/links.rs): a planar face, a construction plane or an origin plane, and edges, faces and vertices to project. Such geometry is named with where it was picked: occurrence, the occurrence path from the root to its component ("O1", "O1/O4", "" for the root), and optionally context, the path the sketch’s own component is seen at (default: the first path to it). The model keeps both as an OccurrenceLink ({"source": "O1", "target": "O2"}):

  • sketch.create with occurrence stores the plane’s link as the sketch’s plane_link; sketch.project with occurrence moves the picked geometry into the sketch, and a linked projection keeps the link in its record (projections[i].link). Geometry in the sketch’s own component needs no link, and none is stored for it.
  • Evaluation finds the geometry in its component at the sketch’s point of the timeline and moves it by placement(target)⁻¹ · placement(source), the occurrences’ placements there. The sketch follows when the geometry changes or either occurrence moves; the cache keys on those placements and on the other component’s bodies the evaluation read. A face’s frame is the frame of every planar face, taken in the sketch’s coordinates; a construction or origin plane keeps its own axes.
  • A target that no longer leads to the sketch’s component (a copy, an occurrence deleted) is replaced by the first path to it; a source path that leads nowhere fails the sketch with the reason. The sketch must come after the features that make the geometry, as with any reference.
  • Without occurrence, another component’s body fails the sketch as before (body F3.b0 (from Extrude2) belongs to A; …), a construction plane of another component is refused, and sketch.project refuses a body of another component (… is a body of A, not of B; pick it where an occurrence of A shows it).

The sketch query shows plane_link. A combine’s tools may be bodies of another component the same way (tools in occurrences or tool_links, combine, mitcad#104, mitcad#544), an extrusion’s and a revolution’s objects (object_links, extrude, revolve, mitcad#762) and a sweep’s path and guide surfaces (body_links, sweep, mitcad#161), and a pulley’s or gear’s shaft (a seat’s link, Seats on shafts, mitcad#578). Tests: core/model-tests/links/src/link_tests.rs, core/model/src/links.rs.

derive 

{"type": "derive", "bodies": ["F12.b0"], "links": {"F12.b0": {"source": "O3/O5"}}}

Copies of bodies of other components as new bodies of the feature’s component (Derive<n>, mitcad#324): each body is read in its own component at the derive’s point of the timeline and moved into the derive’s coordinates by the placements there (links: one occurrence link per body of another component, as a combine’s tool_links; a body without one is the derive’s own component’s), so a copy follows when its source changes or its occurrence moves. The sources stay where they are. The copies are the bodies <derive>.b<j> in the order listed, their faces named <derive>:inst1(<name>). A body is listed once; a link for a body that is not listed, and an empty list, are refused. Paste New and moves of occurrences carry the links like a combine’s (Paste New of a component that holds the source’s occurrence links the copy to its own copy of it).

The .f3d import brings a design’s derived bodies in so: each body’s document is imported from its own file like the other documents the design refers to (Components of other documents), placed as a hidden occurrence of a component filled with its copy, where the derive puts the body (the source design’s placement of the body’s occurrence seen from the deriving design’s placement there), and the derive copies the body from it; report.designs[0].components then lists the documents among references as for occurrences.

Moving features into components

A design often starts in the root: sketches, extrudes and fillets made there, and components only later. The root then holds modelled bodies and components (a hybrid assembly), and Create Components from Bodies moves a body into a component without the features that made it. move_to_component (mitcad#171, document/move_features.rs) moves the features themselves into new components placed where they were, as if they had been made there:

  • Everything (no bodies, features or groups): every modelled feature of component (default the root) goes into one new component, placed in it at the identity and grounded; the component keeps only components and the features that place or relate them (Move and Position of occurrences, joints, rigid groups, assembly constraints). A feature that makes a component (a new-component operation, Component from Bodies) goes too when it uses what goes; the component it made stays placed where it is.
  • Bodies, features, groups: bodies and features go into one new component with the features that made those bodies; groups (lists of bodies) into a component each, named after the body when it is one (otherwise Component<n>; name or names choose). Which features go follows the last recompute (the bodies each feature set, removed or read) and the references (for features after the marker, suppressed or failed): a feature goes with the features it refers to, those that refer to it and those that work on the same bodies.
  • Conflicts: a feature that would belong to two components, or works on a body that stays (a combine or a cut through bodies of two groups, a sketch on a face of a body that stays, a sketch two groups use), refuses the move with the reason (Combine1 ties Body1, Body2, which would go into different components; …), unless "together": true keeps such bodies in one component (a body that would stay goes along). A feature that stays and uses what would go, which no occurrence path can follow (a Move of occurrences about an edge of a moving body), refuses it in every case.
  • Nothing moves: features keep their uids, timeline order, parameters and the topological names of what they make. References from elsewhere take the new occurrence into their paths: sketch planes and projections of other components and combines’ tools (Geometry of other components), joint and constraint origins, Isolate, comments on the moved bodies and the drawings’ recorded view bodies and picks of them (mitcad#1318); a moved feature’s own links are seen from the new occurrence. The move is refused when a feature that worked fails after it, or a definition that checked no longer does.
  • Cut scopes follow (mitcad#859): a moved extrusion’s cut_scope (also a saved one of an extrusion that does not cut) takes the destination as its context (the component and its occurrence path) and so do its targets in the component it left; any scope’s excluded_bodies of the bodies that went name their new place. What the component keeps stays named where it is: an automatic scope’s exclusion of it, and another component’s cut into it, then name both places. The same holds for an explicit destination and for move_history_into_component.
  • move_history_into_component with feature, a component_from_bodies: the features that made its bodies go into the component it made, which then has their history (Paste New copies it), and the feature goes. Refused when one of them also works on a body that stays.
  • Each command is one undo step (Move Features of Root into Component1, Move History into Body1).
Command Fields Result
move_to_component component (default the root), bodies, features, or groups; name or names; together (default false); optional source_occurrence and destination below components: component, occurrence, name, bodies, features; explicit destinations also return created
move_history_into_component feature component, name, features
set_hybrid_assembly allowed (default true)
Query Fields Result
move_to_component as the command, without the top-level name and names component, name, everything, bodies (the component’s at the marker: uid, name), hybrid_assembly, groups (bodies with names, features with uid, name, type), conflicts (feature, name, groups (indices), staying bodies, message), together (the expanded groups, or null), problems, destinations, keep_together (the requested boolean)
feature_references def (a definition as add_feature takes it) features it refers to, components they are in

The application asks before it makes a component in a root with modelled bodies (app/framework/HybridAssembly.cpp): Move into a New Component, Continue as Is or Cancel. “Don’t ask again for this design” runs set_hybrid_assembly (undo step Allow Hybrid Assembly); the document query has "hybrid_assembly": true then, and the design file keeps "hybrid_assembly": true. Tests: core/model-tests/assembly/src/move_features_tests.rs, tools/ui-hybrid-test.sh.

Choosing an existing or new destination

The explicit Move to Component action (mitcad#201) asks for the destination before executing a command. The query is read-only and lists the dependency group that will move. Conflicts still require together: true: selecting a destination never implies permission to take additional bodies.

An existing component is identified by its UID and its full occurrence path from the root:

{"cmd":"move_to_component","component":"C1","features":["F5"],
 "source_occurrence":"O1",
 "destination":{"kind":"existing","component":"C3","occurrence":"O2/O4"}}

To create the component in the same atomic move, specify its parent and optionally its name:

{"cmd":"move_to_component","features":["F1"],
 "destination":{"kind":"new","parent":"C0","parent_occurrence":"","name":"Housing"}}

The empty occurrence path is the root. source_occurrence may be omitted when there is exactly one placement of the source. Both source and target (or a new component’s parent) must have one placement in the whole design; this includes repetitions through an ancestor. A repeated or unplaced component is refused rather than selecting an arbitrary instance of its shared definition. Source and destination paths are checked again when the command executes.

For the picker, destinations contains one row for every placed component context, including the root:

{"component":"C3","name":"Bracket","occurrence":"O2/O4",
 "path":"Root/Assembly:1/Bracket:1","parent_occurrence":"O2",
 "eligible":true,"reason":"","can_create":true,"create_reason":""}

eligible and reason describe a move into that existing component; can_create and create_reason describe creation below it. Full UID paths remain the selection keys even if display names repeat. Supplying a destination in the query also adds its refusal reason to problems. The expanded together group is considered when checking destinations; conflicts remain separate until the caller explicitly consents. An explicit destination accepts one resulting group. Top-level name and names cannot be combined with destination; a new name goes inside it.

An existing destination creates no component or occurrence. To preserve world placement, the model maps source coordinates by inverse(destination_world) * source_world. Origin-plane sketches keep their entities, constraints and parameters, with their stored frame rebased into the target coordinates. Numeric-distance extrudes, fillets, chamfers and combines can accompany them. Definitions requiring other coordinate transformations (for example, a face-supported sketch or an origin-axis revolve) are refused for differing placements with the feature’s name and a reason. At equal placements no frame change is needed. A new component instead receives the source’s world placement relative to its chosen parent, retaining the features’ local coordinates.

Sketch plane/projection links, combine/sweep body links and isolated-body paths follow the geometry to the destination. Explicit moves refuse read-only linked components, the current owner, components created by a modelling feature, moved component-creating features, affected assembly constraint references, and contexts positioned by timeline features. Moving into an existing component is also refused when an affected feature automatically reads all local bodies: the added bodies must not silently become participants of an existing operation. These cases report a reason instead of changing geometry or dropping references.

Validation, optional creation, ownership and reference updates, and the successful recompute are one undo step. Cancelled or rejected commands leave the design, component counters and history unchanged. Explicit results use the full occurrence path in components[].occurrence (empty for the root) and include created. Calls without destination retain the original automatic child-creation behaviour and result format, used by the hybrid-assembly prompt and grouped automatic moves.

core.model covers destination validation, dependency consent and atomic moves; app.unit exercises the destination dialog. The OCCT checks cli.move_destination and cli.move_destination_reopened preserve the world-space bounds, volumes and external face support of three bodies when moving a nested source into a differently rotated existing component, including Undo/Redo and save/reopen.

Moving an occurrence to another parent

reparent_occurrence (mitcad#219, document/reparent.rs) moves one occurrence, with its component and everything placed in it, under another parent: the root or a placed component. It is a hierarchy move, not a copy: the occurrence keeps its uid, number, name, light bulb and grounding, its component keeps its uid, features, bodies, parameters and history. Only its parent changes, and its own placement, to inverse(new_parent_world) * old_parent_world * placement so that it stays where it is in the design at the timeline marker (through the parents the old and the new way do not share; translated and rotated parents alike).

{"cmd":"reparent_occurrence","occurrence":"O1/O2","parent":""}

occurrence is the occurrence’s path from the root and parent the path of the new parent’s occurrence (empty: the root), by uids (O1/O4) or names (Assembly:1/Part:1). The result has occurrence, component, path (the new uid path), path_name, parent (the component), updated (the references that followed it) and features (the features that place it and went with it, below). One undo step, Move Part:1 to Root; undo and redo restore or reapply the hierarchy, the placement, the references and the carried features together.

Several occurrences together (mitcad#1847): with lists more occurrences of the same parent (paths from the root) that go into the new parent in the same step, as Move to Component does for the selected rows or a rigid group’s members:

{"cmd":"reparent_occurrence","occurrence":"O2","with":["O3","O1"],"parent":"O4"}

Each keeps its place in the design as one would. A feature that places only moved occurrences (a rigid group of them, a joint between two of them) goes into the new parent whole, its paths as they were; one that also places occurrences that stay is carried or split as below. The result adds moved (each occurrence’s occurrence, component, path and path_name, the first one first; the other fields are the first one’s), the undo step is Move Bearing:1, Tube:1 to Holder, and occurrences of different parents are refused (Bearing:1 and Plate:1 are in different components; …).

Occurrence paths that lead through the moved occurrence follow it in the same step: sketch planes and projections linked to other components, combine, sweep, split and extrude body links, construction plane, axis and point links (links and datum_links), cut scopes, joints and assembly constraints (their paths are relative to their component), section analyses, Isolate, the model’s annotations, and the drawings (mitcad#743): their views’ occurrence subjects, chosen bodies’ occurrences and the picks of their dimensions, notes, symbols and balloons. A root drawing’s paths go the new way; a component’s drawing keeps paths from its component, which follow while the old and the new parent both lie inside that component, and the move is refused, naming the drawing, when the occurrence would leave it. The changed drawings are listed in updated. Print plate items of occurrences and comment targets whose paths lead through it follow too (mitcad#1318; updated lists Print plates and Comments). Everything is validated before anything changes, in one place (Document::plan_reparent, which design policies extend), and refused with the blocker named.

The features that place it go with it (mitcad#301): its joints and as-built joints (it is the first occurrence of a side’s path), the rows of assembly constraint sets with it, rigid groups with it, and its Moves (move_occurrence) and Capture Positions, wherever they are in the timeline (also after the marker and suppressed). Each becomes a feature of the new parent and keeps its place in the timeline; its occurrence paths are rewritten relative to the new parent. The new parent is the one component where such a feature can still place the occurrence: a joint, constraint or rigid group moves only occurrences placed directly in its component, and a Move or Capture Position places only those, so the lowest component that holds everything the feature refers to after the move must be the new parent itself. Typical: Joint1 of Box joins Part:1 to Box’s own block; moving Part:1 from Box:1 to the root makes Joint1 a root joint from Part:1 to Box:1 (its side b was the empty path, now O1). Moving Part:1 into a component that holds the geometry it is joined to (a joint to Sub:1’s block, Part:1 into Box:1/Sub:1) makes it a joint of Sub to Sub’s own block.

  • A Move turns into the new parent’s coordinates: a free move (free matrix) by relative * move * inverse(relative), where relative takes the old parent’s coordinates into the new parent’s; a move along the axes (translate_xyz) stays as it is when the axes agree.
  • A Capture Position’s placement becomes relative * captured.
  • A rigid group of the old parent holds the moved occurrence, in the new parent (an ancestor of the old one), to the occurrence that places the old parent there (Box:1), which stands for the members that stay.
  • A feature that also places other occurrences is split: the occurrence’s rows of a constraint set (with their parameters), its position of a Capture Position, its place in a rigid group of three or more, or (for a free move) its place in a Move go into a new feature of the new parent right after it (Constraint2, Position2, RigidGroup2, Move2, in the same timeline group), the rest stays.

The query’s plan and the command list them in features: name, from and from_name (its component), to and to_name (the new parent) and split (the new feature’s name, null when the feature goes whole):

{"name":"Joint1","from":"C1","from_name":"Box","to":"C0","to_name":"Root","split":null}

The refusals:

  • the root and an occurrence made by Pattern at Points;
  • a placing feature that could not keep its meaning in the new parent (Joint1: it joins Part:1 to Box:1, which is not in Lid; it places only occurrences placed directly in its component, so it could not place Part:1 there; in Root, which holds both, it would move Lid:1 instead). The reason ends with what to do (mitcad#1847): Move Shaft:1 into Holder as well, or delete it and join Bearing:1 again inside Holder when the other side is an occurrence that could go along (with with), else Delete it and join Part:1 again inside Lid; placing an occurrence inside a component by a joint of its parent is mitcad#1793’s. A rigid group whose other members stay where the new parent cannot hold them says … which would not be in Holder. Move the whole group together; a Move along the old parent’s axes when they are turned in the new parent (Move1: it moves Part:1 along the x, y and z axes of Assembly, which are turned in Root; …) or by geometry of the old parent (an axis or points, which a feature of another component cannot use); a Move by values that also moves other occurrences (its parameters belong to it, so it cannot be split);
  • what a carried feature depends on moving later in the timeline in a way the moved occurrence would no longer follow: an occurrence below the new parent on the way to geometry it is joined to, or a member of its rigid group, placed by a later feature (Joint1: Pin:1 is placed by Move1 later in the timeline, which Part:1 in Root would no longer follow); a parent on the way between the old and the new parent placed by a later Move, Capture Position or Pattern at Points (later joints of the new parent are solved together with the carried ones); for a Move or Capture Position, a parent on the way placed by any later feature (it works in the parent’s coordinates at its point of the timeline);
  • an occurrence whose solved placement differs from its own without a timeline feature that places it (Part:1 is placed by the joints);
  • a source parent placed more than once (the occurrence is in each of them, Assembly is placed 2 times and Part:1 is in each of them; …) and a destination placed more than once (it would appear in each): a single occurrence move never edits other instances of a shared component; other occurrences of the moved component itself stay as they are;
  • linked (read-only) source parents and destinations;
  • the current parent (Part:1 is already in Assembly), the occurrence’s own component and anything placed in it (a cycle);
  • a joint or constraint whose moved occurrence would change, or whose component the occurrence would leave (Joint1: Part:1 would no longer be in Asm:1, the occurrence it moves);
  • Pattern at Points features and instances that refer to it;
  • references across the occurrence (one side through it, the other not) while an occurrence on the way from the old parent or to the new one is placed by a timeline feature (anywhere in the timeline): the relative placement could differ where the reference is evaluated (Sketch2: Assembly:1 is placed by Move1 in the timeline, …).

A component made by a feature (a new-component operation, Component from Bodies) can move: the feature keeps making its bodies, in that component’s coordinates. The command recomputes the new state before taking it and refuses it (the move would make features fail: …) when a feature that built before fails after the move, and when any occurrence would be somewhere else in the design at the marker (the move would change where Box:1 is in the design: Joint1 would place the occurrences differently in Root; e.g. a joint whose side a was the old parent’s own geometry, which cannot move there, while in the new parent a is the old parent’s occurrence, which moves first unless grounded). Carried features are also checked where they stand in the timeline, after the marker too. A refused command changes nothing.

The query takes occurrence and optionally parent and with (as the command’s):

{"query":"reparent_occurrence","occurrence":"O1/O2","parent":""}

It answers occurrence, name, path, path_name (Root/Assembly:1/ Part:1), component, component_name, parent, parent_path, grounded (of the first occurrence), occurrences (every occurrence that moves: occurrence, name, path, path_name), rigid_group (the other members of the rigid groups that hold them, and of the groups that hold those, in the same form: what Move to Component offers to move with them, mitcad#1847), contents (occurrences: the paths placed in it below it, each from its moved occurrence when several move, components, bodies, features), problems (why the occurrence cannot move at all) and destinations: every placement of the root and of each component, as Move to Component lists them, with current (the current parent), eligible, reason and reasons (each blocker on its own; reason joins them with ; ):

{"component":"C3","name":"Bracket","occurrence":"O4","path":"Root/Bracket:1",
 "parent_occurrence":"","current":false,"eligible":true,"reason":""}

With parent, plan is eligible, problems (the blockers), and for an eligible move parent, parent_path, from, from_path, path (the new uid path), moved (every moved occurrence’s new path), transform (the first one’s new placement’s rows), updates and features (the carried features). The query does not recompute: a move the plan allows can still be refused by the command’s recompute (above). Tests: core/model-tests/assembly/src/reparent_tests.rs, cli.reparent_occurrence and cli.reparent_occurrence_reopened (real geometry, undo/redo, save/reopen, a joint that goes to the root with its occurrence), app.unit (the picker), tools/ui-move-test.sh, tools/ui-move-occurrence-group-test.sh (two selected occurrences of a rigid group joined to a shaft, mitcad#1847).

Autoselect profile groups

{"query": "autoselect_profiles"} returns the current profile groups for Solid mode’s Autoselect box (mitcad#193):

{"eligible": true, "sketch": "F3", "component": "C0",
 "projected": [], "drawn": ["r{c9}", "r{c11}", "r{c13}"],
 "hybrid": ["r{c1[c7,c3],c3[c1,c5],c5[c3,c7],c7[c5,c1]}"],
 "all": ["r{c1[c7,c3],c3[c1,c5],c5[c3,c7],c7[c5,c1]}", "r{c9}", "r{c11}", "r{c13}"]}

Only the final item of the whole history can qualify: an evaluated, unsuppressed sketch with closed regions, no feature using the sketch and the timeline marker at the end. A consumer of any of its profiles, curves or points makes the whole sketch used; suppressed consumers and consumers beyond the marker count too. The query never searches older sketches. Otherwise it returns eligible: false, null sketch and component, and empty group lists. The application controls Solid-mode visibility and maps the component to its displayed occurrence.

The three origin groups are disjoint, and all is their union, with each current region key once. Every segment of a region’s outer boundary and holes contributes its original curve’s provenance. reference entities (including unlinked projections) and entities in linked projections are projected; other sketch curves and text contours are drawn. fixed alone does not make a drawing projected. A region with both origins is hybrid. Intersection segments retain their source curve’s origin.

For a projected rectangle containing three drawn circles, the three circle interiors are drawn and the surrounding rectangle region is hybrid: its holes have drawn boundaries. Nested loops likewise produce individual regions with their immediate holes, not one selection per closed curve. Open curves and construction geometry add no candidates on their own; an open curve may help bound a closed region where it intersects other geometry.

This query neither changes selection nor creates features. The application toggles each candidate against the actual current selection, preserving unrelated items; hover only previews. Query again after edits, undo/redo and timeline changes. Keys are current exact identities, not cached or best-matched references; profiles lists the current identities of all evaluated sketches when pruning stale application selection.

Adding to the API

  • A feature type: a module in core/model/src/features/ with its definition struct (generic over the value form P), map_params, FeatureInfo and Evaluate, and one line in feature_types! (features/mod.rs). Its serde form is then its command and file form; the dispatch, the cache, undo, preview and the design file need no change. Add its section under Feature definitions. When every value maps under its field’s name, map_params! (features/mapping.rs, mitcad#586) writes map_params from the list of all fields, each clone, copy, param, option, map (a type with its own map_params), with(helper) or phantom, in the order the values are visited (parameter numbering depends on it); a mapping with other slot names or prefixes is written by hand.
  • Patterns and mirrors of features: FeatureInfo::tool_use() returns the operation and participants of the tool body the feature leaves in FeatureOutput::tool; without it a feature cannot be patterned (extrude, revolve, hole, sweep, loft, pipe, coil, helix, rib, web and the primitives have it). Evaluate::placed_tool(ctx, feature, placement) optionally rebuilds the tool with the feature’s own placement moved by a rigid transform, faces named after feature, for adjust (the primitives and the extrusions whose end depends on bodies, a body face’s too: its face, on its body before the extrusion, moved with the copy, mitcad#2033); without it the stored tool is moved. Reading another feature’s tool goes through EvalContext::feature_tool, which the recompute cache tracks by the version of that feature’s result.
  • A kernel operation: a Kernel method with a default Err(KernelError::Unsupported(…)) (kernel.rs), a family bridge in core/ffi/src/kernel/ with its C++ half in core/cpp/bridge/, and the geometry in geometry/src/<family>.cpp.
  • A command or query: a variant of Command or Query in mod.rs (or of a family’s command enum), a line in the tables above, and its class in classes.rs (see Classes of commands and queries; a test fails without one). The enums are declared with named_enum! (api/dispatch.rs), each variant with its name on the wire before it ("add_feature" => AddFeature { … }), which gives the variant its serde name and the enum its list of names, NAMES (mitcad#585). A family of commands with an enum of its own (components, joints, sketches, …) is one row of Document::command_families (its names and the method that runs it); every other name goes to Command, whose error for an unknown name lists its commands. A test checks that every name reaches its own family and that no name is in two lists.

Sheet rules and base Face

sheet_rules owns fabrication parameters. A sheet_face refers to an earlier rules feature and closed regions of one sketch in its owning component. Rule features may be shared across components. Rules use ordinary numeric or named parameter inputs; allowance.k is dimensionless, all other rule values below are lengths. Editing a shared rule changes all of its consumers.

{"cmd":"add_feature","def":{"type":"sheet_rules","thickness":1,
 "bend_radius":2,"allowance":{"type":"k_factor","k":0.4},
 "reference_side":"front","bend_relief":{"type":"round","width":1,"depth":3},
 "corner_relief":{"type":"rectangular","width":1,"depth":3}}}
{"cmd":"add_feature","def":{"type":"sheet_face","rules":"F2",
 "profiles":[{"sketch":"F1","region":"r{c1[c4,c2],c2[c1,c3],c3[c2,c4],c4[c3,c1]}"}]}}

Lengths must be finite and exceed the modelling tolerance, 1e-7 mm; K must be finite in [0,1]. bend_relief takes rectangular or round and is used where a flange, bend or fold ends inside the sheet. corner_relief also takes tear and supplies the Corner Relief feature when it has no override. Multi-edge flange corners use their own mitres and corner gaps. Corner relief uses width for rectangular and round shapes. Its depth field is retained for saved definitions. Base Face does not create a bend or relief. With front, material runs from sketch offset 0 to +thickness; with back, it runs from -thickness to 0 along the sketch normal. Face creates new bodies; it does not join existing solids.

Face retains exact line, arc, ellipse and spline boundaries, holes and separate islands. Adjacent selected regions form one solid while keeping their semantic panel identities, also after later folded features, whatever curve they meet along (an arc or a spline as well as a line; mitcad#242). Initial panel slots follow canonical profile-key order. Settled panel_slots in saved definitions retain removed references as tombstones, so editing selection order does not reassign a panel. A solid’s body index is its smallest contributing panel slot. Semantic face names include F3:sheet_front(0) and F3:sheet_back(0); source curve aliases remain on walls.

A changed profile is followed as Extrude follows its profiles (mitcad#1444, see SketchOutput::found): a region key is built from the curves around the region, so an edit of the outline (a corner rounded, a curve replaced, moved or added) gives the same region a new key. Each profile reference then finds the region inside the outline its stored key traces on the changed curves, else the region with the most curves in common, and the Face warns region r{…} found as r{…} after a change in Sketch1 (the notice points at the region). The region found keeps the reference’s panel slot, so the panel’s identity, its face names and the later folds, flanges and other sheet features that name it keep working; the walls are named by the region’s current curve segments, so a wall along an unchanged curve keeps its name. A reference that finds no region (its curves deleted) fails with Sketch1 has no profile r{…}. Curves are known by their ids, which continue from the highest one in use: a curve drawn into a sketch emptied of its curves and points takes the id c1 again, and a reference with a c1 then finds that curve’s region, as an extrusion’s profile does. A reference whose region the edit split into pieces fails with region r{…} is split into r{…} + r{…} after a change in Sketch1; select the profiles again, unless each piece other than the main one (the one with the most curves in common) is selected by a reference of its own: then the main piece keeps the reference’s slot and each other piece the slot settled for its own reference. The pieces get no slots made up at evaluation: panel slots are settled in the definition when the Face is edited, and a slot given at evaluation could be handed to another region by a later edit, renaming panels and bodies without notice. So the Face fails until the pieces are selected, and selecting the other pieces (the stored reference still selects the main piece) keeps the existing panel’s slot and names. Two references that find the same region (an old key and the current one) make one panel, under the reference that names it by its own key. A joined Face (body below) finds its profiles in the same way, but adds every piece of a split region (with the warning naming them), since its material has no panel identity of its own.

A Face with "body": "F3.b0" is joined to that sheet in a panel’s plane (mitcad#242): its sketch lies on the front or back surface of a planar panel of the body, it uses the body’s rules, and its regions are added to that panel’s material through the thickness (one union, so the regions must touch or overlap the panel; touching several coplanar panels is refused). The added material has no panel identity of its own: its sketch curves are the panel’s boundaries (lineage), as a coplanar join leaves no seam.

{"cmd":"add_feature","def":{"type":"sheet_face","rules":"F2","body":"F3.b0",
 "profiles":[{"sketch":"F4","region":"r{c1[c4,c2],c2[c1,c3],c3[c2,c4],c4[c3,c1]}"}]}}
{"query":"sheet_state","body":"F3.b0"}

The body query returns body, owner, status, hex version and shape_generation, rules, rules_version, exact panels, invalidated, blockers and textual diagnostics. Each panel has id:{feature,slot}, a component-local sketch frame, and region.loops, each with named exact curve segments. Omitting body returns an array of current sheet entries. A missing or unavailable body returns {body,status:"unavailable"}. status is valid, invalid after an operation without a sheet adapter, or blocked when a failed operation retained geometry but prevents using it as valid material. Invalidity takes precedence when both causes exist; blockers still reports every responsible failed feature. invalidated names the first operation that took the sheet meaning away; later operations on the invalid body do not replace it.

{"query":"sheet_rules","feature":"F2"} returns {feature,status,version,rules} with resolved numeric rules. An unavailable rule returns {feature,status:"unavailable"}. Omitting feature returns all available rule outputs. Both queries are available through MCP’s read-only query interface. Feature previews additionally report sheet_states from the preview result; querying the committed document does not publish the preview.

Shape and sheet domains are one evaluated result, including cache restoration. Ordinary Booleans, scales and face operations invalidate affected sheet meaning; they retain the solid. An ordinary feature (or a base feature) that replaces a valid sheet’s body goes through the sheet-domain adapter first (mitcad#242): where its result is still the sheet’s material changed through the thickness of planar charts (a cut, a hole, a mirror or pattern of them, a rounded or bevelled contour corner), each planar chart’s new outline is read from the result’s faces on its front surface, the material it lost is removed from the domains as sheet_cut removes regions (new curves are generated curves of the feature, F<feature>/g<k>), and the rebuilt sheet must have the result’s volume, area and centre of mass; the body then stays a valid sheet. Otherwise (material added, a bend changed, walls not normal to the material, faces on the surfaces broken by a dressup) the sheet is invalidated with that reason (ordinary modelling replaced this body and the sheet-domain adapter could not re-derive its material: …). An ordinary fillet or chamfer the domains cannot hold (a countersink at a hole’s edge, a rounded surface edge) is instead kept as a change overlay of the sheet (sheet_state.overlays: {"feature", "type": "change", "placement", "removed"}): every later sheet feature rebuilds the solid from the domains and makes the material it changed again (its body before it against its result, moved with the body), and the developed form (Unfold, Refold, Fold, Bend, Flat Pattern) is refused, as for straight cuts. sheet_reference names an edge such an ordinary feature named (a thickness edge at a panel corner) by where it runs: the corner whose vertex it joins on the front and back surfaces. A straight edge such a feature named on a panel’s front or back surface (the outline of material a Join added to a panel in its plane, mitcad#2117) is the boundary it runs along: the answer of a picked wall (boundary, pieces, straight, axial) with its domain and the surface it lies on (front, back), when exactly one straight boundary piece of the panels’ charts holds both its ends; a planar face such a feature named, with at, is the panel whose surface holds that point on its material (domain).

An ordinary Fillet of constant radii, or Chamfer of equal distances, whose edges are all thickness edges at panel corners of a valid sheet, one at least beside a bend (a wall’s side meeting its bend, mitcad#1765), rounds or bevels them as sheet_corner_round and sheet_corner_chamfer do in the developed outline, so the body stays a sheet whose Flat Pattern has them; the feature warns Fillet1 rounds a corner beside a bend: rounded through the thickness in the sheet's flat outline, as Corner Round does (bevels … as Corner Chamfer does), and a corner it cannot trim there fails with the reason in words. sheet_reference on the edge between a panel’s wall and a bend’s side (E{F6:sheet_bend_side0(…)|F6:sheet_side0(…)}) answers the panel’s corner between that wall and its tangent line to the bend.

An ordinary feature that only removes material across one or more folded bends (an extrusion cut through both flanges at a bend, a hole reaching a bend; mitcad#1628) is applied as sheet_cut applies its profiles: every chart’s footprint is read from the result’s faces on its front surface (a panel’s plane, a bend’s cylinder, whose faces’ own parameter curves map exactly into the bend’s developed coordinates), the material each chart lost there is mapped into the developed plane of a panel with the touched bends opened, removed from every chart in that plane in one trim whose seams are the registered ports, and the bends are folded again. The sheet stays valid: Unfold, Refold and Flat Pattern work, and the flat pattern shows the cut’s developed outline. In a bend the cut then runs through the thickness normal to the material, not along the feature’s walls: where the rebuilt sheet differs from the feature’s result (only inside the bends it crosses, and only where the feature cut through the material there), the body becomes the rebuilt sheet and the feature has a warning (Extrude2 cuts across a bend: cut normal to the sheet there, as Sheet Cut does). Material added across a bend, a cut in a bend that does not go through the material, or walls in a panel that are not normal to it invalidate the sheet with that reason as before. A sheet feature on an invalid sheet (Unfold, a flange) fails naming the feature that took the sheet meaning away and its reason in words, without internal ids, and points to Sheet Cut; on a blocked sheet it names the failed feature.

A pattern or mirror of features may repeat sheet features (a joined sheet_face, sheet_flange, sheet_cut, corner rounds, chamfers and reliefs) together with ordinary ones on one valid sheet body (mitcad#242). The copies are made one after another in timeline order and keep the body a sheet: a flange is built again on the copy of its boundary (the panel boundary of the current sheet that the element’s transform carries the original’s boundary onto), its bend turning to the side the transform carries the original’s side to, its offsets and width turned with the boundary; every other feature repeats the material it changed (what it added joined, what it removed cut, both moved by the transform), after which the sheet’s domains are re-derived as above. A straight sheet_cut is cut again from the copy of its sketch’s plane along the copy of its direction (re-derived, or an overlay where it crosses a bend), and the copy of a feature the sheet keeps as a change overlay (an ordinary fillet or chamfer, also on its own in the pattern) is kept as one too, the original’s change moved by the transform. Each copy’s domains and curves carry the pattern’s identity, numbered per copy (slots offset by 100000 for each). Copies of features on several bodies, or on a body that is not a valid sheet, are made as for ordinary features (the material they changed, without re-deriving the sheet). A rigid Move or Align transforms the domains, and Component from Bodies changes their owner atomically. Occurrence placements do not change component-local domains. Generic body copies and split pieces without a sheet adapter report invalid sheet semantics. A failed operation blocks only its intended sheet targets; suppression, rollback and Undo remove that failure when it no longer applies. An automatic participant set is a dependency even when empty. Assembly-scoped cuts track target BodyUid ownership and exclusions.

Paste New copies the sheet rules and their parameter-expression dependency closure, including rules outside the component subtree. The copied rules are independent by default and precede their consumers. Feature, sketch, body and panel provenance references are remapped. Save/reopen recomputes definitions or restores matching geometry and sheet deltas together; old designs without sheet features retain ordinary-solid behaviour. Rules, Face and the folded operations below are native model features. Production Unfold/Refold, Flat Pattern, sheet Cut and DXF follow the sheet-metal contract.

Folded sheet features

The five operations below use add_feature and edit_feature, ordinary parameters, preview, Undo and persistence. They consume a valid native sheet; an invalid or blocked upstream sheet is an error. Body references edit their component definition, including all occurrences of that definition. Geometry, semantic domains, ownership and body consumption publish atomically.

A boundary is {panel:{feature,slot},curve:SheetCurveId}. Sketch curves use {type:"sketch",sketch:"F2",segment:"c2[c1,c3]"}; generated curves use {type:"generated",feature:"F4",slot:13}. Optional piece and directed range:{first,last} disambiguate a split reference. A missing or ambiguous reference fails instead of choosing the first or nearest boundary. The graph records full-side coplanar adjacency even when the kernel merges physical caps.

{"type":"sheet_flange","body":"F3.b0",
 "boundary":{"panel":{"feature":"F3","slot":0},
 "curve":{"type":"sketch","sketch":"F2","segment":"c2[c1,c3]"}},
 "angle":1.5707963267948966,"length":{"mode":"tangent","value":15},
 "position":"inside","offsets":{"start":3,"end":4},
 "relief":{"type":"rectangular","width":2,"depth":3}}

Flange requires a straight free material boundary. Length modes are tangent, inner and outer. The straight length is respectively entered length, length minus r*tan(abs(angle)/2), or length minus (r+t)*tan(abs(angle)/2); it must not be negative, and a straight length of 0 makes a flange of its bend alone, with no wall (a rolled hem, mitcad#1378). Positions inside, outside and default bend_line place the stationary tangent at minus the outer setback, minus the inner setback, or minus half the allowance. The signed angle is nonzero and less than a full turn either way (a flange may bend past 180 degrees, mitcad#1378; Bend and Fold stay at most pi): a flange of 180 degrees or more is a hem (mitcad#242), whose inner and outer virtual sharps do not exist, so inner, outer, inside and outside refuse it. Its developed length is the bend allowance abs(angle) (r + K t) for any angle. Two more references (mitcad#242, the .f3d flanges) use the bend’s outer extent X = (r+t)*sin(min(abs(angle), pi/2)), how far its outer surface reaches past the stationary tangent: position side_tangent places the stationary tangent at minus X, so the outer surface touches the side plane through the selected boundary (normal to the panel) and does not pass it, and length mode outer_tangent measures from the plane touching the outer surface normal to the wall, a straight length of the entered length minus X. At 90 degrees they equal inside and outer. Where the flange’s trim of its panel reaches the seam between that panel and a bend (a flange on an edge next to an earlier flange, or on the side edge of a flange’s wall), the trim goes on through that bend, developed, so the bend ends where the panel now ends: a rectangular relief of the trim’s depth at the corner (mitcad#211). Position edge (mitcad#211, the imports’ flanges whose bend starts at the edge) places the stationary tangent on the selected boundary, so the panel keeps all its material. Where a side of the panel meets the selected boundary at another angle than 90 degrees (mitcad#1576), an end of the whole boundary (no offset, no overhang) follows that side on to the stationary tangent line: the trim takes the panel’s material beside the bend’s end (where the side meets the boundary at more than 90 degrees, followed while it runs straight inward, also past a short side before it), so the side runs on to the line at its own angle, and the bend and its wall span the panel’s material along that line, wider or narrower than the boundary by how far the side leans over the setback. An end with an offset keeps its relief and its place. Positive bends move towards the material front-to-back normal; signs do not change the rule’s reference side. Optional radius overrides the inside-radius rule. Thickness and K always come from the referenced rules.

Omitted offsets are zero. Start/end are nonnegative distances along the canonical axial direction e, chosen with e cross outward = material normal. They leave positive axial width. Instead of offsets a flange may take "width": {"type": "middle", "before": b, "after": a} (mitcad#242): it covers b from the boundary’s midpoint towards the start of e and a towards its end. Such a width may pass an end of the boundary: the bend covers the boundary only, and the wall continues past it beside the bend, cut back at its root by the relief depth so that the bend’s side stays free (the sheet_reference answer for a straight boundary gives its axial start and end, where these are measured from). An optional "root" in the width sets that cut-back instead; 0 starts the overhangs at the bend’s moving tangent line, beside the bend’s side (the .ipt flanges’ overhangs, mitcad#242); it must not be negative. Endpoints inside material receive reliefs outside the selected axial interval, opening through the moving side to its free boundary. Explicit relief overrides the complete bend_relief rule. Width is the actual positive clearance. Depth is penetration behind the stationary tangent and must be positive (mitcad#242; it was at least one thickness before, a convention rules of half a thickness do not follow). Rectangular relief has a flat termination; round relief has a semicircular end and its depth includes that tip, so depth must also exceed half the width. A flange spanning the whole edge does not need endpoint relief. A tear would slit the bend zone through the thickness without removing material. The chart solid and flat pattern do not currently support this construction. New bend relief definitions use a rectangular or round slot. A saved bend tear keeps its original rectangular slot, width, depth and curve references, with a warning. It can be edited in place or changed to a supported shape.

Hem forms of a flange (mitcad#1378, mitcad#2112). An optional "hem" makes the flange a hem whose bends follow from its sizes: {"form":"teardrop", "gap":g}, {"form":"rope","gap":g} or {"form":"double","gap":g, "setback":s} (parameter slots hem.gap, hem.setback), and flat, open and rolled (below). The flange’s length is then the hem’s length L, measured from the plane touching the first bend’s outer surface normal to the panel (the length mode must be outer_tangent), its radius (or the rule’s) the inside radius r of every bend, and its angle gives only the side it folds to (its sign); t is the thickness, a = r + t.

  • teardrop: one bend of pi + alpha and a straight wall coming back towards the panel: the inner corner of the wall’s end lies g above the panel and its outer corner at L, i.e. s sin(alpha) = r (1 + cos(alpha)) - g and s cos(alpha) = L - a (1 + sin(alpha)) for the wall s. The radius must be more than half the gap and L > 2 a.
  • rope: a bend of pi + alpha with cos(alpha) = (g + t) / (2 r + t), at once a bend of alpha the other way, then a wall g above the panel, parallel to it, of L - a - (2 r + t) sin(alpha) (not negative). The radius must be more than half the gap.
  • double: the wall folded back over itself: 90 degrees, a wall of g + t, 90 degrees, a wall of L - 2 a over the panel, 180 degrees and a wall of L - a - t - s back under it, ending s short of the first wall.

The forms of the Hem command (mitcad#2112) fold in one bend and set its radius themselves (the flange’s radius is not used):

  • flat: {"form":"flat"} or {"form":"flat","gap":g}, one bend of 180 degrees whose inside radius is half the gap and a wall of L - g/2 - t back over the panel. The gap is the smallest the model builds, 0.1 times the thickness unless typed.
  • open: {"form":"open","gap":g}, the same with its gap.
  • rolled: {"form":"rolled","angle":a,"radius":r} (radius optional: else the flange’s, else the rule’s), one bend of a, more than 180 degrees and less than a full turn, and no wall; the flange’s length and its mode are not used. Parameter slots hem.angle (an angle) and hem.radius.

They give the bends and walls of the flanges the imports made of these hems before: a flat or open hem the flange of 180 degrees whose inside radius is half its gap, its length from the outer tangent; a rolled hem the flange of its angle with a length of 0 from the tangent line (one of 180 degrees or less stays that flange). The imports write these forms, so that an edit shows the hem. Refused in words, the wall of the hem’s edge painted on hover (the refusal’s place): a gap of 0, a length short of the bend’s outer radius (an open hem's length must be at least its bend's outer radius, 3.0000 mm), a rolled angle of 180 degrees or less or a full turn, a radius of 0, an edge that is not straight (A hem goes only on a straight edge of the sheet.); likewise the teardrop’s and rope’s radius not more than half the gap and the lengths of the forms above.

{"type":"sheet_flange","body":"F3.b0",
 "boundary":{"panel":{"feature":"F3","slot":0},
 "curve":{"type":"sketch","sketch":"F2","segment":"c2[c1,c3]"}},
 "angle":3.141592653589793,"length":{"mode":"outer_tangent","value":0},
 "position":"side_tangent","hem":{"form":"rolled","angle":"270 deg","radius":3}}

Each bend is a bend of the flange (bend slots 0, 1, …; strip curves 40 + 100 k), each wall a panel of it (panel slot k; its root curve 53 + 100 k, its far end 51 + 100 k); a bend followed at once by the next (the rope’s) or by no wall joins it directly. Offsets apply; a width past the boundary needs a flange of one bend and a wall.

{"type":"sheet_flange","body":"F3.b0",
 "boundary":{"panel":{"feature":"F3","slot":0},
 "curve":{"type":"sketch","sketch":"F2","segment":"c2[c1,c3]"}},
 "angle":3.141592653589793,"length":{"mode":"outer_tangent","value":25},
 "position":"side_tangent","hem":{"form":"teardrop","gap":2}}
{"type":"sheet_bend","body":"F3.b0","moving_body":"F5.b0",
 "stationary":{"panel":{"feature":"F3","slot":0},
 "curve":{"type":"sketch","sketch":"F2","segment":"c2[c1,c3]"}},
 "moving":{"panel":{"feature":"F5","slot":0},
 "curve":{"type":"sketch","sketch":"F4","segment":"c4[c3,c1]"}},
 "angle":1.5707963267948966,"port_mode":"tangent_ports"}

Omitted moving_body means body. On one body, virtual_sharp inserts the finite allowance strip at a full shared coplanar seam and moves the unique detachable branch. Separate bodies use tangent_ports: their already placed full-span ports must agree with the requested radius, angle and material sides. Both bodies must have the same owner and the same rule reference. Success keeps the stationary BodyUid and consumes the moving body once; failure retains both. An omitted port mode is resolved and persisted from this body relationship. Radius and relief overrides use the Flange forms. Graph cycles, another path to the stationary domain, incompatible ports or insufficient material fail.

{"type":"sheet_bend","body":"F3.b0","moving_body":"F5.b0",
 "stationary":{"panel":{"feature":"F3","slot":0},
 "curve":{"type":"sketch","sketch":"F2","segment":"c2[c1,c3]"}},
 "moving":{"panel":{"feature":"F5","slot":0},
 "curve":{"type":"sketch","sketch":"F4","segment":"c4[c3,c1]"}},
 "angle":0.7853981633974483,"port_mode":"double","fixed":"stationary"}

Port mode double (mitcad#280) joins two parallel panels of separate bodies by a jog: two opposite bends of |angle| each (more than 0, at most 90 degrees, inside radius radius or the rule’s) and a straight panel between them. The two straight boundaries face each other (their panels’ material on either side, outward directions opposite), cover the same axial interval and their panels lie in parallel planes h apart. The first bend starts on the fixed boundary (stationary, the default, or moving), whose panel keeps all its material, and turns towards the other panel’s plane; with the middle radius rm = r + t/2 the straight between the bends is (h - 2 rm (1 - cos angle)) / sin angle long and the second bend ends 2 rm sin angle + straight cos angle from the fixed boundary, where the other panel is cut back to (through the bends seamed to it along the cut, developed, as a flange’s trim does). A straight that would be zero or negative (the panels too close for the bends), a second bend ending short of the other panel, boundaries of different extent and panels in one plane are refused. A moving body whose front surface lies on the other side of the stationary body’s takes the stationary body’s front and back (its charts keep their material coordinates; a moving body with bends of its own is then refused). The jog’s panel is {feature, slot 0}, its bends slots 0 and 1 of the feature. Between panels of one body the jog would close a loop of material, which the sheet model does not develop: refused. Unfold, Refold and the Flat Pattern develop the jog like any other bends.

A mirror or pattern of a face that made new sheet bodies (a sheet_face without body, alone in its objects) copies each of those bodies as a new sheet body of the pattern (F<pattern>.b<k>), its panels moved by the element’s transform (a mirror turns the material’s side with the planes) and renamed as the pattern’s, slots offset by 100000 per copy, rebuilt from the moved panels (mitcad#280). A pattern whose copies are all of one straight sheet_cut cuts the copies clear of the bends’ seams in one operation and the others one by one after them (mitcad#288): the same result as one copy after another.

{"type":"sheet_fold","body":"F3.b0","panel":{"feature":"F3","slot":0},
 "line":{"sketch":"F4","curve":"c1"},"stationary_side":"left",
 "angle":1.5707963267948966,"position":"bend_line",
 "relief":{"type":"round","width":2,"depth":3}}

Fold requires a directed straight sketch line on the selected panel’s front or back surface (the back surface since mitcad#280: the line lies across the thickness at the same place). stationary_side is explicitly left or right relative to that line. The selected finite interval divides the panel into stationary material, a finite allowance strip and moving material. Interior endpoints use the same explicit relief policy. Existing connected bends move rigidly with their branch; their original sign, radius and material parity remain unchanged. The line may cross holes and cut windows of the panel (mitcad#288): the bend’s two lines then run through material in stretches, each stretch its own piece of the generated curve (numbered along the bend’s axis) with a seam of its own, and the bend’s strip keeps the openings. The line may also cross edges at angles other than 90 degrees, or run past the outline (mitcad#1424): the bend’s strip is bounded by the outline (the crossed edges continued across the strip), so its two tangent lines can end at different places along the line, and each seam covers the part of its line that has material. An end of the line that lies on the outline or past it gets no relief; where an edge oblique to the line carries material past that end within the bend’s reach (the line drawn exactly from edge to edge of a trapezoid), the bend and the moving panel run on past the end, so the whole side folds and its edges stay straight across the strip. The flat pattern of such a fold is the outline it was folded from. A seam that still cannot pair is refused with the bend’s name and the boundary curve where the two sides of the seam part. A fold whose two sides an earlier bend also joins (a first fold whose line crossed both arms of a U- or V-shaped panel, then a fold between the arms) cannot turn one half of that bend and keep the other: it is refused naming the earlier feature as the browser shows it and what to do instead (mitcad#1442), e.g. “This fold would also have to bend SheetFold1, whose bend joins both sides of the fold line. Fold here before SheetFold1, or make SheetFold1 with a separate line on each side.” A sheet_bend whose moving panel such a bend joins to the stationary one is refused the same way.

{"type":"sheet_corner_chamfer","body":"F3.b0",
 "corners":[{"panel":{"feature":"F3","slot":0},
 "incoming":{"type":"sketch","sketch":"F2","segment":"c1[c4,c2]"},
 "outgoing":{"type":"sketch","sketch":"F2","segment":"c2[c1,c3]"}}],
 "distances":{"first":2,"second":3}}

sheet_corner_round uses the same corners and radius instead of distances. Incoming/outgoing follow the directed material contour and meet at one vertex; the first chamfer distance measures away from the vertex along incoming, the second along outgoing. Optional incoming_piece/outgoing_piece disambiguate source pieces. These operations require straight adjacent boundaries. A corner beside a bend (mitcad#1765), where one boundary is the panel’s tangent line to a bend (a wall’s side or a face’s side meeting the bend line at another angle than 90 degrees), is a corner of the developed outline: the bend is opened into the panel’s plane, the corner is the one between the panel’s other boundary and the bend’s side, and the round or bevel is removed from every chart in that plane as sheet_cut removes regions; the bend then folds again. The bend’s side (and the side of the panel beyond the bend, where it runs on in line) is trimmed with the panel’s, and the Flat Pattern has the rounded outline. It is refused in words when it is larger than that straight side allows (The corner beside the bend is larger than the bend's straight side allows; make it smaller.), for an inside corner (it would add material across the bend), between two bends (Corner Relief’s), where the bend’s side is not straight there, and where it would remove a whole wall or bend. Other tangent-port corners (a seam between coplanar panels) are rejected. A corner may take a whole adjacent boundary, to its far vertex (mitcad#242); a longer one is refused, unless the contour continues on an arc beyond it: then a round takes that side whole and is tangent to the arc (mitcad#280). All corners of one feature are found on its input sheet. Convex corners remove material; concave hole corners add the bounded wedge and reduce the void. Oversized, degenerate or ambiguous corners fail. Saved corner_slots retain removed selections as tombstones, so reordering or readding a corner does not change its provenance.

sheet_state keeps its reference-frame panels projection and additionally reports authoritative charts, bends, joins, opened and curve lineage. Charts have a tagged panel/bend domain ID, exact bounded material curves and a plane or cylinder embedding. Plane front_to_back_sign is positive or negative; this is independent of chart winding and remains explicit when a bend is opened by the geometry primitives. A failed or disconnected folded result publishes no partial pieces and blocks only the intended input sheets.

Walls of one sheet that meet (mitcad#1409)

A flange (or another folded feature) whose walls meet walls of the same sheet that no bend joins them to is built only where they touch along a line or at a point: a full open corner, the closing wall’s end on the corner line of the other wall at the exact inside dimension, is accepted as it is, neither fused nor its faces merged. Walls that touch over a face (a half open corner) are refused, sheet walls SheetFlange1 and SheetFlange3 touch over a face, which a sheet body cannot hold: leave a seam gap between them; walls that pass into each other (more than 1e-6 mm deep) are refused, sheet walls SheetFlange1 and SheetFlange3 pass through each other. A wall is named by its feature, a further wall of it SheetFlange3 (wall 2), a bend SheetFlange1 (bend). No clearance is added. See the sheet-metal contract.

Corner joints of a closing flange (mitcad#1410)

A sheet_flange whose wall closes against another wall of the same sheet (the last side of a box section) takes corner, the joint the two walls make: "open" or "half_open" (left out: the wall’s end is free; the list is open for further joints). With a corner the flange’s length is the inside dimension of the closed section, measured by "mode": "inner" (other modes, and a hem with it, are refused), and the joint sets the wall’s end from the sheet’s thickness t:

  • open: the wall ends on the other wall’s inner surface, the two walls meeting only along the corner line (a full open corner, whose outer V is welded); the body holds them as they are (mitcad#1409).
  • half_open: the wall reaches t / 2 further, over half of the other wall’s end. Walls that touch over a face do not make one sound body, so the other wall is cut back by a seam of 0.00001 mm (10 nm) where the wall lies over it (its new end the flange’s generated curves 60 to 63); that seam is the only clearance. It is the smallest seam that is a gap at all, ten times the 1e-6 mm modelling tolerance: the check of mitcad#1409 accepts walls 0.0000005 mm apart and refuses them at 0.0000001 mm, and gaps from 0.000001 mm to 0.01 mm all gave a valid body, a cut through the corner and a hole. The other wall is the flat wall normal to the flange’s wall whose material lies under the wall’s last t / 2 and whose end lies on its surface; none, or more than one, refuses the flange.
{"type":"sheet_flange","body":"F3.b0",
 "boundary":{"panel":{"feature":"F5","slot":0},"curve":{"type":"generated","feature":"F5","slot":51}},
 "angle":1.5707963267948966,"length":{"mode":"inner","value":10},"position":"outside",
 "corner":"half_open"}

On a 1 mm sheet with Outside flanges of Inner Length 10 on both long edges of a 10 mm wide base, this third flange closes the 10 x 10 section: its wall reaches 0.5 mm over the first wall’s end, and the first wall ends 0.00001 mm under it; the inside stays 10 x 10. The Flat Pattern keeps the two walls at the strip’s two ends.

A flange’s profile sketch (mitcad#1648)

A sheet_flange may take profile, a sketch before it whose closed region on the bend line is the wall’s outline instead of the rectangle of length, offsets and width (GitHub mitcad/Mitcad#237). The sketch is read in the wall’s own sketch frame: its origin on the wall’s root line (the bend’s moving tangent line) at the middle of the selected boundary, x along that line (against the boundary’s canonical axial direction e) and y along the wall away from the bend, on the wall’s front surface. Its x axis is the bend line:

  • the wall is the one region of the sketch with a straight side on the bend line and its material above it (holes in it stay holes; regions away from the line are not used). That side, drawn by one line or by several in a row, is the bend’s span: it lies within the boundary (from -L/2 to L/2 for a boundary L long), and the flange’s offsets are where it leaves the boundary free, with the reliefs a flange with offsets gets;
  • the rest of the outline may slant, taper, curve (lines, arcs, circles, ellipses and splines) or pass the boundary’s ends beside the bend (an overhang, as a width from the middle makes one; it starts at the bend’s moving tangent line);
  • the outline’s curves name the wall’s edges ({"type":"sketch", "sketch":"F5","segment":…}), its side on the bend line is the flange’s generated curve 53, as the rectangular wall’s root.

The flange keeps one bend: a profile takes no offsets, width, hem or corner (refused in words), and its length is not used. A region across the bend line, none or more than one with a side on it, a side on the line in more than one place, or one past the boundary’s ends is refused in words without ids, as The flange's profile crosses the bend line; the wall's outline must stay on the wall's side of it. Editing the sketch updates the flange, Unfold and the Flat Pattern; the profile’s 2D outline is used wherever the sketch lies.

The profile sketch’s plane follows the wall (mitcad#1776, GitHub mitcad/Mitcad#310): sheet_flange_profile puts it on a construction plane of the type flange_wall, which is the wall’s sketch frame above, worked out again at every recompute from the sheet before the plane and the boundary, angle, radius and position of the flange whose profile is a sketch on it (the first such flange in the timeline). After the sheet’s edge moves (a base sketch’s dimension changed) or the flange’s angle, radius or position changes, the sketch lies on the wall when it is opened and shown; its curves stay where they are in the wall’s frame. Until a flange names the sketch (while a new flange’s profile is drawn) the plane is the frame stored with it. A design from an earlier version whose profile sketch lies on a fixed construction plane of its own (one no other feature refers to) gets the flange_wall plane when it is opened, with the same frame, so nothing moves in the wall’s frame. A flange whose sketch the user put on another plane, and that no longer lies on its wall, warns The flange's profile sketch no longer lies on its wall; Edit Profile in the Flange panel puts it back there.

{"cmd":"sheet_flange_profile",
 "def":{"type":"sheet_flange","body":"F3.b0",
 "boundary":{"panel":{"feature":"F3","slot":0},
 "curve":{"type":"sketch","sketch":"F2","segment":"c2[c1,c3]"}},
 "angle":1.5707963267948966,"length":{"mode":"tangent","value":15},
 "position":"inside"}}

sheet_flange_profile makes a flange’s profile sketch from its definition def (as add_feature takes it; its values may be expressions), read against the sheet at the timeline marker (while a Flange is edited the marker stands just before it): a hidden flange_wall construction plane on the wall and a sketch on it (Plane1, Sketch2), both at the marker, before the flange, in one undo step Add Sketch2 as a flange's profile. The sketch holds the wall the flange’s length and width give now: a rectangle over the part of the boundary the bend covers (an overhang past the boundary’s ends is left to the sketch), its two corners on the bend line fixed there, its sides vertical, its far side horizontal and its length along the wall a dimension (a flange without a wall starts with 10 mm). For a def that has a profile already, the command makes that profile’s plane a flange_wall plane (a fixed plane of an earlier design) with its stored frame where the definition’s angle, radius and position put the wall (Move Plane1 onto the flange's wall; nothing when it is such a plane there already; a sketch that is not on a fixed or flange_wall plane of its own is refused). Once the flange is in the timeline, the plane follows the flange as it is there. It answers {"sketch":"F5","plane":"F4","added":2} (added: the features it put before the flange, 0 when it moved the plane). The flange then names the sketch: "profile":"F5".

A flange along a straight run (mitcad#2117)

"run": true on a sheet_flange of one edge makes its edge the straight run of its boundary: the boundary and the boundaries before and after it in its loop that continue it in a line and are joined to no other domain (a face over collinear sketch lines has a wall per line). The flange is then one bend and one wall along the whole run, its offsets and width measured along the run (a width from the run’s middle), the face cut back along all of it, as on a body whose edge there is one (the .f3d import’s flange on such an edge). A run that is the boundary alone is the plain flange. It is refused with boundaries, a corner gap or miters, a profile, and at position edge (the bend needs a setback line to cut back to). Left out it is false and not written.

"relieve_ends": true (mitcad#2117) gives a flange over its whole boundary (no offsets, width or profile) the bend relief at each end where the panel goes on along the bend line (the outline turns away from the material there, a concave corner, or goes on straight past the end): that end is an offset end of the relief’s width, the relief cut there as at any offset end, so the bend never meets unbent material. Ends at convex corners stay whole. The .f3d import sets it on its edge flanges (their bend relief). Left out it is false and not written.

A flange on several edges (mitcad#1872)

A sheet_flange may take boundaries, further straight boundaries after boundary (GitHub mitcad/Mitcad#337): one wall on each edge, all with the flange’s angle, length, position, radius and relief. Edge k (0 is boundary) has the flange’s bend slot k and wall panel slot k, its curves numbered from 100 k as a single flange’s (the bend’s strip 40 to 43, the wall’s sides 50, 52, far end 51, root on the bend 53). The edges are connected at their ends, at a common corner of a face or across the side of a bend between two faces (one end on each of its tangent lines, at the same place along it), also on faces turned differently, or across a corner gap the sheet records (mitcad#2098, GitHub mitcad/Mitcad#480); they make one chain or a closed loop. Edges that meet none of the others, more than two at one corner, or edges that leave a corner the same way are refused in words.

Corner gaps. The sheet’s state records each corner gap (gaps in the sheet_state query: the two panels, panels; the corner’s line, line; the gap, width): Convert to Sheet Metal one at each rip (the rip’s edge), a flange on several edges one at each corner between its walls (the line in the corner’s bisecting plane along the walls from where their roots meet). Two edge ends on the two panels of a recorded gap face each other across it when both lie at the same place along its line, neither further from it than the gap and twice the thickness: they are one corner, its point (for a refusal’s places and the sheet_flange_corners query) where the two edges’ lines come closest. So the rim edges of a converted tray, or of a tray whose walls are a flange on several edges, take one flange whose walls meet mitred at the corners. A gap is never guessed from the ends’ distance: ends of panels with no recorded gap between them meet only as above. A state without gaps (from before them) reads as one with none; a design saved before them records them when it is recomputed, its geometry unchanged.

Where two edges meet, their walls are mitred. Sheet walls are cut normal to their surfaces, as a laser cuts them, so a miter is a straight cut of each wall where a plane meets the surface of it that reaches further:

  • "miter": "bisect" (the default): the plane bisecting the corner, the one through the walls’ root lines (where the two lines in the middle of the walls’ thickness come closest) normal to the difference of the two edges’ directions away from the corner. Each flange stays on its side, corner_gap / 2 off it: its wall is cut there, and its bend ends square where all its material clears the plane. Two walls at an angle then meet at most along a line with a gap of 0 (an open corner); two walls in one plane (flanges on the sides of two faces that a bend joins, both turned to the inside of that bend) meet exactly on the bisecting line and need a gap above 0.
  • "earlier_runs_past" / "later_runs_past": the wall of the edge earlier (later) in the list runs on to the other wall’s outer surface and the other wall ends corner_gap short of the passing wall’s inner surface; both bends end at the bisecting plane as above. Not for walls in one plane, and the gap must be above 0 (walls that touch over a face make no sound body, mitcad#1409).
  • corner_miters, [{"edges": [0, 1], "miter": "later_runs_past"}], sets one corner’s miter in place of miter.

corner_gap (a length, expression allowed) is the gap at the corners; left out it is the sheet’s thickness. Where a corner shortens a bend, the face beside it is cut back to the bend’s tangent line up to the edge’s end (generated curves 70 to 73 at the edge’s start and 80 to 83 at its end, plus 100 k), across a bend there as a flange’s trim goes on through it (mitcad#211); the wall runs on past its bend’s end (its root there free: curves 55 before, 56 after the bend) to the miter, also beyond the edge’s end where the corner lets it (a hopper’s walls leaning outward), the miter’s edge the curve 58 at the edge’s start and 59 at its end. A free end of the flange that meets an existing flange of the sheet across a bend ends corner_gap short of that flange’s wall, which is never cut (mitcad#1877); a single-edge flange with corner_gap does the same.
