reverse_normal 

{"type": "reverse_normal", "body": "F3.b0", "faces": []}

The surface body’s faces in faces (every face when left out) turned over: their normals point the other way, which decides the side thicken, offset_surface and the ruled surface’s normal mode go to. The body and the faces keep their names. A solid is refused (its normals point out of its material).

Chains of edges

Blend Surface, Boundary Surface and Match Surface take chains of a body’s edges: body, named edges and free edges of openings (Free edges) that join end to end into one chain (open or closed), and face (target_face for a match), the face beside the chain where an edge lies between two faces (else each edge’s one face; needed for G1 and G2 only). The body may be a surface body or a solid; it is not changed unless the feature says so.

blend_surface 

{"type": "blend_surface",
 "from": {"body": "F2.b0", "openings": [{"opening": {"faces": ["F2:side(c1)"]}, "at": [[10, 0, 5]]}],
 "continuity": "g1", "bulge": 0},
 "to": {"body": "F4.b0", "edges": ["E{F4:bottom|F4:side0}"], "face": "F4:side0", "continuity": "g2"},
 "stitch": false}

A new surface body of one face <feature>:blend bridging the chains from and to (both open or both closed; a closed pair starts the second where it is nearest the first’s start). Each end leaves its chain through the edges (g0: straight towards the other end), tangent to the face beside it (g1, the default) or also curved as it (g2), with a speed of the chord between the chains times 1 + bulge (bulge 0 the plain bridge, more fuller, down to -0.9 flatter). The chains are sampled by length (about a station a millimetre, 16 to 200) and the surface, cubic across (quintic with a g2 end), is fitted through the stations: its edges lie within a few micrometres of the chains. With stitch the blend is sewn onto both bodies within 0.01 mm, into from’s body, which keeps its id; to’s body (when another) is consumed and no new body is made.

boundary_surface 

{"type": "boundary_surface", "boundary": [
 {"sketch": "F1", "curves": ["c1", "c2"], "continuity": "g1"},
 {"body": "F3.b0", "openings": [{"opening": {"faces": ["F3:side(c1)"]}}], "continuity": "g1"}]}
{"type": "boundary_surface", "u": [{"sketch": "F1", "curves": ["c1"]}, {"point": [5, 5, 10]}]}
{"type": "boundary_surface", "u": [{"sketch": "F1", "curves": ["c1"]}, {"sketch": "F1", "curves": ["c3"]}],
 "v": [{"sketch": "F1", "curves": ["c2"]}, {"sketch": "F1", "curves": ["c4"]}]}

A new surface body of one face <feature>:boundary. Each curve is a chain of sketch curves (sketch, curves, chain), a chain of edges (Chains of edges) or a point, one of them.

  • boundary: a closed loop of curves in order (one closed chain, or chains end to end), filled (BRepOffsetAPI_MakeFilling). Each meets the face beside its edges, or along sketch curves the sketch’s plane, with its continuity (g0, the default, g1, g2). No points. See A loop through several sketches.
  • u (two or more) and v (none, or two or more): a network. Without v the surface is lofted through u in order, the first or the last of which may be a point (a cone-like patch); with v it runs through every curve each way (GeomFill_Gordon: a Coons patch of two each way), every u crossing every v. No continuity, no points.
  • Refused: both forms, a curve of none or several kinds, a point in a loop or among crossing curves, one crossing curve.

match_surface 

{"type": "match_surface", "body": "F5.b0", "face": "F5:side(c1)", "target": "F7.b0",
 "edges": ["E{F7:bottom|F7:side2}"], "target_face": "F7:side2", "continuity": "g2"}

A face of a surface body (face; left out: the body’s only face) rebuilt against a chain of target’s edges (another body): the side of the face nearest the chain moves onto it, meeting the face beside the chain through it (g0), tangent (g1) or also curved as it (g2, the default), while the opposite side stays where it was. The face is resampled with the changes fading across it (quintic blends, no change at the opposite side) and fitted again, its slopes across held at both sides. The face must be bounded by its surface’s parameter range alone (four sides, no holes; unsupported: … otherwise); a closed chain is not supported. The body keeps its id and the face its name; its faces are sewn again within 0.001 mm (neighbours along the moved sides come apart). A solid is refused.

fair_surface 

{"type": "fair_surface", "body": "F6.b0", "faces": ["F6:boundary"], "strength": 1, "iterations": 1,
 "keep_edges": true, "tolerance": 0.1}

The B-spline faces among faces (every face when left out) smoothed: each step moves the inner control points strength (more than 0, at most 1) of a damped bi-Laplacian step towards a net of less bending, for iterations steps (1 to 1000), none farther than tolerance (a parameter, mm, more than 0) from where it was. The boundary row of control points stays, so the faces keep meeting their neighbours; with keep_edges (the default) the row next to it stays too, so they keep their tangents there. Faces of other surface types are fair already and stay as they are; a faired face must be bounded by its surface’s parameter range alone. The body keeps its id and the faces their names. A solid is refused.

The .solidcraft import maps SolidCraft’s surface blend, boundary patch, network, match and fair to these (core/import-solidcraft/docs/solidcraft.md).

Tests (surface modelling): core/model-tests/features-solid/src/surface_modelling_tests.rs (mock kernel), geometry/tests/test_surface_modelling.cpp (geometry.surface_modelling, the input check on), the .solidcraft test designs surface-* (cli.import_solidcraft, areas and boxes through the OCCT kernel), core/import-solidcraft/src/tests.rs, tools/ui-surface-test.sh and tools/ui-surface-fill-test.sh (the SURFACE group on a hidden display).

Plastic part features

Molded plastic parts’ features (mitcad#459, core/model/src/features/plastic.rs): a Boss, a Lip, a Groove, a Snap Fit and a Rest, each on a face of one body which it joins (a groove cuts it), and the plastic rules they take their defaults from. The application’s Plastic Feature panel makes them all (app/COMMANDS.md).

A boss, a snap fit and a rest stand on point of face of body: put on the face’s plane for a planar face, else the face’s point nearest to it. They grow along direction ([x, y, z]; default: out of the face). The tools start a little inside the material (5 % of their height, 0.001 to 0.5 mm) so that they overlap the body; sizes are measured at the face, and a draft (draft_angle, radians or an angle expression) narrows the walls from there. Values left out take the defaults below.

plastic_rule 

{"type": "plastic_rule", "rule_name": "ABS (1.5mm)", "material": "ABS Plastic",
 "thickness": 1.5, "draft_angle": "2 deg", "clearance": 0.1, "min_thickness": 1.2,
 "max_thickness": 3.5}

A molded part’s design values; it changes no body. thickness is the nominal wall; nominal_radius (default half the thickness), clearance (0.1 mm), knife_edge (1 mm), reveal_height (0.5 mm), thickness_variation (0.15 times the thickness), draft_angle (2 degrees), min_draft_angle (0.5 degrees), min_thickness and max_thickness (no limit without). A boss, rest or groove names one by its uid in rule: a left-out draft_angle of a boss or rest and a left-out gap of a groove are the rule’s draft and clearance, and the feature warns when its draft is below the rule’s min_draft_angle, or a wall (a boss’s around its hole, a hollow rest’s) is outside the rule’s thicknesses. A suppressed rule is not used (a warning says so); a failed one fails the features that name it. Refused: a thickness not above 0, negative values, drafts of 85 degrees or more, a smallest thickness above the largest.

boss 

{"type": "boss", "body": "F1.b0", "face": "F1:top", "point": [30, 30, 3],
 "diameter": 10, "height": 12, "hole_diameter": 4, "hole_depth": 10,
 "draft_angle": "1 deg", "fillet": 1, "ribs": 4, "rib_thickness": 1.5,
 "rib_length": 6, "rib_offset": 2, "rule": "F2"}

A round post diameter across at the face, height high, narrowing by its draft (default the rule’s, else none). ribs (0 to 64, rounded; a count in a length slot, as pattern quantities) stand round it from half its radius out to rib_length past its wall (default its radius), rib_thickness thick (default 0.3 times its radius), their tops rib_offset below its top; the first along the direction × X (× Y for a direction near X: +Y on a face facing up). fillet rounds the root where the post meets the face (the post’s wall only). The hole of hole_diameter runs hole_depth down from the top (default: to the face), straight. Faces: the post side(c1) and its top end(r{c1}), rib k’s sides side(c<10+4k>…), the hole’s wall side(c2) and its bottom start(r{c2}), the root’s rounds fillet(<edge>). Refused: a draft that closes the post before its top, a hole not inside the top. A boss cannot be patterned or mirrored (its hole cuts after its post joins).

lip, groove 

{"type": "lip", "body": "F17.b0", "face": "F18:offset_cap(F17:top)", "width": 1, "height": 2}
{"type": "groove", "body": "F20.b0", "face": "F21:offset_cap(F20:top)", "width": 1,
 "depth": 2, "gap": 0.1, "outside": true, "rule": "F2"}

A band along a planar rim face: along its largest opening (an inner loop with no material over the face just inside it: the open end of a shelled body), or along its outer edge with outside. A lip raises the band width into the face and height up. A groove cuts it width + gap into the face and depth + gap down, gap defaulting to the rule’s clearance (else 0), the cutter reaching as far past the edge so that none of its walls lies on the body’s. Corners stay sharp; lines and arcs stay lines and arcs. Faces (Kernel::rim_band): band_side(<edge>) along the offset into the face and band_edge(<edge>) along the face’s edge they follow, band_top and band_bottom. Refused: a face that is not planar, one with no inner loop, one whose inner loops are the feet of features standing on it (“not an opening”), one with two openings alike in size (the second more than half the first’s area), a band that does not fit.

snap_fit 

{"type": "snap_fit", "body": "F15.b0", "face": "F15:top", "point": [20, 20, 4],
 "hook": [1, 0, 0], "length": 15, "thickness": 1.5, "width": 6,
 "catch_depth": 1, "catch_length": 3}

A cantilever arm thickness across (away from hook), width wide (centred on the point) and length up from the face, its face on the hook’s side on the point; the catch at its tip sticks out catch_depth towards hook (across the direction) over catch_length (shorter than the arm), a triangle from its foot out to the tip. Faces side(c1) … side(c6) round its side profile (c1 the arm’s foot, c2 its face on the hook’s side, c3 and c4 the catch, c5 the tip, c6 its back), its ends start(…) and end(…). It can be patterned and mirrored.

rest 

{"type": "rest", "body": "F10.b0", "face": "F10:top", "point": [430, 30, 3],
 "along": [1, 0, 0], "width": 10, "length": 20, "height": 4,
 "draft_angle": "2 deg", "thickness": 1, "rule": "F2"}

A pad centred on the point: round (width the diameter) or, with length, a rectangle length along along (default the direction × X, as a boss’s first rib) and width across; height high, narrowing by its draft (default the rule’s, else none), solid or with thickness a wall (thinner than half its width). Faces: its walls side(c1) … side(c4) (round: side(c1)), its hollow’s side(c5) … (side(c2)), its top end(…). Refused: a draft that closes it (or its wall) before its top. It can be patterned and mirrored.

Tests: core/model-tests/parts/src/plastic_tests.rs (mock kernel), cli.plastic (tools/cli/tests/plastic.json: analytic volumes, round rims, the rules’ defaults and warnings, refusals), the .solidcraft test design plastic (cli.import_solidcraft) and tools/ui-plastic-test.sh.

Body transfers

A body_transfer feature (mitcad#465, features/body_transfer.rs) moves bodies of another component into its own component, an existing one, at its point of the timeline. Moving features into components moves the features that made the bodies, as if they had been made in the destination; Create Components from Bodies makes a new component of each body. A body transfer moves only the bodies, from where it is on the timeline:

{"type": "body_transfer", "bodies": ["F2.b0"],
 "link": {"source": "", "target": "O1"}}
{"type": "body_transfer", "bodies": ["F5.b0"],
 "link": {"source": "O2", "target": ""},
 "transform": [[0, -1, 0, 0], [1, 0, 0, 30], [0, 0, 1, 0]]}
  • The feature belongs to the destination. bodies are all of one other component at that point (the source), each named by its id.
  • The bodies keep their ids, display names, attributes (appearance, material, visibility) and the topological names of their faces; their geometry is converted once from the source’s coordinates into the destination’s, so that they stay where they are in the design. From then on they are the destination’s: its later features work on them (in its coordinates), the source’s no longer see them (body F2.b0 (from Extrude1) belongs to Bracket; a feature works on the bodies of its own component), and a later Move of the destination’s occurrence takes them along. A sheet-metal body keeps its sheet state, moved with it.
  • link says where both components are seen, as the links of Geometry of other components: the occurrence path to the source (source) and to the destination (target, the first path to it when it does not lead there); empty paths are the root. The conversion is placement(target)⁻¹ · placement(source) at the feature’s point, so the bodies stay in place when placements before it change. transform (optional; rows of a rotation and a translation) is a fixed conversion used instead, as an import keeps the one its file records.
  • Fails (as features do, with the reason) when a body is not the source’s at that point, the source is the feature’s own component, or the conversion is not rigid. Moves of features, reparented components and copies follow the link like the other links; Paste New and Make Unique copy or refuse a component that takes bodies in as they do one made from bodies (its bodies, as a base feature, are copied).
Command Fields Result
transfer_bodies bodies, source_occurrence (optional: where they are seen, the first path to their component by default), destination: {"component": "C2" or a name, "occurrence": "O2/O4"} (the occurrence path optional, as source_occurrence), name (optional) uid, name, component, component_name, bodies

transfer_bodies adds the feature at the marker in the destination, one undo step Move Body1 into Bracket (Move 2 bodies into Bracket). Refused, changing nothing, when the bodies are not of one component at the marker, the destination is their component, a linked component or a library part, the policy refuses it, or the transfer (or a feature that worked before) would fail. Features after the marker are not computed: one of the source that works on a moved body later fails when the marker passes it, with the reason above.

Query Fields Result
transfer_bodies bodies, source_occurrence component, name (the bodies’ component), source_occurrence, bodies (uid, name), destinations: every placed component by occurrence path, the root first, as move_to_component’s rows (component, name, occurrence, path, parent_occurrence, eligible, reason)

The .solidcraft import maps SolidCraft’s body transfers onto it (the file’s feature is in its destination already): the link from the components’ first placements, and the conversion the file records as transform only where the placements give another (.solidcraft import). The .f3d import translates a cut and paste of bodies into another component as this feature where Move to Component cannot take the features that made them (core/import/docs/f3d-undecoded.md, Copies and cut and paste of bodies). Tests: core/model-tests/assembly/src/body_transfer_tests.rs, cli.import_solidcraft (core/solidcraft/tests/designs/body-transfer.solidcraft.json), mitcad-import’s a_cut_and_paste_whose_features_cannot_go_transfers_the_body.

Drawings

export_drawing (mitcad#471, api/drawing.rs, crate::drawing) writes the bodies at the marker as a drawing on a sheet: orthographic views with hidden lines removed, the overall sizes of the views, the diameters of round holes, a hole table with their threads and a title block, as a PDF, SVG, DXF or DWG file. The views come from the kernel (Kernel::project_view: OCCT’s hidden line removal, geometry/include/mitcad/geometry/drawing.hpp), the holes from Kernel::round_holes, their threads from the threads query. A tangent edge is an edge between faces that meet smoothly (normals within 0.001 rad all along it, a fillet’s edges) however the body was made: the projection finds them on a copy of each body before it projects (mitcad#1438; OCCT’s hidden line removal goes by the continuity stored on an edge, which edges made by later fillets, booleans and imports lack, so such edges were drawn as visible edges with tangent_edges false). Seams and edges between faces of one surface are not drawn at all.

{"cmd":"export_drawing","path":"plate.pdf","bodies":["F2.b0"],
 "sheet":"A3","orientation":"landscape","scale":"fit","projection":"third_angle",
 "views":["front","top","right","iso"],"hidden_lines":true,
 "section":{"analysis":"Section1"},"title":"Plate","date":"2026-10-20"}
Field Default What
path the file; its extension (.pdf, .svg, .dxf, .dwg) gives the format
format by the extension pdf, svg, dxf or dwg
bodies the shown bodies uids or names; each where the design shows it (every placement of a component’s body)
sheet A4 A4 … A0 (ISO 216), ANSI_A … ANSI_E
orientation landscape or portrait
scale fit fit: the largest ISO 5455 scale (50:1 … 1:1000) at which the views fit; or "1:2", "2:1", a number (paper per model length)
projection third_angle or first_angle (ISO 5456-2)
views ["front","top","right"] any of front (from -Y), top (from +Z), right (from +X), iso (from the front, right and above); Z is up
section none a section view: {"analysis": "<Section Analysis>"} (where it cuts) or {"origin": [x,y,z], "normal": [x,y,z]}; what lies on the normal’s side goes, the view looks against the normal
hidden_lines false hidden edges dashed (not in the isometric and section views)
tangent_edges false edges between faces that meet smoothly, thin
dimensions true the width and height of each orthographic view, and one callout per hole size (4x Ø6.6 THRU, CBORE Ø11 DEPTH 6.8, a tapped hole by its thread)
sketch_dimensions false the distances, lengths, radii and diameters of the sketches whose plane faces a view square on, in that view
hole_table true the holes each view shows end on, tagged per view (A1, A2, … B1), with X and Y from the view’s lower left corner, size, depth and thread
units the design’s length unit the unit of the values (mm, in, …), and of a DXF file’s coordinates: the sheet in that unit of paper (mitcad#1408, DXF units); with drawing only the DXF file’s unit (each sheet’s own, else the design’s, when left out)
title Untitled the design’s name in the title block
date today (UTC) the date in the title block
per_body false a sheet per body: pages of one PDF, or SVG, DXF and DWG files <name>-2.svg, …
exact true exact edges; false: from a triangulation (quicker on large bodies; also the fallback when the exact projection fails, and for mesh bodies). Views of bodies with free-form faces (not planes, cylinders, cones, spheres or tori), or with many edges on B-splines against many faces (mitcad#1033), come from a triangulation either way, their edges as lines and arcs where they follow them, polylines elsewhere (mitcad#962: exact edges took half a minute a view on modelled threads): within 0.02 mm of the edges on the sheet at the view’s scale (0.1 mm in the model at 1:5), and never farther than 1.5 times a 2000th of the bodies’ size (mitcad#1671). Only those bodies, and the bodies whose outline in the view overlaps theirs, take the triangulation: the others keep the exact edges when they are not slow on their own
drawing none a drawing kept in the design (D1 or its name, Drawings in the design), written as it is: its sheets, views and title blocks; the fields above are then its own and refused, except title (where its sheets have none) and units (a DXF file’s unit)
sheet all with drawing: one sheet’s index (0 the first)

Without drawing the export lays out a temporary drawing from the fields above (api/drawing.rs, auto_drawing: each view a base view in the grid below, the section a section view without a parent) and draws it as a kept one is drawn, so the two give the same file; add_drawing with layout keeps such a drawing in the design (File › Export Drawing).

The sheet (ISO 5457): a frame 20 mm from the left edge and 10 mm from the others, the title block (ISO 7200) at the bottom right with the title, the bodies, the scale, the units, the date, the sheet, the projection method and its symbol; the hole table at the top right. Views go into a grid by the projection method (third angle: the top view above the front view, the right view on its right, the isometric view top right, the section right of the right view; first angle the other way), aligned with each other, each with room for its dimensions; the views are centred in what the title block and the table leave. Lines after ISO 128’s 0.35 series (mitcad#1112; one table, Pen::width in core/model-drawing/src/sheet.rs, for the PDF and SVG writers and the application’s sheet: visible 0.35 mm; dimensions, leaders, tangent edges and a thread’s roots 0.18 mm; hidden edges 0.18 mm dashed, as ISO 128 draws hidden outlines narrow; hatching 0.13 mm; the frame 0.5 mm; the cutting plane 0.18 mm long dash dotted with its arrows and letter); dimensions after ISO 129 (30° closed filled arrowheads, text 3.5 mm above the dimension line, reading from below or from the right); text in Helvetica (sans serif, as ISO 3098). A hole is coaxial cylindrical faces with the material all round outside them: the narrowest is its drilled wall, a wider cylinder or a cone that meets it on the side it opens to its counterbore or countersink; an end is closed when material lies on the axis within twice its diameter beyond it. A view shows a hole end on when it looks along the axis from the side it opens to (a hole open at both ends from either side).

Details smaller than the pen (mitcad#1112, core/model-drawing/src/convention.rs, simplified): lines closer than twice the visible line’s width (0.7 mm on the sheet, ISO 128-20’s least spacing) merge into a blot, so a view is drawn simplified at its scale. A fillet or chamfer whose size on the sheet is below 0.7 mm (an arc of a smaller radius, the polyline or short lines a triangulation made of it, a chamfer’s shorter line, between two other edges) is drawn as a sharp corner: it is left out with the tangent edges that end at it, and the edges on either side are extended to where they meet. A tangent edge that lies within 0.7 mm of other edges all along is left out, and so is any edge shorter than its pen is wide. This works on the projected lines, so the exact and the triangulated views alike; what a click picks on a view is still the view’s own edges.

Threads by ISO 6410 (convention::with_threads): every thread the threads query lists on a body a view shows, modelled or cosmetic (a hole or a shaft with a thread’s designation and no flanks), is drawn by convention instead of its geometry. In a view across its axis the crests (an external thread’s major diameter, an internal one’s minor) are drawn with the visible pen, the roots with the narrow one, and the thread’s end with a visible line across the major diameter where no face ends it; looking along its axis the crest circle is drawn whole and the root circle as a narrow three-quarter arc (open at the upper right). The thread’s own lines (crests, helices, flanks, the curves where its end chamfers cut them) are left out; the faces’ edges across the thread stay (its end faces, a groove’s), and in a pictorial view the circles about its axis. Only lines on the thread’s own surface are left out, not everything of the threaded body that its outline covers (mitcad#1145): across the axis, a straight line goes when both its ends lie on a crest’s or a root’s radius on one side of the axis, and a curve when it runs like a helix (it turns back across the axis only on the thread’s outline, between the root’s and the crest’s radius, and in a view square to the axis runs one way along it); curves that lie on one circle and together go a quarter of the way round or more (a cross hole’s edge, in pieces where the thread’s faces cut it) stay. In a triangulated view, which gives a helix as straight pieces and arcs, a straight piece goes when it starts on a crest’s or a root’s radius or continues the thread’s lines end to end. Looking along the axis, circles (and the spirals where an end chamfer cuts the flanks) from the root’s radius to the crest’s go, and an external thread’s end chamfer circle a thread’s depth inside the minor diameter; a narrower bore below a tapped hole and a flat’s chord stay. So a cross hole, a socket, a flat or a keyway on the threaded body is drawn as the kernel drew it. Only the threaded body’s own lines are left out and replaced: the kernel’s projection records each line’s body (ViewEdge::source, the index of the shape among those projected; OCCT’s hidden-line removal is asked for each shape’s lines on their own), so every other body’s lines (a nut’s bore and faces, a pin in front of the thread) stay as the kernel drew them. Hidden-line removal: each part of the convention’s lines takes, along the axis, the visibility the kernel’s hidden-line removal gave the lines it replaces, so where a nut, a wall or another body hides the thread its lines are hidden (dashed when the view shows hidden edges, else left out); end on, the crest and root circles each take that of the lines near them. A view at an angle to the axis (isometric; ISO 6410 has no pictorial representation, so the simplified one ISO 128 allows there) draws the thread on its cylinder the same way: the crests’ outlines wide, the roots’ narrow, and where no face ends it the thread’s end as the half of its crest circle the eye sees. A taper pipe thread (the query’s taper) is drawn with its crest and root lines following the taper from the diameters where it starts: an external one widens away from its narrow end, an internal one narrows away from its mouth (which end, from the lines it replaces, else from the face that ends it); end on, its circles are those where it starts.

Files: SVG in millimetres (width="420mm"), a <g class="…"> per group: view (id="view-front", view-top, view-right, view-iso, view-section), dimension, sketch-dimension, hole-tag, hole-table, hole-row (id the tag), hole-datum, section-line, view-label, frame, title-block. PDF 1.4, a page per sheet, the standard Helvetica font in WinAnsi encoding (Ø, °), uncompressed. DXF (R2000) in paper of the file’s length unit (units, else the sheet’s, else the design’s: an inch design’s sheet in inches of paper, its texts scaled with it, mitcad#1408), a layer per kind of line: VISIBLE, HIDDEN, THIN, HATCH, SECTION_LINE, FRAME, EXTRA_THICK (lines and arcs drawn with the extra_thick pen, mitcad#1402), lines and arcs drawn by hand with a width and a pattern no pen of before had (mitcad#1447) on HIDDEN_THICK (thick and dashed), HIDDEN_EXTRA_THICK (extra_thick and dashed), SECTION_LINE_THICK (thick and chain) and SECTION_LINE_EXTRA_THICK (extra_thick and chain; a thin dashed one stays on HIDDEN, a thin chain one on SECTION_LINE, a continuous one on THIN, VISIBLE or EXTRA_THICK), and TEXT (the writer has no dashed line types: hidden edges are told apart by their layer; arrowheads are outlines). DWG (R2000, AC1015, mitcad#728; core/model-drawing/src/dwg.rs) holds what the DXF file holds in paper millimetres, on the same layers, written by MitCad’s own writer (core/dwg/src/write.rs, README): lines, arcs, circles and single-line texts (a text of several lines as a text per line) in model space, the sheet as the layout’s paper and limits; texts in code page 1252, other characters as \U+XXXX.

The answer: path, format, files, sheets, pages (of a PDF; 1 otherwise), sheet, orientation, scale ("1:1", of the first sheet) and scales, views (per sheet), bodies and body_names (each body drawn once), placements (mitcad#2147: the placements drawn over the sheets written, each body once per occurrence path that places it: a component placed 100 times adds its bodies once to bodies and 100 times to placements; a laid-out drawing draws each body at every placement the 3D view shows, a hidden occurrence’s left out), dimensions, holes, hole_table_rows, units (of the values), file_units (DXF: the first file’s length unit), polygonal (a view came from a triangulation) and warnings (a view that shows nothing, views that do not fit at the given scale, rows the table had no room for, holes that could not be found). Refused: an unknown format, unit, view or sheet, no views, a listed body that is not at the marker, an unknown Section Analysis, no bodies to draw. File IO (classes.rs); MCP’s model_export writes one with format: "pdf" or "svg" (or "dxf" with drawing), the options in drawing (docs/mcp.md); mitcad-cli export-drawing runs it. Tests: geometry.drawing (the views, section and holes of a counterbored block), core/model-tests/drawing/src/drawing_tests.rs and core/model-tests/drawing/src/dwg_tests.rs, core/model-drawing/src/convention_tests.rs (the line set, details smaller than the pen, threads), core.dwg (the DWG writer), cli.export_drawing, app.ui-windows-drawing.

A laid-out view of an assembly’s top view on a reported design (mitcad#2174, GitHub #527): cli.drawing_placements_reported exports the top view of a design whose root holds only sketches and suppressed placeholders (items with no MitCad counterpart, which have no bodies and draw nothing) and whose one component, a cylinder, is placed six times; it checks the four corners of each placement’s outline at its place and the line 1 bodies in 6 placements, then hides one occurrence and checks it left out (1 bodies in 5 placements). The design is read from MITCAD_MITCAD_REPORTED (github-527/, by its content id); the test is skipped without it.

Gears

A gear feature (mitcad#472; core/model/src/features/gear.rs the definition and its placement, gear_profile.rs the teeth, the kernel’s gear_sweep and gear_cone (geometry/include/mitcad/geometry/gear.hpp) the solids, api/gears.rs the query and the command) makes a gear with involute teeth from parameters. The application’s Gear panel makes them (app/COMMANDS.md). Tests: features::gear_profile and features::gear_tests, features::seat_tests (seated on shafts), tools/cli/tests/gears.json, tools/cli/tests/gears_link.json, tools/ui-gear-test.sh, tools/ui-windows-gear-test.ps1.

{"type": "gear", "kind": "helical", "plane": "xy", "center": [0, 0], "module": 2, "teeth": 20,
 "face_width": 10, "helix_angle": "20 deg", "backlash": 0.1,
 "bore": {"type": "plain", "diameter": 8}, "keyway": true, "hub": {"diameter": 20, "length": 8},
 "operation": "new_component"}
Field Value
kind spur, helical, herringbone, ring (internal), rack, bevel (straight)
plane, center where the gear’s axis meets its plane (the plane’s normal), in the plane’s coordinates; a rack’s start. Not with mesh_with
angle turns the gear about its axis (tooth 1 centred on the plane’s x axis without it; a rack about its start). Not with mesh_with
module, teeth the normal module (mm) and the number of teeth (a whole number, at least 5; a rack’s at least 1)
pressure_angle the normal pressure angle, 20 degrees without it (10 to 35)
face_width along the axis (a bevel gear’s along its pitch cone, less than half its cone distance)
helix_angle, left_handed helical and herringbone gears (needed), helical rings and racks (optional): up to 45 degrees, right-handed unless left_handed
gap a herringbone gear’s gap between its halves, a groove a quarter module below the roots
rim a ring gear’s rim outside its roots (needed)
height, length a rack’s height from its back to its tips (needed), its length (at least, and without it, teeth times the pitch)
shaft_angle, mate_teeth, pair a bevel gear’s shaft angle (90 degrees), its mate’s teeth (its own) and whether it makes the mate too
backlash mm at the pitch circle: a tooth is thinner (a ring’s space wider) by half of it, so two gears with the same value mesh with it (at most a quarter of the pitch)
profile_shift x in modules, away from the axis (-1 to 0.8; a ring’s teeth outwards)
bore {"type": "plain", "diameter": d} or {"type": "thread", "thread": {"designation": "M8x1.25"}} (the size’s minor diameter, its tap drill; standard as a thread’s): spur, helical, herringbone and bevel gears, through the gear and its hub
keyway a DIN 6885-1 (form A) keyway in a plain bore of 6 to 230 mm: the hub’s width and depth for the bore’s diameter, at the gear’s angle
hub diameter (optional, mitcad#656: without it the bore plus a 2 mm wall all round, or half the root diameter without a bore, at least 4 mm), length: on the end face (a bevel gear’s back)
mesh_with {"gear": "F3", "angle": <angle>, "position": <length>}: in the plane of an earlier gear feature of the same component, at their mesh’s centre distance in the direction angle from its centre (from its plane’s x axis), or position along a rack from the middle of its teeth, turned so that the teeth engage
seat on a shaft instead of plane and center (Seats on shafts, mitcad#578): spur, helical, herringbone and single bevel gears, not with mesh_with; a gear meshing with a seated one lies in its plane. Without bore the bore is plain, the shaft’s diameter plus bore_clearance, and follows the shaft; a thread bore stays the thread’s; a plain bore of its own is refused
bore_clearance mm added to the shaft’s diameter for a seated gear’s plain bore (0 without it; a printed fit 0.2, say); only with seat and without bore
operation, participants as an extrusion’s
  • Teeth: the ISO 53 basic rack (profile A): addendum 1 m, dedendum 1.25 m, root fillet 0.38 m (smaller where it does not fit). An external tooth is what that rack leaves rolling on the pitch circle: the flank is the involute of the base circle (a cubic B-spline within 1e-7 mm), the root the envelope of the rack’s tip fillet, which also cuts the undercut of small tooth counts (below 17 at 20 degrees) into the flank. Helical teeth have the transverse rack’s section (heights in the normal module) turned along the axis by the helix (a screw motion of the section’s curves within about 1e-7 mm; the volume is the section’s area times the width). An internal gear’s space is an external tooth’s shape with a circular root fillet, its tips at the base circle at least. A rack has straight flanks. A straight bevel gear follows Tredgold’s approximation (ISO 23509 nomenclature): the virtual spur gear of z / cos(delta) teeth on the back cone, wrapped onto it, the teeth ruled to the apex and trimmed by the back and front cones; its pitch angle delta from the teeth, the mate’s teeth and the shaft angle.
  • Faces: tooth k (from 1, counter-clockwise about the axis) has tip(k), flank_a(k) and fillet_a(k) on its clockwise side, flank_b(k) and fillet_b(k) on the other, root(k) after it (a rack’s root(0) before its first tooth); the caps start, end, a herringbone gear’s halves #k pieces; rim, back, end_a, end_b (a rack’s back and ends), back, front, back_cone, front_cone (a bevel gear’s), bore, keyway_a, keyway_top, keyway_b, hub, hub_end, groove.
  • Meshes: the gears must share the module, the pressure angle and the helix angle; external helical gears have opposite hands, a ring and its pinion or a rack and its pinion the same. The centre distance takes the profile shifts’ working pressure angle; a rack’s reference line lies r + x m from its pinion’s axis. A bevel gear meshes only through pair; two rings or two racks do not mesh. A gear’s result keeps its frame as the mount gear (x, y and the axis as columns).
  • Joints and links: gears made as components (new_component) turn on joints of their occurrences; link_gears couples two meshed gears' joints.
Query Fields Result
gear_values uid (a gear feature) or def (a definition as add_feature takes it, without type) kind, module, teeth, transverse_module, pressure_angle, circular_pitch; bore_diameter (given, or a seated gear’s from its shaft at the timeline marker, with shaft_diameter and the seat as seat_frame gives it); hub_diameter (given or worked out) and computed (["hub_diameter"] when worked out); pitch_diameter, base_diameter, outside_diameter, root_diameter, tooth_thickness (at the pitch circle), undercut, form_diameter (where the involute starts), helix_angle, lead (external gears); a ring’s inside_diameter, space_width; a rack’s pitch_line_length, length; a bevel gear’s pitch_angle, cone_distance, virtual_teeth, mate_teeth, mate_pitch_angle, shaft_angle; section_area (the transverse section’s, without bore and hub); with mesh_with centre_distance, mate, ratio, pitch_radii; error when the values make no gear
gear_link gear command: the add_motion_link link_gears would run, or reason why it cannot
Command Fields Result
link_gears gear (a gear with mesh_with), name (optional) as add_motion_link: a motion link between the joints the two gears’ components’ occurrences turn on (a rack’s slides on), the mate’s joint driving: gear (internal with a ring) by their pitch radii, or rack_pinion by the pinion’s; reverse when a joint’s axis runs against its gear’s. Refused when a gear has no such joint, a joint’s axis is not along its gear’s, or the two are linked already

The .f3d and .solidcraft imports can map their files’ gears onto the definition later; it is kept in the design file as it is.

Pulleys

A pulley feature (mitcad#562; core/model/src/features/pulley.rs the definition, its placement and the belt, pulley_profile.rs the grooves, the kernel’s gear_sweep the solids, api/pulleys.rs the query) makes a timing belt pulley, a smooth idler or a toothed idler from parameters. The application’s Pulley panel makes them (app/COMMANDS.md). Tests: features::pulley_profile and features::pulley_tests, features::seat_tests (seated on shafts), tools/cli/tests/pulleys.json, tools/ui-pulley-test.sh, tools/ui-windows-pulley-test.ps1.

{"type": "pulley", "kind": "toothed", "profile": "gt2_2mm", "plane": "xy", "center": [0, 0],
 "angle": 0, "teeth": 20, "belt_width": 6, "clearance": 1, "pitch_correction": 0,
 "flanges": {"sides": "both", "diameter": 18, "thickness": 1},
 "hub": {"diameter": 16, "length": 7},
 "bore": {"type": "plain", "diameter": 5}, "keyway": false,
 "set_screws": {"count": 2, "thread": {"designation": "M3x0.5"}, "position": 3.5},
 "operation": "new_component"}
Field Value
kind toothed (a pulley), idler (smooth, for the belt’s back or as a tensioner), toothed_idler (teeth on a bearing bore)
profile gt2_2mm, gt2_3mm, htd_3m, htd_5m, t5, xl: needed with teeth; optional for an idler (the belt’s pitch, and the check that two pulleys share a belt)
plane, center where the axis meets its plane (the plane’s normal), in the plane’s coordinates. Not with belt_with
angle turns the pulley about its axis: tooth 1 is centred on the plane’s x axis without it; the keyway and the first set screw lie in this direction. Not with belt_with (refused: belt_with.angle places the pulley, its teeth then start on that plane’s x axis)
teeth the toothed kinds’ number of teeth: whole, from the profile’s minimum (12 for HTD 5M, 10 for the others) to 1000
diameter an idler’s running diameter (instead of teeth)
belt_width, clearance mm; the toothed (running) width is belt_width + clearance, the clearance 1 mm without it
pitch_correction mm added to the outside diameter (a pitch-diameter correction, e.g. for backlash), at most a quarter of the pitch either way; 0 without it. The belt’s values keep the nominal pitch diameter
flanges sides (none, one, both; both without it), diameter (more than the outside diameter; optional, mitcad#656: without it the outside diameter plus, all round, the profile’s groove depth and 1 mm, MitCad’s default; the outside diameter plus 2 mm without a profile), thickness. One flange lies on the plane’s side, away from the hub
hub diameter (optional, mitcad#656: without it the bore (a seated pulley’s too) plus a wall all round of 2 mm, or of a set screw’s tap drill when that is more; half the root diameter without a bore, at least two walls), length: after the toothed part and the second flange, away from the plane
bore {"type": "plain", "diameter": d} or {"type": "thread", "thread": {"designation": "M8x1.25"}} (the size’s minor diameter, its tap drill), through the whole pulley; it stays 0.5 mm inside the groove bottoms (an idler’s running face) with its keyway
keyway a DIN 6885-1 (form A) keyway in a plain bore of 6 to 230 mm, at the pulley’s angle
set_screws count (1 to 4, 90 degrees apart from angle), thread (a tap drill of that size, radial from the axis through the hub; listed as cosmetic threads by threads), position (mm from the hub’s outer end along the axis; the hub’s middle without it). Needs a hub
belt_with {"pulley": "F3", "center_distance": 80, "angle": <angle>}: in the plane of an earlier pulley feature of the same component, at center_distance from its centre in the direction angle (from its plane’s x axis; 0 without it), for one belt round both. The two share the belt profile (an idler without one takes the other’s); their pitch circles must not overlap
seat on a shaft instead of plane and center (Seats on shafts, mitcad#578): the pulley’s plane (where its first flange starts) at the seat’s offset along the shaft, running along the shaft from it; not with belt_with (a pulley running with a seated one lies in its plane). Without bore the bore is plain, the shaft’s diameter plus bore_clearance, and follows the shaft (a keyway in it too); a thread bore stays the thread’s; a plain bore of its own is refused
bore_clearance mm added to the shaft’s diameter for a seated pulley’s plain bore (0 without it; a printed fit 0.2, say); only with seat and without bore
operation, participants as an extrusion’s

Values are parameters: numbers in mm (radians for angles; teeth and set_screws.count unitless) or names and expressions, as for gears.

  • Diameters: the pitch diameter is z p / pi (the belt’s pitch line); the outside diameter is the pitch diameter less twice the profile’s pitch line offset (PLD), plus pitch_correction; the root diameter is the outside diameter less twice the groove’s depth.

    Profile Pitch PLD Groove
    gt2_2mm 2 mm 0.254 round: 0.764 deep, 1.494 wide, bottom radius 0.555, tip radius 0.15
    gt2_3mm 3 mm 0.381 round: 1.169 deep, 2.31 wide, bottom radius 0.85, tip radius 0.25
    htd_3m 3 mm 0.381 round: 1.289 deep, 2.27 wide, bottom radius 0.86, tip radius 0.3
    htd_5m 5 mm 0.5715 round: 2.199 deep, 3.781 wide, bottom radius 1.49, tip radius 0.43
    t5 5 mm 0.425 straight-sided: 1.75 at the bottom, 1.25 deep, 50 degrees, bottom radius 0.4, tip radius 0.6
    xl 5.08 mm 0.254 straight-sided: 1.32 at the bottom, 1.65 deep, 50 degrees, bottom radius 0.41, tip radius 0.64

  • Grooves: our own construction around the published belt dimensions (the sources per profile are in pulley_profile.rs); one fixed groove per profile, not generated by the belt’s motion. A round groove has a bottom arc centred on its axis and straight flanks tangent to it through the corners its width and depth give; a straight-sided groove a flat bottom with fillets and flanks at half its included angle; both have tip fillets tangent to the flanks and the outside circle. Too few teeth for a groove’s width leave no land and are refused.

  • Faces: tooth k (from 1, counter-clockwise about the axis) has tip(k) (its land on the outside circle), tip_fillet_a(k), flank_a(k) and root_fillet_a(k) (straight-sided grooves) on its clockwise side, tip_fillet_b(k), flank_b(k), root_fillet_b(k) on the other, root(k) the groove bottom after it; an idler’s running; the caps start, end; flange_a, flange_a_end, flange_a_inner, flange_b, flange_b_inner, flange_b_end; hub, hub_start, hub_end; bore, keyway_a, keyway_top, keyway_b; set_screw(k).

  • Mount frame: the result keeps its frame as the mount bore (x, y and the axis as columns, the origin on the axis on its plane), as a library pulley’s: joints and joint origins take it as {"mount": "F3:mount(bore)"} (a plane, the axis or its origin); a joint origin there with a mount (kind hole) is a mount frame of the design for Place Part (Mount frames).

  • Belts: the open belt round two pulleys of pitch radii R and r (an idler’s running radius), C apart: L = 2 C cos(t) + pi (R + r) + 2 t (R - r), sin(t) = (R - r) / C. It wraps pi - 2 t of the smaller pulley and pi + 2 t of the larger. A belt body is not made.

Query Fields Result
pulley_values uid (a pulley feature) or def (a definition as add_feature takes it, without type); belt_lengths (optional: catalogue belt lengths in mm) kind, tooth_width (the toothed width), length (along the axis); bore_diameter (given, or a seated pulley’s from its shaft at the timeline marker, with shaft_diameter and the seat as seat_frame gives it); flange_diameter and hub_diameter (given or worked out, with flanges and a hub) and computed (those worked out, so that a panel shows them as computed until one is typed); with a profile profile, pitch, pitch_line_offset, min_teeth; the toothed kinds’ teeth, pitch_diameter, outside_diameter, root_diameter; an idler’s diameter (and outside_diameter); section_area (the toothed or running section’s, without bore and flanges); with belt_with center_distance, mate (the other pulley’s uid), belt_length (the belt’s pitch length), wrap_angles (on the smaller and the larger pulley), belt_teeth (belt_length / pitch, with a profile), teeth_in_mesh (whole teeth on the smaller toothed pulley), catalogue_length (the nearest of belt_lengths, only when given); error when the values make no pulley or no belt

BUILD: timber frames

A wall, floor or roof frame of timber members made from a few values (mitcad#479), edited afterwards as one. Its members are ordinary BUILD parts (BUILD: timber construction): grounded members by two points of the library’s timber, in the cut list, junctions and lists like any other. The app’s Wall and Floor / Roof (mitcad#520) make them and Timber Frame lays them out again (app/COMMANDS.md, Timber). Code: core/model-build/src/frames.rs; tests core/model-tests/build-frames/src/frame_tests.rs.

{"cmd": "build_frame", "kind": "wall", "part": {"source": "S1", "config": "48x98"},
 "start": [0, 0, 0], "end": [3600, 0, 0], "height": "2400 mm", "spacing": 600,
 "openings": [{"offset": 600, "width": 900, "height": 1200, "sill": 900}],
 "fastener": {"library": "mitcad-parts", "url": "...", "rev": "...", "component": "wood-screw"}}

build_frame (class remote) takes kind (wall, floor or roof), part (the members’ timber: studs, joists, rafters; role: profile, kind: timber, cut to length, with its section) and, by kind, the fields below. Points are in the BUILD host’s coordinates, lengths values (mm or an expression), openings numbers in mm. name (optional) names the frame (Wall 1, Floor 1, Roof 1 by default; unique among the frames); the members’ components are named after it and their role (Wall 1 stud (3)). fastener (optional) is a wood fastener: two of them, sized from the members (Wood fasteners’ default), are driven at every junction of two of the frame’s members that has no connector; a junction they are refused at is left as it is.

  • A wall (kind: wall): start and end, its centre line at its base (made level with the start); height (default 2400 mm, the underside of the bottom plate to the top of the top plate); spacing (the studs’ centre distance, default 600); plates {bottom, top} (1 or 2 each, default 1); plate and header (parts, default part); openings [{offset, width, height, sill}] (offset from the start along the wall to the rough opening’s near side, sill its underside’s height above the base; 0 or left out: a door); joins {start, end, start_on}: the wall frames (any member of each) its ends butt against, start_on: end (mitcad#510) when instead that wall’s end face butts against this wall’s side at its start (left out: side); corner (mitcad#510): how they meet those walls, butt, lapped or straight (mitcad#524: a start on an end face continues in line, its ends otherwise butting) (left out: lapped, as walls saved before it keep their corners), kept in the definition and changed with build_edit.

    • The plates lie flat, the studs stand with the larger section size across the wall: the wall’s depth is the stud’s larger size. The end studs stand flush with its ends; the others at k × spacing from its start (centres), one that would touch the end stud left out.

    • Spliced plates (mitcad#536): a bottom or top plate longer than the plate’s timber’s longest (its length.max, else its longest stock length) is made of pieces butted end to end, from end A each as long as the longest stock length allows (at most its longest), the last one the remainder; each piece at least the timber’s least length (and two stud thicknesses). Each joint lies over the centre of a stud that bears on the plate (one reaching the top plates for a top plate, one standing on the bottom plates for a bottom plate: studs, king studs, junction studs, trimmer and cripple studs), the farthest that keeps the piece within the stock length; where no stud is in reach a backing stud goes in (full height, stud.splice.<n>, as far along as the piece may run, beside the openings’ framing and the other studs). The joints of a second plate (plates.top: 2 or plates.bottom: 2) are at least a stud spacing from the first’s (else a warning, Wall 1: the joints of its top plates are less than a stud spacing apart). A bottom plate is cut at its doors first, each run spliced alone. A plate’s first piece keeps its place (plate.top.0, so a top plate still leads the frame), the others plate.top.0.1, plate.top.0.2, …; a bottom plate’s pieces are plate.bottom.0.0, plate.bottom.0.1, … as at its doors. The pieces are ordinary members: the cut list lists each, cut from the stock. A frame’s fastener goes at the junction of each piece with the stud under the joint (each piece’s end over half the stud); the pieces’ own butt joint is an inline junction, which takes no wood fastener (an inline joint takes a plate), so it gets none. The wall is refused only when a piece cannot be made at all (no stud and no room for a backing stud within reach: Wall 1: its top plate from 0 to 7819 mm is longer than its timber's longest, 6000 mm, and no stud can take a joint between ...) or another member is longer than its timber (a stud taller than the stock: Wall 1: the stud stud.start: the length 6904 mm is longer than the part's longest, 6000 mm). Plates no longer than the timber’s longest stay one piece, as before. Tests: core/model-tests/build-timber/src/wall_splice_tests.rs.

    • An opening: king studs (full height) and trimmer studs (the bottom plate to the header) on each side; a header on edge between the king studs on the trimmers, of as many plies as the wall’s depth takes (floor(depth / thickness), two 48 mm plies in a 98 wall); a window’s sill flat between the trimmers; cripple studs at the stud places in the opening, above the header and below the sill. A door cuts the bottom plates. The studs at the opening’s place give way. Refused: an opening that does not fit between the end studs, openings whose studs overlap, a header above the top plate, a sill below the bottom plate.

    • Load-bearing or not (load_bearing, mitcad#519; kept in the definition and changed with build_edit): true or left out (as walls saved before keep) frames the openings as above; false (a partition, the app’s default for a new wall) leaves the trimmer studs out: the king studs stand at the opening’s sides (opening.<n>.king.a from offset - thickness, .king.b from offset + width), and one header lies flat between them, its wide face down as a plate (opening.<n>.header, role flat header, the header part, from offset to offset + width); the cripple studs above start at its top, the sill and the cripple studs below are as above. The opening’s framing is a stud narrower on each side, so an opening fits nearer the end studs. The preview’s roles and the cut list follow it.

    • Butting (corner: butt, mitcad#510): a wall’s end in joins stops at the face of the wall it names (on the side the wall is on), its end stud and plates square against it, neither lapped nor notched. That wall is neither run on, lapped nor notched; it gets a backing stud on each side of the joining wall (its keys as at a T, junction.<wall>.<end>.a and .b), one that would take its end stud’s place left out, so the sheathing of both walls has a stud behind its edges at the junction. With joins.start_on: end that wall’s end face butts against this wall’s side: that wall is not changed at all, this one runs from its own start and gets the backing studs on each side of that wall’s centre line where they fit (junction.<that wall>.0.a, .b). Either way the walls stay joined: editing one lays the other out again.

    • Corners and T-junctions (corner: lapped, left out): a wall’s end in joins stops at the face of the wall it names (on the side the wall is on); that wall gets a stud for each wall that joins it: where the joining wall’s centre line meets it within that wall’s depth of its end, a corner (it runs on to the joining wall’s outer face, the stud just inside the corner), else a T (a stud on each side of the joining wall). A wall that joins another one lays that one out again with it. At a corner the plates lap (mitcad#493): where each wall has one plate (at the top, and at the bottom), both run to the corner’s outer faces and are half-lapped over the other wall’s depth (a half_lap cut each, no junction, with the other wall’s lead), the joining wall’s half outside (the upper half of a top plate, the lower half of a bottom plate); with two, the joining wall’s outer plate (the upper top plate, the lower bottom plate) runs over the corner to the other wall’s outer face and the other wall’s stops at the joining wall’s inner face, the inner plates as at a butt. At a T the plates butt.

    • A wall started on another wall’s side (mitcad#493): with square: true and joins.start, start is a point on that wall’s side (a click; within its depth of its ends) and the wall starts square to it, at its base, towards the side the point is on (the end’s side when the point is on its centre line, else its left). With corner: butt (mitcad#510):

      • from the side (side): its centre line starts at the point’s place along the wall (snapped, or From and Offset, below), but at least half its own depth from the wall’s end faces (it never hangs past an end: its outer face at most flush with the end face); it butts against that wall’s side, which gets the backing studs;
      • from an end (end): a point on one of the wall’s end faces (within 0.5 mm of the face and inside its depth, or beyond the end; the faces where its plates end now) starts it beyond that end, its side against the end face: its centre line half its own depth past the face, its start flush with the wall’s side away from the side it runs to (the end’s side first here, then the point’s). It stays joined to the wall (joins.start_on: end): that wall is not changed, the new wall gets the backing studs where it meets it.

      With corner: lapped (or left out):

      • an L corner when the point is near one of its ends (within half its stud spacing, at least its depth, at most half its length): the new wall’s centre line starts at that end of the wall’s centre line;
      • a T elsewhere: its centre line starts at the point’s place along the wall.

      From and Offset (mitcad#514): on the side its place along the wall is measured as a side placement’s (mitcad#417), between the wall’s end faces (where its plates end now): from a (end A to the new wall’s near face), b (end B to its far face) or middle (the middle to its centre line, positive towards end B), offset that distance (a value; 0 is flush with that end, or centred). Without either, the point decides, snapped: flush with an end when the new wall’s face would be within its depth of that end (butting; lapped: within the L corner’s reach above), centred within a quarter of its depth of the middle, else the point’s place from the nearer end; snap (mm, optional) is the app’s least snap distance, as at.snap. With either given (end A and 0 when one is left out) they place it, the point only choosing the side (never an end face). It never hangs past an end: a typed offset that would is made flush with that end, with the warning <name>: flush with Wall 1's end A instead. Butting, flush with an end is a clean corner: its outer face in the plane of that end face, its end stud and plates against the side, the wall’s end stud outside it and a backing stud inside it; lapped, flush with an end is the L corner there, any other place a T.

      Its length runs from there: as far as end is along it (a second click, anywhere); else, unless auto_end is false (mitcad#515), to the first wall frame its run meets: one it crosses (not one parallel to it), its centre line between that wall’s end faces (not one it merely touches at a corner), beyond the side it starts from, their heights overlapping; the nearest along the run. It ends there butting against that wall’s side as a start on a side does (joins.end that wall: its end stud and plates square against the side, a backing stud each side of it in that wall; with corner: lapped that wall’s corner or T), its length to that wall’s face. Else (nothing met, or auto_end: false) length. Refused without end or length when nothing is met, and when it would not reach beyond the wall’s side (from an end, beyond its other side). The definition keeps the start, end and joins worked out (not square, from, offset, snap, auto_end). The answer, and build_preview’s with frame, add junction: {kind ("side", "end", "L" or "T"), corner ("butt" or "lapped"), wall (its name), frame (its lead), end ("a" or "b" for an end or an L, else null), at (mm along the wall from its start to the new centre line), length (mm), from ("a", "b" or "middle"; null at an end), offset (mm; null at an end), to ({wall, frame, auto}: the wall its end butts against, auto true when its run met it, false for an end clicked on it; else null), run (mm: the new wall between the faces it butts against, from the wall's side, at an end from its far side)}; null without square.

      Straight (corner: straight, mitcad#524): a start on one of that wall’s end faces continues it in line (kind: "straight", end the end clicked): its centre line that wall’s, its start on the end face, running away from it; the two walls are not joined (neither changes the other). On the side it starts as butt does.

    • A wall started on another body’s face (case B, mitcad#524): with square: true, no joins.start and face {body, face, occurrence} (the body’s uid, the face’s name and the occurrence that places it, its path from the root; left out: the body’s first placement), start the click on the face. A Timber wall frame’s member is case A above, recognised first (the app sends joins.start for it), so its behaviour does not change. The clicked body (an imported wall, a modelled solid, a loose Timber member, a floor frame’s member) is not changed and not linked; everything comes from the geometry:

      • side: the face’s outward side (its normal out of the body’s material, Kernel::face_plane), never into or behind it; direction: square from it, along its normal; a face that is not vertical (its normal more than 0.001 off the horizontal) is refused (<name> starts from a vertical face: the face of <body> clicked is not vertical);
      • base: the floor under the click: the first body a line down from a millimetre in front of the click enters (Kernel::segment_crossings, a slab’s top), else the face’s bottom edge (its box, Kernel::face_boxes, else the body’s), its bottom plate’s underside there, height from it;
      • along the face: at the click, or offset from from (a, the face’s end A: its left end seen from in front of it, b or middle), snapped as on a wall frame’s side with corner: butt (flush with an end within the new wall’s depth, centred within a quarter of it, else from the nearer end), never past an end;
      • an end face (narrower than the body is deep behind it: a solid wall’s thin end) makes a corner: with butt (or lapped, which has nothing to lap here) its side against the end face, running to the side of the face’s middle the end (else the click) is on, its start flush with the body’s far side, longer than the face is wide (kind: "face_end"); with straight in line beyond it, its centre line the face’s middle (kind: "face_straight"); a side face (kind: "face") is the same with any corner.
      • Its length as a start on a wall frame’s: end, else (unless auto_end is false) what its run meets first, else length. The auto end (mitcad#515, both cases) stops the run at a wall frame (as above) or at any other body’s face it meets nearer (the bodies shown other than timber frames’ members), butting it (no link: to.frame null, to.face true). The nearest face along the run is taken (mitcad#536): it looks along lines a quarter, half and three quarters of the wall’s height up and 10 mm under its top (the wall over a door in the wall ahead), each at its centre line and a millimetre inside each of its sides (a post or a wall’s end only its side meets); the body it starts on counts too, beyond its own face (a millimetre on), so a room modelled as one body ends it at its far wall.
      • The definition keeps the start and end worked out (the start at the base’s height), not face. The junction’s kind is face, face_end or face_straight, wall the body’s name, frame null, at along the face from its end A, and base {z, on ("floor", "face" or "origin"), body} names what it stands on. Tests: core/model-tests/build-frames/src/face_start_tests.rs.
  • A floor or ceiling (kind: floor): outline (a closed outline, three points at least, at its first point’s height: the joists' underside), spacing (default 400), direction (the joists’; default square to the outline’s first side, into it), rim (default part), blocking (rows of blocking, default 0), openings [{offset: [a, b], size: [w, l]}] (from the outline’s least corner across the joists and along them), trimmers (default 2).
    • Rim joists on edge along every side, inside the outline; at a corner the side across the joists runs through (exact at square corners). Joists on edge at k × spacing from the outline’s least point across them, from rim to rim (each place cut where the outline is open, as an L or a U), one that would touch a rim along the joists left out.
    • A row of blocking runs across the joists halfway (rows evenly along them), a block between each two neighbouring joists or rims.
    • An opening (a stair’s): trimmers trimmer joists each side, full span; as many header joists each side between the inner trimmers; tail joists from the rims to the headers at the joist places inside it. Refused when it does not fit inside the rims with its trimmers.
  • A roof (kind: roof): walls (two parallel wall frames, any member of each), roof (gable, the default, or mono), pitch (an angle, 5 to 75 degrees; a gable’s default 30; a mono-pitch roof’s default from the walls’ heights), spacing (the rafters’, default 600), overhang (the rafters’ horizontal run beyond the walls’ outer faces, default 300), ridge (default part).
    • The rafters stand on edge at the centre distance along the walls where both run (the first and last flush with those ends), each plumb cut at both ends (ends at the pitch: end A leaning up, its long point the bottom edge at the eave; end B leaning down, its long point the top edge) and notched by a birdsmouth over each wall’s top plate: a birdsmouth cut (Joinery) in its derived part, the box under the top of the plate over its width, with the wall’s lead. The seat is the plate’s width, or less so that the notch is at most a third of the rafter’s depth; a gable roof’s rafters bear on the outer edge of each wall.
    • Gable: the rafters of each side run from the eave to a ridge board on edge halfway between the walls’ outer faces, its top at the rafters' tops; the walls must be of one height. Mono-pitch: from the lower wall over the higher one, notched over both.
    • Warnings: a ridge board shallower than the rafters’ plumb cut, a birdsmouth deeper than a third of the rafter, rafters that do not bear on a wall.
    • Its fastener goes at the junctions of its own members (mitcad#521): through the ridge board into each rafter’s plumb cut end, square to the cut, from the board’s far side (Cut ends after How junctions are found); the two rafters of a pair are no junction, and a mono-pitch roof’s rafters have none among them. The rafters are not fastened to the walls’ plates (junctions of two frames).

The answer: component and frame (the lead), frame_component (the frame’s own component, below), name, kind, members ([{component, member}]), count, fasteners (the junctions given fasteners), relaid (other frames laid out again with it), warnings (the frame’s, the layout’s, and the first ten fasteners’ warnings), splices (a wall’s plates made of pieces, mitcad#536: [{plate, role, at, pieces, longest}], plate the first piece’s place, at the joints in mm along the wall from its start, longest the longest piece); undo step Place wall frame Wall 1, one step with the fasteners.

A frame is a component of its own (mitcad#522). build_frame makes a component named after the frame (Wall 1, Floor 1, Roof 1; Wall 1 (1) when a component has that name) in the BUILD host, placed at the host’s origin, and makes the frame’s members, their fasteners and the fasteners’ joints inside it: the host gets one component per frame, not its members, and a frame’s Joints are only its own. Joints between frames (a fastener connected by hand at a junction of two frames’ members) stay in the host, the common parent. Everything that works on a frame takes its component as well as any member: build_edit with frame (laid out again inside the same component, renamed with the frame), build_preview with frame and component, build_remove with set (the members, their fasteners and the component when nothing else is left in it; the answer’s components lists the parts as before, not the component), joins and a roof’s walls. The definition’s points (start, end, outline, direction) are in the component’s coordinates, the host’s until the component is moved: a frame moved as one (its occurrence moved) is laid out again where it is, and the frames around it read it there; a frame edit’s points are in the component’s coordinates too. build_parts gives each member frame_component; the lead’s record keeps it with the definition (framing.component). Frames saved before keep their members flat in their host and load and edit unchanged: laid out again (MODIFY Timber Frame, or as a frame another one depends on) they stay in the host, their fasteners there too; nothing is re-parented, so paths other parts’ joints and bound lengths name stay valid. Only a new frame is made as a component. The cut list goes by frame: a frame’s members are grouped only with members of the same frame, each row names its frame (frame, null for parts in no frame), the rows of parts in no frame first, then each frame’s by name; the stock is worked out over all of them as before. Tests: core/model-tests/build-frames/src/frame_component_tests.rs.

What is kept. The lead (a wall’s top plate, a floor’s first rim, a gable roof’s ridge board, a mono-pitch roof’s first rafter) keeps the frame’s definition in its record (framing: {frame, count}, its parts as {source, config}, joins and walls as the frames’ leads); every member’s record has frame (the lead) and member, its place in the frame: plate.top.0, plate.bottom.0 (.0, .1, … when a door cuts it or it is spliced; a spliced top plate’s further pieces plate.top.0.1, …, mitcad#536), stud.start, stud.end, stud.<k>, stud.splice.<n> (a backing stud under a plate’s joint), junction.<wall>.<end>, opening.<n>.king.a, .trimmer.b, .header.<ply>, .sill, .cripple.top.<k>, .cripple.bottom.<k>; rim.<side>, joist.<k>, joist.<k>.tail.a, opening.<n>.trimmer.a.<i>, .header.b.<i>, block.<row>.<k>; ridge, rafter.a.<k>, rafter.b.<k>, rafter.<k>. build_parts adds frame, member and the lead’s framing ({definition, count}).

Editing a frame. build_edit with frame (any of the fields above; {} lays it out again as it is) and optionally config (the members' row) through any member: the frame laid out again with these fields over its definition, in one undo step Edit Wall 1. A wall’s length moves its end along it. The members whose place stays keep their components (placed anew, their length, row and cuts; connectors on them stay), new places are made, the others removed as by build_remove; the frame’s fasteners are taken away and driven anew. The frames that depend on it are laid out again too: the walls it joins and those that join it (before and after the edit), and the roofs on any of these walls; one that can no longer be laid out stays as it was, with a warning. The answer as build_frame’s, with changed (frame, config). Members of a frame are otherwise ordinary parts: a member edited alone (its length, ends) keeps its change until the frame is laid out again.

Preview. build_preview with frame (build_frame’s fields, or a frame edit’s with component) answers place: "frame", kind, name, count, roles ({role: count}), members ([{member, role, start, end, length, x, section}] in the design: the axis, the section’s X and its [W, T]), warnings, problems, and for a wall length (as worked out: the auto end’s, mm) and splices (as build_frame’s, mitcad#536). A refused preview (mitcad#536) still answers which frame it is and what its start and auto end worked out: name (the default name given first, Wall 1), kind, junction, length, count: 0, no members, and the reason in problems (the same as build_frame’s refusal, which names the frame too).

Removing. build_remove with "set": true on a member removes the whole frame with its fasteners. A lead removed alone hands the frame to the next member. Walls that join a removed wall keep their layout until they are laid out again (their join is then left out, with a warning).

build_edit with frame is class remote (the fasteners are read from a library).

BUILD: choosing and swapping fasteners

The wood fastener of a timber frame and of a spacing set, its size and count, and fasteners of a design made from another fastener where they are (mitcad#497). The app’s Timber tool chooses them in its Frame and Spacing modes, Swap Fastener swaps them (app/COMMANDS.md, Timber and Swap Fastener). Code: core/model-build/src/frames.rs, spacing.rs, swap.rs; tests core/model-tests/build-timber/src/fastener_tests.rs.

A frame’s fastener. build_frame (and a frame’s build_edit) takes fastener (a wood screw or nail, Wood fasteners) and fastener_count (how many at each junction, default 2). With a row in fastener.config every junction gets that size (a nail 3.1x90); without one each junction’s are sized from its members, as build_connect sizes them. The definition keeps both: a frame laid out again drives the same fastener, size and count. The warnings are build_connect’s (the first ten).

The default fastener (mitcad#516). The model takes the fastener it is given; without fastener a frame has none. The app’s Timber tool sends, until the user chooses another, the library’s default wood fastener: the one marked wood.default (docs/libraries.md, Timber parts; library_build_candidates with kind: wood lists it first). MitCad’s library marks Wood screw, countersunk, seated by its head’s top (flush with the wood, Seating below), not the pan-head Connector screw (head_underside, for a metal connector’s plate), which by name came first and stood proud of every default frame. Without a mark the app takes the first screw seated by its head’s top. Tests: core/vcs/src/tests/library_build.rs (the mark, the picker’s order, the shipped group file’s one default) and tools/cli/build-timber-test.cmake (the generated library’s first wood fastener, a frame with it seated flush).

A spacing set’s fasteners. build_place with spacing takes spacing.fastener and spacing.fastener_count (as a frame’s; none: no fasteners, the default). Each member is then fastened to its hosts: at every junction of a member with a part outside the set that has no connector (a joist on the beams it stands on and reaches, a deck board on each joist it crosses), fastener_count of them as build_connect drives them, in the same undo step as the set. The answer adds fasteners, the junctions fastened, and its warnings the fasteners’. The set keeps them in its definition: build_edit with spacing (which may change fastener and fastener_count) takes the set’s fasteners away and drives them anew with the members, in its one undo step, and answers fasteners too; build_remove with "set": true removes them with the set. A set’s fasteners are the wood fasteners at junctions of exactly one of its members with another part; one connected there by hand is taken away with them when the set is laid out again. build_edit with spacing.fastener is class remote.

{"cmd": "build_swap_fasteners", "fasteners": ["C41", "C42"],
 "part": {"library": "mitcad-parts", "url": "...", "rev": "...", "component": "ring-nail",
 "config": "3.1x90"}}

Swapping fasteners. build_swap_fasteners (class remote; model with part.source) makes each fastener of fasteners (components of role fastener) from part, in place: the component, its occurrence, its derived part (another source and row), its joint (holding it by the new part’s frame of the same kind) and its junction stay, so it stays where it is and what removes or lists it finds it as before; its name becomes the new designation. One undo step, Swap 2 fasteners for Ring nail 3.1x90.

  • Which can replace which. A wood screw or nail (a wood block) only another wood fastener (... is no wood screw or nail: C41 is driven into timber); a connector’s nut, screw or washer only another fastener without wood, and when both name slot systems, one that fits (the systems do not fit: ...). Another part is refused (... is no fastener).
  • The size. part.config names the row. Left out, a wood fastener at a junction is sized from the junction’s members as build_connect sizes it (once per junction); one without a junction (a hanger’s screws) and a connector’s fastener take the source’s default row.
  • The warnings of each wood fastener at its junction for the new size, as build_connect gives them (embedment, edges, the member’s end, through), numbered by the fastener’s place at its junction.
  • The answer: swapped (the components), count, designation, sizes ([{component, config, diameter, length}], the diameter and length a wood fastener’s) and warnings.

Properties

Typed property sets (mitcad#496; core/model-base/src/properties.rs the types, values and the store, document/properties.rs the commands, what the document works out and the answers, api/properties.rs the JSON). A property is a key in a named set with a typed value and its source: Identity / Mark = W-12, Pset_WallCommon / FireRating = EI60, as IFC groups them, so that an export can map them directly. Properties are on three levels:

  • a component (C2, C0 the root): the definition’s, shared by its occurrences;
  • an occurrence (O3): its own values; it shows its component’s as inherited, and its own value of a set and key overrides the component’s for it only;
  • a body (F7.b0).

An owner is given by its id or by its name (a component’s, an occurrence’s Wall:2 or path from the root O1/O4, a body’s at the marker). Set names and keys compare without regard to case; a key has no / (it separates a set from a key in searches; an import writes one as ∕).

Types. The standard types are text, integer, number (a plain number, optionally with a unit label of its own that is shown and not converted, W/(m²·K)), length (kept in mm), area (mm²), volume (mm³), mass (kg), angle (radians), boolean (yes/no; yes/no and bool name it too) and date (YYYY-MM-DD). An own type is defined in the design: a name (not a standard type’s), a base standard type, optional allowed values (a property of the type is then edited as a choice and refuses any other value), an optional unit (a quantity’s shown unit, m, deg, g; a number’s label) and default, and a description.

Values in commands. A JSON number of a quantity is canonical (mm, mm², mm³, kg, radians); text is read in the type’s unit, else the design’s (set_units: a bare 1.2 in a metre design is 1.2 m), unless it names its own (1.2 m, 2 m^2, 500 g, 30 deg; a decimal comma works). yes/no, true/false, 1/0 for yes/no; integers and numbers as text too. A value of another dimension or kind is refused.

Sources. Every value records where it came from: user, rvt, ifc, ipt, f3d (the imports), 3mf (a slicer’s print settings, Print profiles), library (a library or BUILD part’s data) or computed. A user’s value set over an imported one keeps its source and the value the source gave (imported in the file), so the property shows that it differs (edited, source_value); set back to the source’s value it is no longer edited.

Worked out, never stored. computed values (the set Computed) and library values (the set Library) are worked out when asked for and never written to the design file, so a recompute leaves the file as it was:

Level Computed (only with computed) Library
body Volume, Area, Mass (its material’s density), Material
component Volume, Mass (its own bodies), Length (a BUILD member’s), Kind (mitcad#1980) Designation, Supplier, Part number, Library, Version; a BUILD part’s Material, Grade, Finish
occurrence its component’s, inherited its component’s, inherited

A stored value of the same set and key as a library value overrides it (and shows the library’s as its source value); the Computed set cannot hold stored values. A component’s Bill of Materials / BOM Structure is worked out and overridden likewise (mitcad#1985).

Command Fields Result
set_property owner, set, key, value (optional with a type that has a default, or for an existing property), type (a standard or own type; the property’s, else what the value is: text, integer, number, yes/no), unit (a quantity’s: the unit a number or bare text is in; a number’s label), source (default user; never computed) owner, set, key, type, value (as stored), edited. One undo step, nothing recomputed. An empty or blank text for a component’s (not the root’s) Part number or Description removes the stored property instead (its standing row shows again; no step when none is stored; mitcad#2138)
remove_property owner, set, key {}; an occurrence’s component value shows again. Refused when there is none
define_property_type name, base, values, unit, default, description name. Refused for a standard type’s name, a name taken, a unit of another dimension, values not of the base, a default not among the values
edit_property_type name, and what changes: new_name (its properties follow), base (only while no property uses it), values (each property’s value must stay allowed), unit and default (null removes them), description name
remove_property_type name converted: how many properties keep their values under its base type
Query Fields Result
