property_sets body, occurrence, component (at least one; the component follows from the occurrence or the body), computed (also the computed values) levels, the given ones most specific first: level (body, occurrence, component), owner, name, an occurrence’s component, sets: name, properties: set, key, type, base, value (as stored), text (in the shown unit, 1.2 m), unit, source, read_only (computed), inherited, overrides, edited, source_value (the source’s value as text, where it differs), choices (an own type’s values as text), standing (true on a component’s empty Identity/Part number and Identity/Description rows: listed while the component stores no property of that key in any set, never stored, not on the root, an occurrence or a body; mitcad#2138)
property_types standard (the standard types’ names), types: name, base, values (value, text), unit, default, description, uses
property_search text: Key or Set/Key, with a comparison =, !=, <, <=, >, >= (numbers and dates in order, quantities in units: Mass > 10 kg) or ~ (contains), or without one (the key is there) matches: every component, occurrence (with its inherited values) and body at the marker with a matching property, in that order: level, owner, name, component, set, key, text, inherited. Computed values only when the search names one

The properties query of this API is a different one: the bodies' physical properties (Analysis queries).

The design file keeps the own types as property_types and the stored properties as properties, one entry per owner (owner, sets: name, properties: key, type, value, source unless user, imported, unit), only for owners the design has (a deleted component’s are left out). Copies of components, and a design placed as a component, bring their components’, occurrences’ and bodies’ properties (another design’s root’s become the new component’s) with the own types they use.

Imports. Each import gives the values its file holds with its source; values MitCad does not otherwise use come in as well:

  • .rvt: each element’s bodies get Identity (ElementId, GlobalId, Category, Class, Family, Type, TypeId, Level), Instance Parameters (the record’s text, number and element id parameters) and Type Parameters (its family type’s; a wall’s type its Width, the total of its layers). Parameters are named and typed by their definitions (mitcad#501): a project, shared or family parameter by its definition in the file (name, and spec or class), a built-in one by the reader’s table of the common ones (Height, Width, Thickness, Base Offset, Mark, Type Mark, …), else Parameter <id>. Lengths, areas, volumes, angles and masses come in as length, area, volume, angle and mass in the model’s units (mm, mm², mm³, radians, kg, converted from the file’s feet, square and cubic feet, radians and kilograms), so they show in the design’s units; yes/no parameters as boolean, integer ones as integer, numbers, counts and currencies as number. A number of a kind not known or not converted (electrical, mechanical and structural quantities, built-in parameters not in the table, files before the 2021 release, which keep no spec) stays in the file’s internal units as a number with the unit label internal units. An element comes in as bodies of its level’s component, with no component of its type, so its type’s values are on its bodies too; were the import to make a component per element type, they would go on it.
  • IFC: an element’s Identity (GlobalId, Class, Name, ObjectType), its property sets (single and enumerated values) and element quantities (lengths, areas, volumes, counts, weights, times) in MitCad’s units, on its bodies and the occurrences of its type’s shape; its type object’s property sets (and Identity / Type) on the component its type’s shape became, and on its own bodies.
  • .ipt and .iam: the summary’s (Title, Subject, Author, Keywords, Comments, Last Saved By), the document summary’s (Category, Manager, Company), the design tracking set’s (Part Number, Material, Release) and the user’s own named properties (User Defined) on the root; an assembly’s parts’ on their components.
  • .f3d dumps that give them: a component’s Part Number and Description (set Component).

The sketch’s axes and origin as entities

Constraints and dimensions refer to the sketch’s own x and y axes and its origin through entities that stand for them (mitcad#500), made on demand the first time something refers to them:

{"cmd": "sketch.axis", "sketch": "F1", "axis": "x"}
→ {"entity": "c4", "new": true, "entities": ["p5", "c4"], ...}
{"cmd": "sketch.axis", "sketch": "F1", "axis": "x"}
→ {"entity": "c4", "new": false, ...}
  • axis: "x", "y" or "origin" (anything else is refused: unknown axis “z” (x, y or origin)).
  • The origin is the sketch’s fixed point stored at [0, 0] (the one drawing makes when it snaps to the origin, mitcad#355): the first such point that is not projected. Without one, sketch.axis makes it.
  • An axis is a fixed construction line from the origin point (made first when there is none) to a fixed point 100 mm along the axis. The line and that far end carry "axis": "x" (or "y") in the sketch definition and the sketch query; the origin point does not. Only the line’s direction counts: constraints and dimensions take it as the infinite axis (coincident puts a point on it, point_line_distance is a point’s distance from it, angle a line’s angle to it, symmetric mirrors about it), and as construction geometry it bounds no profile. The app draws the axis across the view instead of the line and does not show its far end (app/COMMANDS.md, Sketch Dimension and the constraint tools).
  • One of each. An entity that is there is returned with "new": false, and nothing changes: no undo step. A new one is one undo step Axis in Sketch1, and the result has the editing commands’ fields (entities, status, …) besides entity and "new": true. The app runs it inside the action that needs it and merges the steps (merge_undo), so undo takes the axis back with the constraint or dimension.
  • Sketches saved before have no axis flags and read and save as they were. Copies (move, mirror, patterns) do not copy the flag. The DXF export (export_sketch) leaves the axes’ lines out, also with construction (mitcad#1445).
  • Mirror about an axis (mitcad#876): sketch.mirror takes "axis": "x" or "y" as well as a line; the axis is made (as sketch.axis makes it) in the mirror’s own undo step Mirror in Sketch1, and the copies are symmetric about it. Its made line’s c id works as any line.
  • Not redundant (mitcad#877): a fixed line whose both end points are fixed (an axis line, a projected line) is held in the solve by its points’ fixes alone, so the sketch’s redundant does not list it; the line stays "fixed": true in the definition and the sketch query. So is every fixed curve made only of fixed points (mitcad#1171): an arc with its centre and ends, a spline with its control or fit points (as a projection makes them). A circle or an ellipse keeps its own fix (its radius), and a set of fixes that only repeat each other (a projected arc’s three points, which its own equation ties; a projected circle’s centre) is not listed either.

Code: core/sketch/src/axes.rs. Tests: core/model-tests/sketch/src/sketch_axes_tests.rs, Mirror about an axis core/model-tests/sketch/src/sketch_mirror_876_tests.rs.

Reorient Design

The whole design turned by 90, 180 or 270 degrees about the origin’s X, Y or Z axis (mitcad#502), for a design started on the wrong origin plane. One undo step, Reorient Design:

{"cmd": "reorient_design", "axis": "x", "degrees": 90}
{"cmd": "reorient_design", "plane": "xz"}
→ {"turn": "90 degrees about X", "matrix": [[1, 0, 0], [0, 0, -1], [0, 1, 0]],
 "features": ["Sketch1", "Plane1", "Sketch3"], "moves": ["Move1"],
 "occurrences": [], "views": 1, "analyses": 0, "lights": 0}
  • axis (x, y, z) with degrees (90, 180, 270; -90 is 270), counter-clockwise looking against the axis; or plane (xz, yz): the turn that takes that origin plane’s frame onto XY’s (XZ: 90 about X, YZ: 270 about Y). xy and other turns of nothing are refused.
  • A rewrite, not a move. Every component that is not linked from another file turns in its own coordinates, so that its origin planes are where the turned design wants them:
    • references to the origin’s planes and axes become their turned counterparts: the origin datum the turn takes them onto, frame and sense included (XZ turned 90 about X is XY), else the fixed plane or axis there (XY turned 90 about X faces -Y: {"origin": [0, 0, 0], "normal": [0, -1, 0], "x_axis": [1, 0, 0]}; the Z axis runs along -Y). Fixed planes, axes, points and paths turn, and so do the positions and directions definitions keep (a hole’s points, a split’s direction, picks of surface features, a Move’s and a Move Face’s matrix (a Move Face’s since mitcad#1937), construction geometry given by coordinates, joint frame overrides);
    • a Move’s or a Move Component’s x, y and z go with their axes; a value of an axis the turn reverses is negated (its own dimension parameter; one that other values or features use refuses the command);
    • an Emboss’s Along Axis and Around count along its face’s axis made to point towards +Z of the component (else +Y, else +X): where the turn takes that direction to the other sense (a rod along +Z turned to lie along -Y counts along +Y), both are negated as a Move’s values are (mitcad#1315);
    • a sketch on an origin plane goes onto the origin plane the turn takes its plane onto, with its own frame (frame) set so that its geometry turns with the design, not mirrored. A sketch on a face or a construction plane keeps its plane; where the plane’s frame follows the model axes (a face’s x axis is the model’s X projected) its own frame is set from the turned design’s evaluation so that it stays turned with the design. A sketch that only solves in its turned frame (a projected line that a constraint keeps vertical lies horizontal while its plane’s frame is not yet corrected) gives no frame to correct by; its frame is then read from the turned design up to it with its constraints and dimensions left out (mitcad#1937);
    • an imported body (a base feature) gets a Move right after it that turns its bodies about the origin, named by their own ids (a body kept after Find Repeated Parts took copies out keeps its number, F1.b2 in the second place) (a base feature that joins, cuts or intersects is refused; one without bodies, which only removes the bodies it replaces, gets no Move, mitcad#1937); a body the kernel’s checker finds invalid (an imported shell that is not connected) turns as it is;
    • the pieces of split faces (F2:side(c1[c4,c2])#1) and the edges numbered between the same two faces (E{…}#1) are numbered by the kernel in a geometric order, which the turn changes: references to them (also inside other names, F5:fillet(E{…#1…})) are renamed after the turned design’s numbers, each piece to the one where the turn takes it (its box; an edge’s middle), feature by feature (mitcad#537);
    • occurrences’ placements turn in both coordinates they join (R · T · R⁻¹; an occurrence of a linked component R · T), so a component placed at the identity stays there; joints, constraints and links between components follow from them;
    • named views, section analyses’ planes and the lights placed in the design (not those that follow the camera) turn; what split features remember of their pieces turns with them;
    • image references’ planes turn as section analyses’ do, and comments' free points (at, in their components’ coordinates) and last known places turn with the design (mitcad#1315); comments on faces, edges and bodies follow their targets by name.
  • Faces, edges and bodies keep their names; nothing else is renamed.
  • Checked before it is taken: the command computes the turned design and refuses it, naming them, when a feature that built would fail (a Move it adds too), or a body (its bounding box and centre of mass) or an occurrence would not be where the turn takes it; the document is then as it was. Rules of the model axes that a definition cannot carry (a cylinder’s axis pointing along its largest component, a joint frame’s default x axis) can make a design refuse a turn so. The refusal says where (mitcad#537):
    • a feature with its component and error: Reorient Design cannot turn the design: Fillet3 (in Part) would fail: …, an added Move after the base feature it turns: Move1 (after Base1, in leg) would fail: …;
    • a body with its component, the first feature after which it is not its old self turned (a Move added after a base feature counts with it) and how far: Reorient Design cannot turn the design exactly: Body17 of leg (made by Base1) departs from the turn after Extrude2: its centre is 412.000 mm and its box up to 500.000 mm from where the turn takes it.
  • The application previews it on a command checkpoint (begin_command, restore_command for each choice, discard_command on OK) and logs the bodies’ boxes afterwards (app/COMMANDS.md, “Reorient Design”).

Mount frames

Any part may say where it mounts (mitcad#525; the library’s side in docs/libraries.md, the app’s Place Part in app/COMMANDS.md): a joint origin with a mount is a mount frame of its design.

{"type": "joint_origin", "geometry": {"body": "F1.b0", "face": "F1:top"},
 "mount": {"name": "head", "kind": "shaft", "joint": "cylindrical"}}
{"type": "joint_origin", "geometry": {"origin": [0, 0, 5], "normal": [0, 0, 1], "x_axis": [1, 0, 0]},
 "mount": {"name": "grid", "kind": "grid", "pitch": [42, 42], "cells": [3, 2]}}
{"type": "joint_origin", "geometry": {"origin": [21, 21, 0], "normal": [0, 0, -1], "x_axis": [1, 0, 0]},
 "mount": {"name": "foot", "kind": "foot", "footprint": [1, 1], "pitch": [42, 42]}}
  • name: 1 to 64 of letters, digits, _, -, + and ..
  • kind: face (the default), shaft, hole, grid or foot; what each frame is and what it goes on is the table of docs/libraries.md. Mated frames face each other: the placed frame’s z is opposite the target’s.
  • joint: how the placed part may move, the joint its placement makes: rigid (the default; the only one of grid and foot), planar and revolute on a face, revolute, cylindrical and slider (along the axis) in a hole or on a shaft.
  • pitch (two lengths, mm, along the frame’s x and y) of a grid and, optionally, of a foot; cells (two counts) of a grid, the cells along +x and +y from the frame’s origin; footprint (two counts) of a foot, the cells it covers along its x and y, the frame in their middle. A check of the feature refuses anything else (mount: a grid gives its cells).
  • A joint origin named mount:<name> without a mount (BUILD’s parts, BUILD) is a face frame of that name, fixed. A design’s frames are its joint origins before the marker, not suppressed, each name once (the first); a derived part’s frames (derived_part) are these too.

Inserted parts keep their frames. insert_component (a file or a library part):

  • linked: the design’s frames become joint origins of the new component on fixed planes where the design has them (in its row), each with its mount, named mount:<name> (mount:<name> (2) when the name is taken); update_links and update_library_parts move them with a new version or row (one the design no longer has stays where it was);
  • a copy: the copied joint origins are the frames (a mount:<name> one gets its mount and its name back).

So a part dropped in is joined later with add_joint by a frame as by any joint origin ("a": {"occurrence": "Lamp:1", "geometry": "F12"}). Paste New of a linked part copies its bodies only, not its frames.

Placing by a frame. insert_component with mount:

{"cmd": "insert_component", "library": {"id": "test-mounts", "url": "...", "rev": "v1.0.0", "component": "bin1x1"},
 "mount": {"frame": "foot",
 "at": {"occurrence": "Baseplate:1", "geometry": "F9", "point": [68, 21, 5], "toward": [0, 0, 1]},
 "rotate": "90 deg", "offset": 0, "flip": false}}
  • frame: the part’s frame (its name; the first frame when left out).
  • at: what was picked, as a joint’s origin from the active component: occurrence (a path, uids or names; empty: its own geometry), geometry, the click’s point and the way toward the viewer, both in the active component’s coordinates.
  • rotate (an angle about the frame’s z; a number is radians), offset (a length along it: a gap) and flip (the target turned over: a plane’s other side, a hole’s other end).

The part goes into the active component as without mount, placed where its frame meets the target face to face, and a joint of the frame’s joint is made in the active component: a the new occurrence’s frame, b the target, flip true, angle and offset the values given, its free motions driven at 0 (position) there. So the part moves with what it stands on (a planar joint does not slide when its face moves) and a drag still moves it as the joint lets it (drag_occurrence drives the new values). One undo step, Insert <name>.

The frame Takes Side b
face, grid a planar face, an origin or construction plane, a joint origin the plane’s frame (a face’s: its middle), its shift the click’s place in the plane
shaft, hole a cylindrical or conical face, a circular edge, an axis a cylindrical face’s frame at the end towards toward (the other with flip), z out of that end (frame_override z and shift); an edge’s or an axis’ frame with z towards the viewer
foot a grid of the picked part: its joint origin, else the grid the click is on (any geometry of the part) the grid’s joint origin, its shift the middle of the footprint’s cells

On a grid the footprint is turned by rotate, which must be quarter turns (on a grid Bin 1x1 turns in quarter turns (0, 90, 180 or 270 deg)); its first cell is the one that centres the footprint nearest the click, kept within the grid ((0, 0) without a point). The cells another foot’s joint to the same grid covers (its shift, angle and footprint) are taken: a placement onto one is refused (the cell (0, 1) of Baseplate:1's grid is taken by Bin 2x1:1; several: the cells (0, 0) and (1, 0) ... are taken by A and B). A foot whose pitch is not the grid’s (Bin 1x1 stands on a grid of 40 × 40 mm; Baseplate:1's grid is 42 × 42 mm), a footprint larger than the grid, a pick the frame does not take (Lamp lies on a face: pick a flat face or a plane, not a round one, Screw goes into a hole or onto a shaft: pick its round face or its rim) and a frame the part has not (Lamp has no mount frame wall (its frames: ceiling)) are refused; the document is as it was.

Query Fields Result
mount_frames occurrence (a path from the active component; empty: its own) component, frames: the mount frames at the marker of the component the path ends in and of those placed in it, each name, kind, joint, pitch, cells, footprint, feature, occurrence (its path name), path, frame ({origin, x_axis, y_axis, z_axis} in the design)
mount_preview insert_component’s fields (link, name, transform taken, not used) the part’s name and frames (each frame in the part’s coordinates); with mount what the placement would do: frame, kind, joint, target (occurrence, path, geometry, frame_override and name: side b), at (where the frame goes, in the design), placement (rows, in the active component), world (4x4, in the design), grid (a foot’s: feature, occurrence, path, pitch, cells, cell, footprint, turns, covers: its cells), or problems with the refusal; nothing changes

analysis_shape with {"shape": "mount_preview", ...} and the same fields gives the part’s bodies where the placement puts them, in the design’s coordinates. mount_frames is class model, mount_preview file IO (it reads the part as insert_component does).

Code: features/joint.rs (MountSpec), document/mounts.rs (the frames, inserts, the plan, grids), api/mounts.rs; the library side core/vcs/src/library/mounts.rs. Tests: core/model-tests/joints/src/mount_tests.rs (mock kernel), core/vcs/src/tests/library_mounts.rs, tools/ui-mount-test.sh and tools/ui-windows-mount-test.ps1 (ctest app.ui-windows-mount).

Move face 

{"type": "move_face", "body": "F2.b0", "faces": ["F2:side(c1)"],
 "transform": {"type": "translate_xyz", "x": -1.856, "y": 0, "z": -0.361}}

Moves faces of one body by a rigid motion (mitcad#343; the .f3d import’s moved faces). transform is a move’s (move, align, scale: free, translate_xyz, translate_along, rotate, point_to_point, point_to_position); it must be a rotation and a translation and must move something. Each face keeps its surface, moved; the neighbouring faces stay on their surfaces and extend or shorten up to the moved ones: an edge between a moved face and one that stays becomes their surfaces’ intersection next to where it was, and the vertices follow. A rod’s side moved square to its axis, its ends planes square to it, moves the whole rod. Every face keeps its names, and the body keeps its faces, edges and vertices: a motion that would make a face vanish or split, or leave an edge’s faces apart near it, fails (“the neighbouring faces cannot follow the moved faces”). Its preview reports what a rotate, point_to_point or point_to_position motion was worked out from as motion, as a move’s does (preview, mitcad#854): a circular edge’s axis in its canonical direction, which the app’s Rotate ring turns about.

Code: core/model/src/features/move_face.rs, geometry/src/move_faces.cpp (move_faces_rigidly: OCCT’s BRepTools_Modifier with the moved surfaces, the new edges and the vertices where they meet). Tests: move_face_moves_faces_by_a_rigid_motion (core/model/src/features/f2_tests.rs, mock kernel), geometry (geometry/tests/test_move_faces.cpp, OCCT).

Scale Pattern 

{"type": "scale_pattern", "objects": {"type": "features", "features": ["F4"]},
 "quantity": 3, "scale": 1.5, "compute": "identical"}
{"type": "scale_pattern", "objects": {"type": "bodies", "bodies": ["F2.b0"]},
 "quantity": 2, "scale": 0.5, "combine": false}

Copies scaled where they are (mitcad#539; FreeCAD’s Scaled transformation alone or first in a MultiTransform): element e of quantity is the objects scaled by 1 + (scale − 1) · e / (quantity − 1) about the centre of mass of the first object (a feature’s tool, the first body); element 0 is the original. Otherwise a pattern whose elements do not move: objects (bodies, features; not faces, fillets, chamfers or sheet features), compute, original_bodies, combine (bodies) and suppressed_elements as there; copies of bodies are new bodies <pattern>.b<k>, faces <pattern>:inst<e>(<face>). A pattern or mirror of it (patterns of patterns) places its scaled copies, so that a scale pattern and then a rectangular pattern of it give every scaled copy at every place. A factor must be positive. scale_center, scales (one run per element by default) and skipped_copies as for patterns (mitcad#542).

The patterns’ and the mirror’s scale scales the copies they make instead of adding scaled ones: each copy (of an inner pattern’s copies too) about its own centre by its element’s (or its run’s, scale_groups, over scale_copies) factor; scales multiply.

Code: core/model/src/features/scale_pattern.rs, the scaling in pattern.rs (Scaling). Tests (mock kernel, f4_tests.rs): scale_patterns_scale_copies_where_they_are, scale_groups_scale_runs_of_elements_alike, scaled_patterns_of_patterns_scale_each_copy_about_its_own_centre, a_mirror_scales_its_image_about_the_image_s_centre, patterns_of_bodies_join_their_copies_with_combine, scale_runs_over_the_copies_of_patterns_of_patterns, several_scales_multiply_and_a_scale_centre_is_carried, skipped_copies_are_not_made_but_patterns_of_the_pattern_place_them; OCCT: tools/cli/tests/f4_pattern_scaled.json (cli.f4_pattern_scaled).

Printable bearings

A printable_bearing feature (mitcad#577; core/model/src/features/printable_bearing.rs the definition, its section, placement and checks, bearing_sizes.rs the standard sizes, api/bearings.rs the queries and the parts list’s purchased rows) makes a deep groove bearing that a 3D printer prints in one piece: an inner race, an outer race and the rolling elements, each a body of its own, with clearances between them so that nothing touches; or a variant that takes bought 6 mm airsoft balls in a snap-in cage. It is a bearing to print, not a bought one (bought bearings are library parts). The application’s Bearing panel makes them (app/COMMANDS.md). Tests: features::printable_bearing_tests, tools/cli/tests/bearings.json (cli.bearings, and cli.bearings_3mf: the 608’s bodies as the parts of one 3MF object).

{"type": "printable_bearing", "element": "dumbbell", "size": "608", "plane": "xy", "center": [0, 0],
 "radial_clearance": 0.4, "axial_clearance": 0.4, "element_gap": 0.6, "chamfer": 0.4, "min_wall": 1.2,
 "operation": "new_component"}
{"type": "printable_bearing", "element": "airsoft", "bore": 15, "outside_diameter": 35, "width": 11,
 "flange": {"diameter": 39, "thickness": 1.5}, "plane": "xy", "operation": "new_body"}
{"type": "printable_bearing", "size": "608", "groove": {"body": "F6.b0", "face": "F8:side(c1)"},
 "offset": 2, "operation": "new_body"}
{"type": "printable_bearing", "seat": {"shaft": {"body": "F11.b0", "edge": "E{F11:end(r{c1})|F11:side(c1)}"},
 "offset": 5}, "fit_clearance": 0.5}
Field Value
element dumbbell (the default): a waisted roller touching each raceway on two flanks, centring itself; roller: a cylinder with chamfered ends, line contact; ball: a printed ball (with conical caps, see below); airsoft: bought airsoft balls in a printed snap-in cage
size a standard size: 60x/60xx, 62x/62xx, 63x/63xx, 68x/68xx, 69x/69xx, 160xx, MR.. (miniature), R.. (inch), F.. and MF.. (flanged; their flange comes with them). Case and spaces do not matter. Not with bore, outside_diameter and width
bore, outside_diameter, width custom dimensions (mm), without size
flange diameter, thickness: a flange on the outer race at the face on the plane (an F size’s own without it)
element_diameter the elements’ largest diameter (an airsoft ball’s, 5.95 mm without it); without it the largest that leaves the races made walls of min_wall, or of a sixth of the section (a quarter of the room with groove) when that is more
element_count how many elements, at least 3; the most that fit without it
radial_clearance the gap across the cylindrical faces between elements and races (0.4 mm)
axial_clearance the gap along the axis at the flanks (0.4 mm); a flank’s normal gap is ca sin(a), 0.2828 mm at 45 degrees
element_gap the least gap between neighbouring elements (0.6 mm; airsoft balls 2 radial_clearance + min_wall, room for the cage’s fingers)
chamfer the races’ 45-degree chamfers at the bore and the outside (0.4 mm)
min_wall the thinnest wall a race, an element’s waist or ends and a cage may have (1.2 mm)
flank_angle the flanks’ angle from the axis, 10 to 80 degrees (45 degrees): their overhang printed with the axis vertical
plane, center, angle where the axis meets its plane (the plane’s normal), in the plane’s coordinates, the bearing running along the normal from the plane; angle turns the elements (element 1 on the plane’s x axis without it). Not with groove
groove, offset a cylindrical face of a body ({"body": ..., "face": ...}): the raceway is cut into it, the body becoming one race (a bore’s body the outer race, a shaft’s the inner race), offset from the face’s low end along its axis (the middle of the face without it); new_body only: the bodies stay in the body’s component. The groove runs axial_clearance past the bearing’s faces (at the raceway’s radius there), so the elements’ ends keep that gap from its end walls where the body goes on past them. With a bore the inner race’s bore (or a size’s) is used, with a shaft the outer race’s outside_diameter
seat, fit_clearance on a shaft or in a hole (below): {"shaft": {"body": ..., "edge": ...}, "offset": 5, "flip": false, "near": [x, y, z], "link": {...}} as Seats on shafts takes it; fit_clearance (0.5 mm) for the size that fits. Not with plane or groove
operation new_component (the default: the component named after the size, Bearing 608 (8x22x7), or its dimensions, Bearing 10x30x9) or new_body

Values are parameters: numbers in mm (radians for angles; element_count unitless) or names and expressions. element_diameter, element_count and element_gap are automatic only when left out (mitcad#656): a 0 is refused with the reason (must be greater than zero, at least 3, below the 0.2 mm that a printer keeps open), never taken as automatic; a design could never store one.

  • The section. R the distance from the axis, z along it from the face on the plane (the print bed: the bearing prints with its axis vertical) to the far face at the width W. The elements turn about axes parallel to the bearing’s on the pitch circle (radius Rp); each race is bounded by one function race(z) of the distance from the pitch circle, the inner race at Rp - race(z), the outer at Rp + race(z), so the two mirror each other. With t the flanks' slope (tan(flank_angle)), D and r the elements’ largest diameter and radius, cr and ca the clearances:

    • dumbbell: from face to face, a V waist h = min(D/4, 0.8 t W/2) deep in the middle; the races’ V ridge reaches into the waist, race(z) = min(r + cr, r - h + t ca + t |z - W/2|);
    • roller: from face to face, its ends chamfered by k = min(D/4, t W/4) at the flank angle; the races’ lips over the chamfers, race(z) = min(r + cr, r - k + t ca + t z, r - k + t ca + t (W - z));
    • ball: a sphere centred at W/2 with conical caps tangent to it at the flank angle’s latitude, cut by the faces: it stands on the bed and overhangs by the flank angle at most; race(z) = max(cr, min(r + cr, r / cos(a) + t ca - t |z - W/2|)): a flat cr from the equator and flanks along the caps;
    • airsoft: spheres (bought) in the same grooves, the lands 0.55 r from the pitch circle instead of cr; the cage a ring above the balls to the far face with fingers between them down past their equators, its pockets spheres r + cr round the balls whose openings at the fingers’ tips are 0.2 mm narrower than a ball (they snap in). The races print in place without balls: the balls go in by hand through the crescent with the inner race pushed against the outer one, then they are spread out and the cage, printed on its ring, snaps in from the far face.

    The races’ edges at the bore and the outside have 45-degree chamfers; a flange lies on the outer race at the face on the plane.

  • Count. The most elements that fit round the pitch circle with element_gap between the widest parts of neighbours; airsoft balls at most those that go into the crescent: where the groove bottoms’ gap 2 (r + cr) - 2 land cos(phi) holds a ball, an arc of 2 (pi - acos(cr / land)), touching (one more than the arc over the angle between touching balls).

  • Checks (an error, nothing resized): too many elements for the pitch circle (or fewer than 3), a wall of a race, an element or the cage below min_wall, a clearance or gap below 0.2 mm, an element not held (it must reach 0.2 mm past the ridge, the lips or the lands), an overhang steeper than 45 degrees printed with the axis vertical (a flank angle above 45 degrees), a printed ball below 3 mm (it sticks or rattles) or one that does not reach the bed (D >= W sin(a)), airsoft balls that do not fit the section (the walls, the cage’s ring above them, its width, its fingers), a chamfer not smaller than the walls, a flange not larger than the outside or as thick as the width.

  • Faces: the inner race’s side(c1…) (its section’s lines from the bore’s lower chamfer round), the outer race’s side(c101…), the first element’s side(c201…) and the others’ inst<k>(…) (copies turned about the axis), an airsoft ball’s side0, the cage’s side(c301…), the raceway cut into a body side(c401…).

  • Bodies, in order: the inner race (not with a groove in a shaft), the outer race (not with a groove in a bore), the elements from element 1 counter-clockwise, the cage.

  • Mount frames: bore (on the axis at the face on the plane, z the axis), face_a (that face, z out of the bearing), face_b (the far face, z out of it), taken as {"mount": "F3:mount(bore)"} as a pulley’s (Mount frames).

  • Printing: the 3MF export writes the bodies as the parts of one object in their places, so a slicer prints the bearing in one piece; an STL file holds one body. The airsoft balls are bodies too, to see and check the bearing; leave them out of the print.

  • Parts list: an airsoft bearing’s balls are a purchased row of parts_list after the components’ rows: name and designation Airsoft ball 6 mm (the bought diameter rounded), quantity the balls per bearing times the placements of the component they are in (its row’s quantity; the root’s once), component that component, purchased true, features the bearings; rows of the same designation in one component add up.

  • On a shaft or in a hole (seat, mitcad#578, Seats on shafts): a shaft’s circular end edge or side face, or a hole’s rim or wall, followed through its topological name. The bearing lies on the plane through the seat’s origin normal to its axis and runs along the axis into the shaft or the hole: on a shaft seat.offset is how far from the shaft’s end, in a hole how deep (0: flush with the face); seat.flip measures from the other end. Without size or custom dimensions the bearing takes the standard size whose bore fits the shaft (in a hole: whose outside diameter fits the hole) within fit_clearance (0.5 mm), the nearest, the table’s order among sizes as near; none within it is an error (no standard bearing's bore is within 0.5 mm of the 11 mm shaft: choose a size or give custom dimensions). A size given is used as it is. Not with plane, center, groove or offset. A new component without a size is named Bearing (the panel gives the size it fitted, so its component is named after it).

Query Fields Result
bearing_values uid (a bearing feature) or def (a definition as add_feature takes it, without type) element, designation, bore, outside_diameter, width, flange, element_diameter, element_count, max_elements, pitch_diameter, radial_clearance, axial_clearance, element_gap, chamfer, min_wall, flank_angle, min_gap (the least normal gap between an element and a race), inner_wall, outer_wall (null for a body’s own race), element_wall (an element’s thinnest), hold (how far an element reaches past its ridge, lips or lands), max_overhang, raceway_depth; a dumbbell’s waist_diameter; airsoft cage (ring, width, pocket_diameter) and purchased (designation, quantity); with groove groove (diameter, race: outer or inner); with seat seat (as the seat_frame query gives it), shaft_diameter (the shaft’s or the hole’s) and fits (the designations within fit_clearance, the nearest first); component_name with new_component; error when the values make no printable bearing (then only element beside it)
bearing_sizes fit (bore for a shaft, outside for a hole) with diameter and clearance (0.5 mm), or neither; series (optional) sizes: designation, series, bore, outside_diameter, width, flange (diameter, thickness, or null); with fit those within clearance of diameter, the nearest first

The sizes are our own compilation of the standards’ boundary dimensions: ISO 15 for the metric series (the dimension series 18, 19, 00, 10, 02 and 03 of the deep groove type, and the miniature sizes under their common MR designations), ISO 8443 for the flanges of the F and MF sizes, ANSI/ABMA 12.2 for the inch R series (converted at 25.4 mm to the inch); the widths are the open bearings'.

Seats on shafts

A part that sits on a round shaft or in a round hole is placed by it instead of by a plane and a centre (mitcad#578; core/model/src/features/seat.rs the definition and its one resolver, api/seats.rs the query): a pulley, a gear with a bore, and a printable bearing (mitcad#577) take a seat, and the application’s panels take it with the same inputs (Shaft, Offset, Flip, Bore Clearance; app/commands/SeatInputs.hpp).

{"type": "pulley", "kind": "toothed", "profile": "gt2_2mm", "teeth": 20, "belt_width": 6,
 "seat": {"shaft": {"body": "F2.b0", "face": "F2:side(c1)"}, "offset": 3, "flip": false,
 "near": [4, 0, 28], "link": {"source": "O1", "target": ""}},
 "bore_clearance": 0.2, "operation": "new_body"}
Field Value
shaft a circular edge (a shaft’s end edge, a hole’s rim) or a cylindrical face (a shaft’s side, a hole’s wall) of a body. An edge must end a cylindrical face of its radius on its axis; anything else is refused with its name
link the shaft’s body is another component’s (a BUILD shaft, a library part): the occurrence link {"source": <path to the shaft's component>, "target": <path the feature's component is seen at>} as a sweep’s body_links take it (Geometry of other components); the shaft is read in its component and moved by the placements at the feature’s point of the timeline, so the part follows when the shaft’s occurrence moves
offset mm along the axis from the end measured from; 0 without it. A parameter
flip measured from the shaft’s other end, the part facing back along the shaft
near where a face was picked (mm, in the coordinates of the shaft’s component, as a pick gives it): the end of the face nearer it is the end measured from, wherever the shaft’s occurrence moves; the face’s low end along its axis without it. An edge is its own end
  • The seat: the end measured from (the picked edge, or the face’s end nearer near; flip the other end of the cylindrical face), the axis from that end into the shaft (into the hole), the origin offset along it and the shaft’s (hole’s) diameter. The part’s plane goes through the origin normal to the axis (its x axis as a plane’s without one: References to geometry) and the part runs along the axis from it: a pulley at offset 0 starts at the shaft’s end and runs along the shaft; flipped it starts at the other end and runs back. A hole picked at its rim gives the axis into the hole: a part at offset depth sits depth below the face, flush at 0.
  • Bores: a seated pulley or gear without bore has a plain bore of the shaft’s diameter plus bore_clearance (a keyway goes into it); it follows the shaft’s diameter. The wall rules of a too large bore apply to it (a pulley’s 0.5 mm to the groove bottoms, a gear’s module to its roots). A threaded bore stays its thread’s tap drill.
  • Belts and meshes: a pulley or gear on a shaft can be the first of a belt pair (belt_with) or a mesh (mesh_with): the second lies in its plane. The second is not seated itself.
  • Recompute: the seat reads the shaft’s body (and, with link, the occurrences’ placements); a shaft made thicker, longer or moved rebuilds the part, and a shaft face or edge that no longer resolves fails it with the reason (seat: …).
  • Copies, moves and reparents carry the seat’s link like a sweep’s body_links; the occurrences a feature refers to and the design policy see it.
Query Fields Result
seat_frame seat (as a feature takes it), component (the seated feature’s; the active one without it) where the seat puts a part at the timeline marker, in that component’s coordinates: origin, axis (unit, into the shaft or hole), end (the end measured from), diameter, length (the cylindrical face’s along the axis), hole (a hole’s wall); an error when the shaft is not round or does not resolve

pulley_values and gear_values resolve a definition’s seat the same way (bore_diameter, shaft_diameter, seat). Tests: features::seat (the frame), features::seat_tests (pulleys and gears on the mock kernel), tools/cli/tests/pulleys.json, tools/cli/tests/gears.json, tools/ui-pulley-test.sh, tools/ui-windows-pulley-test.ps1, tools/ui-gear-test.sh, tools/ui-windows-gear-test.ps1.

Printed fit parameters

The Thread, Gear, Pulley, Bearing and Hole panels offer ordinary user parameters for different printed fits. Their names, defaults, fields and comments come from one table in core/model/src/print_fits.rs:

Parameter Panel field Default
thread_radial_clearance modelled thread radial_clearance 0.1 mm
thread_flank_clearance modelled thread flank_clearance 0.1 mm, at most what each thread’s pitch takes (see the thread’s flank_clearance)
shaft_bore_clearance seated gear or pulley bore_clearance 0.2 mm
gear_backlash gear backlash 0.2 mm
bearing_radial_clearance printable bearing radial_clearance 0.4 mm
bearing_axial_clearance printable bearing axial_clearance 0.4 mm
bearing_element_gap printable bearing element_gap 0.6 mm
bearing_fit_clearance printable bearing fit_clearance 0.5 mm
press_fit_interference press-fit hole press_fit.interference (mitcad#1517) 0.1 mm
print_in_place_gap none: Print Analysis’ narrow gap reads it (Narrow gaps between bodies printed in place, mitcad#1519) 0.3 mm
hole_roof_sag flat-roofed hole roof_sag (mitcad#1515) 0.4 mm

An explicit feature-field expression referencing one of these names creates the missing user parameter with its default, unit and a comment describing the fit and the printer quality that affects it. Creation and add_feature or edit_feature share one undo step: undo removes both, redo restores both, and a rejected command leaves neither behind. Previews use a private definition-state copy; canceling a panel adds no parameters. An applied feature with a geometry error keeps the parameters its definition uses, like other applied features.

An existing parameter always wins: its value, unit and comment stay as they are. Features bind parameter IDs, so renaming keeps their references; the next explicit use of the old default name creates a new parameter. Deleting an in-use parameter is refused as for any other user parameter.

Omitted fields keep their existing JSON API defaults. Numeric definitions, old files and imports acquire no fit parameters merely by opening or recomputing. Plain Hole has no new clearance field; its Press Fit offers press_fit_interference in Interference, and its Flat Roof print shape hole_roof_sag in Roof Sag (mitcad#1515).

{"query":"printed_fit_parameters"} returns the table as an array of name, field, features, value (millimetres), unit and comment. The panel’s evaluate query can pass "printed_fits":true to evaluate not-yet-created fit names against a temporary parameter copy. Without that opt-in, unknown names remain errors. Definition-based gear_values, pulley_values and bearing_values also understand these prospective defaults; none of these queries changes the document.

Tests: print_fits::tests, the shared tools/ui-scripts/printed-fits.mitcad-ui workflow, ui-print-fits-test.sh, app.ui-windows-print-fits, app.ui-macos-print-fits and app.ui-macos-native-print-fits.

Print analysis

Where bodies will print badly and what they will take, before they go to a slicer (mitcad#620): overhangs, walls thinner than the printer makes, and an estimate of the filament, its mass and its cost. It is an analysis only: no body, feature, timeline or export changes, and the bed face only sets the analysis’ print direction (no body moves; 3D Print’s files stay as they are). The work is done in Rust (core/model/src/print_analysis.rs, the queries in api/print.rs) on what the kernel already gives: each body’s Kernel::triangle_mesh (the 3MF export’s mesh, the one a slicer gets) and Kernel::physical_properties.

A print analysis is kept in the document as an analysis with "type": "print" (default name Print1, Print2, …):

{"type": "print", "bodies": ["F2.b0"], "bed_face": null,
 "overhang": {"enabled": true, "angle": 45},
 "thin_wall": {"enabled": true, "minimum": 0.8},
 "estimate": {"enabled": true, "material": null, "line_width": 0.4, "walls": 2,
 "layer_height": 0.2, "top_bottom_layers": 4, "infill": 0.15,
 "filament_diameter": 1.75, "price_per_kg": null}}
Field Value
bodies body uids, at least one: solids and mesh bodies
bed_face a planar face of one of the bodies (face reference) lying on the bed: its outward normal is the print direction (down). It follows the model by its topological name, as a section’s plane does. null (the default): the design’s −Z is down and each body lies on its lowest point
overhang enabled, angle (degrees from the vertical, 0 to 90; 45 by default)
thin_wall enabled, minimum (mm, greater than zero; 0.8 by default, two line widths)
min_gap enabled, gap (mm, greater than zero; null, the default: the design’s print_in_place_gap, else 0.3 mm): Narrow gaps between bodies printed in place (mitcad#1519)
estimate enabled, material (a material id or name, Visibility and display lists them; null: each body’s own material, PLA for a body without one), line_width (mm, 0.4), walls (a whole number, 2), layer_height (mm, 0.2), top_bottom_layers (a whole number, 4), infill (a fraction from 0 to 1, 0.15), filament_diameter (mm, 1.75), price_per_kg (a number in any currency, null for no cost)

Fields left out take these defaults, also inside overhang, thin_wall and estimate; other fields are refused, in commands and in design files. add_analysis and edit_analysis refuse settings out of range, an unknown material, a body that is not there at the marker and a bed face that is not a planar face of one of the analysis’ bodies. The analyses query gives each print analysis its file form with down (the unit print direction in design coordinates at the marker) or error (why a body or the bed face is not there; the analysis stays and the application shows it red with the reason). enabled is the application’s: the queries below are asked for the parts that are on.

Three queries do the work; the application asks them with a definition’s settings. All take bodies (body uids; all bodies at the marker when empty or left out). A body is analysed where it is shown in the design: moved by its first shown occurrence (else its first one; a mirroring placement keeps its triangles facing out), so triangles and points are in design coordinates.

Query Fields Result
print_overhangs bodies, down ([x, y, z], any length) or bed_face (a face reference; not both; neither: [0, 0, −1]), angle (45), deviation (mm; the 3MF export’s 0.03 when left out) down (unit), angle, bodies: [{body, name, area (mm²), overhang_area (mm²), share (0 to 1), triangles: [[x, y, z, x, y, z, x, y, z], …]}], overhang_area, area and share of all of them
print_thickness bodies, minimum (0.8), deviation, triangles (true; false: the summary only, mitcad#689), max_triangles (at most this many pieces per body) minimum, bodies: [{body, name, thinnest (mm, or null when no ray met the other side: an open mesh), at (the point of the thinnest wall on the surface, or null), to (the point on its other side), regions (connected groups of the thin pieces), thin_triangles (how many pieces), triangles (where the walls are under the minimum, as above: a thin triangle of the mesh whole, or the thin pieces of one thin only in part; left out with "triangles": false), truncated (true when max_triangles left some out)}], thinnest, at, regions, thin_triangles (and truncated) of all of them. Over MCP triangles is false unless the query gives it
print_estimate bodies, the estimate fields (enabled taken and ignored) volume, area (mm³, mm²), shell_volume, infill_volume, filament_volume (mm³), mass (g), length (m of filament), cost (or null without a price), material (its name; the names of several, comma-separated), material_id (null for several), density (g/cm³; of several, the filament’s mean), and bodies: the same per body with body and name
  • Overhangs: a triangle of the body’s mesh whose outward normal is within 90° − angle of straight down (normal · down > sin(angle)) overhangs; a face exactly at the angle prints. Triangles facing down with every corner within the mesh’s deviation of the bed lie on the bed and do not overhang: the bed is the bed face’s plane, or the body’s lowest point along down without one. Curved faces are flagged where they are steep, not as a whole.
  • Thin walls: from sample points on each triangle (its centroid; on a triangle longer than 2 mm the centroids of an even subdivision, up to 8 per edge) a ray along the surface’s inward normal to the first triangle of the same mesh where it leaves the material (a bounding volume hierarchy written in Rust); the triangle’s wall is its shortest ray. The surface’s normal at a sample is interpolated from the normals at the triangle’s corners: there, the triangles that meet at the vertex and face within 40° of the triangle, their area normals added up (a triangle’s own normal would miss the centre of a curved wall by the triangle’s tilt). On planar walls the value is exact (next to a tangent blend within the blend’s facet angle); on curved ones it is within the mesh’s deviation. A wall under minimum (by more than 0.000 001 mm) is thin; thin triangles that share a corner, and the two sides of one wall, are one region. The rays run on all cores.
  • Thin pieces (mitcad#767): what is answered and shown is where the wall is thin, not the whole triangle. A triangle whose samples are all thin is answered whole. A triangle thin at only some of its samples (a long triangle of a large planar face that reaches a thin rim) is subdivided 4 times more finely than its samples (at most 32 × 32 pieces, 1024 more rays, the cancel request asked every 256 of them) and only the pieces whose centroid’s wall is thin are answered; the finer samples include the coarse ones, so the thinnest wall is as before. Regions are the connected groups of these pieces: pieces that touch at a corner or along an edge, in one triangle or across the mesh’s vertices and edges, and the two sides of one wall. A thin rim at the edge of a large face is then a band along the rim, and two rims that the face’s triangles span are two regions.
  • Edges are not walls (mitcad#689): next to an edge whose faces meet at an acute angle (a split plane through a fillet, the rim of a hole through a curved wall), the ray along the normal leaves through the neighbouring face at once. A ray is left out when the face it leaves through meets its start across an edge of the body within one sample distance (2 mm) of the start: the planes of the two triangles meet within 2 mm of the sample (and within 8 mm of the exit), and the surfaces around the start and the exit, each across its smooth neighbours (normals within 40°), share a vertex. The two sides of a real thin wall, a fin or a lip, are parallel (within 1°) or do not meet there, so such walls are still found next to edges.
  • Estimate: volume and area from physical_properties; shell = area × walls × line width (the top and bottom layers counted in it, at most the volume), infill = (volume − shell) × infill, filament = shell + infill, mass = filament × density, length = filament / (π × (diameter / 2)²), cost = mass × price per kilogram. layer_height and top_bottom_layers are kept with the settings and do not enter these formulas.
  • Errors: a body that is not there at the marker, a bed face that does not resolve to a planar face, or a mesh or volume the kernel cannot make answer {"error": "..."} with the reason; settings out of range, unknown fields and an unknown material are refused as other queries' inputs are.
  • Cancellation: run inside a model job (Document::attach_job, the job’s RecomputeMonitor, Progress and cancellation), print_overhangs and print_thickness check the job between bodies and the rays check it every 256 triangles; a cancelled one is rejected with the computation was cancelled and keeps nothing. Without a job (mitcad-cli) they run to the end.
  • Cache: the meshes and results are kept in memory (the last 8 meshes and 32 results) by the body, its shape’s version, its placement, the mesh tolerance and the settings, so showing an analysis again computes nothing; a body that changes is meshed again.

Tests: print_analysis_tests (the functions on meshes built in the test: a box, a bridge, a T, a tilted box, a sphere against the analytic share, a lying cylinder, a plate, a shelled box, a thin lip at the edge of a plate and lips at both edges (thin pieces and regions), a uniformly thin plate shown whole, the estimate of a 20 mm cube), api::print_tests (the definition, the queries on the mock kernel, the cache, cancellation, no change to bodies and the 3MF file), tools/cli/tests/analysis.json (a box and a sphere on the OCCT kernel).

Materials

What bodies are made of (mitcad#640; core/model/src/material.rs, document/materials.rs, api/materials.rs). A material is an object: its id, name, density (g/cm³), the appearance a body gets with it (an id of the appearances), an optional filament (values of the Print Filament set of the print key map by key: filament_type, temperature, …; no filament_colour, which is its appearance’s (A filament’s colour is its appearance); the density is the material’s own, not a filament_density; a key that names a slicer’s own preset, filament_settings_id, holds {"<slicer id>": "<name>", ...}: the slicer’s filament preset the material is based on, which a 3MF export writes as the filament’s preset and as the preset it inherits from: in inherits_group for the Bambu Studio family, in PrusaSlicer’s inherits_cummulative (mitcad#1065); a material without one is written under its own name, inheriting from nothing, mitcad#1062, print_files_tests), slicer (a slicer’s filament settings the key map does not have, by slicer id: its keys as text, written back only to that slicer; Print profiles), based_on (the material it was made from), version (its version in its library) and origin ({"library", "id", "version"}: where the design’s copy came from; a library’s or an import’s, Print profiles).

  • Built-in materials keep the ids bodies always had (steel, pla, … in Visibility and display), now with an appearance each (steel steel_satin, stainless_steel steel_polished, cast_iron, aluminum aluminum_anodized, copper, brass brass_polished, titanium steel_satin, abs plastic_black, pla plastic_white, nylon plastic_white, polycarbonate plastic_clear, glass glass_clear; water none; resin_standard, Resin - Standard, 1.15 g/cm³, resin_grey, mitcad#1102) and the plastics with a filament_type (ABS, PLA, PA, PC), which makes them FDM plastics. After them, common woods and panels of the bundled dataset (mitcad#1706, Material properties), of the class wood, each with the dataset entry’s density, a solid wood’s Young’s modulus (nothing the dataset does not give), its look and its reference, taken from core/model/data/wood_materials.json (material::BUILT_IN_WOODS): wood_pine (Wood - Pine, wood/pine), wood_oak (Wood - Oak), wood_birch (Wood - Birch), plywood_birch (Plywood - birch, panel/plywood_birch) and mdf_raw (MDF - raw, panel_mdf). Their ids hold _, which no library item’s id (a slug of its name) and no design’s own (custom1) does; a design’s own material of one of their names (made from the dataset before) opens unchanged and keeps changing under its name, while a new one of such a name is refused as for any built-in one.
  • Classes (mitcad#655, mitcad#1102): metal, plastic (General Plastic: moulded, cast, machined or sheet plastic; the id and its group plastics as before, so library parts and scripts that name it are unchanged), fdm_plastic (FDM Plastic, the filaments), resin (the photopolymer resins of resin printers), wood (solid wood and wood-based panels, mitcad#1552) and other, listed in that order. A material with print settings (filament values, slicer keys or variants) is an FDM plastic whatever class it stores (a filament stores plastic or none), worked out when read: the file is not rewritten, and a filament made or edited keeps plastic. fdm_plastic and resin are written only when chosen (for a material without print settings, fdm_plastic). Older versions (before mitcad#1102) open a design or a library file unless it holds a material of class fdm_plastic or resin (an unknown value, as embedded images), and versions before mitcad#1552 one of class wood.
  • The design’s materials are kept in the design file. One with a built-in’s id takes that built-in’s place in the design (a library’s copy of pla with its filament values); deleting it brings the built-in back. Ids are letters, digits, _, -, and / between parts (<vendor>/<product>); names are unique among the materials shown.
  • What a body is made of: its own material, else the default material of the nearest component up the occurrence path that places it (its own component first), else the root’s, else steel. Without a path (a body’s mass in properties, print_estimate, the computed Material property) the body’s own component and the root count. That last steel is no body’s material (mitcad#1817): Physical Properties (properties), the computed properties, the Center of Mass marker, the parts list’s and drawing tables’ material columns and a drawing’s title block (MATERIAL, MASS) say a body without a material has none (No material, or nothing) and give it no mass, nor its component or the total while it has such a body; the marker leaves it out and says how many it left out. Only print analysis gives such a body the print default (below).
  • A part placed from a library is made of its library’s material (mitcad#1817), as it shows its library’s appearance: the material the source design’s shown bodies all name, else the one the material block of its library’s build block names for the part’s row: a timber member’s species (Spruce, the block’s 450 kg/m³ as 0.45 g/cm³, class Wood), a sheet’s or metal part’s product (Steel, galvanised), or both (Plywood - spruce). That material is the design’s own, its reference the library, found again by name and density for every part that names it (a design or built-in material of that name and density is used instead); a block with a density only is the built-in material of that density, if one has it. BUILD gives it when it places, connects or edits a part (a member’s row changed takes the new row’s, a material set by hand stays), and a design saved before gets it on open for every body of a library part without a material of its own. The cut list and the parts list use the same material.
  • Appearance: setting a body’s material sets its appearance to the material’s (appearance: "replace"), keeps the body’s ("keep"), or, left out, replaces it unless the body’s appearance was set by hand: it has one, and it is not the appearance of the material it is made of. The bodies query marks such a body appearance_set_by_hand; the application asks before replacing one (material_conflicts). A component’s default material does not change its bodies’ appearances.
  • The commands are undo steps that recompute nothing.
Command Fields Result
create_material id (the next free custom<n> when left out), name (Material 1, Material 2, … when left out, never New …, mitcad#828; a copy <its source's name> (copy), (copy 2), …, a copy of a copy counted on from its source’s name, mitcad#655, mitcad#828; free among the design’s and the libraries’ names), density, appearance, filament, class (metal, plastic, fdm_plastic, resin, wood or other, mitcad#655, mitcad#1102, mitcad#1552: stored on the material, but plastic for fdm_plastic when the material has print settings, which make it an FDM plastic anyway; left out, a copy keeps its source’s class and a new one is stored as worked out, see library_items; a new wood one without appearance or appearances gets the class’s look, wood_oak, mitcad#1552), based_on (a material whose fields it starts from, by id, or a library’s item {library, id}: Duplicate, with the appearance it carries; 1 g/cm³ and nothing else without it), version, origin, project, properties, reference and dataset (Material properties); with library see Items where they live (Print profiles) id; undo step Create Material Acme PETG (with a library item’s appearance, one step)
edit_material id, and the fields that change: name, density, appearance (null: none), filament (its keys are set, a key with null removed), class, version, origin, properties, reference (Material properties); with library see Items where they live (Print profiles) undo step Edit Material Acme PETG unless nothing changes; a built-in one is refused (create_material with based_on, or with its id, makes one the design can change)

Query Fields Result
materials the built-in materials the design does not replace, in their order, then the design’s: the fields above, built_in, replaces_built_in (a design’s material with a built-in’s id), class (its own or worked out, as in library_items), class_fixed (true when print settings make it an FDM plastic, mitcad#1102), display_color (its appearance’s), bodies (uids of bodies that name it) and components (whose default it is)

The design file keeps the design’s materials as "materials": [{"id", "name", "density", "appearance", "appearances", "filament", "slicer", "variants", "based_on", "class", "version", "origin"}] (fields left out when not set) and the components’ defaults as "component_materials": [{"component", "material"}], both left out when there are none (files without them have none); a body’s "material" may name either. Copies of components into another design bring the materials their bodies and components name (a different one of the same id gets another id, <id>_1) and the components’ defaults; a BUILD part brings a material of its library design. The comparison of versions lists the design’s materials by id and a component’s default material with the component.

Tests: material_tests (built-in ids and their looks, replace and keep, the design’s materials made, edited, deleted and taking a built-in’s place, components’ defaults up the occurrence path, the design file and the comparison), material::tests, tools/ui-material-test.sh (Material… in the context menus).

Print settings key map

MitCad’s keys of print settings, in three sets (mitcad#640; core/print-keys/src/): Print Printer (only what MitCad uses: bed_shape, bed_exclude_area, max_print_height, nozzle_diameter, filament_slots, printer_model, printer_settings_id), Print Process and Print Filament. A key is PrusaSlicer’s where PrusaSlicer has the setting, else Bambu Studio’s (else OrcaSlicer’s); one that would carry a vendor’s name gets a neutral one. Each has a type, a unit, choices, a plain name for the interface and, per slicer dialect (bambu_studio, orcaslicer, qidi_studio, prusaslicer, cura), the slicer’s key and how a value converts (percentages, ratios written as percentages, choices by meaning, percentages of another value resolved through their basis, yes/no, settings split over two keys, Cura’s bed by its sizes). The module documentation names the slicers’ sources it was built from and what the Bambu family’s loader needs to take a 3MF’s settings.

Categories (mitcad#655). Every key has one place in the settings form, the same in the material editor, the profile editor and Property Sets: a category of its set (a tab) and a group in it (a headed section), and is advanced or common. Advanced keys show only with Advanced on, or when an item sets them. The order of the categories, of the groups and of the keys in a group is the display order; the keys come in that order (by set, category and group, common keys first in each group), so that the application keeps no table of its own.

  • Printer: basic_information (groups printable_space, printer_presets), extruder (nozzle).
  • Process: quality (layer_height, line_width, seam, precision, ironing, wall_generator, order_and_flow, bridges_and_overhangs, travel), strength (walls, top_and_bottom_shells, sparse_infill, infill_details), speed (first_layer, other_layers, overhangs, slow_down_by_height, travel_speed, acceleration, jerk, smoothing), support (support, raft, contact_and_interface, support_body, tree_supports, support_filament, support_ironing), others (bed_adhesion, prime_tower, filaments, interlocking, special_modes, fuzzy_skin, gcode_output, process_presets).
  • Filament: filament (filament_basics, flow, nozzle_temperature, bed_temperature, chamber, volumetric_speed, scarf_seam, purge (Purge volumes), filament_presets), cooling (part_cooling_fan, slow_down_for_cooling, overhangs_and_bridges, auxiliary_fan, exhaust_fan), setting_overrides (retraction, toolchange_retraction, override_speed), advanced (filament_change, filament_prime_tower, loading_and_ramming, circle_compensation).

Group ids are unique over the sets; their titles are not (travel and travel_speed are both “Travel”). A choice’s values are MitCad’s (in commands, files and properties), each with a plain name for the interface (inner_outer, “Inner, then outer”).

Query Fields Result
print_keys set (printer, process or filament; all when left out) keys in display order: key, set, name, kind (boolean, integer, number, percent, number_or_percent, text, color, choice, points), unit, category, group (ids), advanced, of (a percentage’s basis), choices ({value, name}), per_dialect (the value names a slicer’s own preset: one per slicer), for a number (integer, number, percent, number_or_percent) min and max (mitcad#746: the widest range the key’s slicers take, in its unit, a number_or_percent key’s for its numbers; each left out where there is no bound: an angle of a direction or a compensation has neither, a length only min 0), dialects: {dialect, key, list} (list: one value per filament or extruder), with that dialect’s own min and max where it takes less (Bambu Studio’s -1 for “automatic” is out of OrcaSlicer’s range of Tree support walls, min 0 and max 2), for a number_or_percent key also percent (mitcad#655: whether that dialect takes a percentage, a form of its own or the same as MitCad’s; Bambu Studio’s line widths do not); layout: per set asked for, {set, categories}, each category {id, title, groups} and each group {id, title}, in display order

Tests: print_keys::tests (the table’s consistency and conversions in both directions between the dialects; every key in a group of its set’s category, no group empty, the rows in display order, every choice named, the layout as the enums), material_tests (print_keys_are_listed_for_the_interface).

Print profiles

Printer and process profiles, the print settings of components, occurrences and bodies, the libraries of materials and profiles, and slicers’ files (mitcad#640; core/model/src/print_profile.rs, document/print_settings.rs, print_library.rs, document/print_library.rs, print_files/, document/print_import.rs, api/print_profiles.rs).

Profiles. The design keeps printer and process profiles: id, name, kind (printer or process), values (keys of the Print Printer or Print Process set of the key map in their JSON form: numbers in the key’s unit, a percentage as its number, a number or a percentage of another value as 0.45 or "110%", choices by name, an outline as [[x, y], ...]; a key that names a slicer’s own preset, printer_settings_id, print_settings_id, printer_model, as {"<slicer id>": "<name>", ...}), slicer (a slicer’s settings the map does not have, by slicer id: its keys as text, written back only to that slicer), raw (a printer’s whole block from a Bambu-family project, by slicer id: not shown, not edited, written back to that slicer only; the queries list only raw_slicers), based_on, version and origin (as a material’s). A printer carries only what MitCad uses: the bed (bed_shape, bed_exclude_area), the printable height, the nozzle, the filament slots, the printer model and the slicers’ preset names; a profile is complete in the design. Values given as text are read in the key’s form ("15%" is 15).

Command Fields Result
create_print_profile kind, id (the name’s when left out, bench-printer; else printer1, process1, …), name (Printer 1, Process 1, then Printer 2, … when left out: one pattern for every kind, mitcad#655, never New …, mitcad#828; a copy <its source's name> (copy), (copy 2), …; free among the design’s and the libraries’ names), values, slicer, based_on (a design profile whose fields it starts from, by id, or a library’s item {library, id}: Duplicate), version, origin, project, choose (true: the design, the root, chooses it in the same undo step, mitcad#655); with library see Items where they live (Print profiles) id; undo step Create Profile Bench printer. Refused: keys of another set, values not of their key, a name another profile of the kind has
edit_print_profile id, and what changes: name, values (a key’s null removes it), slicer (a key’s null removes it), version, origin; with library see Items where they live (Print profiles) undo step Edit Printer Bench printer (Edit Process ...) unless nothing changes; the kind and id cannot change
delete_print_profile id; with library (and kind when the library has a printer and a process of the id) see Items where they live (Print profiles) owners: the components, occurrences and bodies that chose it, which no longer do; undo step Delete Profile Bench printer

The Print property sets. On a component (C0 the root: the design’s), an occurrence or a body (Properties):

  • Print Printer and Print Process hold the profile chosen there (profile, of the own type Print printer profile or Print process profile, whose values are the design’s profiles of the kind) and values set there under MitCad’s keys, typed by the key: yes/no, integers, lengths in mm (length, shown in the design’s units), areas and volumes, other numbers with their unit as a label (°C, mm/s, percentages %), a number or a percentage, text, colours and outlines as text, choices as an own type Print <key> with the choices as its values. set_property takes the key and a value of it (its type and unit are the key’s); a key of another set, a value not of the key, a profile the design has not and a key kept per slicer are refused. The queries give each such property its plain name too. The profile choice is the undo step Use Printer Bench printer (Use Process ...); with library (base, user, project) and project the profile value is that library’s item, copied in first (or the design’s copy of it reused) in the same undo step (mitcad#655).
  • Print Slicer (<slicer>) (Print Slicer (PrusaSlicer), or by the slicer’s id) holds a slicer’s own keys as text, written only to it.
  • Print Filament is the material’s (edit_material): set_property refuses it.
  • An imported value has the source 3mf (Properties: edited and source_value as for the other imports).

Inheritance. A body prints with the values of the root, then of the components down the occurrence path that places it (each occurrence after its component), then its own: the nearest wins. On a level a value set there comes before the values of the profile chosen there, so that a component that chooses a profile prints with that profile whatever the root set, unless it sets a value itself. The filament is the body’s material’s (Materials): its filament values, its density as filament_density and, when it sets no colour, its appearance’s colour as filament_colour; its own slicer keys follow those of the levels and profiles. Without a path a body inherits from its own component and the root. property_sets is unchanged: an occurrence shows only its component’s values as inherited.

Query Fields Result
print_profiles the design’s profiles: their fields (without raw), raw_slicers, chosen_by (the owners that chose each)
print_settings body (uid or name) with occurrence (the path that places it), or occurrence (a path), or component; the root’s when none is given levels (owner, level, name: nearest first), printer and process: profile (id, name, owner, level, owner_name: the nearest chosen) and values, filament: material (id, name) and values; each value key, name, value, text, unit, from (property: owner, level, owner_name; profile: profile, profile_name, owner, level, owner_name; material: material, material_name); slicer: each slicer key’s slicer, key, value and where it comes from
build_volume the root’s printer: printer (id, name) or null, bed (its outline moved so that its middle is on the origin; null without one), excluded, height, shift (what the bed was moved by), outside: the shown bodies whose box is beyond the bed’s outline or height, below the bed or over an excluded area: body, occurrence (uids O1/O4), name, path_name, min, max, reasons

Libraries. Materials and profiles come from three libraries, one JSON item file each (docs/libraries.md, “Materials and print profiles”): the base library (MitCad’s parts library mitcad-parts, its newest version fetched on this computer, through the library resolver), the user’s (print-library in MitCad’s data folder beside libraries, MITCAD_PRINT_LIBRARY_DIR) and the project’s (print-library in the project’s folder, given as project). The same kind and id in several: the nearest wins (project, user, base); the others are listed as shadowed. The design keeps complete copies of the items it uses, with their origin ({"library", "id", "version"}, and declined: a library version the design kept its own values over; an import’s 3mf and the file’s name), so that a library change never changes the design by itself; a material’s appearances (its default and the others of its list, mitcad#1067, A filament’s colour is its appearance) come with it as design appearances.

Command Fields Result
copy_from_print_library library (base, user, project; the nearest when left out), kind (material, printer, process), id, project id in the design, library, version; a copy of the same item is replaced (an update), another of the same id keeps its id and the copy gets <id>_1; undo step Copy Acme PETG from Library
update_from_print_library kind, id (the design’s copy), project version taken: the copy’s fields become the library item’s of its origin, its id stays; undo step Update Draft from Library
decline_print_library_update kind, id (the design’s copy), project version declined (mitcad#655, “Keep these”): the copy keeps its fields and its origin remembers the library’s version as declined, so the change is not offered again until the library changes again; undo step Keep Draft
save_to_print_library library (user or project), kind, id (also a built-in material), project path, version: the next version of the item the copy was saved as before, else a new item (version 1) under the design’s id, a free one (bench-2) when the library has another item of that id; a name another item of the library has gets a counter (Bench 2), which the design’s copy takes too; the design’s copy then names it as its origin. The file and the copy are one undo step (Save Bench to Library): undo takes the file back. The base library is not written
Query Fields Result
print_library project items: library, kind, id, name, version, path, shadowed, in_design (the design’s copies of it), item (its fields; a material’s display_color); updates: the design’s copies whose library item was changed elsewhere (see changed below: kind, id, name, library, library_id, version, newer); folders; problems (files that could not be read)

Items where they live (mitcad#655; document/library_items.rs). The user never handles a copy: choosing an item copies it in, and an item is edited where it lives. An item has a place: mitcad (the built-in materials and the base library; read-only), user, project, or design (the design’s own, in no library: made in the design, imported, or its library item deleted). The app shows only two states: built-in (read-only) or the user’s own, saved in a library or not yet.

  • One list. library_items gives one row per item of a kind the user can choose: the built-in materials the design does not replace (in their order, first), the nearest of each library item (shadowed ones are left out) and the design’s items that are in no library (a copy of a library item that is shadowed now keeps that item’s row), sorted by name. An item and the design’s copy of it are one row, showing the copy’s fields (what the design uses).
  • Made in a library. create_material and create_print_profile with library (user or project) write a new item file (version 1) and change nothing in the design: from based_on (an item of the design, a built-in material, or a library’s item {library, id}: Duplicate) or empty (a material of 1 g/cm³; a profile needs its kind). The name is <name> (copy) (then (copy 2), …, mitcad#828) after the item it is based on, else Material 1, Printer 1, Process 1 (then … 2), free among the libraries’ and the design’s names; the id is the name’s (acme-petg-copy) when not given, free among the libraries’ items. A material’s appearance that is not one of MitCad’s goes with it into the file. The file is an undo step of its own (Create Material Material 1): undo removes it. The print managers (mitcad#704, mitcad#1135, app/COMMANDS.md) make them in the library the user chooses with these commands, on the open design’s model or, with no design open, on an empty design of their own, so that the empty window does not change.
  • Edited in its library. edit_material and edit_print_profile with library read that library’s item, apply the change key by key on top of its newest version (so an older copy never overwrites newer keys) and write it as the next version. The design’s copies of it take the same change; a copy that had the library’s version is then at the new one, an older copy stays older. The file and the copies are one undo step (Edit Material Acme PETG, Edit Process Draft): undo and redo write the file back too, unless another design saved it since (then it stays as it is). An edit to the values the library’s newest version has already (another design made them, this one kept its own) writes no file and keeps the version; the design’s copies that differ still take it, as an undo step of its own (mitcad#758). version and origin are the library’s own and refused.
  • Changed elsewhere. A row’s changed is true when the library has a newer version than the design’s copy (another design or a hand changed the item), the design did not decline that version, and its fields differ from the copy’s. The app asks once: the changes are taken with update_from_print_library, the design’s values kept with decline_print_library_update (asked again only when the library changes again). An edit made here keeps a declined change declined.
  • Deleted from its library. delete_material and delete_print_profile with library remove the item’s file. A design copy that bodies or components use (a material) or an owner chose (a profile) stays as the design’s own unsaved item (its origin goes); an unused copy goes. The file and the design are one undo step: undo brings the file back.
  • Chosen in one step. set_body_material, set_component_material and set_property (the profile of Print Printer or Print Process) take library (base, user, project) beside the id, and project: the design’s copy of that item is used, else the item is copied in, in the same undo step as the choice (named as the choice).
  • The base library (mitcad) is read-only: a write there is refused. These commands and library_items read or write folders (class file IO).
