Tests: annotation_tests (added with a group, format, tolerance and places, the stored form and reading back, refused fields; datums and feature control frames: letters, ISO 1101’s rules, a frame under a dimension, edited, saved and read back, the characteristics’ list, a frame following its renamed dimension and not drawn under a hidden one, on refused for a leader, itself and nothing and null for a leader, datum names and frames’ datums following their letters, letters past Z, points refused, a frame under a dimension from a point, frames of a deleted dimension on leaders again, the next datum letter (not one a frame refers to), a new letter refused when a frame would refer to it twice, a saved state opened again, a frame under a dimension from a body, a frame’s zone in inches; older files’ measurements opened unchanged in value, written so while they need nothing more, both lists read; a note on a component’s face following its occurrence, a body without a point refused; a view seen along a length; a length’s drawing in its plane, its text and line moved, following a parameter, back to the defaults, a picked plane and a broken one; a view’s plane and places; notes pointing at a face’s point, following it, refused fields, broken; fit codes’ deviations and the size range; several edited, undone, renamed, given other picks and deleted as one step; rolled back with the features after the marker without a warning, broken with the marker at the end, mitcad#1756), api::annotations::tests (values, prefixes, decimals, own text and every tolerance in words, with their own decimals, a radius’ fit; the layouts of a length, a circle, an angle and a note), iso286::tests (ISO 286-2’s classes at 20 mm, range bounds, intermediate ranges, Δ, K8, JS rounding and half micrometres, a size a hair over a bound, codes refused), document::annotations::tests (checks of fields, older measurements read and written the same).

Parameter limits

Any user or model parameter can have limits (mitcad#665), so that a value with a real minimum and maximum needs no min(max(…)) formula: a driven dimension’s reference parameter cannot have them.

  • min and max are expressions in the parameter’s unit (a bare number is read in it, as in its expression) and may use other parameters ("min": "Wall * 2"); they take part in the dependency order and the cycle check like the expression (dependencies lists their parameters too; a limit that uses the parameter itself, or closes a circle through others, is refused as a circular reference; a parameter a limit uses is not deleted, and a rename rewrites the limit).
  • step is a positive value in the parameter’s unit (1 for whole numbers, 0.2 mm; it may be an expression too).
  • strict (default false).

add_parameter and set_parameter take min, max and step as an expression text or a number (in the parameter’s unit), null or "" removing one in set_parameter, and strict as a boolean; fields left out keep what the parameter has. set_parameter with limits and an expression (or value, unit) changes them in one undo step (Change Limits of Width), so that a new expression is checked against the new limits; the same limits and expression again are no command.

The value. The expression’s result is clamped to [min, max] and snapped to the step; the parameter records which limit took effect (limited). The step rule: steps are counted from the minimum (from zero when there is none), and a result goes to the nearest step; one halfway between two steps goes to the upper one (33.5 with steps of 1 from 8 gives 34). A step above the maximum is replaced by the step below it (never below the minimum), so a snapped value always stays within [min, max]. A result within a billionth (relative, at least 1e-9 in mm or rad) of a bound or a step is not limited. When a limit clamps the value, limited is min or max even if the step also moved it.

A strict parameter refuses a result outside [min, max] or off its steps instead, as it refuses a wrong unit: parameter count: 12 is above the maximum 10, … 0 is below the minimum 1, … 2.5 is not on a step of 1. Limits that are wrong are refused for every parameter: a limit that does not parse or evaluate, or of another kind (parameter b: minimum: …), a minimum above the maximum (the minimum 20 mm is above the maximum 10 mm), a step that is not positive.

The parameters query. A parameter with limits also has:

  • limits: min, max, step (the expressions as written, or null), strict, and for each of min, max, step: <limit>_value (evaluated, mm or rad, or null), <limit>_text (in the parameter’s unit, "300 mm") and <limit>_number (the number in the parameter’s unit);
  • unclamped (the expression’s result before the limits, mm or rad) and unclamped_text; value and text are the limited value;
  • limited: min, max, step or null;
  • limit_message: what the limit did, in words (Width is limited to its maximum 300 mm (its expression gives 372 mm), Width is rounded to its step of 1 mm: 33 mm (its expression gives 33.3 mm)), or null;
  • limit_references: the parameters its limits use.

A parameter without limits has none of these fields. The names min, max, step and strict are the same in the commands, the query’s limits and the design file, for clients that read or write parameter tables (such as a CSV export of the parameters).

A feature’s own limits of the slots a parameter gives its value to are reported in the same form, as fixed, read-only limits, so that a client can show them before the feature fails: intrinsic, a list of feature (uid), feature_name, slot, fixed (true), describe (1 to 10000, whole) and the <limit>_value, _text and _number fields. They are not applied to the parameter (the feature refuses the value). Known ones (parameters::slot_limits): a pattern’s quantity (also direction1.quantity), a pattern’s or mirror’s scale_copies and scales[i].copies (1 to 10000, whole), a gear’s teeth (at least 5, whole), pressure_angle (10 to 35 degrees) and profile_shift (-1 to 0.8).

Elsewhere. The document query lists the parameters a limit changed in limited_parameters (name, limited, text, unclamped_text, message; left out when there are none). The sketch query’s dimensions have limited and limit_message when their parameter’s value is limited. The evaluate query with "parameter": "Width" evaluates the expression as that parameter’s new expression, in its unit, and adds limited, limited_value (mm or rad) and limited_text; for a strict parameter a result outside its limits rejects the query with the reason, so a client can say at once that a typed value will be clamped or refused.

Files, undo and configurations. The design file stores min, max and step (each only when set) and "strict": true with the parameter; a file whose strict parameter’s result is outside its limits is refused (parameters[1]: …). Limits are part of the parameter, so undo and redo restore them, a copied feature’s parameters keep them (with renamed references), and a configuration row, which sets only expressions, is clamped by them (or refused when strict, as the table’s problems say).

Tests: api::parameter_limits_tests (clamping at the minimum and the maximum, step snapping, limits as expressions of other parameters, cycles through limits refused, strict errors, the evaluate query, save, load, undo and redo, configurations, a feature’s own limits, a limited sketch dimension), expr::limits::tests (the clamp and step rule); tools/ui-parameter-limits-test.sh (the mark and the tooltip in Change Parameters, the warning while typing, the strict refusal, the slider, the “Only limited” filter).

Parameters as CSV

The parameters are exported to and imported from CSV (mitcad#666; parameters_csv.rs, document/parameters_csv.rs, api/parameters_csv.rs). The CSV is the text of the query or the command: the application reads and writes the file.

Fields Result
query parameters_csv csv: MitCad’s table of all parameters, parameters: their number
query parameters_csv_preview csv what import_parameters_csv would do; nothing changes
command import_parameters_csv csv what it did, as the preview; one undo step Import Parameters, none when nothing changes

Both formats are UTF-8 (a byte order mark is skipped) with RFC 4180 quoting: a field with a comma, a quote, ;, a line break or leading or trailing space is quoted, a quote in it doubled. Numbers have decimal points. MitCad writes CRLF after each row and reads any line break. A header with semicolons and no comma is read with ; between fields. Columns are found by their names in the header (any case, any order); name and expression are needed, the others are optional.

  • MitCad’s table, header name,kind,unit,expression,value,comment,favorite,min,max,step,strict: one row per parameter in creation order, its kind (user, model, reference), its unit as the parameters query gives it ("" for unitless, Text for a text parameter, whose value column is its text as it is), its expression, its value as a number in its unit (the shortest decimal that gives the value back: 12.5, 90 for 90 deg; the limited value), its comment, true or false for a favourite, and its limits: min, max and step as written (10, count * 20 mm, 0.5 mm; empty when not set) and true or false for strict.
  • The parameter table CSV of the .f3d application, header Name,Unit,Expression,Value,Comments,Favorite exactly: an empty unit for unitless parameters, ° for degrees, Text for text parameters (with expressions such as '6qt'). The import reads it directly; MitCad does not write it. Its expressions are in the language of Values, which reads those of .f3d designs.

An import takes the rows as the .f3d import takes a design’s parameters (core/import-replay/src/params.rs):

  • Names. A name MitCad cannot use (a unit such as mil, a function, other characters) gets a free one as the .f3d import gives it (mil_1, a b as a_b, 2nd as p_2nd), chosen among the table’s other names so that importing the same table again finds it; the expressions that use it follow (whole names). A second row of a name and a row without a name are refused.
  • Existing names change, new ones are added as user parameters (a model or reference row of a name the design lacks too, noted). A user parameter takes the row’s expression, unit, comment and favourite; a new unit is refused where a feature uses the parameter as another kind of value. A model parameter (a feature’s) changes only its expression and limits: its unit, comment and favourite stay, and the row notes what it kept. A reference parameter (a driven dimension’s) is read-only and has no limits: a row with another expression or with limits is refused.
  • Limits (Parameter limits). The min, max, step and strict columns the table has replace the parameter’s limits: an empty cell removes that limit, an empty or missing strict keeps what the parameter has, and a column the table lacks keeps the parameter’s limit (the .f3d application’s table has none). Their names follow renames as the expressions do. A limit that is wrong (one that does not parse or evaluate, a minimum above the maximum, a step that is not positive, a circular reference) refuses the row with the reason; a strict parameter whose result is outside its limits takes its value instead, or is refused. A new value is clamped and snapped as the limits say, and the row’s limited says which limit took effect.
  • Order. Rows are taken in dependency order (of their expressions and limits), so an expression or a limit may use a parameter of a later row. Rows in a circular reference, or that use one, take their value.
  • The value column is used only where the expression does not evaluate (an unknown name, a wrong unit, a cycle): a number read in the row’s unit, or a value with its unit, kept as the expression (7.5 mm) with from_value and the expression’s reason. Without a value that evaluates, the row is refused with the reason.
  • Units. The unit column’s unit (mm, in, deg, °, "" for unitless, any unit the Values take); one that does not parse refuses the row. Without a unit column a new parameter gets the unit of its expression’s value, as add_parameter gives it.
  • Text parameters (unit Text, or kind text; mitcad#664) are text parameters: their expressions are text expressions ('6qt', 'Box ' & GridX); a value cell, used where the expression does not evaluate, is the text itself (plain words, kept as 'plain words') or a quoted text ('6qt'). Without a unit column, a new parameter whose expression gives a text is a text parameter.

A table that is not a parameter CSV (no name or expression column, a quoted field not closed, nothing at all) refuses the query or the command with the reason.

The preview and the import answer: format (mitcad or parameter_table), the counts added, changed, renamed (rows added or changed under a name of MitCad’s own), unchanged, refused, skipped, summary (5 to add, 1 to change, 1 renamed, 1 refused, 1 skipped, the nought counts left out; nothing when all are) and rows in the file’s order:

Field
line the line the row starts on (the header is line 1)
name the name in the file
renamed the MitCad name, when the file’s cannot be used
action add, change, unchanged, refuse or skip (no row is skipped since mitcad#664; kept for clients)
changes of a change: expression, unit, limits, comment, favorite
expression, unit after the import (the file’s for a refused or skipped row)
value, text after the whole import (mm or rad; "35 mm"; the limited value), not for a refused or skipped row; a text parameter has only text, its text
limits min, max, step (as written, or null) and strict after the import (the file’s for a refused row); left out when there are none
limited min, max or step: the limit that changed the value after the import; left out when none did
from_value true when the value column was used
reason why the row is refused or skipped, or why its expression was not used
notes what else stayed (a model parameter keeps its unit mm, its comment)

Tests: parameters_csv::tests (quoting, lines, the header’s format, free names), parameters_csv_tests (a design exported and imported into itself, nothing changing, and into a new design, the same parameters with their limits, also one using a later parameter and a strict one; a synthetic parameter table of the .f3d application with unitless counts, floor and round of length ratios, °, quoted comments with commas, a text parameter, a unit’s name, forward references, a cycle and unknown names; existing parameters changed as their rows say, limits given to a model and a user parameter, a new one clamped, a wrong limit refused; tables refused; a text row exported and imported again, a text row taking its value, type errors refused), api::parameters_csv::tests (the query, the preview and the command); tools/ui-parameters-csv-test.sh (Change Parameters’ Export and Import with its preview, a maximum that clamps a dimension).

Text parameters

A parameter whose unit is Text has a text as its value instead of a number (mitcad#664), such as the label of a lid. Its expression is a text expression; the full rules are in core/expr/src/lib.rs (grammar, rules 23 to 30), as a superset of Values: every expression that parsed before parses and evaluates the same.

  • Texts in expressions. A text is in single quotes, as .f3d designs write it ('6qt'), or in double quotes ("Box "). A quote of the same kind inside is doubled ('It''s', "say ""hi"""); the other kind is an ordinary character ("It's"). The quoted unit of value(x; "mm") is still a unit.
  • Joining. a & b joins its operands as text: "Box " & GridX & "x" & GridY is Box 6x4. A number is written as text(x) writes it: in the document’s unit of its dimension with at most six decimals (15 mm, 30 deg, 6 for a unitless one). & binds less tightly than + and - and more tightly than comparisons.
  • Functions. concat(a; b; …) joins as & does. text(x; [format]) writes a number; the format is a pattern of zeros and #s with at most one decimal point ("0.00", "0.0#", "000"), optionally followed by a unit ("0.0 in", or only "in") that the value is written in (a unitless value is read in it); without a unit the document’s unit of the value’s dimension follows the number, and halves round away from zero (text(Width; "0.00") is 15.00 mm; text(value(Width; "mm"); "0") is 15). left(t; [n]) and right(t; [n]) give the first and last n characters (one by default), len(t) the number of characters (unitless). Function names are case-insensitive; the names of these five are functions only before (, so parameters named Text, Left or len keep their names.
  • Choices and comparisons. if, ifs, switch, choose, iferror and let take texts as values (the values of one choice are all texts or all numbers); == (and = in parentheses) and <> compare two texts, case included.
  • Never mixed. A text is never accepted where a number is expected, nor a number where a text is: '5' + 1, sin(Label), a text parameter as a feature’s length or count, left(5; 1), a text compared with a number, and a number as a text parameter’s value are refused (“text where a number is expected”, “a number where text is expected: make text of it with text(…) or &”). Only &, concat and text make text of numbers.
  • Commands. add_parameter with a text expression and no unit makes a text parameter ({"cmd": "add_parameter", "name": "Label", "expression": "'6qt'"}), as does "unit": "Text". set_parameter with unit Text makes a parameter a text one (its expression must give a text), and another unit a number again; a parameter a sketch text follows keeps its unit (… Sketch1 uses it as a text). A text parameter has no limits: min, max or step for one is refused (“a text parameter has no minimum, maximum or step”).
  • The parameters query gives a text parameter "unit": "Text", "text" its text and "value" 0. The evaluate query takes "kind": "text" (or a text parameter’s name as parameter) and answers text, references and expression, no value.
  • Sketch text. A sketch text can follow a text parameter: the sketch definition’s text_values, or value in sketch.add_text and sketch.edit_text: a text parameter’s name ("value": "Label"), or a text expression ("value": "'Box ' & GridX"), which becomes the sketch’s own text parameter of the text (the next free d<n>, comment Sketch1 t9 text, deleted with the sketch; a new expression changes it). "" in sketch.edit_text stops the text following one; it keeps its string. A number parameter or a number expression there is refused. The text is laid out with the parameter’s text, and so is an emboss or an extrusion of it: a change of the parameter (or of what its expression uses) lays the sketch out again and recomputes what uses it, and a change that leaves its text as it was recomputes nothing. The sketch query gives such a text its parameter’s text and value: {"parameter": "Label", "expression": "'6qt'", "own": false} (own: the sketch’s own parameter).
  • Files, undo, CSV. The design file stores a text parameter with "unit": "Text" and its expression, and the sketch’s text_values by parameter name; undo, redo, renames, copies and configurations treat it as any parameter. The CSV export writes its unit Text and its text as its value, and the import reads text rows of both tables.
  • The .f3d import creates the file’s text parameters (unit Text) with their expressions ('6qt', Label & ' lid'); an expression that does not evaluate (a text without quotes, as older designs keep it) is taken as the text itself and reported with the parameters taken as values. The text parameter a design keeps for each sketch text (role Text1-Text, the sketch’s model parameter) becomes the sketch’s own, and the sketch’s text follows it when its string is the parameter’s text: the text of that number, or the only one with that string; a text is never changed by the link. A link the model refuses leaves the texts as they are.

Tests: expr::tests (text_literals_and_their_quotes, ampersand_joins_texts_and_numbers, text_functions, texts_and_numbers_do_not_mix, choices_and_comparisons_of_texts, text_function_names_stay_parameter_names, expressions_without_texts_read_as_before, texts_have_a_length_limit, text_parameters_in_a_table), expr::lexer::tests, expr::units::tests::the_text_unit, parameters::tests, api::text_parameter_tests (a sketch text following a text parameter and an expression of its own, its recompute on a change and only then, the type errors both ways, no limits, save and load), api::evaluate::tests::evaluates_texts, parameters_csv_tests (text_parameters_go_out_and_come_back), and the import’s text_parameters_are_imported_and_sketch_texts_follow_them (a synthetic design).

Formula assistance

formula_help is a read-only query for expression fields and larger editors:

{"query":"formula_help","expression":"FLOOR(length / pitch)","cursor":6,"selection_end":20,"kind":"unitless"}

cursor and optional selection_end are UTF-8 byte positions. kind accepts length (default), angle, unitless and text (mitcad#664: result is then {"text": …} and no selection is inspected); optional parameter evaluates in that existing parameter’s unit. The response always contains functions, the supported function catalog with argument labels, descriptions and examples. An unfinished call can return signature with its current zero-based argument. A complete formula returns result; selection describes the smallest AST node containing the cursor or selection, its byte range and evaluated text. It retains lexical LET bindings and reports actual dimensions rather than promoting a selected ratio to the field’s length unit. Errors include a message and source range. The query never changes the formula, parameters or limits.

For the formula editor’s colors and completion (mitcad#2179) the response also has units, the unit names a value may take (mm, deg, in, …), and tokens, the formula’s pieces in order, {kind, start, end} with UTF-8 byte ranges (white space is in none), from the parser’s own tokenizer (expr::assistance::tokens): number, unit, name (a parameter of the design), unknown (a name no parameter has, or a table the design has none of), local (a name a LET binds), table and column (Screws.dk), function, keyword (LET, PI, E), operator (also the . of a column), bracket, separator (;, ,), text (quoted, also one not closed yet) and error (a character the tokenizer refuses, a name after a value that is no unit, an unknown function). An unfinished or wrong formula keeps its pieces: after a refused character the rest is cut again. With "tokens_only": true the response is only {"tokens": […]} (nothing is evaluated), for coloring the text on each key.

The editor’s templates are ordinary expression text. Limits continue to use set_parameter with min, max, step and strict; setting a formula and its limits together remains one undoable parameter command.

Purge volumes

How much the printer purges when it changes from one filament to another (mitcad#705; core/model/src/print_purge.rs, document/purge_volumes.rs, api/purge_volumes.rs, print_files/): a table of the filament slots, a row per filament changed from and a column per filament changed to, in mm³, which the 3MF export writes for the slicers that keep one.

  • A material’s values. Two keys of the Print Filament set, MitCad’s own (no slicer keeps them per filament; the key map’s group purge in the category filament): purge_into (purging into it, when the printer changes to it) and purge_out (purging out of it, when it changes from it), mm³, zero or more. A material that sets neither takes them from the colour it prints with (its filament_colour, else its appearance’s): by the colour’s lightness L (CIE L*, 0 black to 1 white), into 70 + 140 · L and out of 70 + 140 · (1 − L), whole mm³. Mid grey takes 140 each way, black 70 into and 210 out, white 210 into and 70 out.
  • The multiplier. flush_multiplier of the Print Process set (category others, group filaments; the Bambu family’s key), 1 when unset; the design’s is the first body’s.
  • The computed table: from one filament to another, out of the first plus into the second, times the multiplier, whole mm³; 0 from a filament to itself. Dark to light so takes more than light to dark (black to white 420, white to black 140).
  • Pairs set by hand (“overrides”): the design keeps a volume for an ordered pair of materials (from, to), as it is: the multiplier does not apply to it. Resetting it gives the computed volume again.
  • The slots are those the 3MF export makes: the bodies in their order (sheet and empty bodies are not printed), a slot per distinct material in the order of first use, each body’s material and settings in each placement written (the shown ones, all when none is shown): a body whose placements print otherwise is in the slot of each of their materials (mitcad#1061).
  • Export (export with a dialect): the Bambu family (Bambu Studio, OrcaSlicer, QIDI Studio) gets flush_volumes_matrix (the table divided by the multiplier, which the slicer applies; one table per extruder), flush_multiplier (a list, one entry per extruder) and flush_volumes_vector (out, then in, per slot, unmultiplied). The extruders are as many as the printer’s nozzle_diameter entries, or as the slicer’s own preset of the printer has when it has more (mitcad#2207: a printer named only by its preset keeps one nozzle diameter, and the slicer loads the preset’s extruders): the preset the project names (printer_settings_id, else the printer profile’s name), the one its kept block inherits from, else one of its printer_model, looked up in that slicer’s data folder (its user presets and system presets, with what they inherit); one extruder when none is found. PrusaSlicer, which has no multiplier, wiping_volumes_matrix (the table as it purges), wiping_volumes_use_custom_matrix = 1 and wiping_volumes_extruders (out, then in, per slot, multiplied). Cura has no table, and its per-material prime volumes are extruder settings, which its export does not write: nothing.
  • Import (import_print_profile into the design): a Bambu-family project’s flush_volumes_matrix (its first extruder’s table, times the first entry of its flush_multiplier) or a PrusaSlicer project’s or configuration’s wiping_volumes_matrix (unless wiping_volumes_use_custom_matrix is 0) becomes the pairs set by hand of its materials, in the same undo step; a table of another size is left out (the report says so). None of these keys is kept as the slicer’s text; the report counts them as read.
Command Fields Result
set_purge_volumes volumes: [{from, to, volume}], material ids (built-in or the design’s) and mm³ (zero or more); a volume of null or left out resets the pair undo step Set Purge Volume PLA Plastic to ABS Plastic, Reset Purge Volume …, or for several Set Purge Volumes (Reset Purge Volumes when all reset), which recomputes nothing; none when nothing changes. Refused: an unknown material, a material to itself, a negative volume, no pairs
Query Fields Result
purge_volumes bodies (uids of the bodies printed, in order; the design’s when left out) multiplier; slots: {material, name, color, purge_into, purge_out, bodies} (the values used: the material’s own or its colour’s); volumes[from][to]: {computed, volume, edited} (volume the one used, edited set by hand)
purge_defaults color (#RRGGBB; mid grey when left out) {purge_into, purge_out}: what a material of that colour without its own values takes (the material editor’s empty fields)

The design file keeps the pairs set by hand as "purge_volumes": [{"from", "to", "volume"}], left out when there are none. Deleting a design material (delete_material, or a library’s delete that removes an unused copy) takes its pairs away in the same undo step, so that a new material that gets its id (the first free custom{n}) starts computed; undo brings them back with the material (mitcad#758). A design material that took a built-in’s place keeps them for the built-in of its id.

Tests: print_purge::tests (the colour rule, the multiplier, overrides in the table, a project’s table as pairs), print_files::purge_tests (the computed table, a material’s own values, pairs set, kept, reset, saved and refused, the Bambu-family and PrusaSlicer exports, both imports), tools/ui-purge-volumes-test.sh (3D Print’s Purge volumes table).

The reference in parts over MCP

This reference is about 1 MB, more than an agent’s context. The MCP servers (headless and live, docs/mcp.md) give it in parts through the read-only tool model_reference (mitcad#714), parsed from this file in core/mcp/src/reference.rs; the resource mitcad://reference/commands holds all of it as agents see it (below).

Arguments Result
none contents (the ## and ### headings), and queries, commands, features: the names MCP permits
section one section with its subsections, found by its heading, a name its heading lists (split_body) or a part of its heading
query, command its entry (mitcad#1897): the rows of its tables (tables whose first column is Query or Command, or a row whose first cell is command `name` or query `name` ), with their headers and the headings above them; else the section that describes it in prose. With section and path, brief, also_in, and a command’s JSON Schema (schema) where one exists
feature the section of the feature type: the heading that lists it, or the section of its first example definition (a code block with "type": "<name>"), and that example
search the headings and the lines that contain a text, each line’s headings and an excerpt

Each answer holds at most 64 kB of text; a longer one gives next_offset for offset. A section or feature answer is brief by default (mitcad#1587): the heading, the first code block, the tables, and each paragraph and top-level list item up to 800 bytes (cut after a sentence), without nested list items, later code blocks, the subsections’ texts (their headings are listed) and parenthesized issue numbers; "extended": true gives the whole section. So that the brief form keeps what matters, put a field’s meaning in the first sentences of its top-level item and details in nested items or subsections. So that the tool finds things, keep to the forms it reads: a feature type’s section is a ### heading that names the type (### rib, web, or a list after a colon) or has an example {"type": "<name>", …}; a command’s or query’s row is in a table whose first header cell is Command or Query and names it in backticks in its first cell.

A command’s or query’s entry (mitcad#1897, Reference::item_entry): the rows of its tables when it has any; else the section that describes it, the one whose paragraphs, list items and code blocks name it most (a JSON example {"cmd": "<name>", …} or {"query": "<name>", …} counts three, a backticked name in prose one). That section comes whole up to 16 kB; a longer one gives its blocks that name it, with the paragraph ending in a colon that introduces an example, the examples and lists such a paragraph introduces, and the paragraph after an example. The answer says section and path, and also_in the other sections that name it. "extended": true adds what the other sections say of it (for rows: every paragraph and example elsewhere that names it; for prose: the whole section first). brief: true says that extended gives more; a cut for size is truncated with next_offset, both in note. A command described only in prose gets a complete answer this way, so keep its fields, result and example in one section.

Commands’ JSON Schemas (mitcad#1897, core/mcp/src/schemas.rs): a command lookup adds schema, a JSON Schema (2020-12) of the command’s fields with their types, enums, units, defaults, alternatives and examples, and a feature definition’s types and where their fields are, for the commands schemas.rs lists (the contents’ schemas) and only when the server permits the command. x-mitcad-server and x-mitcad-restrictions say the server’s restrictions (live or headless, undo and redo alone, the array’s as and ref). They are given on demand only: the tool listing stays short. The test core/model-tests/api/src/mcp_schema_tests.rs checks each against the fields the API reads (the field list of its unknown-field error, its missing-field errors and its examples); a field added to such a command needs its schema too. Every command MCP permits has one: the sketch commands (mitcad#1912, core/mcp/src/schemas/sketch.rs) and the others (mitcad#1918), one module per family under core/mcp/src/schemas/. A new permitted command needs a schema in its family’s module, or a place with its reason in that test’s WITHOUT_SCHEMA (empty now) when a schema cannot describe it; UNPROBED there names the commands whose fields the API reads only after looking at the design (link_gears, edit_render_light), whose examples alone are checked.

What agents see (mitcad#1509): the tool and the resource give the reference without what an agent cannot use, and this file stays as it is for the developers:

  • A section whose command and query tables name only names MCP does not permit, and whose heading and examples name no permitted feature type (Files, Version history, Projects, Edit locks, …), is left out of the contents, the sections, the rows, the search and the resource. Its subsections go with it, except one that names permitted names of its own. A command or query asked for that only such a section describes gets “not available through MCP” with the permitted names.
  • A section about how the code works inside, not the API, is marked by the line <!-- mcp: internal --> as the first line under its heading (a Markdown comment, so the document reads as before). It is left out the same way. Mark new sections of that kind (caches, workers, how to add to the API, how a class of names is chosen).
  • Headings lose their issue numbers: ## Linked designs read again while open (mitcad#1416) is shown as ## Linked designs read again while open, and section finds it by either.

mitcad_mcp::reference_losses names the permitted names whose rows or sections agents would no longer find; the test core/model-tests/api/src/mcp_reference_tests.rs checks with the names the backend permits that it names none.

The names come from api::classes: external_queries() (the model class), external_commands() (the model class, and the commands that are the model’s own in some form: create_appearance, edit_appearance, set_render_settings without a file, build_place, build_connect, build_panel, build_swap_fasteners with a source of the design) and FeatureDef::TYPE_NAMES. The MCP server’s errors name the same lists: an unknown query or command lists the permitted ones, and a refused command that misses a field gets the section of its feature type, or its command’s rows, in reference (docs/mcp.md, “Transport, errors and limits”).

Drawings in the design

Drawings kept in the design (mitcad#707, phase 1; core/model/src/drawing/def.rs, document/drawings.rs, api/drawings.rs): the root’s and each component’s Drawings folder. A drawing is a definition only: its sheets and their views, each with its place on the sheet, scale, style, label and subject. The lines are projected from the model whenever the drawing is asked for, so a drawing follows the model; nothing computed is stored. A drawing of a component shows that component in its own coordinates and belongs to it: a copy of the component (Paste New, Insert Component as a copy) brings copies of its drawings, with their bodies and occurrences mapped, and deleting the component deletes them. A component a feature made (a new-component operation, a component from bodies) that is filled into an existing empty component (move_made_component) moves its drawings there (a name the folder has gets the next free one); an edit that would remove it (the feature no longer a new-component operation) is refused while it has drawings (Component1 has drawings in its Drawings folder; delete them first, or keep the new-component operation), as while it has features or occurrences; deleting the feature keeps it, with its drawings, as a plain component. Dimensions, centre marks, notes and symbols on views: Annotations on drawing views (phase 2).

Ids: a drawing is D<n> (uid), named uniquely in its folder (Drawing1); commands take the id or a name only one drawing has. Its sheets are numbered from 0 in their order; its views have ids from 1, unique in the drawing. Points on a sheet are millimetres of paper from its lower left corner.

Command Fields Result
add_drawing component (uid or name; the root when left out), name (the next free Drawing<n>), the first sheet’s size, orientation, projection, title_block, units, annotations (below), layout (instead of an empty sheet: export_drawing’s fields without path and format, laid out as the export lays them out; the root’s only) drawing, name, component, sheets, warnings; undo step Add Drawing1
edit_drawing drawing, name undo step Rename Drawing1
delete_drawing drawing undo step Delete Drawing1
add_drawing_sheet drawing, sheet (where it goes; the end), name (Sheet<n>), and the sheet’s fields; the others are the last sheet’s (not its views and text notes, mitcad#742) sheet; undo step Add Sheet2 to Drawing1
edit_drawing_sheet drawing, sheet (0), and the fields to change undo step Edit Sheet1 of Drawing1
delete_drawing_sheet drawing, sheet; refused for the last one undo step Delete Sheet2 of Drawing1
add_drawing_view drawing, sheet (0), type, and the fields of its type (below) view; undo step Add view 3 to Drawing1
edit_drawing_view drawing, view, and what changes (below) undo step Move view 3 of Drawing1 (a move alone) or Edit view 3 of Drawing1
delete_drawing_view drawing, view deleted: the view and the views that come from it; undo step Delete view 3 of Drawing1

The commands change no geometry and recompute nothing; nothing changed is no undo step.

The views’ projections in answers (mitcad#1033). A drawing command (above, and the annotation, revision and template commands) and the drawing query answer with projections when their work asked for any view’s projection: one entry per view, {"view": 1, "bodies": 1, "ms": 2252.7, "cached": false, "polygonal": false}: how many bodies the view shows (a view of the design: the bodies it recorded, shown in the 3D view when it was placed, mitcad#1293), whether the kernel projected them (cached false, its milliseconds) or the projection came from the document’s projection cache (cached true, the lookup’s milliseconds), and whether the projection was made from a triangulation (polygonal: the quick path, exact above, or the polygonal style) instead of the exact edges, for some of its bodies at least. A move projects nothing: the cache’s key is the bodies’ shape versions and placements and the view’s direction and style, never its place on the sheet; a projection made from a triangulation is kept by the view’s scale too (its lines follow it, mitcad#1671), so a new scale projects such a view again, never an exact one. The application writes one line of each to its log (Drawing projection of view 1: 1 bodies, 2252.7 ms, projected exactly, …, projected from a triangulation, or …, from the cache).

Projected once, inside the command (mitcad#1997). A view added or edited is projected at the scale it keeps inside its command: add_drawing_view, edit_drawing_view (all but a move or a label’s move) and edit_drawing_sheet (when its projection method turns views) work their sheet out before they keep it, so the drawing query after them takes every view from the cache, and the work is the command’s job in the application (its progress after 400 ms, its Cancel). A base view’s scale that fits the sheet ("fit", left out, or "parent" on a base view) comes from the boxes of its bodies seen along it, not from a projection: the view is projected once, at that scale (only a kernel without bodies’ boxes projects it first to measure it). In a job the kernel’s projection is given up on a Cancel (OCCT’s hidden-line removal looks at no progress, core/ffi/src/kernel/abandon.rs) and the command is refused (the computation was canceled), the drawing as it was; the kernel’s time limit (300 s, MITCAD_KERNEL_TIME_LIMIT) gives a projection up too, and the view is then not drawn (its error). For tests the job’s delay (RecomputeMonitor::set_test_delay; the application’s MITCAD_TEST_RECOMPUTE_DELAY_MS=add_drawing_view=3000) holds each projection that long, ending early on a cancel.

A view of many bodies (mitcad#1997). The bodies’ boxes that fit a base view to its sheet (Kernel::bounding_boxes), the boxes that split a view between the exact and the quick path, and the quick path’s copies and triangulations are made body beside body on the kernel’s threads, each as it would be alone, so the lines are those made one body after another. The automatic centre marks find the visible lines near each circle through a grid of the lines’ boxes instead of measuring every line for each point. The bodies an occurrence moves are placed beside each other too (Kernel::transform_shapes, mitcad#2021: each the copy transform_shape makes alone), and the hiding pass of the polygonal hidden-line removal runs on the kernel’s threads, each segment tested only against the faces near it (OCCT port patch 1810), its lines the same: a view of 884 bodies placed them in 0.2 s instead of 2.7 s and hid its lines in 0.5 s instead of 7 to 8 s. What stays on one thread is the removal’s setup (HLRBRep_PolyAlgo::Update, about 1.3 s there).

The triangulation follows the view’s scale (mitcad#2014). The quick path’s triangulation keeps its lines within 0.02 mm of the edges on the sheet (SHEET_DEVIATION, by its deviation in model millimetres), and the angle between two of its chords along a round edge (ViewSpec::quick_chord_angle) is 0.2 radians on a view at full size or larger, that divided by the scale on a reduced one, up to a twelfth of a turn from 1:3 on: a round edge stays an arc to the fitting of the lines (a whole circle five points at least, a quarter of one three chords), and a reduced view no longer triangulates its round faces that are small on the sheet more finely than it draws them. A view of 884 bodies at 1:17 went from 67 s of hidden-line removal to about 9 s (writing its drawing from 78 s to 16 s), its lines the same on the sheet.

Sheets. size: A4 (default) … A0, ANSI_A … ANSI_E; orientation: landscape (default) or portrait; projection: third_angle (default) or first_angle; title_block: title (the component’s name, or the design’s: the query’s title, else the root’s name unless it is Root), number (the drawing number; without one the block names the bodies drawn), author (DRAWN BY; without one MADE WITH Mitcad), date (today’s when drawn); "" clears a field; units: a length unit symbol (the design’s when left out, ""); annotations: {"dimensions", "hole_table", "sketch_dimensions"}, File › Export Drawing’s automatic annotations (all off for a new drawing; those of its options for one laid out). A drawing of several sheets numbers them in the title block (A3 1/2).

Views. Each view has a place: where its anchor lies on the sheet, the component’s origin as the view sees it (a detail’s centre), so views that share an axis share a coordinate of their places at the same scale.

type Fields when added What it shows
base direction (front (default, from -Y), back, top (+Z), bottom, left, right (+X), iso (front, right, above), iso_top_left, iso_bottom_right, iso_bottom_left; {"toward_eye", "x_axis"}; or {"toward_eye", "up"}: the application’s camera), subject, at (where its box’s middle goes; the sheet’s middle, moved right clear of the other views; a view placed for itself is moved on while it overlaps another, then the other way, never out of the sheet’s area for views, and stays where it would go, overlapping, when there is no room), scale ("fit" or left out: the largest ISO 5455 scale at which it takes two fifths of the sheet at most each way) the subject from that direction
projected parent, side (right, left, above, below, or a corner above_right, …; from at when left out), at (where its box’s middle goes; beside its parent, moved away from it clear of the other views, never back past it: with no room that way it stays beside its parent, overlapping) an orthographic view seen from that side of its parent (third angle) or from the opposite one (first angle); at a corner, the view from that corner (an isometric view of a standard one)
section parent, line (two sheet points on the parent), flip (look the other way), letter (the next free: A, B, … without I, O, Q), hatch (true), at (where its box’s middle goes; beside its parent on the side it is seen from in third angle, on the other side in first angle, clear of the other views, moved away from its parent only) the parent’s subject cut by the plane through the line and the parent’s direction; what lies on the normal’s side (left of the line as drawn, flip: right) goes and the view looks at the cut along -normal; the line, its arrows and letters are drawn on the parent
detail parent, center (a sheet point on the parent), radius (sheet millimetres on the parent, 10), letter, at (where its centre goes; right of its parent, clear of the other views, moved away from its parent only) what the parent shows inside the circle, projected in the detail’s own style as its parent looks (a detail of a section cut by the section’s plane), at twice the parent’s scale unless given; the circle and its letter are drawn on the parent

Every view also takes scale ("1:2", "2:1", a number; a projected and a section view take their parent’s when left out), style ({"hidden_lines", "tangent_edges", "shaded", "polygonal"}; a view other than a base view takes its parent’s when left out; an isometric view and a section show no hidden edges; shaded fills the faces in grey under the lines from the kernel’s triangles; polygonal projects a triangulation, as every view of bodies with free-form faces or many B-spline edges is projected anyway, export_drawing’s exact above, mitcad#962, mitcad#1033) and label (written under the view; a section’s SECTION A-A and a detail’s DETAIL B (2:1) when left out). A base view’s subject: {"type": "design"} (default: every body of the drawing’s component and its occurrences that the 3D view shows now, recorded as the view’s bodies, below), {"type": "occurrence", "occurrence": "O2/O5"} (every body of that occurrence, a path from the drawing’s component, and of its occurrences), {"type": "bodies", "bodies": [{"body": "F2.b0", "occurrence": "O2"}]} (each where the occurrence places it, or wherever the design places it when occurrence is left out). Views of other types show their parent’s subject.

A drawing keeps what was put into it (mitcad#1293, GitHub #144). Visibility in the 3D view decides nothing a view draws: a view placed with the whole component (design, the default) records the bodies shown at that moment, each with its occurrence (none for the component’s own bodies), so that hiding or showing in the 3D view later does not change it and a component added later does not appear in it; more comes in only by editing the view (edit_drawing_view with subject: the application’s Shows list). edit_drawing_view with "subject": {"type": "design"} records what the 3D view shows then (the application’s Update from Model; undo step Update view 1 of Drawing1 when nothing else changes); with nothing of the component shown it is refused (nothing of the design is shown in the 3D view: …) and the view keeps its subject. Its projected, section and detail views follow, as they show their parent’s subject. A recorded body or occurrence that is deleted from the design leaves the view drawing the rest with a warning naming it (warnings of the view, the occurrence O3 is gone, the body F9.b0 is gone, and the sheet’s view 1: …); only a view with nothing of its subject left is not drawn (error). A design file written before mitcad#1293 has no subject on such views (the whole component, as the 3D view showed it): the first recompute after it is read pins each of them to the bodies shown then, no undo step and no change to save (a save writes the list), and the recompute command’s answer has one info notice per drawing pinned (Drawing1 now keeps what its views showed when the design was opened (2 bodies): hiding, showing or adding components no longer changes them; Document::take_drawing_notes). The title block’s material and mass are those of the bodies the drawing’s views show (its component’s shown bodies while it has no view). File › Export Drawing’s layout records its bodies where the 3D view shows them (wherever the design places them when nowhere).

edit_drawing_view takes place (the anchor’s new place) or move ([dx, dy], a drag), scale ("parent": the parent’s again; a base view, which has no parent, takes the one that fits the sheet, as "fit" does), style, label ("": the default), a base view’s direction and subject, a projected view’s side, a section’s letter, hatch and flip, a detail’s center and radius (on the sheet) and letter, breaks (all of them, [] none) or add_break, and aligned. A view that moves takes the views that come from it along. A projected or section view is kept in line with its parent (aligned, true): one beside its parent keeps its parent’s y, one above or below its x (a section the axis its view shares with the parent’s; a view of a detail lines up with the detail’s centre); "aligned": false lets it go. A break: {"direction": "horizontal" | "vertical", "from": [x, y], "to": [x, y], "gap": 6}, two sheet points whose coordinates along the view’s x (horizontal) or y (vertical) bound the band taken out; the two sides close up to gap millimetres of paper with a break line at each. A break is its own view’s: the views in line with it keep their length.

Refused: a parent that is not an earlier view of the sheet, a subject on a view other than a base view (a laid out section without a parent keeps its sheet’s bodies as its own), a section line of no length, a detail circle of no size, overlapping breaks, a field the view’s type does not have, "fit" for a view other than a base view, an unknown unit, two drawings of a folder with one name, the last sheet’s deletion and a drawing of a linked component. Turning a view that has sections or details drawn on it or on a view from it (a base view’s direction, a projected view’s side, a section’s flip, the sheet’s projection) was refused until mitcad#729; they now follow it (Drawing defaults, sketches, patterns and turned views).

The drawings query lists the drawings: drawing, name, component, component_name, exported, sheets (name, size, views: their count). exported numbers the drawings add_drawing laid out from a layout, in the order they were made (1, 2, …; 0 for the others): File › Export Drawing offers the highest one first and writes it as it is (mitcad#725). A drawing is never laid out again: what was made on it by hand stays.

The drawing query (drawing, sheet (0), geometry (true), title, cached (false)) gives the drawing’s sheets, each with name, size, orientation, projection, width, height, title_block, units, annotations and views: id, type, parent, place, scale and scale_text, own_scale, automatic_scale (what it would be without its own: its parent’s, twice that for a detail, 1:1 for a base view), style, own_style, label, aligned ("x", "y" or null), breaks, and a base view’s direction and subject, a projected view’s side, a section’s letter, hatch and span, a detail’s letter and circle (center and radius on the sheet). The sheet asked for is drawn: each view’s box on the sheet (null when it shows nothing), a base view’s warnings (the recorded bodies and occurrences that are gone, the rest drawn, mitcad#1293), or error (why it is not drawn: the body F9.b0 is gone when nothing of its subject is left, the occurrence O3 is gone, its parent, view 2, is not drawn, a kernel failure) with broken and a 30 mm box about its place, so that it can be picked and deleted; the sheet’s scale (the first base view’s) and warnings, and with geometry its groups as the export writes them (class, id, items: {"line": [a, b], "pen"}, {"arc": {"center", "radius", "start", "end"}, "pen"}, {"polyline": points, "closed", "pen"}, {"fill": points}, {"shade": points, "grey"}, {"text", "at", "height", "angle", "anchor"}; pens thick, extra_thick, thin, hidden, hatch, chain, frame, and for lines and arcs drawn by hand dashed_thick, dashed_extra_thick, chain_thick, chain_extra_thick, mitcad#1447) and pens, the writers’ widths and dashes of those pens in sheet millimetres ({"thick": {"width": 0.35, "dashes": []}, "extra_thick": {"width": 0.7, …}, …}, mitcad#1112 and mitcad#1402: the application draws the sheet with them). Groups: view (id view-front, … by its direction, view-section, view-detail, else view-V<id>), view-label, section-line, detail-circle, the automatic annotations’ groups, frame, title-block. Each view drawn names the group of its lines (view-front, mitcad#1997: the application draws them scaled while a new scale is worked out).

With cached (mitcad#1997) the sheet is drawn only from the projection cache: when a view of it would need the kernel (a projection or a shading the cache does not have: a model change, an undo, a drawing opened), the answer is the drawing with its sheets listed but the one asked for not drawn (no box, group, scale or groups), with "uncached": true and no projections; the kernel is not asked. The application asks so first and draws such a sheet in a job of its own.

How a view is worked out: a base view’s subject is found in the drawing’s component at the timeline marker (Document::instances below the component’s first placement, moved into its coordinates); the kernel projects it (Kernel::project_view, the drawing family: hidden-line removal and sections by OCCT); the projection is kept in the document’s projection cache (the 64 used last) by the bodies’ shape versions and placements and the view’s spec, so asking again projects only what changed; the bodies’ edges and faces that picks are found among are kept by a bound of their own (4096 bodies, a body’s newer version replacing its older one), so a sheet of many bodies does not throw them out on every draw. A detail is projected in its own style and cut to its circle, and breaks take their bands out (mitcad_model_drawing::clip: lines and polylines cut where they cross, arcs split at the circle or, across a break, as polylines, cut faces clipped as polygons), all in Rust on the projected lines. A shaded view’s faces are those that face the eye (a mirroring placement turns their triangles over). The sheet is then drawn by the export’s code (mitcad_model_drawing::compose::render); each view tags the round holes of the bodies it shows, not those inside its breaks, and a kernel failure finding a body’s holes is a warning of the sheet.

Files: "drawings": [{"uid", "name", "component" (unless the root's), "exported" (when a layout laid it out), "sheets": [{"name", "size", "orientation", "projection", "title_block", "units", "annotations", "views": [{"id", "kind": {"type": "base", "direction"} | {"type": "projected", "parent", "side"} | {"type": "section", "parent", "origin", "normal", "span", "letter", "hatch"} | {"type": "detail", "parent", "center", "radius", "letter"}, "place", "scale", "style", "label", "subject", "breaks", "aligned"}]}]}], left out when there are none and each field at its default left out; the comparison of versions lists drawings by id with their changed fields (sheets[0].views[1].place). Since mitcad#1293 every base view (and a laid out section without a parent) is written with its subject, a view placed with the whole component as {"type": "bodies", "bodies": [{"body", "occurrence"}, …]}; a view without one, which only older files have, is pinned when the design is read and recomputed (above), and older MitCads read the list as chosen bodies.

Classes: the commands and both queries are the model’s (classes.rs). export_drawing with drawing writes one (Drawings); mitcad-cli export-drawing <design> <out> --drawing D1 [--sheet N] too (the sheet from 1; the options that lay out a new drawing are refused with it). Tests: core/model-tests/drawing/src/stored_tests.rs (directions of projected and section views; the definition, its checks and file form; views placed, projected, cut and detailed; moves in line with parents; breaks; the model changed under a drawing and projections kept; undo, the design file, the comparison; refusals; a component’s drawings copied and deleted with it, and inserted with a design; a kept drawing exported; a laid out drawing the same as the export’s; the drawings laid out numbered and one written again as it is, mitcad#725; per-body sheets; hole tags per view and under breaks; first-angle placement; a detail of a section; sections and details on a broken view; the refusal to turn a view; a view that cannot be drawn; a made component’s drawings; a view that keeps what it showed when placed and an older file’s view pinned, mitcad#1293), the tests in core/model-drawing/src/clip.rs; tools/ui-drawings-test.sh, tools/ui-windows-drawings-test.ps1 (app.ui-windows-drawings); tools/cli/drawing-keeps-content-test.cmake (cli.drawing_keeps_content), tools/ui-drawing-keeps-content-test.sh, tools/ui-windows-drawing-keeps-content-test.ps1 (app.ui-windows-drawing-keeps-content).

Annotations on drawing views

Dimensions, centre marks and centrelines, leader notes, datum labels, feature control frames and surface finish symbols on a drawing’s views, and text notes on its sheets (mitcad#707 phase 2; core/model/src/drawing/annotate_def.rs, core/model-drawing/src/annotate.rs, api/drawing_annotations.rs). One engine with the annotations of the model (Annotations, mitcad#702): a dimension’s value is written by the same code, with its prefix (Ø, R), decimals, own text (format: decimals, prefix, before, after, replace), tolerance (tolerance: symmetric, deviations, limits or an ISO 286 fit code) and the same checks; a datum label’s letter and a frame’s frame are those of Datums and feature control frames.

Picks are model topology seen through the view. A pick is {"body", "occurrence", "edge" | "face", "point"}: a body the view shows, where an occurrence places it (a path from the drawing’s component; none for its own placement), and one of its edges or round faces by its topological name, or a point of an edge ("start", "end", "center": a circle’s centre, a straight edge’s middle; a round face’s "center": its axis). Commands take a pick, or a sheet point ([x, y], mm) where the view’s nearest pick is found: the bodies’ named edges (Kernel::edge_geometries) and round faces (Kernel::face_geometries, cylinders, their ends the body’s circles on their axis), projected as the view sees them (a circle end on as a circle, from the side as its diameter; a round face from the side as its axis between its ends); an edge’s end or a circle’s centre within 2 mm of paper first, else an edge or face within 3 mm, of what the type wants (an ordinate a point, a circle’s rim or a round face giving its centre; an angle a straight edge; a radius, a diameter and a centre mark a circle or a round face). A view sees what it shows (mitcad#717): an edge’s part nearest the click must lie inside a detail’s circle and outside a break’s band (a long edge across a band or into a detail is picked where it shows); a section sees what lies behind its plane (an edge in front of it is no pick, one across it is cut there) and picks a planar face where its plane cuts it (the cut face’s edge in the face’s plane, found again on every draw among the projection’s cut faces). The cut edges in the face’s plane, joined end to end, are that face’s cut line in pieces (mitcad#1361: a face cut beside a hole is cut in two); a click picks the piece under it, {"body", "face", "on_cut": [u, v]}, its middle in the face’s own coordinates (as on_face’s below), found again on every draw as the piece that point lies on (one it lies on no piece of makes the annotation broken: the point picked on the cut of the face … lies on no piece of it), and its ends ("point": "start" or "end", the piece’s ends along the line, picked as corners where no edge’s end is seen) and middle ("center"). A face picked without on_cut (older files) is its whole cut line, from its first piece’s start to its last piece’s end across the gaps; no point but center goes with it. Picks as near as one another (within 0.25 mm of paper) are told apart by the view: the one the projection draws as a visible line first, then the one nearest the eye. An arc is where it is (seen end on its range of angles, from the side its reach), and a whole circle has no start or end to pick. A round face reaches between the circles of its own edges (not those of another face on its axis). Whenever the sheet is drawn each pick is found again by its name (Kernel::edge_geometry, Kernel::face_geometry), so the annotation follows the model; one that is gone (its body no longer shown by the view, its edge or face not in the body, a face that is not round) makes the annotation broken: it is not drawn or exported, the drawing query says why and gives it a small box beside its view, and the sheet’s warnings say annotation 2 on view 3: the face F4:side(c1) of Body1 is gone.
