Bindings: values from expressions

A body’s appearance and material, a face’s appearance, a feature’s suppression and the visibility of a body or an occurrence can follow an expression of parameters instead of a value set by hand (mitcad#800; docs/configurations.md, “Bindings”). A configuration only sets parameters, and these follow; they work as well in a design without configurations. Code: core/model/src/document/bindings.rs.

Command expression Undo step
set_body_appearance a text: an appearance id, else the name of one appearance (switch(Color; 'Black'; 'paint_black'; 'White'; 'Paint - White'; 'plastic_white')) Set Appearance of Body1
set_face_appearance as above, for the faces given Set Appearance of Face of Body1
set_body_material a text: a material id, else the name of one material Set Material of Body1
suppress_feature a condition: suppressed while it holds (Holes = 'No') Suppress Extrude2 When
set_body_visible a condition: shown while it holds Show Body1 When
set_occurrence_visible a condition: shown while it holds Show Board:1 When
  • The value and the expression are alternatives. A command gives one of them; both are refused. Setting the value by hand removes the expression in the same undo step (Hide Body1, Unsuppress Extrude2). An empty expression removes the expression and keeps the value it gave (Clear Appearance Expression of Body1, Clear Show When of Board:1, Clear Suppress When of Extrude2). The same expression again is no undo step.
  • Checked when set. The expression must evaluate with the design’s parameters: an appearance’s or a material’s must give a text, a condition a number (true when it is not 0: Color = 'Black', Length > 1 m, and(Tables = 1; Power = 1)). A text that names no appearance or material is accepted and gives the warning below.
  • Values follow. Every command settles the bound values after its edit, in the same undo step: changing Color in Change Parameters, a configuration row, a CSV import or undo all switch the look. The value is stored next to the expression, so readers that ignore bindings (the exports, older versions) see the value as if it were set by hand.
    • A changed suppression recomputes from that feature on, as suppress_feature does; the features before it keep their results.
    • Appearance, material and visibility recompute nothing.
    • A material that follows an expression gives the body the new material’s appearance by the rule of Materials: unless the body’s appearance was set by hand or follows an expression of its own.
  • Warnings. A text that names no appearance or material, or names two, gives the body a warning, and the body has the default look: no appearance of its own (its material’s) or no material of its own (its component’s). A face shows the body’s look. A condition that cannot be evaluated (a text, a parameter that is gone) leaves the value as it was, with a warning.
  • Parameters. Renames rewrite the expressions (in the rename’s undo step). A parameter that a binding uses cannot be deleted: parameter Color is used by the appearance of Body1. A feature’s own parameter that a binding uses stays as a user parameter when the feature is deleted.
  • Queries.
    • bodies: appearance_expr, material_expr, visible_when and face_appearance_exprs ({face name: expression}) when bound, with dependencies (the parameters the body’s bindings use) and warnings (one line each, appearance: there is no appearance Gloss Purple; the body has the default look).
    • timeline and feature: suppressed_when, dependencies and, when the condition cannot be evaluated, binding_warning.
    • components: each occurrence of the tree has visible_when, dependencies and warnings.
  • Design file. A body keeps appearance_expr, material_expr, visible_when and face_appearance_exprs beside its values, a feature suppressed_when beside suppressed, an occurrence visible_when beside visible. Opening the file settles the values with the file’s parameters.

Tables

A design keeps named tables of data (screw sizes, standard dimensions) that parameter expressions look values up in with Table.Column and the lookup functions XLOOKUP, MATCH and INDEX (mitcad#667; the design is docs/table-lookups.md; tables.rs, document/tables.rs, api/tables.rs):

Size = 'M5'
HeadDia = XLOOKUP(Size; Screws.Size; Screws.dk) → 8.5 mm
Fields Result
command set_table name, table: comment, columns [{name, unit}], rows (arrays of cells: numbers in the column’s unit, texts, null) changed: the parameters whose values changed; moves: the configuration options it moved (Configurations and tables, mitcad#806); creates the table or replaces it; one undo step Edit Table <name>, none for the same table
command rename_table name, new_name {}; the expressions, limits and configuration values that use it follow; undo step Rename Table <name> to <new_name>
command rename_table_column table, name, new_name {}; the same; undo step Rename Column <table>.<name> to <new_name>
command delete_table name {}; refused while a parameter or a configuration row uses it, naming them; undo step Delete Table <name>
query tables name (optional: only that table) tables: each with name, comment, columns, rows, used_by (the parameters that use it), problems (first cells more than one row has: lookups find the first)
  • Names. A table’s name follows the parameter name rules (case-sensitive, not a unit, function or constant) and the tables share the parameters’ namespace: a table cannot take a parameter’s name, nor a parameter (added, renamed, copied) a table’s. Column names use the same characters, are unique in their table and may be reserved words (in, Max): a column is only ever written after Table..
  • Cells are constants. A column’s unit is any unit a parameter takes (mm, in, deg, mm^2), "" for unitless, or Text; a number cell is in the column’s unit (5.5 in an mm column is 5.5 mm), a text cell a string, an empty cell null. A row has a cell per column; a text in a number column, a number in a Text column, a number that is not finite or a text over the text limit is refused with its row and column. At most 10 000 rows and 100 columns.
  • Edits re-evaluate. set_table re-evaluates every parameter that uses the table, and the parameters that depend on them, in one step. When one of them would fail (a key no longer found, a column of another kind) the command is refused with that parameter and its error, and nothing changes; a column a parameter uses cannot be left out (column Screws.dk is used by HeadDia). The features then recompute by the usual rule: only those whose parameters changed value, so an edit that changes no used value recomputes nothing.
  • Renames rewrite every expression and limit that uses the table or the column, keeping the rest of their text, and the configuration rows' values; values do not change.
  • Copies. Copying parameters into another design (Paste New, inserting a design’s copy) brings the tables they use: the same table there is used as it is, a different one of the same name gets a free name (Screws_1), and the copied expressions follow.
  • Configurations stay separate: a row can set only the key (Size = 'M5'), and the lookups follow when it is applied.

The other queries:

  • parameters: each parameter’s table_dependencies, the columns it looks values up in (["Screws.Size", "Screws.dk"]).
  • evaluate: table_references, the same for the expression, beside references.
  • formula_help: tables, each table’s name and columns (name, unit), for completion.
  • diff: a tables section (the “Tables” lines of the text), by name: tables added, deleted, renamed (the same content under another name), and changed ones by their comment, columns (column Pitch added, column dk mm -> in) and rows (table Screws row 3 (M5): dk 8.5 mm -> 8.7 mm); rows are matched by their first cell when it tells them apart.

The design file keeps them as "tables", left out when there are none, each {name, comment, columns, rows} (comment left out when empty); a table with a problem, a name twice or a parameter’s name is refused.

Classes: all of them are the model’s own. Tests: tables::tests (the file form, refused tables), tables_tests in the model (recompute only what a changed value reaches, refused edits, renames, deletes, undo, copies, configurations), api::tables_tests in core.model.api (the commands and queries) and files::tables_tests in core.model.files (saved and read back, the diff’s rows).

Tables as CSV

A table of the design (mitcad#667, docs/table-lookups.md) is exported to and imported from CSV, one file per table (mitcad#804; tables_csv.rs, document/tables_csv.rs, api/tables_csv.rs). It is separate from the parameters CSV. The CSV is the text of the query or the command: the application reads and writes the file.

Fields Result
query table_csv name csv: the table as CSV, rows: its number of rows
query table_csv_preview name, csv what import_table_csv would do; nothing changes
command import_table_csv name, csv what it did, as the preview, and moves: the configuration options it moved, as set_table’s (Configurations and tables, mitcad#849; empty when the table is already as the file has it); one undo step Import Table <name>, none when the table is already as the file has it

The file is UTF-8 (a byte order mark is skipped) with RFC 4180 quoting and CRLF, read and written as the parameters CSV is; a header with semicolons and no comma is read with ; between fields.

  • The header has a field per column: its name with its unit in brackets, Size [Text],d [mm],dk [mm],Pitch [mm], [] for unitless, any unit a parameter takes (mm, in, deg, mm^2). A unit that is not one refuses the file.
  • Cells. A cell of a number column is read as a constant expression in the column’s unit: 5,5 (a decimal comma) is 5.5, a plain 5 in an mm column is 5 mm, 0.25 in there is kept as 6.35. A cell that is not a number of the column’s kind (abc, 5 deg in an mm column, a parameter’s name: cells are constants) is refused with the reason. A Text column takes its cells as they are, numbers too (8). White space around a cell is dropped; an empty cell is empty (null). Rows of empty cells at the end of the file are left out; one in the middle stays.
  • Inferred columns. A header without brackets is a Text column when any of its cells is not a number; else a column of the unit of its first cell with a unit, in the design’s default units (10 mm makes an mm column, and a plain 12 in it is 12 mm), and a unitless one when no cell has a unit.
  • Names. A column name the model cannot use gets a free one, as the parameters CSV renames: other characters as _ (Head diameter as Head_diameter), c_ before one that does not start with a letter (2nd as c_2nd), column_<n> for an empty one, and _1, _2, … for a name already taken (a second d as d_1). Reserved words (in, Max) name columns as they are. A column without a name and without cells (a separator too many) is left out.
  • Sizes: at most 10 000 rows and 100 columns, a text cell at most MAX_TEXT_BYTES; a larger file is refused.
  • Export writes every unit in brackets ([Text] too) and numbers with decimal points, the shortest decimal that gives the value back (5.5, 1e-12), so export and import give the same table.

An import creates the table name or replaces it whole; a table it replaces keeps its comment. It goes through the same atomic check as a table edit: the parameters that name the table, and their dependents, are evaluated again with the new one in one step, and features recompute only when a value changed. It is refused, and nothing changes, while a cell of the file is refused, while a parameter would fail with the new table (a key no longer found, a column gone or of another kind), and for a name no table can have (a parameter’s, a reserved one).

columns in the file’s order: name (the file’s), renamed (the table’s, when the file’s cannot be used; left out otherwise), unit (mm, "", Text), inferred (the header had no unit)
rows the cells as the table keeps them: numbers in their column’s unit, texts, null for an empty or refused cell
refused cells: line (the header is line 1), column (the table’s name; empty for a cell beyond the last column), text, reason

failing parameters that would fail: name, error

Recompute workers

Document::set_recompute_workers(n) (mitcad#842) lets a recompute evaluate the features of independent components on up to n threads at once, each with a fork of the kernel; 1, the default, evaluates every feature on the recompute’s own thread as before. The environment variable MITCAD_RECOMPUTE_WORKERS gives every document of the process its starting value (the ctests core.model.assembly.workers, core.model.links.workers and core.model.joints.workers run those model tests with 4). No JSON command or query sets it yet, and the application and mitcad-cli leave it at 1.

The recompute cuts the timeline into windows that end at barriers (joints, rigid groups, constraint sets and motion links; Move, Capture Position, Joint Origin, Pattern at Points, Component from Bodies, Body Transfer and any feature that made a component; sketches with driven dimensions and Bound Length, which write parameters; an extrusion with a cut scope across components, and a feature whose last result moved occurrences, measured parameters or gave bodies to another component). Within a window, each component’s features run ahead on a worker, except a feature that reads other components (links in its definition, or reads of other components’ bodies, placements or results in its last result) and the features of its component after it, which the recompute evaluates itself. A window runs ahead only when at least two components have a feature there that the cache likely lacks.

The recompute still goes through the timeline in order and takes a worker’s result only where the cache would take a stored one (the same definition, every read the evaluation recorded holding where the recompute is, the definition’s parameter values the same) and the evaluation succeeded; otherwise it evaluates the feature itself. The document, results, versions, topological names, statuses, warnings, the memory cache, the result store’s writes and the monitor’s progress are therefore those of one thread. A stop cancels every worker (their monitors are part of the recompute’s) and keeps nothing a worker returned; results not yet taken count against the memory cache’s budget, and before the cache drops results for its budget the recompute stops the workers and waits for them, so that it drops what it drops with one thread. Previews, commands that add base features from shapes (written_from) and recomputes on a worker’s thread use no workers. The OCCT kernel installs its crash handlers on each worker thread (Kernel::worker_thread).

Tests: core/model-tests/assembly/src/parallel_recompute_tests.rs (two components at the same time; a linked feature, a driven dimension’s reader and a moved occurrence’s reader waiting for what they read; stops while workers evaluate and while the recompute waits for one; each against the same design with one thread).

Cut sheets

A cut sheet (mitcad#853; core/model/src/drawing/cut_sheet_def.rs, core/model-drawing/src/cut_sheet.rs, api/cut_sheets.rs) is a drawing of its own kind in a Drawings folder: it collects flat parts at 1:1 on a sheet of material and writes their outlines as DXF or SVG for cutting (a laser, a water jet, a plasma cutter). It has no title block, frame, scale, dimensions, hole table, hidden or tangent lines: only the edges to cut. It is kept with the design’s drawings (drawings lists it with "kind": "cut_sheet", the others "drawing"), is copied and deleted with its component as they are, and follows the model: its outlines are worked out whenever they are asked for.

A part is a body seen along the normal of one of its planar faces, from outside the body: its largest planar face unless one is chosen (of faces as large, the one facing up most: +Z, then +Y, then +X). Its outline is the body’s silhouette along that normal: the outer boundary of its whole extent and the holes and cut-outs that go through it, so a through hole is one inner loop however many faces its wall has, and a blind hole or a pocket is none. Each part has an id (from 1, unique on the cut sheet), a place, where the middle of its outline’s box lies on the sheet (millimetres from the sheet’s lower left corner), and a rotation about that middle (degrees counter-clockwise), so a part that grows or shrinks stays where it was put. A count adds that many parts (2 × Rib 3: two parts of the same body). Parts are moved and turned by hand; nothing nests them. A part whose body (or the occurrence placing it) is gone stays on the sheet, marked as missing; one whose face is gone or no longer planar says why.

Command Fields Result
add_cut_sheet component (uid or name; the root when left out), name (the next free CutSheet<n>), width, height (the material, mm; 600 × 300), bodies (parts to start with, below), count (1) drawing, name, component, parts (their ids), warnings; undo step Add CutSheet1
edit_cut_sheet drawing, name, width, height undo step Rename CutSheet1 or Edit CutSheet1
add_cut_sheet_parts drawing, bodies, face (a planar face of the one body given; its largest when left out), count (1 to 1000), at (where the first one’s middle goes; each in a free place of the sheet when left out, in rows from the top left 5 mm apart, beside the sheet when none is left) parts, warnings; undo step Add part 3 to CutSheet1 or Add 4 parts to CutSheet1
edit_cut_sheet_part drawing, part, place or move ([dx, dy]), rotation (degrees) or turn (degrees more: 90 a quarter turn left, -90 right), face (null: the largest) undo step Move part 3 of CutSheet1, Turn part 3 of CutSheet1 or Edit part 3 of CutSheet1
delete_cut_sheet_parts drawing, parts (ids) deleted; undo step Delete part 3 of CutSheet1 or Delete 2 parts of CutSheet1
export_cut_sheet drawing, path, format (dxf or svg; from the extension when left out), labels (false), units (a DXF file’s length unit; the design’s when left out, DXF units) path, format, parts (written), outer, inner (loops written), labels, width, height, units (a DXF file’s unit; null for SVG), warnings

A body in bodies is its uid or name ("F2.b0", "Rib 3"), or {"body", "occurrence"} with the occurrence that places it (a path from the cut sheet’s component, "O2/O5"); left out, wherever it is shown. Refused: a body without a planar face (Body1 has no planar face to lie on), a face that is not a planar face of its body, a body that shows nothing along the face’s normal, a face with several bodies, a count of 0 or over 1000, a material of no size or over 100 m, and a cut sheet’s views, sheets, notes, templates or revisions (CutSheet1 is a cut sheet: it holds parts only, on one sheet).

The generic drawing commands work on a cut sheet’s parts as on views: edit_drawing_view with place, move or rotation (any other field is refused), delete_drawing_view, edit_drawing (its name), delete_drawing; add_drawing_view is refused. export_drawing with the cut sheet as drawing writes it as export_cut_sheet does, without labels.

Warnings (the query’s and the commands’ warnings): part 2 (Rib 3) overlaps part 3 (Rib 3) (their material overlaps; touching is no overlap, nor a part inside another’s hole), part 4 (Rib 5) leaves the sheet, part 5 (F9.b0) is missing: the body F9.b0 is gone, and part 6 (Body2): … for a part that cannot be worked out.

The cut_sheet query (drawing, geometry (true)) gives drawing, name, component, component_name, kind, width, height, warnings, counts (each body, occurrence and face once: body, name, face, occurrence, count, parts) and parts: id, body, body_name, occurrence, face (the face it is seen along), own_face (chosen rather than the largest), faces (the body’s planar faces with their area, mm²), place, rotation, size (its outline’s box before it is turned), box (on the sheet; a 30 mm box about its place when it is not worked out), outer and inner (its loops), missing, error, off_sheet, overlaps (the parts it overlaps), and with geometry its loops on the sheet: {"outer", "pieces"}, the pieces end to end with the material on their left (outer boundaries counter-clockwise, inner loops clockwise): {"line": [a, b]}, {"arc": {"center", "radius", "start", "sweep"}} (radians; a positive sweep counter-clockwise, a whole circle ±2 pi), {"polyline": points}, {"spline": {"degree", "knots", "poles", "weights"}} (from the piece’s start to its end; weights empty when not rational). A part also gives splines: the B-splines of its outline on the sheet, as the pieces’ spline.

The drawing query of a cut sheet draws it for the application: its kind (cut_sheet), one sheet of the material’s width and height whose views are the parts (type part, id, place, rotation, label (the body’s name), box, broken and error when it is not worked out, and the query’s fields of a part), its warnings, and with geometry its groups: a view group part-<id> of each part’s outline (pen thick) and a view-label group of its name.

B-splines. The kernel’s projection gives a B-spline or Bézier edge as its B-spline (its degree, full knot vector, poles and weights, cut to the edge’s range), and another curve that is no line or circle (an ellipse, an offset curve, …) as a B-spline within 1e-6 mm, each with a polyline of it within the view’s deflection (ViewCurve::Spline; drawings draw, cut and pick that polyline). A cut sheet keeps such a curve as the curve it is: split where other lines meet it and joined again (the crossings and ends found on the curve itself), turned and moved by its poles, and cut to a part of its range by knot insertion (mitcad_model_drawing::bspline). Lines and arcs of a polyline stay a polyline.

The files. DXF (R2000, 1:1, in the design’s length unit unless units names another, mitcad#1408): outer boundaries on the layer CUT_OUTER, inner loops on CUT_INNER (the Flat Pattern’s names, DXF export of Sheet-metal), lines as LINE, arcs as ARC, whole circles as CIRCLE, B-splines as SPLINEs with their own degree, knots, control points and weights (weights only when they differ), a polyline (from the polygonal projection) as a SPLINE of degree 1 through its points; with labels each part’s name as TEXT on LABEL at the middle of its box (5 mm high, smaller on small parts). SVG (the material’s size in millimetres, viewBox in millimetres, y down from the top): a layer (<g id="CUT_OUTER">, inkscape:label) of the outer boundaries (red) and one of the inner loops (CUT_INNER, blue), each loop one closed <path> (data-part its part’s id) of lines (L), arcs (A) and, for a non-rational B-spline of degree 3 or less, its Bézier pieces as cubic Béziers (C, exactly; a quadratic raised to a cubic, degree 1 as lines); a rational B-spline or one of a higher degree as lines within 0.0001 mm (cut_sheet::SVG_DEFLECTION); with labels a layer LABEL of the names as <text>. A part that cannot be worked out is left out (a warning says why); a cut sheet with no part to write is refused.

How a part is worked out: its body where its occurrence places it in the cut sheet’s component; the face’s plane (Kernel::faces, Kernel::face_plane); the kernel’s projection along the face’s normal with hidden lines removed, sharp, tangent and silhouette edges (Kernel::project_view); then, in Rust (mitcad_model_drawing::cut_sheet::silhouette), the lines seen are split where they cross or end on each other, the regions they bound are asked once each whether the body lies behind them (a line of sight across the body, Kernel::segments_crossings), and the lines with material on one side only are followed into loops, pieces of one line or circle joined again. The result is kept in the document’s drawing cache by the body’s shape version, its placement and the face chosen. Overlaps and parts off the sheet are found on the loops flattened (arcs in steps of 2°).

Example:

[{"cmd": "add_cut_sheet", "width": 600, "height": 300,
 "bodies": ["Rib 3", "Spar"], "count": 2},
 {"cmd": "edit_cut_sheet_part", "drawing": "CutSheet1", "part": 2, "turn": 90},
 {"cmd": "export_cut_sheet", "drawing": "CutSheet1", "path": "ribs.dxf", "labels": true}]

Classes: the commands and the query are the model’s, export_cut_sheet writes a file (classes.rs); MCP’s model_export takes cut_sheet (and labels) to write one as DXF or SVG. Tests: core/model-drawing/src/cut_sheet_tests.rs (a plate with two holes and a slot seen with its edges twice and a seam: one outer loop and three inner within 1e-6 mm; a blind hole; placing and turning; overlaps, touching and nesting; the DXF and SVG read back with their layers and sizes; a polyline as a spline; B-splines cut, turned and as Béziers; a plate whose top is a cubic B-spline split by a seam: one spline again with its degree, knots and control points within 1e-6 mm, read back from the DXF as a SPLINE and written in the SVG as a cubic Bézier; the spline turned with its part), core/model-tests/drawing/src/cut_sheet_tests.rs (the commands and queries on the mock kernel: a part added with a count, a parameter change, a deleted body marked missing, overlaps and parts off the sheet, the generic drawing commands, undo, the design file, the files written and read back), tools/cli/tests/cut_sheet.json (cli.cut_sheet: a plate with two holes and a slot through OCCT, and a plate whose top is a B-spline of degree 2, its control points on the sheet), tools/ui-drawings-test.sh (New Drawing › Cut Sheet, two bodies added, DXF written).

Rounded rectangles and fillets of several corners

(mitcad#867) sketch.rectangle with radius (a value: a number or an expression) makes the rectangle of its mode and rounds its four corners: four tangent arcs (made: the four lines, then the four arcs), the first with a radius dimension (comment fillet radius) and the other three Equal to it, so the one parameter drives all four. A radius of half the shorter side or more is refused (the corner radius 10 mm must be less than half the shorter side (10 mm)), and nothing is added.

sketch.fillet rounds several corners at once with curves and/or points in place of a and b (giving both forms is refused):

  • curves (lines): every corner where two of them end at one point. Construction lines count only among construction lines, so a rectangle’s construction diagonal does not spoil its corners; a point where three or more lines of one kind end is refused; two lines in line make no corner. Two lines without a shared end are the corner where they meet, as with a and b.
  • points: each a point where exactly two lines of one kind end (the drawn ones, else the construction ones); any other point is refused (p9 is not the corner of two lines or arcs (no curve ends there)).

Each corner is filleted as with a and b (the corner stays as a point on both lines, a length dimension of a line becomes the distance from its other end to the corner); one radius dimension on the first arc and Equal from it to each other arc. Before anything changes, the corners on each line must leave some of it: otherwise the refusal names the line and the largest radius that fits (the fillet radius 12 mm does not fit on c2: its corners take 24 mm of its 20 mm, the radius must be less than 10 mm). One command: one undo step, Fillet in <sketch>. Circular arcs count as lines do, see Fillets at corners of arcs; any other curve is refused.

{"cmd": "sketch.rectangle", "sketch": "F1", "mode": "two_point",
 "a": [0, 0], "b": [40, 20], "radius": 5}
{"cmd": "sketch.fillet", "sketch": "F1", "curves": ["c1", "c2", "c3", "c4"], "radius": 5}
{"cmd": "sketch.fillet", "sketch": "F1", "points": ["p5", "p7"], "radius": "r1"}

The application’s 2-Point and Center Rounded Rectangle and Sketch Fillet’s Curves or Corners send these (app/COMMANDS.md). Tests: core/model-tests/sketch/src/sketch_rounded_rectangle_867_tests.rs (a 40 × 20 rounded rectangle of r 5 fully constrained by width, height, radius and position, all four arcs following the radius parameter; the centre variant; Sketch Fillet on a whole rectangle with length dimensions giving the same, undone in one step; a Center Rectangle with its diagonal; two corners by their points; the refusals).

Fillets at corners of arcs

(mitcad#1192) sketch.fillet rounds a corner where a circular arc ends together with a line or with another circular arc, as it rounds two lines. The corner is the point where the two curves end:

  • a and b: a line and an arc, or two arcs, that end together at one point. Curves that end together at both ends (a half disc’s line and arc, the two arcs of a lens) name no one corner and are refused (c1 and c2 end together at p3 and p4: pick the corner point to round), as are curves that do not end together (c1 and c2 do not end at one point: …).
  • curves: lines and arcs; every point where two of them end is a corner, as for lines (a whole profile of lines and arcs at once).
  • points: each a point where exactly two lines or arcs of one kind end.

Two ends at the same place (within 0.01 mm) are one corner too when a coincident holds them together: point to point, or one end on the other curve (point-on-curve), as a Trim or an import leaves a corner. The two curves, or either end point, name it. Both ends stay, each then a point on its own curve, held together as before.

Of the circles of the radius tangent to both curves, the fillet is the one on the side where the two curves bound the corner (between the directions in which they leave it, as for two lines), nearest to the corner: inside an arc’s circle where the corner is convex on the arc’s side (a ring’s outer corner), outside it where it is concave (a ring’s inner corner). The fillet arc is tangent to both curves (tangent), both are trimmed back to the tangent points, and the corner stays as a point on both curves (coincident with each, its constraints and dimensions kept), as for lines. The arc keeps its centre point and its radius, with their constraints and dimensions; an arc length dimension of it and the midpoints on it, which measured the piece cut off, are removed. A length dimension of a line becomes the distance from its other end to the corner, as for lines. A sketch fully constrained before stays fully constrained with the radius dimension.

Several corners get one radius dimension and the other arcs Equal to the first, as for lines. Before anything changes, every corner must have a fillet that touches both curves ahead of the corner, and the corners on each curve must leave some of it (along an arc, its length); otherwise the refusal names the curve and the largest radius that fits, found by bisection (an arc’s fillets do not take of it in proportion to the radius): the fillet radius 14 mm does not fit on c5: its corners take 22.254033 mm of its 20 mm, the radius must be less than 13.333333 mm, or, inside an arc’s circle too small for the radius, the fillet radius 3 mm does not fit on c3 at its corner with c6, the radius must be less than 2.5 mm. Curves tangent where they end together make no corner (a slot’s joins): curves leaves them out, a and b are refused (c1 and c3 are tangent at p2: there is no corner to round), as is such a point (p2 is no corner: c1 and c3 are tangent there). Circles, ellipses, elliptical arcs and splines are refused (c4 is a circle: Sketch Fillet rounds corners of lines and circular arcs).

{"cmd": "sketch.fillet", "sketch": "F1", "a": "c5", "b": "c2", "radius": 2}
{"cmd": "sketch.fillet", "sketch": "F1", "points": ["p3"], "radius": 2}
{"cmd": "sketch.fillet", "sketch": "F1", "curves": ["c5", "c2", "c6", "c3"], "radius": 2}

The geometry is core/sketch/src/fillet.rs (with unit tests of the tangent circles), the edit SketchEdit::fillet_curves in core/sketch/src/modify.rs. Tests: core/model-tests/sketch/src/sketch_fillet_arcs_1192_tests.rs (a fully constrained quarter ring: its line–arc corners inside and outside the arcs’ circles by the two curves, a corner by its point and all four corners at once by curves and by points, fully constrained after the radius and following its parameter; the two corners of a lens of two arcs by point, by curves and at once; a corner whose line end is held on the arc apart from the arc’s end, by either point, by curves and as a and b; the refusals). The application’s Sketch Fillet takes arcs and such corner points (app/COMMANDS.md; tools/ui-sketch-fillet-arc-test.sh, tools/ui-windows-sketch-fillet-arc-test.ps1).

Annotations’ look: text height, Auto colour and placement

mitcad#894 (core/model/src/document/annotations.rs, core/model-api/src/annotations.rs, api/analysis.rs): the annotations of the model drawn as a technical drawing’s dimensions (ISO 129-1, ISO 3098, ISO 1101).

Text height. The annotations’ texts are one height in model units (mm), in their planes, so that they grow and shrink with the model like their lines: the design’s setting, or, left unset, the automatic one — of the ISO 3098 series 2.5, 3.5, 5, 7 and 10 mm the largest at most a fiftieth of the size of what is annotated (the diagonal of the box of the bodies the shown annotations’ picks are on), at least 2.5 mm; 3.5 mm when no body is known (datums only). Each annotation’s drawing has it as text_height. The application keeps a text at least about 9 pixels high on screen when zoomed out.

Command Fields Result
set_annotation_text_height text_height: mm, 0.1 to 1000, or null for the automatic one undo step Annotation Text Height (nothing to recompute), none when nothing changes; out of range refused (an annotation text height is 0.1 to 1000 mm, got 0)

{"query": "annotation_text_height"} gives {"text_height" (the one set, null for the automatic one), "in_use" (mm), "automatic" (the one the size gives), "series": [2.5, 3.5, 5.0, 7.0, 10.0]}. The design file keeps a height set as annotation_text_height.

Auto colour. A new annotation’s color is auto when none is given (add_annotation, add_measurement): no colour of its own, the neutral annotation colour the application draws it in, which follows the view’s background tone (near-black on a light background, light grey on a dark one). color takes auto in any case as it takes #rrggbb. The six colours new annotations took in turn before (#d9480f, #1971c2, #2f9e44, #c2255c, #7048e8, #e67700) were the program’s, not the user’s: an annotation stored in a design file with one of them is read as auto (and saved so). A colour given in a command, or any other stored one, stays the annotation’s own.

Placement of a length. Left out (line_offset not set: added without a view, or set back to the default with null, the editor’s Automatic), a length’s dimension line lies outside its bodies’ extent in its plane: of the corners of the boxes of the bodies its picks are on, projected across the ends in the plane, on the side they reach less far past the ends (y’s when as far; when added in a view, the side towards the view’s eye, mitcad#902), 6 text heights past the farthest corner there (1.5 before mitcad#902); a parallel line laid out before it (by the order of the annotations, a shown length in a parallel plane, along the same direction, overlapping it along the length) that it would come within 2.5 text heights of moves it 2.5 text heights past that line, on its side. A line set (by a view when added, or dragged) keeps its place. The places are worked out from what measure_picks keeps for the picks (MeasuredPicks::extent, MeasuredPicks::faces: the bodies’ boxes placed by their occurrences, the planar faces at the picks), measured again only when the picks’ bodies change (mitcad#716).

Tests: api::annotations::tests (a length outside a box’s extent and a second one stacked outside it, one elsewhere along it not, one set by hand kept; an offset of planes leaving the box at its outline; a view’s plane of the part), document::annotations::tests (old default colours read as Auto, the ISO 3098 series by size, heights refused), core/model-tests/analysis/src/annotation_tests.rs (lengths_are_placed_outside_the_body_and_stack_outside_each_other, old_default_colours_are_read_as_auto, the_text_height_is_automatic_or_set_for_the_design).

Clearance holes and recesses by screw size

mitcad#903 (core/model/src/features/hole_sizes.rs, core/model/data/hole_sizes.json, core/model-api/src/hole_sizes.rs): the clearance holes and the screw head recesses of the ISO metric screw sizes M1.6 to M24 (the sizes of MitCad’s fastener tables), which the Hole panel’s Hole Tap Type Clearance fills its fields from. The data file has one section per standard, each naming it:

  • ISO 273 (ISO 20273): the clearance hole of the fine, medium and coarse series; the panel’s Fit Normal is the medium series.
  • DIN 974-1, series 1: the counterbore for an ISO 4762 socket head without a washer; its depth is ISO 4762’s head height k plus an allowance (0.2 mm for M1.6 to M2.5, 0.4 mm for M3 to M6, 0.6 mm for M8 to M20, 0.8 mm for M24). A counterdrill takes the counterbore’s diameter and depth, its cone 90°.
  • ISO 10642: the theoretical head diameter dk of the 90° countersunk socket head (M3 to M20), and ISO 15065: the countersink diameter for the heads of ISO 7721 (M1.6 to M10). A size’s countersink is the larger of the two, so that either head is at or just below the face; M24 has none.
  • A tapped hole’s countersink: 1.1 times the thread’s major diameter, rounded to 0.1 mm and at least 0.1 mm over it, at 90°.

For printed parts (mitcad#1518):

  • ISO 4032 (hexagon regular nuts, style 1): the nut’s width across flats s and its height m (max), M1.6 to M24, the same values as MitCad’s nut library. A nut pocket is the nut with a clearance on both: MitCad’s own default of 0.3 mm, or the query’s nut_clearance.
  • Heat-set threaded inserts, M2 to M6: the hole diameter is the drill size ruthex publishes for its threaded inserts (its drill bit set for threaded inserts: M2 3.2 mm, M2.5 and M3 4 mm, M4 5.6 mm, M5 6.4 mm, M6 8 mm); the insert’s length is that of ruthex’s standard insert of the size (RX-M2x4, RX-M2.5x5.7, RX-M3x5.7, RX-M4x8.1, RX-M5x9.5, RX-M6x12.7); the hole’s depth is the length plus MitCad’s own allowance of 1 mm for the plastic the insert displaces. Other inserts need other holes: type the values in.

Licences: every number of the table is MitCad’s own data under the MIT licence (core/model/data/hole_sizes.json, each section naming its source): dimensions tabulated from the standards named (ISO 273, DIN 974-1 with ISO 4762’s head heights, ISO 10642, ISO 15065, ISO 4032) and from the insert maker’s published product dimensions. These are facts; no text, table layout or drawing of a source is copied. The clearances and allowances (a counterbore’s depth allowance, the tapped countersink’s factor, the nut pocket’s clearance, the insert hole’s depth allowance) are MitCad’s own choices.

Query Fields Result
hole_sizes size (M6, case and spaces ignored; every size when left out), major (a thread’s major diameter, mm), thread (a tapped hole’s thread as thread_sizes names it, mitcad#980: standard, iso_metric when left out, size (6) and designation (M6x1, optional)) sizes (smallest first): size, diameter (the thread’s nominal d), clearance (fine, normal, coarse), counterbore (diameter, depth), counterdrill (diameter, depth, angle 90), countersink (diameter, angle 90; left out for M24), iso_10642_head and iso_15065 (the two diameters the countersink is the larger of, where the standard has the size); fits (fit, title: fine Fine, normal Normal, coarse Coarse), default_fit (normal), default_size (M6), standards (the sections’ titles: clearance, counterbore, countersink_head, countersink); with major also tapped_countersink (diameter, angle 90); with thread also tapped_countersink (from the size’s major diameter unless major is given), thread_size (the screw size of an ISO metric size’s nominal diameter, 6 is M6, as an entry of sizes: a tapped hole’s counterbore and counterdrill; left out for a size the table lacks, 5.5, and for the other standards) and thread_bore (the designation’s basic minor diameter D1, the tapped hole’s bore; left out without a designation the standard has). For printed parts (mitcad#1518) each size also has nut (across_flats, height: ISO 4032’s), nut_pocket (across_flats, depth: the nut with the clearance) and, in the insert series, insert (diameter, depth, length: the hole and the insert); the answer has nut_clearance (the clearance used: the field nut_clearance, mm, 0 or more, else 0.3) and standards also nut and insert (naming the insert’s source). A size the table lacks is refused (no clearance hole for the screw size M7: the sizes are M1.6, …), and so are a major not greater than zero and a negative nut_clearance

Lengths are millimetres, angles degrees. A hole stores the values the panel filled in as plain values, and names its size and fit in clearance (hole); the table does not change a hole later.

Tests: features::hole_sizes::tests and features::hole::tests::clearance_holes_keep_their_size_and_fit (core.model), core/model-tests/features-profile/src/hole_size_tests.rs (the query for M2, M6 and M24, a tapped M6x1’s thread_size and thread_bore; a clearance hole with a counterbore, a typed value kept, the refusals), features::hole_sizes::tests::a_tapped_hole_takes_the_screw_size_of_its_thread, tools/cli/tests/f1_hole.json (the volumes of M6 clearance holes counterbored, Normal and Fine, and countersunk, through a 60 x 40 x 20 block); nut pockets and insert holes (mitcad#1518): features::hole_sizes::tests::nut_pockets_are_iso_4032_nuts_with_the_clearance, features::hole_sizes::tests::insert_holes_come_from_the_series and core/model-tests/features-profile/src/nut_pocket_insert_tests.rs.

Hole callouts and the reference look

mitcad#902 (core/model-api/src/hole_callouts.rs, core/model-api/src/annotations.rs, core/model-drawing/src/compose.rs): hole callouts on the model, and what the annotations give the application for the look of a technical drawing’s dimensions.

Hole callouts. An annotation of the kind hole_callout points at a hole: its a is a body’s round face or edge (a hole’s wall, its counterbore’s or countersink’s face, or a rim between them), with at, where the hole was clicked. It is a leader as a note is (no value, format, tolerance or text of its own; name HoleCallout1, …), stored and listed as the other annotations, edited and deleted by the same commands. add_annotation needs kind: "hole_callout"; it is refused for a pick that is no face or edge (a hole callout points at a hole: its round face or edge) and for a face that gives no hole or circle. Its label is {"text": "4x Ø6.6 THRU / ⌴ Ø11 ↧ 6.8", "lines": ["4x Ø6.6 THRU", "⌴ Ø11 ↧ 6.8"]}, worked out whenever the annotations are asked for, so it follows the hole’s size, depth and thread:

  • A hole of a hole feature (its face named F5:hole2.wall, F5:hole2.cbore_wall, … or named after one): the exported drawing’s callout engine (mitcad_model_drawing::compose::hole_callout, there in words, here in ISO 129-1’s symbols) — the count of the feature’s holes (4x, none for one), the thread of a tapped hole (M6x1 - 6H, LH for a left-handed one, a custom thread’s size and starts, 10x1.5 2 STARTS) or Ø and the drill’s diameter (a tapped hole’s bore, its thread’s minor diameter), then THRU or ↧ and the depth (a hole to an object: its wall’s length); a thread along part of the wall has its depth on the first line and the drill’s size and depth on the second; then the counterbore (⌴ Ø11 ↧ 6.8; a counterdrill’s too) or the countersink (⌵ Ø12 × 90°). Lengths in the document’s unit as the drawings write them (two decimals in millimetres at most).
  • A round face of a thread feature: its thread (M10x1.5 - 6g) and ↧ its length when it has one.
  • Any other round face or edge: its diameter (Ø20).

Its drawing is a note’s: the leader from the text to the arrow on the hole’s edge, at the end of the round face picked towards the side its plane faces (the view’s when added), at the point of the rim nearest at. A broken pick or a hole feature that does not build breaks it with the reason, as other annotations. A feature control frame can stand under it (on, as under a dimension: its position frame on the same leader).

What the drawing gives the look. Each leader’s drawing has align, start or end: its text starts at the leader’s end, or ends there when it lies on the arrow’s side along the text; a frame under a hole callout has the callout’s align and under_lines (the callout’s lines it stands below). A note’s and a frame’s leader on a face ends in a dot ("terminator": "dot"), on an edge or outline in an arrow; a datum label’s in its triangle ("datum"). A length’s extension line from a planar face picked starts at that face’s own outline (the corners of its box, MeasuredPicks::outlines), on the line’s side, never at the edge of the bodies’ box in mid-air; from an edge or a vertex at its point. The places left to the defaults are in text heights, which follow the design’s text height, and keep the annotations out of the part as a drawing does: a length’s line 6 text heights past its bodies (2.5 more for each parallel one), on the side towards the eye of the view it was added in; a length between two planes picked has its ends slid within both faces to their common edge on that side and to their far edge along its plane’s normal (the plane faces the eye: away from it), so that its extension lines run from the faces’ corners to a line outside the part; a view’s ties between planes facing it alike go to the one most along its up (a horizontal plane). A leader’s text (a note’s, a frame’s, a callout’s) goes the shortest way out of the part in its plane on an oblique leader, never along the text nor straight up: of the directions up and out to its own side (45 degrees, then steeper), up and out to the other side, and down and out (in that order of preference), the one that leaves the bodies' extent soonest without crossing a leader or a text laid out before it in a parallel plane, 2 text heights past the extent, after a landing of 1.5 text heights level with the text’s first line (the leader’s dimension_lines: the leader to the point, then the landing; the other lines hang below), and moves on up past the leaders’ texts laid out before it (their size estimated from their words) and on past the lengths’ dimension lines laid out before it as seen in its plane; without a body four along and three across from its point. A leader’s text moved (text_offset) nearer its point along the text than its landing is long takes a landing of at most half that way back, so that the leader meets it at an obtuse bend, and none right above its point (mitcad#1168); the application draws the landing in proportion to its text as drawn (longer where the text is held to its least height on screen). A datum label on a face stands on a stem 3 text heights long square to that face (its normal in the label’s plane), its square centred past the stem’s end ("align": "middle", no landing); on a planar face its triangle stands on the face’s outline where the stem leaves the face (the convex outline of the face’s box corners seen in the label’s plane), its base along that outline and the stem square to it in the plane. A round face’s circle (a radius, a diameter) is drawn at the face’s end towards the default isometric view’s eye. A radius, and a diameter without a plane, lie in the circle’s plane, the text out from the bodies’ middle, one and a half radii and at least three text heights past its rim, a diameter on a leader from outside with its one arrow on the rim and no centre mark. A diameter added in a view takes the view’s plane as a note does (its plane, the view’s horizontal its x): there it is a leader from outside to the rim’s point that lies out from the bodies’ middle, its arrow on the rim, its text level on a landing (align as a note’s), laid out as a note’s; a frame under it stands below its text as under a hole callout; an angle’s arc is five out without its picks’ reach. A view no longer freezes pixel sizes when an annotation is added. The automatic text height takes the size of the design (its root’s bodies with the annotated ones).

Tests: api::hole_callouts::tests (a hole found in its faces’ names), api::annotations::tests (extension_lines_start_at_the_picked_geometry_not_at_a_box, a_datum_stands_on_its_faces_outline_and_a_diameter_on_a_leader, the defaults in text heights), compose::tests (hole_callouts_in_words_and_in_symbols), document::annotations::tests (the kind), core/model-tests/analysis/src/annotation_tests.rs (hole_callouts_write_their_holes_from_the_feature: a simple, a through counterbored, a countersunk, a tapped, a partly tapped and a custom-thread hole, the drill’s size changed; a_hole_callout_takes_a_frame_and_breaks_with_its_hole).

Readers of files in the application’s process

The application reads whole CAD files only in its import process (mitcad --import-worker), including the listings asked before an import (list_references of import_f3d_timeline, list_links of import_rvt; mitcad#922). The queries and commands that read a file the user chose in the application’s own process run that reader guarded: a panic in it (a reader’s bug that a broken or hostile file reaches) is the query’s or command’s error, <file>: the file's reader failed (an internal error): <the panic's message>, instead of an abort of the application at the bridge. Guarded: the dxf_info and svg_info queries, sketch.import_dxf and sketch.import_svg, and the read of import_print_profile (a 3MF project, a preset or a bundle), and the read of each installed preset import_slicer_presets imports (the preset with those it inherits from; a broken preset file is that command’s error, not an abort). The readers return data of their own, so nothing of the document is half changed by such an error (mitcad_model::reader_guard::catch_panic).

For tests, MITCAD_TEST_PARSER_PANIC=<file name or path> makes the reader of that file panic: the guarded readers return the error above, and the listings in the import process end that process.

Tests: reader_guard::tests (core.model_base: a panic with its message, a result passed on), test_reader_panic_is_an_error (core.bridge: dxf_info with the hook returns the error, the process goes on and answers the query again), tools/ui-import-listing-test.sh.

Feature inputs

mitcad#957 (core/model/src/features/inputs.rs, core/model-api/src/feature_inputs.rs; the kernel’s Kernel::edge_polylines, geometry/include/mitcad/geometry/input_edges.hpp): what a feature picked and its result no longer shows, kept with the feature’s result so that the application can draw it where it was when the feature is selected or hovered on the timeline (app/COMMANDS.md, “Timeline feature inspection”). Today a Fillet and a Chamfer keep their picked edges: the edges their sets name and the edges bounding the faces their sets name (every edge of a set of every edge), each edge once, as polylines in the component’s coordinates. The rounding or the bevel took those edges away, so the lines run where the edges were in the body before the feature.

Cheap by design. The feature’s build works the lines out once, from the body before it, with the names it has just resolved (one kernel call after the rounding or the bevel succeeded): each edge’s curve cut into straight pieces within the view’s display tolerance (0.01 mm from the curve, at most 5° between neighbouring pieces), a few kilobytes per feature. They are kept with the result in the memory cache and in the result store, so a warm open has them as a build does. The query only reads them: asking it runs no geometry operation and never starts a build. A kernel that cannot give them leaves the feature built as before, with none.

Query Fields Result
feature_inputs uid (the feature) uid, name, stored (whether the feature’s last build kept inputs), edges (the picked edges, one polyline each: [[x, y, z], …], millimetres in the feature’s component; empty when none are kept)

None are kept (stored false, edges empty) for a feature not built since the document was read without building (its next build keeps them), one that failed, is suppressed or lies after the history marker, and a feature of a kind without picked inputs. A feature that does not exist is refused (feature F99 does not exist).

The inputs are of kinds of their own, each a field of the answer, so that other kinds (the faces of a Shell or a Draft, a Hole’s points) can follow beside edges without changing it.

Tests: core/model-tests/features-solid/src/feature_inputs_tests.rs (a fillet of four edges keeps four polylines and the query, asked twice, makes no kernel call; a document read without building answers none and computes nothing, its next build keeps them; a chamfer of a face and an edge keeps each edge once; an extrude, a rolled-back, a suppressed and a failed fillet have none; a kernel that refuses the polylines still builds the fillet).

Joins that touch only another component’s body

A feature changes only the bodies of its own component (mitcad#958): a Join (an extrusion’s, a revolution’s, any feature whose operation is join) with participants empty works on all of its component’s own bodies, and a body of another component listed there fails as before (body F9.b0 (from Extrude1) belongs to Bracket; a feature works on the bodies of its own component …). Joining into a component placed inside the feature’s is not supported: the body belongs to that component’s definition, which every occurrence of it shows.

When the tool touches none of its participants (or the component has no bodies of its own) but touches a body of a component placed inside the feature’s, through any occurrence on any depth, the error names it:

the extrusion does not touch any participant body of Brace; it touches body F9.b0
(from Extrude1) in Bracket:1, a body of another component, and a feature of Brace
joins only Brace's own bodies: choose New Body, or activate Bracket and add the
feature there

(there is no body of Brace to join; … for a component without bodies; at most three bodies are named, then N more). The bodies are each occurrence’s under the feature’s component, moved into its coordinates by the placements on the occurrence’s path at the feature’s point of the timeline; the test is the one Extrude’s automatic operation makes (Kernel::enclosing_box, then Kernel::tool_contacts), and only a failed Join reads them. Without such a body the error stays the extrusion does not touch any participant body. The application’s panel shows the message (app/COMMANDS.md, Extrude in a turned occurrence). Code: core/model/src/features/join_elsewhere.rs. Test: core/model-tests/links/src/link_tests.rs (a_join_that_touches_only_a_child_occurrences_body_names_it).

The sketch query’s frame is in the sketch’s component’s coordinates (as the bodies of the component are); a client that draws a direction from it in the design moves it by the world placement of the occurrence it shows the sketch at (the components query).

Dogbone 

{"type": "dogbone", "body": "F1.b0", "edges": ["E{F2:side0|F2:side1}"],
 "faces": ["F2:bottom"], "diameter": "6.35 mm", "extra": "0.1 mm",
 "dogbone_type": "along_side", "axis": [0, 0, 1]}

Relief cuts at a body’s inside corners, so that a router bit of the tool’s diameter clears the sharp corner a square part fits into (mitcad#1011). For each inside (concave) corner edge it takes, a cylinder of the tool’s diameter runs along the whole edge, parallel to it, placed so that its circle passes extra beyond the sharp corner, and is cut from the body; the body keeps its id, and its faces keep their names.

  • edges: inside corner edges, taken whatever their direction. Each must be straight and an inside corner: an edge that is not fails the feature with the reason (edge E{F1:side0|F1:side1} is not an inside (concave) corner, edge E{F4:side0|F4:top} is not straight).
  • faces: of each face, its edges that are straight inside corners parallel to the tool axis (a pocket’s wall: its two corners); of a planar face across the axis (a pocket’s floor, a top face), every such edge of the body that ends on the face.
  • Neither edges nor faces: every straight inside corner edge of the body parallel to the tool axis. Picks that give no corner fail (the body has no inside corner along the tool axis).
  • diameter (> 0, default 6.35 mm) and extra (>= 0, default 0.1 mm): value slots diameter and extra; without them the defaults.
  • dogbone_type: diagonal (the default) puts the cylinder’s centre on the corner’s bisector, diameter / 2 - extra from the corner; along_side (a T-bone) keeps it diameter / 2 off one face of the corner and moves it extra beyond the corner along that face, so that it notches only the other face: the picked face (in faces) the edge came from, otherwise the longer of the corner’s two faces (the one that reaches farther from the edge).
  • axis: the router bit’s axis in the component’s coordinates (any length, not zero), [0, 0, 1] by default; it chooses the corners of faces and of the body.

The reliefs’ faces are named <feature>:dogbone(<edge>) along each cylinder and dogbone_start(<edge>), dogbone_end(<edge>) at its ends, <edge> the corner’s edge name (Kernel::dogbone_tool). The preview’s tool is the cylinders; the timeline shows the picked edges and faces (Feature inputs). A mesh body is refused as in the other surface operations.

Code: core/model/src/features/dogbone.rs, geometry/src/dogbone.cpp (the corners: each edge’s faces’ outward normals across it, an inside corner told by a point beside the edge inside the material). Tests: core/model-tests/features-solid/src/dogbone_tests.rs (mock kernel), tools/cli/tests/dogbone.json (ctest cli.dogbone, OCCT: a pocket’s four corners in a block, analytic volumes of both types), the UI tests tools/ui-dogbone-test.sh and app.ui-windows-dogbone.

Mortise and Tenon

A mortise_tenon feature (mitcad#1012, core/model/src/features/mortise_tenon.rs) grows a tenon out of a planar end face of one body and cuts its mortise into another body where the tenon reaches. The application’s command is Mortise and Tenon in SOLID > MODIFY (app/COMMANDS.md).

{"type": "mortise_tenon", "body": "F1.b0", "face": "F1:side1", "mortise_body": "F2.b0",
 "width": 40, "thickness": 8, "length": 25, "offset_width": 5, "offset_thickness": -2,
 "turned": true, "clearance": 0.1, "corners": "rounded", "tool_diameter": 6}
{"type": "mortise_tenon", "body": "F4.b0", "face": "F4:side1", "mortise_body": "F5.b0",
 "width": 40, "thickness": 8, "through": true}
{"type": "mortise_tenon", "body": "F7.b0", "face": "F7:side1", "mortise_body": "F8.b0",
 "width": 10, "thickness": 8, "length": 25, "count": 3, "start_offset": 5, "end_offset": 5}
  • The tenon is a rectangle width x thickness on face (planar) of body, grown length along the face’s outward normal; with through (and no length) up to where the mortise body’s material ends last along the line out of the tenon’s middle: flush with the mortise body’s far face. Its width runs along the face’s longest straight edge (across the normal; the face’s normal × X, or × Y for a normal near X, when the face has no straight edge), turned to point along its largest component’s positive direction; with turned the width runs across that edge. The thickness runs along normal × width.
  • Its place: the middle of the face’s extent along those two axes (the face’s edges projected on them), moved by offset_width and offset_thickness (default 0: centred). What the face leaves round the tenon are the shoulders.
  • The mortise is the tenon grown by clearance (default 0.1 mm) on every side and past the tenon’s tip: width + 2 clearance x thickness + 2 clearance, length + clearance deep from the end face’s plane (a through mortise runs on 1 mm past the mortise body, so that its end lies on none of the body’s faces). Its volume in the body is therefore the tenon’s plus the clearance’s.
  • Corners: square (default) or rounded: the mortise’s corners round by tool_diameter / 2, as the cutter leaves them, and the tenon’s four edges along its length round by that radius less the clearance (square when the clearance is as large), so that the mortise is the tenon grown by the clearance there too.

The tenon starts a little inside its body (5 % of its length, 0.001 to 0.5 mm) and joins it; the mortise cuts the other body (a piece a mortise splits off becomes a body of the feature, as a cut’s pieces do). Both bodies keep their ids and names; the input shapes are not modified, and an edit of any value builds both again. The feature’s tool (for previews) is the mortise.

Several tenons (mitcad#1063): count (unitless, a whole number from 1 to 100; default 1) tenons, each with its mortise, in the one feature. They are spaced evenly along the face’s long direction (its longest straight edge as above, pointing along its largest component’s positive direction, whether or not turned): the first tenon’s side lies start_offset from the face’s end where that direction starts, the last one’s end_offset from the other end (both default 0, not negative), with the same gap between each two. Width, thickness, length (or through), clearance and corners apply to every tenon; the offset along the long direction (offset_width, or offset_thickness when turned) is not used then, the other one moves them all. At a count of 1 the start and end offsets are not used, and a definition without count (every design saved before it) is the single tenon as before. Through tenons each run to where the mortise body ends along their own middle; tenons one after another of one length are extruded together (one extrusion of their regions), and the extrusions of several lengths make one compound tool. The feature’s tool is the mortises.

Face names: the tenon’s sides side(c1) … side(c4) counter-clockwise from the side along the width at -thickness / 2 (rounded: the lines c1, c3, c5, c7 and the rounds c2, c4, c6, c8), its tip end(…); the mortise’s walls side(c11) … side(c14) (c11 … c18) in the same order and its bottom end(…). Of several tenons, tenon k (from 0, the first at the start) has the same names with the curve numbers raised by 20 k: the second tenon side(c21) …, its mortise side(c31) ….

Refused when the feature is added: the same body for both, a size not above 0, a negative clearance, a blind tenon without length, rounded corners without tool_diameter or with a tool not narrower than the mortise (the tool diameter (9 mm) must be smaller than the mortise's thickness (8.2 mm)). Refused when it is built, with the reason in the timeline: an end face that is not planar, a tenon larger than the end face (the tenon (70 × 8 mm) is larger than the end face (60 × 20 mm)), one an offset takes past the face’s edge (… (shoulders 25, -5, 6, 6 mm)), and a tenon that does not reach the mortise body (the tenon does not reach body F12.b0: the blind mortise cuts nothing of it, or nothing of a through tenon’s mortise body lies ahead of the tenon’s middle). Of several tenons: a count that is not a whole number from 1 to 100 or a negative start or end offset when the feature is added (the count of tenons must be a whole number from 1 to 100, got 2.5: use floor(…) or round(…) for a whole number, the start offset must not be negative, got -1); when it is built, offsets that leave less than a tenon (the start and end offsets (30 and 25 mm) leave less than a tenon's 10 mm of the end face (60 mm)), tenons that overlap or touch (the 3 tenons overlap: 20 mm along the face each, their middles 15 mm apart) and mortises that would (the mortises of the 3 tenons overlap: 20.1 mm along the face each with the clearance, their middles 20.05 mm apart).

Uses only the existing Kernel methods (face_plane, curves_of, extrude_feature, boolean, and bounding_box with segment_crossings for a through tenon). Tests: core/model-tests/parts/src/mortise_tenon_tests.rs (mock kernel), cli.mortise_tenon (tools/cli/tests/mortise_tenon.json: OCCT volumes of crossing boards, blind, through and rounded, edited, three tenons, two through tenons of different lengths, refusals), tools/ui-mortise-tenon-test.sh and app.ui-windows-mortise-tenon (tools/ui-windows-mortise-tenon-test.ps1).

Constraints a drawing tool adds automatically

The sketch tools add the constraints the geometry they have just drawn already satisfies (mitcad#1024; app/COMMANDS.md): an end at a circle’s quadrant is held on the circle and level or plumb with its centre, a line drawn level gets horizontal, a line ending where it touches a circle gets tangent. They add them with sketch.add_constraint and "auto": true, which adds the constraint only when that is safe (SketchEdit::add_constraint_if_safe, core/sketch/src/auto.rs):

  • the others do not imply it, in full or in part: the redundant count does not rise. Unlike a plain sketch.add_constraint, no older constraint is removed in its favour (A constraint that replaces one it makes redundant), no Symmetry is fitted, and a coincident of two curve ends is refused instead of joining them into one point;
  • the sketch still solves with it (no conflict);
  • the solve moves no point and changes no radius by more than 1e-9 mm (AUTO_CONSTRAINT_TOLERANCE): the geometry stays as drawn.

Otherwise the command is refused and nothing changes; the message says why after auto constraint k<n>: : redundant, conflict: <the solver's reason> or moves p3 by 1.000e-2 mm (the point or curve that moved most). The tools skip such a constraint without a hint and log the reason. Accepted, the result is that of any sketch.add_constraint (constraints: the new id). Order matters for a tangent: a line end first held on a circle (coincident) is then tangent there, at the shared point; the tools add the end holds first.

Example: a circle of radius 10 about the origin and a line from (-20, 10) to (0, 10). coincident of the line’s end with the circle, vertical_points of that end and the centre, and tangent of the circle and the line are added; a horizontal of the line is then refused as redundant (the end above the centre on the circle and the tangent make the line level), and so is the same tangent again. A horizontal of a line 0.01 mm off level is refused as moves p… by 5.000e-3 mm, where a plain sketch.add_constraint would level it.

Tests: core/model-tests/sketch/src/sketch_auto_1024_tests.rs (mock kernel); the application’s use in app/tests/sketch_snap.cpp (autoConstraintTests), step 7 of tools/ui-sketch-tools-test.sh and app.ui-windows-sketch-auto-constraints.

New designs in other units

A design’s length unit is its own (set_units, Timeline and parameters), and a new design starts in millimetres. The application’s Preferences › General › Default units for new designs (mitcad#1036) makes new designs start in another unit, as their initial state rather than a change: no undo step, and the design is not modified, as a new design in millimetres is not. Three ways make one:

  • Document::new_design_in(kernel, length): as Document::new_design (the root and an active Component1, Design policy), with length as the document’s length unit; bare numbers in its expressions are read in it (1 is 25.4 mm in inches). The bridge’s new_design_document_in(unit) takes the unit’s name and refuses a name that is not a length unit.
  • A project’s new_design with units (Folders and designs): the file mitcad_model::file::empty_design_in(length) writes, the same as Document::new_design_in(..).to_json(); a name that is not a length unit, a value that is not a string, or units with text is refused and nothing is written; null is as left out.
  • mitcad_model::file::parse_length_unit(text) reads the unit’s name as set_units does (mm, cm, m, in, ft, …).

The unit is saved in the file’s units as any design’s; a design opened or imported keeps the units of its file, and an open design is never changed by these.

Tests: a_new_design_can_start_in_other_units (core/model-tests/api/src/metric_defaults_tests.rs, mock kernel), a_new_design_takes_the_units_given (core/vcs/src/tests/folders.rs); the application’s in tools/ui-units-test.sh and app.ui-windows-default-units.

Filling a closed table

A closed table with parameter columns (mitcad#999) is the classic design table: a row per size, a column per parameter the row sets. Its rows are filled whole from a table of the design or from a CSV file (mitcad#1044; docs/configurations.md, “Filling a closed table”, decision 12). The logic is mitcad_model::configurations::{RowSource, RowFields, NewParameter} and Configurations::fill_rows (core/model-base/src/configurations/fill.rs); the CSV is document/configuration_rows_csv.rs and api/configuration_rows_csv.rs.

Generated rows with columns. generate_configuration_rows takes columns, other columns of the table (Configurations and tables):

{"cmd": "generate_configuration_rows", "table": "Screws", "column": "Size",
 "option": "Size", "columns": ["d", "k"]}
  • Each column sets the parameter of its name in every row, from the first row of the table with the row’s key (a column of the option’s kind and dimension, or a unitless one read in the parameter’s unit, as for the key). A parameter that is an option of the table takes it as the option’s value; any other becomes a parameter column of the table (parameters), and the table becomes closed. An empty cell takes the row’s value of that parameter out.
  • A parameter the design lacks is made with the column’s unit (Text for a text column, none for a unitless one), its expression the value of the row the options choose now, else of the first row; created lists them. A column whose name no parameter can have (in, m) is refused.
  • A row of the same name is updated (listed in updated when a value changed), the others added. In a closed table, a row without a value of an option takes the option’s current value (its constant expression).
  • The parameters, the rows and the table are one undo step (Generate Rows from Screws); undo takes the parameters made back too.

The rows as CSV.

Fields Result
query configuration_rows_csv none csv: the rows as CSV, rows: their number
query configuration_rows_csv_preview csv what import_configuration_rows_csv would do; nothing changes
command import_configuration_rows_csv csv what it did, as the preview, and moves (the cascade’s, as generate_configuration_rows’s; empty when nothing changed); one undo step Import Configuration Rows, none when the table is already as the file has it; nothing recomputed

The file is read as a table CSV is (Tables as CSV: UTF-8, RFC 4180 quoting, semicolons, units in the header’s brackets, decimal commas, inferred columns, free names, at most 10 000 rows and 100 columns).

  • Name, Designation, Part Number and Supplier URL (in any case, with or without spaces, _ or -) fill the rows’ fields; an empty cell clears a field. A row without a name is named by its key. A field twice is refused.
  • The first other column is the key option (made with its column’s unit when the design lacks it); every other column sets the parameter of its name (its free name when the file’s cannot be used), as the columns of a generated row do, one row per line. A row twice in the file is refused (the row M4 is in the file twice); a file without a column of values too.
  • A cell of a number column that is a formula (d * 0.6; the tables CSV reader refuses it as a cell) is kept as the row’s expression of a parameter column. Any other refused cell refuses the import.
  • Rows of the same name are updated, others added, and the table’s rows the file does not have are kept (kept). The import is refused, and nothing changes, with the table’s first problem afterwards (problem).
  • Export writes the options’ and the parameter columns’ values in their parameters’ units (a text without quotes, a formula as its text), then Name, then Designation, Part Number and Supplier URL when a row has one: size [Text],d [mm],k [mm],Name [Text]. Export and import give the same rows.

The preview and the import answer:

Field
key the key option
columns in the file’s order: name (the file’s), renamed (the parameter’s, when the file’s cannot be used), unit, inferred, role (key, option, parameter, name, designation, part_number, supplier_url)
rows the cells as the file has them (numbers in their column’s unit, texts, a formula as its text, null for an empty or refused cell)
refused cells, as a table CSV’s: line, column, text, reason
added, updated, kept row names
created the parameters the import makes
closed the table is closed after the import
unchanged the table is already as the file has it
problem the table’s first problem afterwards, which refuses the import (left out when none)
summary 3 rows from the file: added M3, M4, M5; updated M2; made the parameters size, d; kept Old; 1 cell refused (all up to date when nothing changes) 
{"query": "configuration_rows_csv"}
{"query": "configuration_rows_csv_preview", "csv": "size,d [mm],k [mm]\r\nM3,3,1.86\r\n"}
{"cmd": "import_configuration_rows_csv", "csv": "size,d [mm],k [mm]\r\nM3,3,1.86\r\n"}

Add Option on a closed table with rows is set_configurations with the option in options and every row’s value of it (the application gives each row the parameter’s current value, a parameter column keeps its rows’ values): a closed table refuses an option that a row has no value of (M3: no value for Color).

A filament’s variants per printer and nozzle

One filament is one material (mitcad#1054; core/model/src/material.rs, print_files/filaments.rs, document/material_variants.rs). Its settings for different printers and nozzles are the material’s variants, not separate materials: the user picks “this filament”, and the right values follow from the printer and nozzle in use.

  • Variants. A material keeps its own filament values (its base) and variants: [{"printer", "nozzle", "filament", "slicer"}], each holding only the filament values (and a slicer’s own keys) that differ from the base. printer names the printer as its printer profiles do: a profile’s printer model (printer_model), else its name without the nozzle (“Bench X 0.4 nozzle” is Bench X; “(0.4 nozzle)”, “0.4mm nozzle” too); nozzle is the diameter in mm, left out for any nozzle of the printer. One level: a variant inherits nothing but the base. A variant never sets filament_colour: a filament whose colours print differently is a material per colour, each with its colour. Two variants of one printer and nozzle are refused.
  • Resolution. What a body prints with (Print profiles, print_settings, the export) takes the material’s values with the variant its printer picks over them: the variant of the printer and its nozzle (match exact), else one of the printer for any nozzle, else the printer’s of the nearest nozzle (printer), else none (the base). The printer profile’s names (its printer model, its name and its slicers’ preset names, each also without the nozzle) and its nozzle_diameter (else the nozzle its name says) are what is matched, in any case and spacing.
  • The nozzle. A printer profile’s nozzle_diameter (the key map’s printer key) is its nozzle: read from the slicers’ printer presets on import and edited as any of its values. library_items of printers gives each row’s variant_printer and nozzle: the printer and nozzle a material’s variant names for it.
  • Import. import_print_profile and import_slicer_presets merge the presets of one filament into one material: the same name before its @ (any case: “Shop PLA @Bench X”, “Shop PLA @Bench Y 0.6 nozzle”) and the same colour. A preset is for the printers it is compatible with (its slicer’s compatible_printers), else for the printer its name’s @ part names ("@Bench X 0.6 nozzle", “@MK4 0.6”; a bare last number is a nozzle only when it has a decimal point and is 0.1 to 2 mm, so “@Ender 3” is the printer Ender 3), else for any. A preset for any printer is the base and the others its variants with the values that differ from it; without one the base is the values all of them share and each preset’s other values its variants. A preset for several printers gives each a variant. Two presets for any printer, and a filament of one preset, stay as they were. The merged material is named as the filament; each variant keeps its preset’s own filament_settings_id, so that a slicer finds its preset. A project’s purge volumes follow its merged materials.
  • The printers in use. import_slicer_presets’ printers ([{"printer", "nozzle"}], a nozzle null or left out for any) keeps only the presets and variants of those printers and nozzles; a preset for any printer always comes in. All when left out.
  • Materials kept apart. Designs and libraries from before have one material per preset (“Shop PLA @Bench X” and “Shop PLA @Bench Y”); they load unchanged, without variants. slicer_presets’ merge lists the target’s groups of them (two or more plastics of one filament and colour, one of them for a printer, that can be merged: [{"name", "items": [{"id", "name"}]}]), import_slicer_presets with merge_separate merges them first in the same undo step (merged in its answer; presets may then be empty), and merge_materials merges some by id.

In the design the first takes the merged values and the filament’s name (unless another material shows it), the others go and the bodies and components that named them name it; one undo step Merge Materials Shop PLA.
