Pipe and Sweep along 3D sketch curves (mitcad#1523)

A Pipe’s or a Sweep’s path (and a sweep’s guide_rail, guide_rail2 and auxiliary frame curve), a loft’s centerline, rails and auxiliary frame curve, a path pattern’s path and a construction plane’s or point’s path (along_path, normal_at_point; mitcad#1550) may be curves of a 3D sketch of the same component before it, named by the typed path form:

JSON Meaning
{"spatial_sketch": "F3", "curves": ["c3", "c6", "c9"]} the curves, in any order, joined end to end
{"spatial_sketch": "F3", "curves": ["c3"], "chain": true} also every curve joined to them end to end (construction curves only when listed)
"reversed": true (with either) the path runs the other way

Pieces. Lines, arcs, elliptical arcs and splines (control-point and fit-point ones) in any mix; a construction curve when it is listed. A curve without ends (a circle, an ellipse, a closed fit-point spline) is a closed path by itself, and so is a curve that starts and ends at one point; with other curves it is refused at the recompute (c7 is a closed curve: it is a closed path by itself, not a piece of a longer one). A reference curve is refused (3DSketch1's c12 is a reference curve, geometry from outside the sketch: it is no path piece (draw a curve on it)). Each piece is the curve’s model curve in the component’s coordinates (a line, an arc as a circular conic, an ellipse as a conic, a spline as a B-spline, a fit-point spline by its solved control net), mapped once from the sketch’s frame and turned round where the path runs against it.

Closed paths (mitcad#1550). Curves that close a loop without branching are a closed path: from the first listed curve’s start (its end when reversed) round to it again; one chained pick of any of its curves takes the whole loop. A Pipe and a Sweep along a closed path are closed (a Sweep’s Distance 2 is none, as along a closed planar path).

Joints and order. Curves join where they share a point, or where their ends are points made coincident (a coincident relation; in a sketch converted from a planar one also an in-plane coincidence of two points, whose ends must still meet). Ends that only lie near each other do not join, and curves that cross do not meet there. The curves must make one chain, open or closed, without branches; the joints, not the positions, decide the order, so it stays the same whatever a recompute solves. Chain selection adds the curves joined to the listed ones the same way.

Direction. The path runs through the first listed curve along its own direction (a line from start to end, an arc counter-clockwise about its normal, a spline from its first point), against it with "reversed": true; first curve and direction are kept across edits and recomputes. Use the existing Pipe corners and Sweep orientation options: tangent joins (tangent relations) give a smooth path, a sharp corner a mitered or rounded one; no bend is added.

Associativity and failures. The path is found from the sketch’s current solve on every recompute: a dimension, a parameter or a moved support moves the pipe or sweep. When the feature is added or edited the selection is checked (the sketch is a 3D sketch before the feature, of its component; every listed curve is a curve of it that can be a piece, listed once; no curves selected, 3DSketch1 has no curve c99); a planar path form naming a 3D sketch, or the 3D form naming a planar one, is refused naming the right form. Whether the curves still make one chain is found by the recompute, so an edit of the sketch that breaks it is taken and fails the Pipe or Sweep with the reason (the path branches at p2 (10, 0, 0): c3, c5 and c8 meet there, c9 does not join the others); deleting a curve a path lists is refused (Pipe1 would no longer work: ...). A sketch that fails (a lost support or source, conflicting relations) fails the feature using it, and no last geometry is used. A failure of the pipe’s or sweep’s own geometry is the consumer’s: the sketch stays solved and editable.

Chains in the query. The sketch3d query’s chains lists what chain selection finds: [{curves (an open chain’s in order from the free end of the end curve with the smaller id, a closed one’s from its smallest curve, a branched one’s in id order), closed, branches (the points where three or more meet, when any), path (the typed path that takes the chain whole, for an open or closed one without branches)}]; a curve without ends (a circle, an ellipse, a closed spline) is a closed chain of its own; construction curves and reference curves are in none.

Routes in the query (mitcad#1527). {"query": "sketch3d", "uid": "F3", "path": {"curves": ["c6", "c3"], "chain": false, "reversed": false}} adds route to the answer: how a Pipe would run along those curves of the sketch (chain and reversed as in the typed path, both optional), found from the sketch’s joints as the recompute finds it: {curves (in order along the path), forward (for each, whether the path runs along its own direction), start, end (the points the path starts and ends at; null for a closed curve), closed (mitcad#1550: it ends where it starts)}, or {error, message, places} with the reason a Pipe along them would fail or be refused: error for agents with the ids and points (the path branches at p2 (40.000000, 0.000000, 0.000000): c3, c5 and c8 meet there, c9 does not join the others: ..., c7 is a closed curve: ..., 3DSketch1 has no curve c99), message the same in plain words (the path branches at a point: 3 curves meet there, mitcad#1644) and places the points it is about, when it has them. The application lists a picked path’s route with it while a path input is open (app/COMMANDS.md, “Pipe and Sweep along 3D sketches”).

Every curve input (mitcad#1550). Besides the paths above:

  • a path pattern’s path and a construction plane’s or point’s path take the typed form, measured along the path’s exact pieces as along an Intersection Curve (a fraction of the whole length, a length from the start with physical, the point nearest to a point); Pattern on Path along a 3D sketch’s route moves the copies along it, and turns them with its tangent with along_path;
  • an axis or a line reference (a construction axis through an edge, a plane at an angle to a line, a plane through two lines or a line and a point, a point where two lines or a line and a plane meet, a helix’s or a revolve’s or a circular pattern’s axis) takes a 3D sketch’s line, {"sketch": "F3", "curve": "c4"}, from its start to its end, and for an axis also its arc or circle, the line through its centre along its normal;
  • a point reference ({"sketch": "F3", "point": "p2"}) takes a 3D sketch’s point where it is now;
  • an Intersection Curve’s first or second, a boundary surface’s curves and a surface loft’s sections of curves take a 3D sketch’s curves in the sketch-curves form ({"sketch": "F3", "curves": [...], "chain": true}): curves anywhere in space, as a set, chain selection by the sketch’s joints; an Intersection Curve sweeps them along the normal of the 3D sketch’s support plane, as its Project takes geometry onto it.

All of these follow the 3D sketch’s edits and fail with it, as a Pipe does. What grows from curves in their sketch’s plane (a rib’s or web’s curves, thin walls, the curves a surface extrusion, revolution or sweep sweeps) takes a 3D sketch’s curves in its sketch plane in the planar form (“Curves of 3D sketches that grow walls and surfaces” below); a tool of sketch curves takes a planar sketch’s alone. A path’s planar form naming a 3D sketch says which form to use (3DSketch1 (F3) is a 3D sketch: as a path its curves are {"spatial_sketch": "F3", "curves": [...]}).

The browser and the timeline. The timeline query’s sketches of a feature (mitcad#177) lists the 3D sketches it uses beside the planar ones: the browser lists a Pipe under its route’s sketch, and editing the Pipe shows that sketch for the edit. A 3D sketch is not hidden when a feature uses it (planar sketches are, mitcad#7): its route stays in view.

Planar paths in a conversion. mitcad_model::features::path::spatial_rewrite gives the typed path that a planar path along a sketch’s curves becomes when that sketch turns into a 3D sketch in place (mitcad#1544): the same curve ids and chain, reversed set so that it runs the way the planar path ran, a closed one too (mitcad#1550). rewrite_spatial_paths does it for every path a feature holds (a Pipe’s, a Sweep’s, a loft’s centre line, rails and auxiliary curve, a path pattern’s, a construction plane’s or point’s) and refuses a surface sweep’s curves, which grow from their sketch’s plane.

Tests: core/model/src/spatial_path_tests.rs (mock kernel: the route on a turned support driving a Pipe and a reversed Sweep, BC at 50 and the support turned, saved and read again; a subchain of a branching sketch, an explicit construction line, a Coincident joint, the failing and refused selections, an edit that breaks a chain, the query’s chains; a failed sketch and a failing pipe; lines, a tangent arc and splines either way with W11’s edits; a planar path rewritten), core/model-tests/api/src/sketch3d_tests.rs (the commands, the query’s chains and a pipe from them; routes_are_ordered_and_refused_as_paths, mitcad#1527: the query’s routes either way, from one pick and of a sub-chain, their refusals, a Pipe’s sketches in the timeline and a rib’s planar form refused) and CLI sketch3d_pipe (a pipe and a sweep along a line, a tangent arc and a spline on the geometry kernel, their volumes, AB edited). Closed paths and every curve input (mitcad#1550): core/model/src/spatial_consumers_tests.rs (a circle, a closed spline and a closed chain either way and from one chained pick, a closed curve with others refused, the chains; a loft’s centre line, rails and curve sections; planes, points, an axis, a point and a path pattern along a 3D sketch following AB’s edit; an Intersection Curve; every planar path rewritten by a conversion, a closed one too) and CLI sketch3d_consumers (the datums and the pattern’s copies on the geometry kernel, before and after AB’s edit; a pipe round a 3D sketch’s circle, a torus).

Fillet of 3D sketches (mitcad#1548)

sketch3d.fillet rounds the corner between two lines of a 3D sketch that share an end with a tangent arc of a radius, the bend of a tube route:

Command Fields Result
sketch3d.fillet sketch; a, b (two lines that share an end: their corner) and/or points (corners: points where exactly two ordinary lines end; construction lines are rounded by naming them); radius (value: a number, a parameter’s name or an expression) one undo step Fillet in 3DSketch1 for all the corners; made the arcs, fillets [{corner, lines [first, second], arc, center, tangent_points [on the first line, on the second], corner_lines (the two construction lines to the corner), full_lines (construction lines that took the lines’ segment relations)}], dimension (the radius dimension), and the edit’s entities, points, curves, constraints, dimensions, parameters and status

What a corner becomes. Both lines are trimmed back to the tangent points: they keep their ids, their direction (start and end stay in their order) and their other relations (an alignment, a tangency at the far end). A tangent arc of the radius in the lines’ plane joins them, counter-clockwise about its normal from the tangent point on the first line to the one on the second, with two tangent relations (the first line and the arc, the arc and the second line) and a driving radius dimension. The corner point stays where the lines’ extensions meet, with its own relations and dimensions (a Fix, an attachment, offsets typed for it): two construction lines run from the tangent points to it, the first tangent to the first line (in line with it) and both equal, which together hold it there with nothing redundant. What took a line as a segment to the corner, its length dimension, an equal of lines, a point_on or a midpoint relation, moves to a construction line between the line’s other end and the corner, so that a typed length keeps measuring to the corner. In-plane relations of a converted sketch stay on the trimmed line. Construction lines make a construction arc.

Several corners. Corners are rounded in the order given, a and b first: the first arc gets the radius dimension, the others are equal to it, so one value sets them all. A corner given by its point takes the two ordinary lines that end there when its turn comes, so both ends of a line can be rounded in one command (the second fillet trims what the first left of it).

Refusals (the edit then changes nothing: definition, parameters, ids, history): a line named twice, a curve that is no line; lines that do not share an end (c3 and c7 do not share an end: a fillet rounds the corner where two lines meet); lines collinear at their corner, straight on or folded back (c7 and c9 are collinear at p6: there is no corner to round); a radius whose tangent point would not lie inside either line (a radius of 35 mm does not fit c5: the arc would touch it 35 mm from the corner p2, and it is 30 mm long), or that is not above 1e-6 mm; a point where not exactly two ordinary lines end (p1 is no corner of two lines: ..., or p2 is an end of the lines c3, c5, c7: name the two lines to round); neither a and b nor points, and a without b.

Editing it later. The radius is a dimension like any other: sketch3d.set_dimension (or a parameter bound to it) moves the tangent points and the centre, the corner stays. Undo restores the corner whole: the lines end at it again with their own lengths.

Paths through a fillet. A Pipe’s or a Sweep’s path along curves of the 3D sketch (above) runs through the arc: a chain selection finds it by itself (the corner’s construction lines are in no chain), and a path that lists both lines of a corner takes the arc into its curves in the fillet’s undo step, so that the pipe still runs through the corner, now bent.

The application’s Fillet in a 3D sketch (app/COMMANDS.md “3D sketch Fillet”) sends one sketch3d.fillet with points or a and b per corner picked.

Tests: core/model/src/spatial_fillet_tests.rs (mock kernel: the route’s corner trimmed with its ids, alignments and lengths kept, the arc tangent to both lines, nothing free or redundant; an obtuse corner in a slanted plane by its lines; the radius edited; both corners in one edit, the second Equal to the first; the refusals; undo restoring the corner; a pipe that lists the lines taking the arcs and a chained one finding them), core/model-tests/api/src/sketch3d_tests.rs (corners_are_filleted_and_their_radius_edited) and CLI sketch3d_fillet (a three-segment route rounded at both corners and piped, its volume; the radius edited; undone).

Plane-bound shapes of 3D sketches (mitcad#1550)

The SKETCH tab’s circle, ellipse, rectangle, polygon and text tools draw in a 3D sketch on a frame plane, plane xy, yz or zx (the plane square to Z, X or Y), through the first point given; new points of the shape are put in that plane. Each command is one undo step with all it makes, or refused with nothing changed:

Command Fields Result
sketch3d.add_ellipse center, major (point inputs: the end of the major axis, a new one put in the plane through the centre), minor_radius (mm, where the solve starts), plane, major_value, minor_value (driving major and minor radius dimensions), construction made the ellipse
sketch3d.add_rectangle mode: two_point (a, b: opposite corners), center (center, corner) or three_point (a, b: the first side, c [x, y, z]: a place of the opposite side); plane; width, height (driving lengths of the first and second side); construction made the four lines counter-clockwise about the plane’s axis from the lower left corner (in the plane’s own first and second axis), corners the four points, center (a centre rectangle’s), construction (its diagonal), relations
sketch3d.add_polygon center, vertex (the first corner of an inscribed polygon, an existing point too; the middle of the first side of a circumscribed one, a place), sides (3 to 256), inscribed (default true), plane, radius (driving radius of its circle), construction made its sides, corners, center, construction (its circles), relations
sketch3d.add_text text, at [x, y, z] (the anchor), plane, height; frame [x, y, z] (the frame’s opposite corner: a text in a frame), angle, font, bold, italic, align, valign made [t5], texts

sketch3d.add_circle with plane (and through) is the circles' command.

What they store, as the planar tools make them, in the shape’s plane:

  • A rectangle or a polygon is lines through points with the planar relations as in-plane relations of its plane (in_plane with normal: x, y or z, the axis square to the plane; a converted sketch’s are z and leave it out): a 2-point or centre rectangle’s sides horizontal (along the plane’s first axis: X of XY, Y of YZ, Z of ZX) and vertical (along its second: Y, Z, X), a 3-point one’s perpendicular, a centre rectangle’s construction diagonal with the centre at its midpoint; an inscribed polygon’s corners coincident with its construction circle (bound to the plane) and its sides equal, a circumscribed one’s sides tangent to the inner circle and its corners on the outer one. One plane_bound relation (points, normal) keeps the shape’s points in one plane square to that axis: their coordinates along it stay equal, wherever the plane is. So a shape has the planar shape’s freedoms and one more, its plane’s place; nothing is redundant.
  • A circle on a plane is bound to it (plane {axis, sense}). An ellipse (or an elliptical arc) is plane-bound with normal (z when left out): its major point and an arc’s ends stay in the plane through its centre, and its minor radius is solved: minor_radius is where the last solve left it, a point_on relation holds a point on the ellipse, and the dimensions major_radius and minor_radius ({"type": "minor_radius", "curve": "c5"}) drive it. The sketch3d query’s geometry of an ellipse is major, minor and normal.
  • A text is the planar text in its plane at z along its normal, its at and frame in that plane’s coordinates; a framed text’s frame is a construction rectangle of the plane whose corner, x corner and y corner it follows. The query lists each text with id, plane (XY, YZ, ZX) and its outline (polylines of local points, laid out with the kernel’s fonts), or outline_error. sketch3d.remove deletes a text by its id (t5); its frame stays.

Deleting a shape’s line leaves its corners while other lines use them; a point only a plane_bound relation lists goes with the last curve that used it, and the relation goes when fewer than two points are left.

Shapes and lines on a rotated plane of 3D sketches (mitcad#1661)

The drawing tools’ placement plane rotates freely (app/COMMANDS.md “3D sketch drawing tools”); what they draw on it is stored with the rotated plane’s frame {"x": [x, y, z], "normal": [x, y, z]} (local directions: x in the plane, normal across it, y = normal × x; made unit and square, x taken across the normal; refused when they have no length or x lies along the normal). The frame gives the plane’s directions only: the shape’s own points place it, and the sketch’s frame never changes.

  • sketch3d.add_circle, add_ellipse, add_rectangle, add_polygon and add_text take the frame as their plane in place of xy, yz or zx. The shapes are what the frame planes’ are (above) with the frame’s x and y as the plane’s first and second axis: a rectangle’s sides horizontal along x and vertical along y, its points kept in one plane square to the normal. A circle’s normal is free, held along the frame’s normal by a normal_along relation; an ellipse stores frame beside normal; a text stores frame, its at, angle and frame in the frame’s x and y and z along its normal (the query’s plane says rotated).
  • sketch3d.add_line takes frame: its axis (with sense, Keep Axis and Axis and Length) and offsets are then along the frame’s x, y and normal, stored as an align_along relation and offset_along dimensions.
Relation or dimension Fields Rows
in_frame relation (a planar relation, as in_plane’s), frame the planar relation on the points’ coordinates along the frame’s x and y (the solver’s rotated planes, SpatialSystem::add_in_plane_frame)
frame_bound points, frame their coordinates along the frame’s normal equal the first’s (one each but the first)
align_along line, direction (unit), sense the line along the direction, anywhere (2), its sense validated as align’s
normal_along curve (an arc or circle with a free normal), direction (unit) its normal along the direction, either way (2)
offset_along (dimension) a, b, direction (unit) (b - a).direction - value (1), signed

in_frame relations come with the shapes only (sketch3d.add_constraint refuses them, as in_plane); the others can be added to any sketch. A sketch with them turns back into 2D only where its geometry lies in the sketch plane: they go with it as another frame plane’s do, a tilted ellipse, a text on a rotated plane and a circle’s normal held across the sketch’s normal are named. Tests: core/model-tests/api/src/sketch3d_tests.rs (shapes_on_a_rotated_plane_are_solved_saved_and_read_again: a circle, a rectangle, an ellipse, a polygon, a text and lines along the frame’s axes solved, saved and read again).

Turning a planar sketch into a 3D sketch (mitcad#1544)

{"cmd": "sketch3d.convert", "sketch": "F3"} turns the planar sketch F3 into a 3D sketch in place, as one undo step (Convert Sketch1 to 3D Sketch). Undo takes it back, and sketch3d.convert_to_2d turns a 3D sketch that all lies in its sketch plane back into a planar one (below); a 3D sketch is refused here (is a 3D sketch already).

Command Fields Result
sketch3d.convert sketch (a planar sketch) the same feature as a 3D sketch with its ids kept: kept, in_plane, coincident, fixes, on_sketch_plane, attachments, references, dropped, rewritten and status (below); refused as a whole, naming the features in the way

What is kept. The feature (its uid, name, place in the timeline, visibility), its support and its own frame (frame, the planar sketch’s; its normal is the 3D sketch’s local +Z), and every point, curve, text, constraint and dimension id, construction flag, driving dimension’s parameter (name and expression), driven dimension and text. Points start where the planar sketch last solved them, at z = 0.

Planar 3D sketch
point (x, y) point (x, y, 0)
line line; a centre line becomes a construction line
arc, circle arc or circle whose normal is bound to +Z (plane; sketch3d.release_plane frees it)
ellipse, elliptical arc, text plane-bound ellipse, elliptical arc, text
spline (control-point or fit-point, open or closed) spline of the same kind, degree, weights and knots
coincidence of two points 3D coincidence (coincident)
a fixed point or curve in-plane fix (in_plane_fixed: its x and y)
every other constraint and dimension in-plane relation or dimension (in_plane), evaluated on the x and y of its points, with its id, value, expression and driving state

One on_sketch_plane relation keeps the geometry in the sketch plane: it lists the lowest id of each group of points whose elevations are tied (by coincidences and plane-bound curves), so a fully constrained planar sketch stays fully constrained (dof 0) and nothing becomes redundant. A group that something else holds (an attached point, a point on a projected curve) is not listed. sketch3d.release_from_plane frees a point’s group (DOF +1 per group: its elevation); relations and dimensions added after the conversion are 3D ones (an in-plane length stays in plane until it is removed and dimensioned again).

Linked projections keep following their sources (mode Project): a projected point of a vertex or another sketch’s point is attached to it (attach with projected); a projected line stays a construction line whose ends are attached to the source curve’s start and end (matched by where they are); any other projected curve becomes a reference curve of its source (reference with projected), with its ends attached where something uses them, a point on it (a planar coincidence with the curve) a point_on of the reference curve and a midpoint of it a midpoint. Unlinked projected geometry stays fixed (in-plane fixes), as construction geometry.

Consumers. In the same step, later features’ planar paths along the sketch’s curves (a Pipe’s or Sweep’s path, guide rails, an auxiliary curve) are rewritten to the typed path with the same curves and direction (above), and later sketches’ linked projections of its points and curves keep following.

Profiles (mitcad#1550): the features that use the sketch’s profile regions (Extrude, Revolve, a Sweep’s or Loft’s profile, every other region user) keep them: the 3D sketch’s closed loops in its sketch plane bound the same regions under the same keys (below).

Kept in the plane (mitcad#1550): what 3D sketches have no own form for is kept in the 3D sketch’s planar records (planar in the definition and the sketch3d query; planar in the result names them) and acts in the sketch plane as it acted in the planar sketch: patterns and offsets (their copies and results bound in the plane; the curves of derived offsets, of ellipses and splines, computed there after every solve), the placement on the plane (an offset, a move, a rotation), a plane of another component (found through its link), texts that follow text parameters, inactive constraints and dimensions (kept in plane, holding nothing), and every linked projection a reference record cannot stand for (a face’s edges, section curves, a chain of edges, a source as an earlier feature left it, several curves of one source, a projected curve other than a line whose centre is used or that a relation other than a point on it names): its entities stay geometry held in the plane by in-plane fixes, moved to their sources at every evaluation. The planar flags (projected entities, centre lines, the sketch’s axes, where the dimensions’ values are shown) are kept too, so the sketch turns back into the same planar sketch.

Refused, nothing converted, naming why or the features in the way: a later feature that takes the sketch in a form only a planar sketch has (every path, closed ones too, is rewritten; the curves a rib, a web, thin walls or a surface sweep grow from keep their form, which the 3D sketch’s curves in its sketch plane have too, mitcad#1550), a feature or a parameter that uses a driven dimension’s reference parameter (a 3D sketch’s driven dimensions have none) and a change that would make an evaluated feature fail.

Result. uid, name, type (spatial_sketch), kept {points, curves, texts, constraints, dimensions} (the planar ids kept), in_plane (the constraints and dimensions kept in plane), coincident (kept as 3D coincidences), fixes (the new in-plane fixes), on_sketch_plane {relation, points}, attachments (made for linked projections), references (projected curves made reference curves), dropped (points of those curves that nothing else used), rewritten [{uid, name}] and status (as an edit’s). The sketch3d query then flags in-plane relations and dimensions (in_plane), plane-bound curves (plane_bound) and the points kept on the sketch plane (on_sketch_plane).

{"cmd": "sketch3d.convert", "sketch": "F1"}

→ {"uid": "F1", "name": "Sketch1", "type": "spatial_sketch", "kept": {"points": ["p5", "p6", "p7", "p8"], "curves": ["c1", "c2", "c3", "c4"], "texts": [], "constraints": ["k1", "k2", "k3", "k4"], "dimensions": ["k5", "k6"]}, "in_plane": ["k1", "k2", "k3", "k4", "k5", "k6"], "coincident": [], "fixes": ["k7"], "on_sketch_plane": {"relation": "k8", "points": ["p5", "p6", "p7", "p8"]}, "attachments": [], "references": [], "dropped": [], "rewritten": [], "status": {"dof": 0, "fully_constrained": true, ...}}

The app’s Sketch Palette has a 3D Sketch box for the open sketch, and the Browser’s and timeline’s menus of a planar sketch Convert to 3D Sketch (app/COMMANDS.md); an agent’s sketch3d.convert of the sketch it has open switches the editor the same way.

Profile regions of 3D sketches (mitcad#1550)

A solved 3D sketch’s closed loops in its sketch plane (|z| at most 1e-6 mm: its On Sketch Plane geometry and any loop drawn there) bound profile regions as a planar sketch’s curves do, with the supporting face’s edges, its texts and derived offsets, and under the keys a planar sketch’s same curves have (r{c1[c4,c2],...}). Loops out of the plane bound none. Extrude, Revolve, Sweep and Loft profiles and every other profile user take them as {"sketch": "F3", "region": "r{...}"}; the profiles query lists them, and the sketch3d query’s regions names them.

Turning a 3D sketch back into 2D (mitcad#1550)

{"cmd": "sketch3d.convert_to_2d", "sketch": "F3"} turns the 3D sketch F3, whose geometry all lies in its sketch plane, into a planar sketch in place, as one undo step (Convert 3DSketch1 to 2D Sketch). The sketch3d query’s flat says whether it can (off_plane names what lies out of the plane, with the ids; off_plane_messages says the same in plain words, mitcad#1644).

Command Fields Result
sketch3d.convert_to_2d sketch (a 3D sketch) the same feature as a planar sketch with its ids kept: kept {points, curves, texts, constraints, dimensions}, dropped, projected, notes, rewritten [{uid, name}] and dof; refused naming what lies out of the plane or the features in the way

What it becomes. Every point, curve, text, relation and dimension id; in-plane relations and dimensions back as the planar ones they were, active or not, with their values’ places; the planar records back in place (patterns, offsets, placement, plane link, text parameters, linked projections). 3D relations as their planar equivalents: a coincidence as a coincidence, an alignment along X or Y as horizontal or vertical, a point on a curve as a coincidence with it, midpoint, tangency, equal; a fix and an in-plane fix as a fixed entity; a true length as a length, an offset along X or Y as a signed horizontal or vertical distance, radius, diameter and arc length as theirs. An arc about -Z runs counter-clockwise with its ends swapped. What the plane holds by itself is left out (dropped): On Sketch Plane, a normal along Z, an offset along Z, a spline’s driven length, a point on a planar face in the sketch plane. Attachments become linked projections with the point on them (a vertex or another sketch’s point as a projected point, a curve’s start, end or middle as the projected curve with the point on its end or middle; the origin as a fixed point), and reference curves linked projections of their sources keeping their ids (projected). A fit-point spline’s free end becomes a natural one (notes).

Consumers. In the same step, later features’ paths along the sketch’s curves (a Pipe’s and a Sweep’s path, rails and auxiliary curve, a Loft’s centre line and rails, a path pattern’s, a construction plane’s or point’s along a path) are rewritten to the planar form with the same curves, and each keeps its direction: where the planar chain of its curves would run the other way (a path against its first curve, an arc about -Z that runs counter-clockwise in 2D with its ends swapped), the planar path gets "reversed": true (see Paths); the profile users keep their regions.

Refused, nothing changed: geometry out of the sketch plane, named (p3 is 7 mm off the sketch plane, a curve whose normal is not the plane’s, a line kept along Z), a point on a face that is not a plane in the sketch plane (Detach it first), a later feature in the way, a change that would make an evaluated feature fail.

{"cmd": "sketch3d.convert_to_2d", "sketch": "F1"}

→ {"uid": "F1", "name": "Sketch1", "type": "sketch", "kept": {"points": ["p5", "p6", "p7", "p8"], "curves": ["c1", "c2", "c3", "c4"], "texts": [], "constraints": ["k1", "k2", "k3", "k4"], "dimensions": ["k5", "k6"]}, "dropped": ["k7", "k8"], "projected": [], "notes": [], "rewritten": [], "dof": 0}

The app’s 3D Sketch Palette has the 3D Sketch box checked: unchecking it turns the open sketch back into 2D, and the Browser’s and timeline’s menus of a 3D sketch have Convert to 2D Sketch (app/COMMANDS.md).

Tests: core/sketch/src/spatial_planar_tests.rs (a rectangle back to the same planar sketch, a point off the plane named, the region of a loop in the plane and none of one out of it, a kept pattern binding its copies), core/sketch/src/spatial_convert_tests.rs (what is kept), core/model/src/sketch_conversion_tests.rs (an extruded sketch both ways keeping its profile, a 3D sketch drawn in its plane back to 2D with its Pipe’s path, refused off its plane, a pattern through both conversions), core/model/src/spatial_sketch_tests.rs (W9), core/model-tests/api/src/sketch3d_tests.rs (a_3d_sketch_is_turned_back_into_2d) and CLI sketch3d_to_2d.

Curves of 3D sketches that grow walls and surfaces (mitcad#1550)

What grows from curves in their sketch’s plane takes a 3D sketch’s curves in its sketch plane, in the planar form, as its profiles are taken (“Profile regions of 3D sketches” above): a rib’s or web’s curves, thin walls along curves (thin.curves of an extrusion), and the curves a surface extrusion, revolution or sweep sweeps:

{"cmd": "add_feature", "def": {"type": "rib",
 "curves": {"sketch": "F1", "curves": ["c3", "c5"]}, "thickness": 2,
 "extent": {"type": "depth", "depth": 10}}}

The curves are those of the sketch plane’s planar form (|z| at most 1e-6 mm), with the ids the 3D sketch has; the feature grows in and along the sketch plane as from a 2D sketch on the same plane (the rib’s thickness across it, a web’s and a surface extrusion’s along its normal), and follows the 3D sketch’s edits. Chain selection ("chain": true) adds the curves joined end to end to the picked ones in the sketch plane (construction curves left out), as in a 2D sketch. The sketch3d query’s plane_curves lists the curves that lie in the sketch plane now.

Refused. Before the evaluation, as a path’s selection is: an id the sketch does not have, one listed twice, a reference curve (draw a curve on it). At the evaluation, a curve out of the sketch plane fails the feature, naming the sketch and the curves (3DSketch1's c7 does not lie in its sketch plane: walls and surfaces grow from a 3D sketch's curves in its sketch plane); no other plane is taken in its stead. A planar sketch whose curves a rib, a web, thin walls or a surface sweep use turns into a 3D sketch and back with them (sketch3d.convert, sketch3d.convert_to_2d).

The app’s Rib, Web, Extrude (Thin Extrude) and Surface Extrude, Surface Revolve and Surface Sweep panels take a 3D sketch’s curves in its sketch plane and refuse a click on one out of it, saying why (app/COMMANDS.md); Surface Sweep’s Path takes a 3D sketch’s curves as a Pipe’s does.

Tests: core/model/src/spatial_plane_curves_tests.rs (mock kernel: a rib and a web from a route’s curves in the plane, chained without the one out of it, thin walls and a surface extrusion, revolution and sweep following an edit, the curve out of the plane refused naming the sketch, a planar sketch with a rib, a surface extrusion and a surface sweep converted both ways), core/model-tests/api/src/sketch3d_tests.rs (routes_are_ordered_and_refused_as_paths), CLI sketch3d_plane_curves and the UI step in tools/ui-sketch3d-test.sh.

Design review

A read-only review of the current design (design_review, mitcad#1513). It returns modeling guidance from the existing definitions and computed results; it does not repair references, change geometry, recompute or add an undo step. The ordinary non-print checks do not request meshes.

Query Fields Result
design_review scope (all by default, a component uid or name, or an array of feature uids), checks (rule ids; all when omitted, none for an empty array), print (auto by default, true, false) findings: rule, level (error, warning, info, the Notice levels), target (feature uid, body uid, plate id or user parameter name), message, advice, guide (topic, anchor); errors (print checks that could not run: rule, target, message); print (enabled, bodies, contexts, default_nozzle_diameter, default_layer_height)

Examples through the model query tool:

{"query": "design_review", "print": false}
{"query": "design_review", "scope": "C2", "checks": ["failed-feature", "fixed-placement"]}
{"query": "design_review", "scope": ["F2", "F5"], "checks": ["sketch-underconstrained", "fixed-placement", "volatile-parent"], "print": false}

A component scope selects features owned by that component; C0 selects only the root’s own features, while all selects the whole design. A feature array selects exactly those features, each once; an empty array selects none. Unknown components, feature uids and check ids are refused. User parameters are global, so unused-parameter runs only with scope all. Geometry and sketch guidance is for unsuppressed features before the timeline marker; names and grouping also describe rolled-back and suppressed definitions.

Rule id Level What it checks
failed-feature error A feature’s current failure.
auto-fixable warning References which the model found under another name and Auto Fix can write back.
sketch-underconstrained warning A solved sketch with degrees of freedom greater than zero.
sketch-fixed-heavy warning Ordinary sketch entities held by fixed flags; projected geometry and the sketch axes are excluded.
fixed-placement warning A primitive on a fixed plane, including its picked-geometry placement, or a sketch on a fixed construction plane.
volatile-parent warning A selected face, edge or vertex whose topological name refers to a fillet, chamfer, pattern or mirror. Merely modifying a body after a fillet is not enough.
repeated-literal info The same literal length in at least three independent feature-owned parameter slots within the scope. Angles, counts, raw coordinates, shared named parameters and computed expressions are excluded.
unused-parameter info A user parameter not referenced by feature slots, parameter expressions or limits, bindings or configurations.
default-names info A feature name still formed from its type’s default base followed by digits.
ungrouped-timeline info A feature outside every timeline group.
overhang warning Unsupported area from the existing print-overhang query, using the assigned bed face or design -Z, at 45 degrees.
thin-wall warning Thin regions from the existing print-thickness query, with a minimum of two nozzle diameters.
outside-build-volume warning The existing build-volume query lists the body’s current shown placement outside the printer bed, height or permitted area.
min-gap warning Two checked bodies on the same plate (or, without plates, in the design) are apart but closer than the design’s print_in_place_gap, else 0.3 mm, as print_min_gap finds them (mitcad#1519); the target is the pair’s first body.
stray-bodies warning A piece that a feature in the scope split off a body (a cut that leaves a body in several pieces gives the extra pieces new bodies) still has a default name while another piece of the same split was named (mitcad#1731). The target is the unnamed piece. Splits where no piece is named are left to the user’s naming.
no-bed-face warning A checked body on a print plate whose piece has no usable print bed face, so the 3D print export orients it automatically. A body on its own plate item, or on none, is a piece of its own; bodies on a plate through an occurrence item print as assembled, are one piece that turns onto a bed face of any of its bodies, and are reported once, at their first checked body (mitcad#1731).
no-print-profile warning A plate whose checked bodies include one without an effective printer profile: its 3MF names a placeholder printer the slicer cannot slice with (mitcad#1727, mitcad#1731). The target is the plate’s id.
split-profile warning A feature whose profile region references a sketch change found as several regions (the region was split) or as fewer regions than the feature selected (selected regions merged). The feature builds with the regions found and otherwise keeps only its region warning; auto_fix writes them into the definition (mitcad#1731).

With print: auto, only scoped final bodies with an assigned print bed face, a print plate or an effective printer profile are checked. Explicit true checks all scoped printable bodies; false runs no print checks. If checks selects no print rule, none runs regardless of print. no-bed-face and no-print-profile are print checks that apply only to a design with print plates; like outside-build-volume they request no meshes. A selected modifying feature includes the final bodies its output sets. The review uses the current body’s first shown occurrence (else its first occurrence, else its own coordinates), as the underlying print queries do. Printer settings and the assigned plate are resolved through that same occurrence path, including body overrides. The build-volume check uses that placement’s effective printer, which can differ from the root’s printer used by the ordinary build_volume query. The contexts list identifies each checked body’s occurrence path, assigned plate, effective printer, nozzle diameter and layer height, including defaults and body overrides. The build-volume check describes assembly placement, not the later export’s automatic arrangement; inspect the exported plate layout too.

Without an effective nozzle size the print checks use 0.4 mm, and the assumed layer height is 0.2 mm. These defaults do not invent a printer’s bed dimensions: without a bed, build-volume fit is reported in errors as unchecked. A failed print query likewise appears there, not as an empty successful check. Findings link to the modeling guide topic and anchor: look it up with model_reference {"guide": "<topic>"}.

Modeling hints in MCP command results

The MCP model_command tool returns hints by default: up to three short findings about features the call added or edited. Each has rule, target (the feature uid), message (the finding and advice), and guide (topic and anchor, read with model_reference {"guide": "<topic>"}).

The rules are sketch-underconstrained, fixed-placement, and volatile-parent, shared with the design_review query. Untouched features, merely recomputed dependants and old failures are not included. An empty hints array means no finding for the edited features. A stopped command array reviews only the entries that actually ran; a refused and rolled-back array returns its refusal without hints. Undo and redo produce no hints.

Set "hints": false beside command to omit feedback and avoid the review query. It is a boolean. This works with timeline: "changed", "full", or "none" in both headless and live MCP; it is not a field of an individual model command. These are modeling suggestions, not errors or extra edits.

Narrow gaps between bodies printed in place

mitcad#1519: parts printed in place (a hinge and its pin, a captive part) fuse when the gap between them is under about 0.3 mm. interference finds bodies that overlap; print_min_gap finds those that lie too close where they do not touch. It is an analysis only: no body, feature or export changes. The logic is Rust (print_analysis::gap_candidates, gap_kind, face_gap, the query in api/print.rs); the distances are the kernel’s exact ones (Kernel::measure_between of the two whole bodies, the same minimum distance measure gives, and for bodies that touch Kernel::face_separations, the same distance between pairs of their faces, mitcad#1672).

Query Fields Result
print_min_gap bodies (body uids; empty or left out: the printed bodies at the marker, solids and mesh bodies), or plate (a print plate by id or name: the printed bodies that print on it; not both), gap (mm, greater than zero; left out: the design’s user parameter print_in_place_gap when it is a length greater than zero, else 0.3 mm) gap, gap_from (query, parameter or default), bodies (how many were checked), pairs: [{a, b (body uids), names, distance (mm), on_a, on_b (the closest points, design coordinates), touches (the bodies touch elsewhere: the gap is beside their contact)}], the closest first, closest (the smallest distance, null without pairs), touching (pairs that touch or overlap; their contact is interference’s), unmeasured (pairs that touch whose faces the kernel could not measure: a narrow gap beside their contact is not ruled out)
  • Narrow: a pair whose smallest distance is more than 0.000 001 mm and less than the gap by more than 0.000 001 mm. A pair at the gap or farther is not reported.
  • Touching pairs (mitcad#1672): bodies that touch or overlap are counted in touching; a body inside the other’s material is left at that. For the others the faces are measured pair by pair (only faces whose boxes lie within the gap of each other): a pair of faces that touch or cross is the contact and left out; any other pair narrow by the rule above whose faces face each other across air is a gap, and the smallest is reported with touches: true, its distance and closest points. Faces face each other when each one’s outward normal at its closest point lies within 30° of the line to the other face. So a peg in its hole beside a face the bodies lie on together is found (the walls of the peg and the hole face each other), while a face that only meets the contact at its edge (the side of a block above the face it stands on, the top of a plate beside the peg at the hole’s rim) is not a gap, and walls of bodies that overlap face away from each other and are not either. A face pair that touches anywhere is a contact as a whole: a peg leaning on one side of its hole has no gap reported on the other. A kernel that cannot measure the faces leaves the pair in unmeasured.
  • Where: each body where it is shown in the design, as the other print queries place it (its first shown occurrence, else its first one), so a plate’s occurrence item is measured as assembled. The 3MF export lays separate pieces of a plate apart; this query measures the bodies in place.
  • Cost: only pairs whose boxes lie within the gap of each other are measured; their distances are kept by the two bodies’ shapes and placements, so asking again, with another gap too, measures nothing again. A touching pair’s faces are kept by the two bodies and the gap asked for. Run inside a model job, the query checks the cancel request between pairs (the computation was canceled).
  • Errors: a body that is not there at the marker, or a distance the kernel cannot measure, answers {"error": "..."}; an unknown plate, bodies with plate, a gap that is not greater than zero and unknown fields are refused.
  • Print Analysis: a print analysis’ min_gap ({"enabled": true, "gap": null} by default, see Print analysis) asks this query for its bodies when it has two or more. The application lists the pairs with their distances, draws each gap’s closest points and a marker at the smallest one, and logs narrow gaps under 0.3 mm: Body1-Body2 0.20 mm. Without pairs it says no bodies are closer than the gap where they do not touch, or, when touching pairs were unmeasured, that none was found and how many touching pairs could not be checked (the log adds (1 touching not checked)).
  • Design review: the rule min-gap (Design review) asks it for the checked bodies of each plate.
{"query": "print_min_gap"}
{"query": "print_min_gap", "plate": "Hinge", "gap": 0.4}
→ {"gap": 0.4, "gap_from": "query", "bodies": 2, "closest": 0.2, "touching": 0, "unmeasured": 0,
 "pairs": [{"a": "F2.b0", "b": "F4.b0", "names": ["Pin", "Knuckle"], "distance": 0.2,
 "on_a": [20, 10, 10], "on_b": [20.2, 10, 10], "touches": false}]}
{"query": "print_min_gap", "bodies": ["F9.b0", "F11.b0"]}
→ {"gap": 0.3, "gap_from": "default", "bodies": 2, "closest": 0.1, "touching": 1, "unmeasured": 0,
 "pairs": [{"a": "F9.b0", "b": "F11.b0", "names": ["Plate", "Wheel"], "distance": 0.1,
 "on_a": [112.6, 10, -2.5], "on_b": [112.5, 10, -2.5], "touches": true}]}

The second is a wheel lying on a plate with its peg in the plate’s hole, 0.1 mm wider all round: the bodies touch, and the gap is the peg’s.

Tests: print_analysis_tests (the kinds of a gap, the pairs measured), core/model-tests/print/src/print_min_gap_tests.rs (mock kernel: blocks 0.2 mm and 0.5 mm apart and touching ones, the gap from the query, the parameter or the default, a plate’s bodies, the distances kept, cancellation, the analysis’ settings, the min-gap rule), tools/cli/tests/print_min_gap.json (the same blocks on the OCCT kernel), app/tests/print_analysis.cpp and tools/ui-print-gaps-test.sh.

Filament changes at print heights

mitcad#1596 (core/model/src/print_changes.rs, document/filament_changes.rs, api/filament_changes.rs, print_files/layer_events.rs): a schedule of print heights and what happens there on a single extruder: a manual change to another filament (a material with one of its appearances) or a pause (for inserts, magnets, nuts). The design keeps it, the 3MF export writes it into the slicer’s project, and model_render and the USDZ export can show it as print colours. The design’s geometry is never cut or changed for it.

  • Scope: a plate. A manual change swaps the one filament loaded, so it changes the whole layer of every object on the plate. The design’s own schedule (no plate) is that of an export of bodies and of every print plate without one of its own; a plate may have its own (plate), which is deleted with the plate. Below the first event every part on the plate must print with one filament (one material and appearance): a plate whose parts print with several is a conflict, which the export reports, writing none of that plate’s events (several filaments at once are a multi-material print: give the bodies their materials).
  • Heights are millimetres above the print bed (JSON numbers, whatever the design’s length unit), the bed’s Z after the export’s turn (a print bed face, the automatic orientation) and drop, not the design’s Z: in a 3MF each object is measured from its own lowest point, where the slicer lays it; a plate’s top is its tallest object’s. An export that does not put the bodies on the bed (no on_bed) measures each object as it is written, from its lowest point, as a slicer that drops it onto the bed prints it.
  • Layers. An event happens at a layer boundary: its height moves to the nearest top of a layer (the plate’s process: first_layer_height, then layer_height, 0.2 mm each when unset; a tie upwards), never within the first layer, which always prints with the plate’s own filament (the bodies’ material and appearance). The slicer gets the top of the first layer printed after it (print_z), which it assigns to that very layer. Variable layer heights are not known to the design.
  • Left out, with a warning: an event at or above the plate’s top, the earlier of two events on one layer boundary, a change to a material the design no longer has, every event of a plate in conflict.
  • Limits: heights above 0 and at most 2000 mm, one event per height, at most 64 events per schedule; a change names a material (and optionally one of the design’s appearances; the material’s default when left out) and no message; a pause names no material and may carry a message of one line, at most 120 characters.
Command Fields Result
set_filament_changes plate (a print plate’s id or name; the design’s own schedule when left out); changes: the whole schedule, [{height, kind, material, appearance, message}] (or at and body in place of height: at planes and faces) (kind change, the default, or pause); [] takes it away (a plate then prints with the design’s) {"changes"}, the schedule as kept (sorted upwards); undo step Set Filament Changes, Set Filament Changes of Short, or Clear Filament Changes…, which recomputes nothing; none when nothing changes. Refused: an unknown plate, material or appearance, a height out of range, two events at one height, a change without a material, a pause with one, a message on a change
Query Fields Result
filament_changes plate (id or name; the design’s own schedule when left out), trial (an event not in the schedule: a trial event) plate ({id, name} or null), inherited (the plate takes the design’s), layer_height, first_layer_height (the plate’s process), changes: [{height, kind, material, appearance, message, material_name, color, boundary, print_z, layer}] (boundary the layer boundary it happens at, print_z what the slicer gets, layer that layer’s number from 1; left_out for the earlier of two on one boundary; error for an unknown material), notes, schedules: [{plate, name, events}] of the whole design; with trial also trial: {height, place, body, warning}

Export (export of a 3MF with a dialect; the result’s filament_changes lists each event written: {plate, height, print_z, layer, kind, material}, plate from 0 in the design’s plates’ order):

  • PrusaSlicer (Metadata/Prusa_Slicer_custom_gcode_per_print_z.xml, as PrusaSlicer 2.9.7’s own reader and writer in src/libslic3r/Format/3mf.cpp take it): a custom_gcodes_per_print_z element per bed (bed_idx; bed 0 always, the others with events), a code per event and the mode. A change is a colour change (type 0, M600 from the printer profile) of the plate’s extruder (extruder 1 in a project of one filament) with the filament’s color; a pause is type 1 with its message as extra. A colour change keeps the first filament’s settings: a warning says so when the two differ in type or temperatures.
  • The Bambu family (Bambu Studio, OrcaSlicer, QIDI Studio: Metadata/custom_gcode_per_layer.xml, as their bbs_3mf.cpp / qds_3mf.cpp take it): custom_gcodes_per_layer with a plate per plate (plate_info id from 1), a layer per event (top_z) and the mode. Their G-code export leaves colour changes out, so a change is a filament change (type 2) to the filament’s own slot (extruder from 1), which the export adds to the project’s filaments, in MultiAsSingle mode; a pause is type 1. A change to the filament already printing changes nothing there: left out with a warning (a pause stops for a new spool).
    • Prime tower off. When every plate’s parts print with one filament (the second filament slot is only the manual change’s), the project’s enable_prime_tower is written 0 (and named in the process’s different_settings_to_system), with a warning when the design had turned it on. With it on, the slicers build a tower for every plate of two filaments at the project’s wipe_tower_x / wipe_tower_y (per plate; their defaults are a corner of their own printers’ beds, and the export does not know the tower’s depth, which they compute from the purge volumes): on a printer of another bed it falls outside the printable area, and Bambu Studio and QIDI Studio stop with -104 (“G-code outside of the printable area”). A manual change needs no tower: the printer purges the old filament in its own filament-change G-code, and the tower’s other layers would only print waste. A project with a plate whose parts print with several filaments keeps the slicer’s tower.
    • Filament count. The slicers count a project’s filaments by its filament_diameter list (OrcaSlicer’s ToolOrdering: num_filaments = filament_diameter.size()), and with one entry they take a filament change as a colour change, whose G-code their export leaves out (GCode.cpp, emit_custom_gcode_per_print_z: “inserting color gcode is removed”): a real OrcaSlicer run wrote no change. So a project of several filament slots always has filament_diameter with an entry per slot (1.75, their default, where no slot sets it). With two, a MultiAsSingle change becomes a tool change of that layer (ToolOrdering’s custom_tool_changes), which runs the printer’s change_filament_gcode and writes T<n>.
    • Filament change G-code. For such manual changes (the prime tower off) on a printer without a change_filament_gcode of its own, the export writes {if previous_extruder > -1}{if previous_extruder != next_extruder}M600{endif}{endif}, with a warning: M600 (Marlin’s filament change, PrusaSlicer’s default colour change) at each change, not at the print’s first filament, for which the slicers run the same G-code with previous_extruder -1 (GCode::set_extruder). The slicers still write the tool change T<n>, which a printer of one extruder ignores or reports. A printer’s own G-code stays. The M600 is written only where the change G-code that counts is the file’s (mitcad#2235, the rule of the relative extrusion reset below): the printer names no system preset of the export’s own slicer (no preset name, or only a name another member of the family has), or its printer block (one kept from an imported project included) lists change_filament_gcode in different_settings_to_system. A printer that names a preset of the export’s own slicer and does not list it keeps the key to that preset (for a printer of several extruders or a filament changer, its own tool change): it is not written or listed, and there is no warning.
    • Relative extrusion. Every Bambu-family export (with changes or without): with use_relative_e_distances on (the slicers’ default when the printer does not say) and no line resetting E (G92 E0) in before_layer_change_gcode or layer_change_gcode, the export adds G92 E0 as the last line of before_layer_change_gcode (where the family’s own printer profiles keep it), writes use_relative_e_distances 1 when the printer did not say, and names both in the printer’s different_settings_to_system. OrcaSlicer refuses a project with relative E and no reset at each layer (its Print::validate). Relative E stays, as the prime tower needs it; a printer with relative E off is left as it is. This is done only where the layer G-code that counts is the file’s (mitcad#2211): the printer names no system preset of the export’s own slicer (no preset name, or only a name another member of the family has, which this slicer may lack and then uses its built-in defaults), or its printer block (one kept from an imported project included) lists before_layer_change_gcode or layer_change_gcode in different_settings_to_system. A printer that names a preset of the export’s own slicer and does not list either keeps both keys and use_relative_e_distances to that preset: none of them is written or listed by this step, so the slicer does not report modified G-code the design never set.
  • PrusaSlicer is not changed by these: it writes a colour change (M600 from its printer profile) and no second filament.
  • Cura keeps no such events in a project (they are post-processing scripts of the machine’s settings): nothing is written, and a warning names each event’s layer and height to add in Cura (Extensions, Post Processing: Filament Change or Pause at Height).
  • Without a dialect nothing is written, with a warning.

The slicer emits its printer profile’s own filament change and pause code; the export writes printer G-code only for the Bambu family’s manual changes on a printer without filament change G-code of its own or of its own slicer’s preset (M600, above) and the G92 E0 of relative extrusion.

Print colours (opt in): model_render’s print_colors: true and the export of a USDZ with print_colors: true draw each placement in the colours of the filaments it prints with by height, in place of the appearances: the schedule of the plate the body prints on (the design’s without plates), its own filament below the first change, measured along its print direction (away from its print bed face, else +Z) from its own lowest point, its triangles cut at the layer boundaries of the changes (edges drawn there). Both use the same cuts; USDZ writes the first band as the mesh’s material and each other band as a subset PrintColor_<n> with a material print color rrggbb. Pauses change no colour. Other formats refuse print_colors.

The design file keeps the schedules as "filament_changes": [{"plate", "changes": [...]}] (plate left out for the design’s own), left out when there are none.

{"cmd": "set_filament_changes", "changes": [
 {"height": 10, "material": "pla_two", "appearance": "blue_pla"},
 {"height": 4, "kind": "pause", "message": "Insert the magnets"}]}
{"query": "filament_changes"}
→ {"plate": null, "inherited": false, "layer_height": 0.2, "first_layer_height": 0.2,
 "changes": [{"height": 4.0, "kind": "pause", "message": "Insert the magnets",
 "boundary": 4.0, "print_z": 4.2, "layer": 21, ...},
 {"height": 10.0, "kind": "change", "material": "pla_two",
 "appearance": "blue_pla", "material_name": "PLA Two", "color": "#0000FF",
 "boundary": 10.0, "print_z": 10.2, "layer": 51, ...}], ...}

Tests: print_changes (validation, layer rounding, the events placed, the triangles cut into bands), core/model-tests/print/src/filament_change_tests.rs (mock kernel: the two-colour box edited, undone, redone, saved and reopened; each slicer’s file read back; a rotated print bed; two bodies sharing a plate and a conflict; a plate’s own schedule; model_render’s and USDZ’s print colours).

Filament changes at planes and faces

mitcad#1643: an event’s place is either a height (as above) or at a plane: a construction plane ("F5"), an origin plane ("xy", "xz", "yz") or a planar face of a body ({"body": "F2.b0", "face": "F2:end(…)"}), by the model’s usual references (a face found again after edits, as other references are). Its height is worked out whenever it is asked for, so it follows the model: a change at the top of a base stays there when the base gets thicker, at a construction plane when its offset changes.

  • Measured from a body: along the print direction (the bed’s normal after the export’s turn) from the lowest point of the body it is measured from to the plane. That body is the face’s own for a face; for a plane the one the event names (body), else the plate’s first body (a print plate’s first item; the design’s first printed body as the design places them for the design’s own schedule, in an export the first body written on the plate). In an export each object is measured from its own lowest point, as the slicer lays it on the bed; the query and the print colours measure the body’s first shown placement in the design, turned by its print bed face (else as designed). A construction plane of the body’s own component, or of the root, is taken where that component and the body’s placement put it.
  • Left out, with a warning in words (the plate’s warnings, the query’s warning, the export’s warnings), never moved: a plane or face that is not level in the print orientation (the filament change at Plane3 is not level in the print orientation, so it is left out: after the automatic orientation picked another bed face, for example), one that is gone or no longer flat, one at or below the bottom of its body, a plane of another component than the body (but the root’s), a body not printed on the plate.
  • Several objects on a plate: the change is the plate’s, written once at the height of the body it is measured from, on that layer for every object. When another object of the plate stood at another level in the design (an export on the bed lays each piece on the bed itself), the export says so once per plate: Plate 1: the filament changes at planes and faces are measured from Body1, and other objects of the plate stand at other levels: each change happens on the same layer for all of them.
  • Auto Fix: a face an edit renamed is found again under its new name (as a feature’s reference is), and the query’s row says so (found_as); auto_fix of every feature (no features) writes the names found into the schedules, in its one undo step (Auto Fix Filament Changes when no feature changes), counted in its result’s filament_faces and message (the face of a filament change found again).
  • Whole sentences: each warning and refusal is one sentence for each kind of event (a change, a pause) and place (a height, a plane by its name, a face of a body), so that each translates whole (docs/translations.md); the place is never a phrase put into another sentence.
  • Validation: an event has a height or an at, not both; body only with at (a face’s own body for a face); at must be a plane or a planar face at the timeline marker when it is set, and a named body a solid or mesh body; one event per plane or face (and body). Events at heights come first, upwards, then those at planes and faces in their order.
  • Texts name planes by their names in the timeline and the browser (Plane3, an origin plane XY) and faces by their bodies (a face of Body1), never by topological names or coordinates (mitcad#1327); a face’s places give agents and the hover the face.
Field In Meaning
at set_filament_changes events, the file The plane or face (a reference) instead of height
body the same The body an event at a plane is measured from (none: the plate’s first)
height filament_changes rows The height used: given, or worked out (null when left out)
source filament_changes rows, the export’s filament_changes height, plane or face
place filament_changes rows Where it is, in words (10 mm, Plane3, a face of Body1)
at, body, places filament_changes rows; at, body in the export’s events The reference, the body measured from, a face’s place
left_out, warning filament_changes rows Left out, and why in words
found_as filament_changes rows A face an edit renamed, by the name it is found as (Auto Fix writes it)
event filament_changes rows The event as the schedule keeps it (to edit and set again)
start, choices the filament_changes result The filament the plate starts with (its first body’s {material, appearance, name}) and what a change can change to: each of the design’s own materials in each appearance it offers, {material, appearance, name, color} (Send to Slicer’s rows)
Query Fields Result
filament_change_preview bodies (uids; every shown printed body when left out) What Send to Slicer draws over the view while its Filament changes section is open: bands ([{color: "#RRGGBB", triangles: [x, y, z, …]}], nine numbers per triangle, design mm: each shown placement cut at its plate’s layer boundaries in the colours it prints with, as print_colors), rings (six numbers per segment: where each change’s boundary crosses the placement), notes (events left out)

 {"at": "F5", "material": "pla_two", "appearance": "blue_pla"},
 {"at": {"body": "F2.b0", "face": "F2:end(r{c1[c4,c2],c2[c1,c3],c3[c2,c4],c4[c3,c1]})"},
 "kind": "pause", "message": "Insert the nuts"}]}
{"query": "filament_changes"}
→ {"changes": [{"height": 12.0, "source": "plane", "at": "F5", "body": "F2.b0",
 "place": "Plane1", "boundary": 12.0, "print_z": 12.2, "layer": 61, ...},

A trial event (mitcad#1800)

The filament_changes query also takes trial, one event as set_filament_changes takes it, which is not in the schedule (Filament Change’s plane or face picked, before its OK): the result’s trial is {height, place, body, warning}, where it would be on the plate (plate; the design’s schedule when left out), measured as the schedule’s own events are: height above the print bed (null when it would be left out, then with its warning in words), place in words and, at a plane or face, the body it is measured from. Nothing changes. Test: a_trial_event_gives_its_height_without_changing_the_schedule.

{"query": "filament_changes", "trial": {"at": "F5", "kind": "pause"}}

Pick marks as wide as their lines (mitcad#1618)

The drawing_pick query’s items of a line, a circle or an arc carry the pen (a name of the drawing query’s pens table) of the lines the view draws there: of the projected lines that lie on it, the widest one’s, with the view’s chosen line styles (mitcad#1546); a line along a centre mark (center_line) is chain unless it lies on a line of the view. An item the view draws no line under has no pen; a point never has one. The application draws a hover’s or a pick’s mark that wide at the zoom (at least a pixel) and 2 pixels more on each side, never narrower than 2 pixels (the hover) or 2.5 (a pick), and see-through so that the line shows under it; a point keeps its own size (mitcad#1338). Tests: line_style_tests.rs (a_picks_mark_carries_the_pen_of_the_lines_it_lies_on) and app/tests/drawing_sheet_view.cpp (the mark’s width at two zooms and its pixels beside the line); pictures of a hovered and a picked edge, fitted and zoomed in: tools/ui-drawing-mark-width-look.sh <dir>.

Drawing templates of one’s own: sizes, images and the title block (mitcad#1625)

Company and standard drawing formats (core/model/src/drawing/mod.rs, template_def.rs, core/model-drawing/src/template.rs, pdf.rs, pdf_image.rs, svg.rs, dxf.rs, api/drawing_templates.rs): sheets of a size of their own, images such as a logo in a title block, and a title block edited on the sheet (the application’s title block editor, app/COMMANDS.md The title block editor).

Custom sheet sizes. Wherever a sheet size is given (a sheet’s size in add_drawing, add_drawing_sheet, edit_drawing_sheet, a template’s size, export_drawing’s sheet, the design file) it is a name (A4 … A0, ANSI_A … ANSI_E) or {"width": 500, "height": 300} in mm, each side 10 to 10 000 mm. Such a sheet lies as given: its orientation turns nothing. A template of such a size brings it to a new drawing as a named one does, and save_drawing_template keeps it. The drawing query’s sheet size is the name, or custom with the sheet’s width and height; the drawings query, the title block’s {size} and the simple block’s SHEET cell name it 500 x 300 mm. Exports are written at that size (the PDF’s page, the SVG’s width and height, the DWG’s paper). Refused: a side out of range (a sheet of its own size is 10 to 10000 mm each way), an object with other fields than width and height, an unknown name.

Images in the title block. A template’s title_block.images: [{"at": [x, y], "size": [w, h], "data": "<base64>"}], mm from the block’s lower left corner, the file a PNG, JPEG or SVG image of 4 MB at most (known by its bytes: the PNG and JPEG signatures, an SVG’s root element). The sheet’s copy of the template keeps them, so a drawing carries its logo wherever its design goes. An image is drawn whole in its box, its proportions kept (a PNG’s and a JPEG’s pixels, an SVG’s viewBox, else its width and height), in the box’s middle, under the block’s lines and texts. The drawing query’s title-block group has it as {"image": "<base64>", "format": "png", "at": [x, y], "size": [w, h]} (the fitted box on the sheet); the exports: SVG an <image> with the file as a data URL; PDF a PNG decoded (any colour type, bit depth and interlacing) as an image with its transparency as a soft mask, a JPEG as it is, each file once per document; an SVG image (mitcad#1627) in PDF, DXF and DWG as its paths, read with usvg (CSS, use, transforms and shapes resolved): in a PDF as vector paths fitted in its box as the sheet draws it, its fills and strokes in their colours (a gradient as its mean colour), opacities as transparency, strokes’ widths, caps, joins and dashes, clip paths; in DXF and DWG as lines (curves flattened within 0.01 mm) on a layer per colour and line weight, IMAGE_<colour index>_<weight> (the nearest colour index of the colour on white paper, 7 for black), a fill as its path’s closed outline, a stroke on the weight nearest its width. An SVG image’s text (mitcad#1637) goes in as the outlines of its glyphs, filled and stroked as its paths: laid out by usvg in the first font of its font-family the computer has (the system’s fonts, read once per run, and the bundled Droid Sans, embedded in the model as sketch text embeds it in the geometry), else in Droid Sans, which is also every generic family (sans-serif, serif, monospace, cursive, fantasy) and the font of text that names none, so that such text has the same outlines on every machine; a character the font lacks from another font of the computer that has it. A PNG or JPEG image in DXF and DWG (which hold no raster image), and an SVG file usvg cannot read in any of the three, is its outline. The export’s warnings say what is left out or drawn otherwise (a DXF file holds no raster images: the title block's PNG and JPEG images are written as their outlines, an SVG image of the title block cannot be read: the PDF file has its outline, for text in fonts the computer does not have the title block's SVG images name fonts this computer does not have (Corporate Sans): the PDF file draws their text in Droid Sans (each font-family list as the file names it, several with ; between), for characters no font of the computer has the text of the title block's SVG images has characters no font on this computer has: the DWG file cannot draw them, and for pictures inside an SVG image the pictures inside the title block's SVG images are left out of the DXF file). Masks and filters of an SVG image are not applied, and DXF and DWG draw its paths without its clip paths. Refused: an image of no box, one that is no image, larger than 4 MB or no base64. Template files may be 16 MB.

The title block edited on the sheet.

Command Fields Result
edit_drawing_title_block drawing, sheet (0), title_block: the whole block as a template has it (width, height, lines, fields, images, projection_symbol) drawing, sheet; undo step Edit title block of Sheet1 of Drawing1; nothing changed is no undo step

It replaces the title block of the sheet’s copy of its template; a sheet of the simple title block gets a copy of the ISO template (id custom, name Custom, without its size and projection method) around the block given, which save_drawing_template can then save. Refused as a template is (a field without a cell, an image that is none) and when the block with the revision table’s room does not fit in the sheet’s frame. The drawing query’s drawn sheet gives what the editor edits: frame (its corners), title_box (the block’s corners on the sheet) and title_block_layout (the block; the ISO template’s for the simple block).

{"cmd": "add_drawing", "size": {"width": 500, "height": 300}, "template": "iso"}
{"cmd": "edit_drawing_title_block", "drawing": "D1", "title_block": {"width": 180, "height": 36,
