Tests: core/model-tests/drawing/src/title_block_tests.rs (a custom size kept, saved and exported at that size, and refused out of range; a template of a custom size with a logo round-tripping through the design file and a library and exported to PDF, SVG and DXF; an SVG logo fitted and its paths in the PDF, the DXF and the DWG without a warning, mitcad#1627; a block edited, undone and refused; the simple block edited into a template), the tests in core/model-drawing/src/template.rs (sizes' JSON, images’ kinds, proportions and boxes), core/model-drawing/src/pdf_image.rs (PNG decoding, filters, Adam7, JPEG) and core/model-drawing/src/svg_image.rs (paths, paints, transforms, clips, the box, flattening); tools/ui-drawing-title-block-test.sh.

Copy and paste of 3D sketch geometry (mitcad#1661)

The sketch_fragment query (“Copy and paste of sketch geometry”) copies a 3D sketch’s points and curves too, and sketch3d.paste adds a copy to a 3D sketch: another 3D sketch’s (its z, relations, dimensions and linked references kept) or a planar sketch’s (onto a frame plane at a place). Cut is the copy and then sketch3d.remove of the same items.

{"query": "sketch_fragment", "sketch": "F1", "items": ["c3", "c5"]}
→ {"sketch": "F1", "sketch_name": "3DSketch1", "kind": "3d", "base": [0, 0, 0],
 "entities": 5, "texts": 0, "kept": 5, "left_out": 0, "references": 1,
 "fragment": {"version": 1, "sketch": "F1", "base": [0, 0, 0],
 "points": [...], "curves": [...], "constraints": [...],
 "dimensions": [...], "left_out": 0}}
{"cmd": "sketch3d.paste", "sketch": "F2", "fragment": {...}}
{"cmd": "sketch3d.paste", "sketch": "F2", "fragment": {...}, "at": [100, 10, 5]}
{"cmd": "sketch3d.paste", "sketch": "F2", "fragment": {<a planar sketch's>},
 "plane": "yz", "at": [0, 5, 7]}
→ {"made": ["p1", "p2", "p3", "c4", "c5"], "kept": 5, "left_out": 0, "dropped": 0,
 "entities": [...], "constraints": [...], "dimensions": [...], "status": {...},
 "warnings": [...]}
Command Fields Result
sketch3d.paste sketch; fragment (a sketch_fragment answer’s, of a 3D or a planar sketch); at [x, y, z] (where the base point goes: where it was for a 3D sketch’s copy, the origin for a planar one); plane (xy, yz or zx: a planar copy’s plane through at, xy by default) one undo step Paste in 3DSketch2; made (new points, curves and texts in the fragment’s order), kept, left_out, dropped (linked references left out), values, warnings (in words), and the edit’s entities, points, curves, constraints, dimensions, parameters and status
  • What is copied (items: points p3, curves c4, texts t5; relations and dimensions listed are ignored, they come with their geometry): the selected points, curves and texts, the points the curves use and the points of a text’s frame, each point with its three local coordinates. A relation or dimension is kept when it names copied geometry and nothing else but the sketch’s reference curves (a reference curve it names comes with it); one that names copied geometry and other geometry of the sketch is left out and counted (left_out). On Sketch Plane and a shape’s Plane-Bound relation keep the copied points they list. Attachments, points on faces and reference curves keep their sources as they are (references counts them). Driving dimensions keep their value and expression as a planar copy’s do.
  • The fragment has curves and no entities (a planar fragment always has entities): that tells the two apart. sketch is the sketch it was copied from; base the first selected item’s first point (a line’s or an arc’s start, a circle’s centre, a spline’s first point, a text’s anchor) in local coordinates.
  • sketch3d.paste adds the copy with new ids (made: points, curves and texts in the fragment’s order), as one undo step Paste in 3DSketch2. A 3D sketch’s copy is moved by at - base (without at it goes where it was: the same local coordinates and z); it takes no plane. A Fix is fixed where the point goes; the copy’s On Sketch Plane points join the sketch’s own relation. A planar sketch’s copy (its held does not apply) goes onto the frame plane plane (xy, the default, yz or zx) through at (the origin by default), its base point at at: its points on that plane, its arcs and circles bound to it (their normal its axis), its ellipses, elliptical arcs and texts on it, a coincidence of two points a 3D coincidence, its other constraints and dimensions in-plane ones of that plane (in_plane with normal), a fixed point a Fix where it goes, all its points kept in the plane by one Plane-Bound relation; a centre line becomes a construction line. Constraints and dimensions on the planar sketch’s origin and axes, inactive ones and common spacings are left out and counted.
  • References outside the copy are kept as the same references where the sketch can use their sources: the origin; geometry of features before the sketch in the timeline, of its own component; another component’s (through a link) only when the copy’s sketch is of the same component, where the link starts. Otherwise the attachment, the point on a face or the reference curve is left out (dropped counts them) with the relations that named a dropped reference curve (in left_out). A reference curve of a source the sketch has a record of already is that record (mitcad#1543). When a source kept does not evaluate in the sketch (a copy of another design), the paste is made again without its sources and says so.
  • Warnings, in words with no ids (mitcad#1327): N relation(s) and dimension(s) left out: they name geometry the copied geometry lacks (what this paste or the planar copy’s move onto a plane left out; what the copy left out was said at the copy), N link(s) to geometry outside the copy left out: this sketch cannot use their sources, and the dimensions that took their values (as a planar paste’s).
  • Refused: a fragment of a newer version, one whose curves use points it lacks or that names an id twice, an empty one, a place that is not finite, plane with a 3D sketch’s copy, and a paste that does not solve (nothing changes). sketch.paste refuses a 3D sketch’s copy: 3D sketch geometry cannot be pasted into a 2D sketch: paste it into a 3D sketch.

The application’s Copy, Cut and Paste in a 3D sketch use these (app/COMMANDS.md, “3D sketches”): a 3D sketch’s copy goes where it was, a planar one onto the active placement plane at the anchor.

Classes: sketch3d.paste is the model’s. Code: core/sketch/src/spatial_clipboard.rs, core/model-api/src/sketch_clipboard.rs (the query), core/model-api/src/sketch3d.rs (the command). Tests: core/model-tests/api/src/sketch3d_clipboard_tests.rs (a route between 3D sketches keeping z, relations, dimensions and the origin attachment as one undo step; a copy moved to a place with what it left out; a cut’s copy pasted; a reference left out in words or kept; planar geometry onto the YZ plane; a 3D copy refused by a 2D sketch), tools/ui-sketch3d-keys-clipboard-test.sh and tools/ui-windows-sketch3d-keys-clipboard-test.ps1.

The key of a sketch’s body geometry (mitcad#1646)

{"query": "plane_geometry_key", "sketch": "F3"} answers {"key": "<32 hex digits>"}, a fingerprint of what the sketch’s plane_geometry query reads: the sketch’s frame and, for each body it looks at, the body, the version of its shape (the result that made it), the occurrence path it is seen at and the transform into the sketch’s coordinates. The same key means the same plane_geometry answer, in the plane and with out_of_plane alike, so a client keeps what it read while the key stays. An edit of the sketch itself (an entity, a constraint or a dimension added) changes the document’s revision but not the key, as the bodies before the sketch stay; a body before it built again differently, shown or hidden (by its light bulb or by Isolate, mitcad#1702), or an occurrence moved changes it. The key is cheap (no kernel call), unlike the out-of-plane answer of a large assembly: hundreds of thousands of items, seconds to list. Refused as plane_geometry is: an unknown feature, one that is not a sketch, a sketch with no plane yet. Tests: core/model-tests/analysis/src/plane_geometry_tests.rs (plane_geometry_key_*).

A drawn line’s own edge, the hovered body and the preview’s value (mitcad#1691)

A line the view draws is its straight edge’s. A click for anything (drawing_pick’s want any, dimension or datum, the Dimension tool’s Auto, a linear dimension, a note) that finds a round face seen from the side ("seen": "axis") on its outline, nearer the outline than half its radius from its axis, picks instead the straight edge drawn along that outline within 3 mm of paper, parallel to the axis: the edge where a rounded tube’s corner meets its flat side lies on the tube’s long line, which is also the round face’s outline. Alone that edge is the tube’s length. A click on the face’s axis keeps the face, and the radius, diameter and centre mark types (want circle) pick the face on its outline too.

The hovered body. drawing_pick takes "outline": true: its answer then has outline, {"body": <the body's name>, "lines": [[[x, y], …], …]}, the visible lines the view draws of the picked body (each a list of sheet points; an arc in steps of at most 10 degrees), so that the application shows which of bodies that meet at a corner the pick is on. lines is empty when the kernel does not say which body a line is of.

The preview’s value. drawing_snap’s answer to a placing click (add_drawing_annotation with at) also gives label, what the annotation writes there as the sheet writes it (a dimension’s value with its prefix, decimals and tolerance, its own words before and after), and a dimension’s value (mm or radians); neither when it would be broken.

Code: core/model-api/src/drawing_annotations.rs (pick_at’s own_edge, body_outline, placed_label), core/model-api/src/drawing_spacing.rs (snap_new). Tests: core/model-tests/drawing-views/src/chosen_dimension_tests.rs (a_click_on_a_rounded_tubes_long_line_dimensions_its_length), tools/ui-drawing-hover-body-test.sh.

A center pattern’s bolt circle and center lines as picks (mitcad#1693)

A flange’s hole pattern is dimensioned the way it is made: the bolt circle’s diameter and the angle between the holes’ centre lines.

Picks of what a view draws. A pick may stand for a centre line or a centre pattern’s circle that the view draws, with drawn beside its body and edge or face (which name the circle it is drawn for, picked whole: no point, on_face or on_cut):

  • {"kind": "pattern_circle", "pattern": 3}: the circle through the centres of the circles of the center_pattern annotation 3 of the same view (an arc over them where it draws one), seen end on; the pick one of its circles.
  • {"kind": "pattern_line", "pattern": 3}: that pattern’s radial line through the pick’s circle, from the pattern’s centre out past the circle’s rim.
  • {"kind": "center_mark", "arm": "right"} (up, left, down): one line of the centre mark of the pick’s circle, from its centre toward that side of the sheet, past its rim (an automatic mark or a center_mark annotation’s).
  • {"kind": "centerline", "centerline": 4}: the line the centerline annotation 4 of the same view draws (its axis, halfway between its edges, or through its two centres, run on past them); the pick its first.

Each is found again on every draw from the circles and the annotation that draws it, so it follows the model as the pattern or the line does; the annotation drawing it gone (deleted) makes it broken: the center pattern it is drawn by is gone, the centreline it is drawn by is gone. A centre mark, a centreline, a centre pattern, an edge extension, a table and a balloon take no such pick (a centerline is of the model's edges and faces, not of a center line or a center pattern's circle); dimensions, notes, datum labels, frames and finish symbols do.

Clicks. drawing_pick and a command’s picks given as sheet points:

  • With no type (the Dimension tool’s Auto, want dimension), and with type radius or diameter (want round), a click within 3 mm of paper of a centre pattern’s circle or arc picks it, unless a model edge or face is as near (a point within 2 mm still comes first for Auto). drawing_pick answers "seen": "circle", "pattern_circle": true, its circle or arc in items.
  • With type angle (want straight), a click within 3 mm of a centre line the view draws (a centre mark’s line, a pattern’s radial line where it is drawn, a centreline) picks that line, unless a straight edge is as near. drawing_pick answers "seen": "line", "center_line": true, the drawn line first in items. An edge extension (want line) and a centre mark or pattern (want circle) pick model edges only, as before.
  • With Auto, a click on a centre mark’s line or a pattern’s radial line picks the circle’s centre, as for a corner to a centre line (mitcad#1338).

Dimensions. A centre pattern’s circle alone makes a diameter (Auto too, on an arc as well): its value the circle’s diameter, its words by default Ø60 B.C. (format.after B.C., set when no format is given; edited as any dimension’s, e.g. {"after": "PCD"}). An angle takes two centre lines, or a centre line and a straight edge: the arc about where their lines cross, as for two edges; two radial lines of a pattern meet at its centre. One centre line alone measures nothing (a center line alone measures nothing: ...).

A centre pattern draws radial lines through its circles, not their centre marks: a click on a line through a pattern’s circle that the pattern does not draw picks nothing there.

A radius on a fillet seen from the side (mitcad#1694)

A fillet round a turned part (a torus face, say between a boss and a flange) seen from the side, its axis in the view’s plane, has no model edge along most of its outline. Its outline either side of the axis is an arc of its tube: the circle of its minor radius in the plane of the axis and the view’s across, between the tube’s angles at the face’s two ends (the circles round the axis that bound it; the shorter way round), where the face reaches round its axis. Each side is a pick of its own, {"body", "face", "side": [x, y, z]}: side a direction from the axis that way in the body’s coordinates, so it keeps its side when the model or the view changes (the outline on the side nearest it). It is seen as an arc ("seen": "circle"), so the Radius type, Auto and Diameter take it: Auto makes a radius of the fillet’s. A torus face picked without side is refused (a rounded face is picked on one side of its axis); one whose ends are not two circles round its axis offers no outline.

Auto on a small arc. With no type (want dimension or any), a point within 2 mm of paper still comes first, except an edge’s end (not a centre) when an arc or a circle is nearer the click than it by more than 0.25 mm: the arc is then picked. A small fillet’s arc lies within 2 mm of its edges’ ends almost everywhere; a click on it picks the arc, a click at an end the end.

The arrow on its leader (mitcad#1770, replacing the first fix of mitcad#1694, whose arrow pointed out from the centre on the far side of the arc from its leader). A radius seen end on has one arrow, its tip on the arc at the end of the line that reaches it, pointing along that line’s last segment, on the sheet and in every export alike:

  • its text inside the circle: a line from the centre out to the rim towards the text (an arc’s nearer end when its sweep misses that way), the arrow on it pointing out;
  • its text outside, the arc there: a leader from the text straight to the rim, the arrow on it pointing in (no line from the centre);
  • its text outside on the arc’s hollow side (the sweep misses the text’s way but takes the opposite one, as a fillet in an inside corner with its text beyond the fillet’s centre): a leader from the text through the centre to the rim opposite, the arrow on it pointing out;
  • otherwise: a leader from the text to a bend 5 mm of paper (RADIAL_LEADER) out from the arc’s nearer end, in radially from there to that end, the arrow on it pointing in.

A diameter keeps its line across with an arrow at each end pointing out, run on from the rim to its text; beyond an arc’s sweep from the arc’s nearer end, out radially 5 mm before it bends to the text.

The order of a sketch’s items

The sketch query’s order (mitcad#1492) lists the ids of the sketch’s points, curves, constraints and dimensions (p1, c3, k1, …) in the order they were made; sketch mode’s list of the sketch’s work steps in the timeline’s place follows it (The work steps of a sketch, mitcad#1750; app/COMMANDS.md, “The sketch’s work steps in the timeline’s place”). Texts, patterns, offsets and projections are not listed.

A sketch stores no order across its two numberings, but each numbering gives out its numbers in the order things are made (one more than the largest in use, see Sketch commands), so the points and curves are in creation order by their numbers and the constraints and dimensions by theirs. The two are merged by what a constraint or dimension names: it comes right after the newest point or curve it refers to (and after the constraints and dimensions numbered before it), ahead of the points and curves made later. A curve comes with its points: those numbered after it (the rectangle numbers its lines first, then its corners) follow it at once, so a rectangle lists each line with its new corner and its horizontal or vertical constraint. A constraint that an edit moved onto a newer curve (a trim, a merge of points) is listed after that curve. Code: core/sketch/src/order.rs (SketchDef::creation_order); tests: core/model-tests/sketch/src/sketch_order_1492_tests.rs.

The last feature of each body

{"query": "bodies", "last_features": true} (mitcad#1704) adds each body’s last_feature: the last feature before the marker whose result set the body (made it or changed its shape: the box that made it, a fillet, a move, a join that kept it), "F4". A body that no feature before the marker set (none such at the marker) has no field. The application asks for it with the browser’s snapshot: while a body, or a face, edge or vertex of it, is selected in the view, the timeline marks the feature that made it, and a face whose name gives its creating feature (F3 of F3:side(c1)) marks that one instead (app/COMMANDS.md, “Selection”). Without last_features the field is left out. The model reads the results' change heads only, so results read from the result store stay packed (mitcad#858).

Code: Document::body_last_features (core/model/src/document.rs), the bodies query (core/model-api/src/lib.rs). Test: core/model-tests/api/src/body_last_features_tests.rs.

Flex (mitcad#1713)

A Flex item is a flexible item laid through the model: a wire, a cable, a hose, a flat cable, a strip, a belt. It is a feature type of its own, flex, with its own commands (flex.*) and queries (flex, flex_items, end_ports, flex_types). What is stored is the item (its type’s data), the nodes and the options; the route between the nodes is derived on every evaluation: the shortest one that passes through no body and stays within the item’s bend radius, along the surfaces the nodes lie on. A route with problems still makes the solid, with warnings whose places show where. Code: core/model-base/src/flex.rs (the stored type and the kernel’s inputs and results), core/model/src/features/flex.rs (the feature), core/model/src/document/flex.rs (its results and edits), core/model-api/src/flex.rs (commands and queries), core/model/src/flex_library.rs (the library of types), geometry/include/mitcad/geometry/flex.hpp (routing, the solid, end ports).

The flex feature 

{"type": "flex",
 "item": {"name": "Hose 10", "section": {"type": "round", "diameter": 10},
 "wall": 1.5, "bend_radius": 30},
 "nodes": [
 {"id": "n1", "at": [0, 0, 40], "port": {"body": "F2.b0", "face": "F2:end"}},
 {"id": "n2", "at": [30, 10, 20], "on": {"body": "F3.b0", "face": "F3:top"}},
 {"id": "n3", "at": [60, 10, 5], "on": {"body": "F3.b0", "face": "F3:side1"}, "twist": 0},
 {"id": "n4", "at": [90, 40, 0]}]}
  • item: the item itself, a copy of a Flex type or one written here; the design keeps it whole, so it opens the same without the library:
    • name;
    • section: {"type": "round", "diameter": d}, {"type": "rectangular", "width": w, "height": h, "corner_radius": r} (corner_radius 0 when left out) or {"type": "outline", "loops": [[<segment>, …], …]}: closed loops of curves in section coordinates (millimetres; the first loop the outside, the others holes; segments as a sketch profile’s: line, arc, circle, ellipse, ellipse_arc, bspline). Section coordinates: the origin is on the route, x is the section’s width (it lies along the surface the item rests on), y its height, away from that surface; the route’s direction is x × y. A rectangle is centred on the route; an outline lies where it is drawn, and rests on the surface with its lowest point (its least y);
    • wall: makes a round or a rectangular section hollow, the wall inside the section; less than half the diameter or half the smaller side. An outline is hollow by its own inner loops, and takes no wall;
    • bend_radius: the smallest radius of the route’s centre line. One value for a round section. For another section it is the radius of bending over its flat side (about the section’s x), and bend_radius_edge the radius of bending over its edge (about its y); either left out (or null) says the item does not bend that way. A round section must have a bend_radius;
    • max_twist: the most the section may turn about the route, radians per millimetre of length (a non-round section only; left out: no limit);
    • appearance, material: ids of an appearance and of a material: the design’s own or built-in ones. The item’s body gets them when the item is made, and again when an edit changes what the item names (a look set on the body by hand stays through the item’s other edits); a material brings its own appearance unless the item names one. Left out, or an id the design does not have: the component’s defaults;
    • mass_per_length: grams per metre (reported with the length; the hanging slack’s shape does not depend on it);
    • origin: {"library": "built_in" | "user" | "project", "id": …, "version": n} where the copy came from; left out for an item written in the design.
  • profile: {"sketch": "F4", "region": "r{…}"}, a closed region of a sketch before the feature as the section instead of the item’s section, followed when the sketch changes. The sketch’s own coordinates are the section coordinates above (its origin on the route, its y axis away from the surface); where the sketch lies in the model does not matter. Saved as a type, its loops become an outline.
  • bend_radius, bend_radius_edge: this item’s own bend radii in place of its type’s (values: a number, a parameter’s name or an expression; slots bend_radius, bend_radius_edge).
  • fixed_length: a value (slot fixed_length): the item is that long. Longer than the route, with a direction of gravity in the design, its slack hangs that way (Hanging slack below); without one the route is not changed and the flex query reports slack, the fixed length less the routed one. Shorter than the route, the item warns too_short.
  • length: the item’s own reference parameter (slot length), which every evaluation sets to the route’s length: a driven parameter (kind reference, comment Flex1 length (driven)) that expressions and later features use, and that nothing sets. Left out of a definition, the item keeps the one it has or gets a new one with the next free name; the flex query names it (length_parameter). A parameter that is not the item’s own is refused.
  • nodes: two or more, in order from the item’s start to its end. Each:
    • id: n<k>, unique in the item; the commands make them;
    • at: [x, y, z] in the feature’s component. For a free node (no on, no port) it is the node’s place. For an attached one it is where the node was last put: the node is the point of what it is attached to nearest to at, so it slides on its face or along its edge; and it is where the node stays when what it was attached to is gone. The model keeps it up to date: after every evaluation that finds the node on what it is attached to, at is where the node is then (also when its face or its pipe moved it), so a node whose attachment is lost later stays where it last was;
    • on: what the node is attached to, a reference: a face of a body ({"body", "face"}: the node lies on the face and the item rests on it there), an edge ({"body", "edge"}: the nearest point of the edge), a vertex, a sketch point, a construction point or the origin (that point);
    • port: the cap face of a Pipe or of another Flex item ({"body", "face"} with a face F5:start or F5:end, an end port), only at the first or the last node: the item begins at the middle of the cap, leaves along the cap’s outward normal, takes the port’s section orientation there, and follows when the pipe changes. A node has on or port, not both;
    • twist: radians the section is turned about the route at the node, right hand about the route’s direction, beyond what the route gives it (0 when left out; a half turn of a flat cable is pi).
  • links, datum_links: the occurrence links of bodies and of construction features or sketches of other components that nodes are attached to, as a construction plane’s (a body’s or a feature’s uid to {"source", "target"} paths). A caller need not write them: a node’s on or port may say where the geometry was picked, with occurrence (the occurrence path to its component) and context (optional: the path the item’s component is seen at), as sketch.project takes them (Geometry of other components); add_feature, edit_feature, their previews and the node commands turn those into the links, and the stored reference is the plain one. A link no node uses any more is dropped by the flex.* commands.

The feature makes one new body in its component, and nothing else: it joins and cuts no body.

Routing. Between two neighbouring nodes that lie on faces of bodies that touch (or of one body) the route runs along the surfaces, held off them by the distance from the route to the section’s resting side (a round section’s radius, half a rectangle’s height, an outline’s lowest point), crossing from face to face; over a sharp edge it rounds with the bend radius and leaves the surface for that stretch. Any other stretch is a smooth curve through the air around the bodies in its way. Every solid of the design at the feature’s point of the timeline is an obstacle: the bodies of the feature’s component, and the bodies of every other component at each place its occurrences put it (moved into the feature’s component as its first occurrence places that), other Flex items among them; the item’s own earlier run is one too. Shown or hidden makes no difference: the route is the same whatever is on display. Items may touch.

Hanging slack (mitcad#1713, Part B). With a fixed_length longer than the route and a direction of gravity in the design, the slack hangs: it is shared among the stretches between two neighbouring nodes that run mostly through the air, by their lengths, and each such stretch passes through points of a curve that hangs from its two nodes toward gravity (in the plane of the stretch’s chord and gravity, its sag along the part of gravity square to the chord): a parabola while its bottom bends no tighter than the bend radius, else straight sides into an arc of the bend radius. A point of the curve whose way down meets a body rests on it, the section’s reach above it. The route is then made through those points (by the same router: around bodies, within the bend radius), and again, up to three times, asking for what it lacked of the fixed length, until it is within 0.1 % of it or no longer grows (the slack lies on what is below; slack then says how much is left). Stretches on faces do not hang. The direction is the design’s in the feature’s component’s coordinates; the item is evaluated again when it changes.

Orientation. On a surface the section’s resting side (-y) stays against the surface. Through the air the section goes from the orientation at one end of the stretch to that at the other with the least twist. A node’s twist turns it there. At a port the orientation is the port’s.

Faces of the body: start and end (the caps, each an end port), side0 for a round section and inner0 for its bore; for a rectangle side0 (the resting side) to side3 counter-clockwise about the route’s direction, corner0 to corner3 after each when the corners are rounded, and inner<i> likewise for the bore; for an outline side<i> in the order of its outer loop’s segments and inner<i> in the order of the inner loops’ segments.

Refused (the feature fails, or the command is refused): fewer than two nodes; a node id used twice; a node with both on and port; a port at a node that is not the first or the last, or on a face that is not a cap of a Pipe or a Flex item before the feature; a section size, wall or bend radius that is not greater than zero; a wall that fills the section; a round section without a bend radius; an item whose nodes are all at one point.

Warnings, not failures

A route that is not clean does not fail the feature: the item is made on the best route found, and the feature carries warnings (level warning, Notices) whose places are points and boxes along the route where the trouble is; the application paints them while the pointer is over the message. The messages are plain words, without names, ids or coordinates:

kind Message
passes_through the item passes through a body
bend_too_tight the item bends more tightly than its bend radius allows
edge_bend_too_tight the item bends over its edge more tightly than its type allows (a section that is not round; bend_too_tight is then its bends over the flat side)
twist_over_limit the item twists more than its type allows
no_clean_route no route was found that passes through nothing within the bend radius; the item is drawn on the nearest one
face_lost a face a node was on no longer exists; the node stays where it was
reference_lost what a node was attached to no longer exists; the node stays where it was
port_lost the end the item was attached to no longer exists; the node stays where it was
too_short the item's fixed length is too short to reach between its ends (places: the route’s two ends; the route is the shortest one)

A lost node keeps its last place (at) as a free node until it is attached again (flex.attach_node). The flex query’s problems give agents the detail the messages leave out: each problem’s kind, the stretch of the route (from and to, millimetres along it), the node (node) and what it was attached to (was) for a lost one, the body it passes through (body), and its places.

Only what leaves no item at all is an error: a definition refused as above, or a solid the kernel cannot build along the route; the route and its nodes are then still given by the flex query, so the nodes can be moved.

Commands

The item is made with add_feature and a flex definition, and may be changed whole with edit_feature; both have their preview (Preview), which the flex query reads with "preview": true for the route under the pointer. For pointer moves and node drags the previewed definition carries "route_only": true: the nodes are placed and the route is worked out (by the same router, with what it keeps between calls), and no solid is built, so the preview has no body and costs the route alone. That route is a quicker, rougher one: its points at the coarser steps only, with fewer of the passes that bend it within its limits (the item, and its preview without route_only, take the full route). The flex query’s preview then gives the nodes, the polyline, the frames, the length and the problems with their places. route_only is refused in a command that is not a preview. The flex.* commands change one thing each, as one undo step (Edit Flex1), and answer with the item as it is now: flex (its uid), node (the node made or changed), nodes (the ids in order), length and warnings.

Command Fields Result
flex.add_node flex (the feature’s uid), at [x, y, z], on or port (optional, as a node’s); with occurrence and context for geometry of another component, twist (optional), place: "end" (default: after the last node, the item grows), "start" (before the first) or {"after": "n2"} (between that node and the next) node the new id
flex.move_node flex, node, at [x, y, z] the node put there: a free node at the point, an attached one at the point of its face, edge or point nearest to it (its attachment stays)
flex.attach_node flex, node, one of on (a reference), port (a cap face) or "free": true; at (optional: where on the new face or edge; left out, where the node is now) the node attached to that instead, or free in space where it is
flex.delete_node flex, node the route goes straight from the node before to the node after; refused when two nodes would not be left
flex.set_twist flex, node, twist (radians)
flex.set_item flex, and what changes: item (the whole item, as in the definition) or type (the id of a Flex type, copied into the item: a built-in one, or with library (user, project; project then the project’s folder) one of that library), profile (null: the item’s own section again), bend_radius, bend_radius_edge, fixed_length (values; null takes one away)

A node id or a feature that does not exist, or a feature that is not a Flex item, is refused in plain words; nothing changes then.

Through the design’s changes. A node on another component’s geometry follows when its occurrence moves, and its links follow when features or components are moved, copied (Paste New), reparented or saved as a design of their own (nodes on geometry left outside become free nodes where they are). Reorient Design turns the nodes’ places. An item before the timeline marker’s position that is rolled back keeps its definition; the flex query then gives status rolled_back without a route.

Queries

Query Fields Result
flex uid; preview (default false: true reads the previewed definition’s evaluation instead, the uid left out for a previewed add_feature); frames (default false) below
flex_items every Flex item before the timeline marker, in timeline order: {"uid", "name", "item" (its name), "type" (its origin's id, when it has one), "body", "length", "length_parameter" (the name of the parameter that holds it), "mass" (grams, when the item has a mass per length), "warnings" (how many)}; the rows of a cut list. The parts_list query’s row of an item’s body has the item’s name as its designation, and flex (the item’s uid), length and flex_type (its origin’s id) beside it; the body’s computed properties have its Length
end_ports feature (optional: only that Pipe’s or Flex item’s), body (optional: only the ports of that body, the one under the pointer; only its faces are looked at), occurrence and context (optional: where the ports’ component was picked, as a node’s on), component (optional, with occurrence: the component of the item that will use the ports; the active one when left out) End ports
flex_types text (optional: only the types whose name or id holds every word), project (optional: the project’s folder, for the project’s types) Flex types

The flex query’s answer, lengths in millimetres, points in the feature’s component:

{"uid": "F7", "name": "Flex1", "status": "ok",
 "item": {"name": "Hose 10", "section": {"type": "round", "diameter": 10}, "wall": 1.5, "bend_radius": 30},
 "bend_radius": 30, "bend_radius_edge": null,
 "length": 143.2, "length_parameter": "d7", "fixed_length": null, "slack": null,
 "nodes": [{"id": "n1", "point": [0, 0, 40], "normal": null, "along": 0,
 "support": "port", "ref": {"body": "F2.b0", "face": "F2:end"},
 "lost": false, "twist": 0}, …],
 "smallest_bend": {"radius": 31.4, "along": 62.0, "point": [58, 10, 9]}, "smallest_bend_edge": null,
 "polyline": [[0, 0, 40], …],
 "frames": [{"along": 0, "point": […], "tangent": […], "normal": […]}, …],
 "runs": [{"from": 21.5, "to": 58.0, "body": "F3.b0", "face": "F3:top"}, …],
 "problems": [{"kind": "bend_too_tight", "message": "the item bends more tightly than its bend radius allows",
 "from": 60.1, "to": 66.4, "places": [{"kind": "point", "at": […]}]}]}
  • status: as a feature has it (ok, error with the error when no item was made, suppressed, rolled_back), or preview for the previewed definition; the fields below are given whenever the nodes were placed, the route’s when a route was found. The previewed one has no uid, name or item, and its nodes no ref or twist: the caller holds that definition.
  • nodes: each node where it is now (point), the surface’s outward normal there for a node on a face (normal), its length along the route (along), its support (free, face, edge, point or port), its reference as stored (ref), whether what it was attached to is gone (lost) and its twist. The in-view handles are drawn at point.
  • polyline: the route’s centre line as points, close enough to draw; frames (only when asked for) the samples behind it: the unit tangent and the section’s y direction (normal) at each.
  • runs: the stretches that lie on a face, for agents.
  • bend_radius, bend_radius_edge: the radii the route was held to (the item’s own or its type’s); slack: with a fixed_length, that length less the routed one (negative: too short).
  • smallest_bend: the route’s tightest bend, to show beside the radius it may not go below (bend_radius): the radius of the circle through three neighbouring samples that is the smallest, where it is (along, point); null for a straight route. Of a section that is not round its bends over the flat side alone (about the section’s x: the circle’s radius over its share along the sample’s normal), and smallest_bend_edge its bends over the edge (about y), beside bend_radius_edge (null for a round section or a route that does not bend that way). Estimates as close as the samples are; whether the route is too tight is the bend_too_tight and edge_bend_too_tight problems’ to say.

End ports

The ends of a Pipe and of a Flex item are end ports: where another item begins or ends. A port is the feature’s cap face (F5:start, F5:end) in the body that holds it now (the pipe’s own, or the body it was joined to). The end_ports query lists them:

[{"feature": "F5", "name": "Pipe1", "kind": "pipe", "end": "end",
 "ref": {"body": "F5.b0", "face": "F5:end"},
 "position": [40, 0, 0], "direction": [1, 0, 0], "x_axis": [0, 1, 0],
 "size": [8, 8]}, …]

ref is what a node’s port stores. position is the middle of the cap (of its outer boundary, so also of a hollow one), direction the cap’s outward normal: an item that begins there leaves along it. x_axis is the section’s orientation: the direction of the cap’s width, square to direction (for a round cap any such direction, the same on every evaluation), and size the cap’s extent along x_axis and across it. kind is pipe or flex. A cap that a later feature removed (a pipe joined end to end with another body) is not listed.

The points and directions are in the coordinates of the component the port’s body is in. With occurrence (the path its component was picked at) they are the ports of that component, in the coordinates of component (the item’s): where the item’s node will be. The ref is the same either way; the node’s port takes it with the same occurrence and context.

Flex types

A Flex type is an item as above, kept apart from any design, with an id and a version. The flex_types query lists them, {"types": [{"id", "library", "built_in", "version", …the item's fields}], "problems": […]} (problems: the files that could not be read): the built-in ones (library built_in: round wires, cables and hoses of common sizes, flat cables, strips), then the user’s own (user) and the project’s (project, given the project’s folder as project), each library’s by name. The user’s and the project’s live beside the materials of those libraries (Print profiles, Items where they live), one file for a type: flex-types/<id>.json in the library’s folder, {"format": "mitcad-flex-type", "version": n, "type": {…the item}}. An item taken from a type is a copy with its origin (the library, the id and the version copied); a later change of the type does not change the design.

The built-in types, by id: wire-1, wire-1-5, wire-2, wire-3, wire-4 (single wires by their outer diameter), cable-5, cable-6, cable-8, cable-10, cable-12 (sheathed cables), hose-4, hose-6, hose-8, hose-10, hose-12, hose-16, hose-19, hose-25 (hollow, by their outer diameter), flat-cable-12, flat-cable-25, strip-10 and strip-10x5 (rectangular, bent over the flat side only). They are generic: a kind and a size, with a bend radius and a mass per length that are plausible for it; a design that needs a certain product’s values sets them in its item or saves a type of its own.

Command Fields Result
flex.save_type library (user, the default, or project), project (the project’s folder, for its library), id (optional: the next free one from the name; lower-case letters, digits and hyphens), the type’s fields (name, section, wall, bend_radius, bend_radius_edge, max_twist, appearance, material, mass_per_length) or flex (a Flex item of the design whose item is saved: its profile as an outline, its own bend radii as the type’s; fields given beside it change the copy saved) id, library, version (1), path (the file)
flex.edit_type library, project, id, and the fields that change (null takes away one that a type may leave out) id, library, version (one more when something changed), path; a built-in type is refused
flex.delete_type library, project, id id, library, version, path; a built-in type is refused; designs keep their copies

Each is one undo step of the design (Save Flex Type …, Edit Flex Type …, Delete Flex Type …) that puts the file back as it was, as a library’s material does; the design itself does not change. They and the flex_types query read and write files (class file IO), so external clients (MCP) do not have them; flex.set_item with library likewise. An agent takes a built-in type by its id above, {"cmd": "flex.set_item", "flex": "F7", "type": "hose-10"}, or writes the item whole.

The kernel

core/model reaches the geometry through three methods of the Kernel trait, each Unsupported by default (core/model-base/src/kernel.rs, “Flex”; the mock kernel has stand-ins for the model’s tests):

  • flex_route (FlexRouteSpec to FlexRoute): the obstacles, the nodes in order (each with its point, the face it lies on and the normal there, a port’s direction and orientation, its twist), the section’s reaches and the bend radii in; the route’s curve, its samples (point, tangent, the section’s y direction, the face under it) and its problems out. It never fails for a route that is not clean: it gives the best one with its problems.
  • flex_solid (FlexSolidSpec): the solid of a section that is not round along the route, turned as the samples say. A round section is built by pipe (a circular section, rounded corners), hollow by its thickness.
  • end_port: the position, direction, orientation and size of a cap face of a Pipe’s or a Flex item’s body.

Tests: core/model/src/features/flex.rs (the definition and its node edits), core/model-tests/features-solid/src/flex_tests.rs (create, add, move, attach and delete a node, twist, the item, a port, warnings that are not failures, a lost face; mock kernel).

Gravity (mitcad#1713)

The design’s direction of gravity. It is for flexible items only: a Flex item’s fixed length hangs its slack toward it (Hanging slack in Flex), and a Flex item can be let hang (Hanging cables). Code: core/model/src/gravity.rs (the stored direction, the hanging slack’s curve), core/model/src/document/gravity.rs, core/model-api/src/gravity.rs. Tests: core/model-tests/features-solid/src/gravity_tests.rs. (Rigid parts that fell, tipped and were dragged under gravity were taken out on 15.11.2026; that code is kept on the branch archive/flex-rigid-gravity.)

The direction of gravity

Stored in the design file (gravity, left out without one) and undone as any change: a unit vector in the design’s coordinates and what it was taken from.

{"gravity": {"direction": [0, 0, -1],
 "source": {"geometry": {"body": "F1.b0", "face": "F1:top"}, "occurrence": "O1",
 "reverse": false}}}
  • From a planar face or a plane (an origin plane, a construction plane, a fixed plane) gravity pulls against its normal; from an axis (an origin axis, a construction axis, a straight edge, a sketch line, a fixed axis) along it; reverse the other way. A face of another component is picked where an occurrence shows it (occurrence, its path from the root), as a joint origin is.
  • Recompute reads the vector only: what it was taken from may change later without the design changing; the gravity query says what that gives now (source_direction), and gravity.set with it again takes it.

Commands

Command Fields Result
gravity.set direction [x, y, z] (any length), or geometry (a reference) with occurrence (optional, the path it was picked at) and reverse (default false) the gravity query’s answer; undo step Set Gravity
gravity.clear the same; undo step Clear Gravity
Query Fields Result
gravity direction (null without one), source, source_direction (what the source gives at the marker now), hanging (the uid of the Flex item that hangs, null when none does)

The app sets and clears the direction in the Let It Hang panel (app/COMMANDS.md, “Hanging cables”); there is no tool of its own.

A Flex item that hangs while the direction changes (the Let It Hang panel’s Direction From) goes on hanging and settles again toward the new direction, among the bodies as they are after the change; gravity.clear leaves no direction, so it is let go (put back as it was). The change is an undo step of its own all the same; undoing it, as any other change of the design, ends the hanging (The session in Hanging cables).

Hanging cables (mitcad#1713)

With a direction of gravity in the design, a Flex item can be let hang: it becomes a hose that falls toward gravity, lies limp on what is below it, wraps round curved faces and edges and never passes through a body; it can be grabbed by any point and dragged, and settles again when it is let go; then it is locked where it rests, an ordinary Flex item again. Code: core/model/src/document/flex_hang.rs (the session), core/model-api/src/flex_hang.rs (the commands’ fields and answers), core/model-base/src/flex_drape.rs (the kernel’s inputs and results), geometry/include/mitcad/geometry/flex_drape.hpp (the chain and its nodes). Tests: geometry/tests/test_flex_drape.cpp (the chain over a cylinder, hanging from one end, a pinned middle, stiff and limp, a swing that settles within seconds and its rest, the nodes of a drape, the work of a step in proportion to the time it simulates), core/model-tests/features-solid/src/flex_hang_tests.rs (the commands, with the mock kernel’s stand-in of the chain).

  • The chain. Its centre line as points at even steps (a segment is twice the section’s resting distance, at most half its bend radius, and there are at most 400 of them), as long as the item’s route when it is let hang. The length stays as it is unless flex.hang_set sets it.
  • Pins. Each node is a point of the chain (its ends the chain’s ends). By default (flex.hang without pins) both ends are pinned, and so is every node attached to a face, an edge, a point or a port (a clip: it stays attached to what it is attached to; one whose attachment is lost stays where it was); only the nodes placed freely in space are let go. Given pins replace the default; any node can be pinned or let go (an end hangs free) with flex.hang_set. An end pinned on a port also holds the next point, so the item leaves along the port. Every other point is free.
  • How it hangs. Position-based dynamics: each step moves the free points by their velocities and gravity (9810 mm/s²: it moves as it would) in substeps of 1/360 s: a step simulates as many as its seconds hold (12 for 1/30 s, 6 for 1/60 s) and carries what is left of a substep over to the next step, so that its work is in proportion to the time it simulates however often it is asked. Each substep holds three times the segments’ lengths and each point’s reach from the nearest pinned point on either side (it does not stretch) and its bending (as stiff as the bend radius says: the length over which its own weight bends it as much as its stiffness holds it straight is twice the bend radius, so a thick hose bends more gently than a thin wire); then, once, the obstacles (its points and segments’ middles kept the section’s resting distance off them, sliding with friction 0.5; a point asks the obstacles again only once it may have come that near them since it last asked); then three times its bend radius (never tighter) and lengths; then its own run (twice the resting distance apart) and its pins. A point moves at most half the resting distance per substep. A flat section’s flat side lies against what it lies on (its normals there are the surface’s).
  • Damping. It settles as a real hose does, with a slight swing: the air holds every point back, as strongly as the session’s damping says (0 to 1, 0.5 by default; given with flex.hang, changed with flex.hang_set, for a panel to set): its velocity falls by e^-(damping × 12) each second while it swings, and by up to e^-(damping × 48) as the whole chain slows below 30 times its rest speed (below), so that its last small swings die out (the default: 6 per second, a slight overshoot; it rests within about two seconds). 0 is no air at all: it swings on. Besides, whatever the damping, the item’s own material damps its short wiggles (the rate of each joint’s change of bend, by e^-60 a second; nothing of the chain’s swing as a whole), and a push off an obstacle gives it no speed away from it (it does not bounce). The bending’s constraint is the joint’s vector x0 + x2 - 2 x1 with a vector of multipliers, so that a nearly straight joint puts no energy into the chain.
  • The obstacles. Every body of the design at the marker where its occurrences place it, in the item’s component’s coordinates (hidden ones too), but the item’s own and those of features after it: the bodies its route passes round. A step gives the kernel only those whose boxes come within the item’s reach of every pinned point (its length, 2 % more, and twice its resting distance; a grabbed point is no pin), all of them while none is pinned: the chain cannot come nearer the others. They are meshed as the router meshes them but coarser for a thicker item (a deflection of a twentieth of its resting distance, 0.1 to 0.5 mm).
  • Rest. The chain rests once none of its points has moved faster than 0.5 % of its length per second (at least 0.5 mm/s; its mean speed over each frame, so that a tremble within a frame is no motion) for 0.3 s; its velocities are then zero. The time it has been still carries over from step to step until something moves it. A step while it rests and nothing holds it simulates nothing; a grab, a pin set or let go and a new length wake it (a new damping alone does not), and so does a new direction of gravity (The session).
  • The session. Runtime state of the document, as a preview is: the design does not change until the lock, and any change of it (an edit, an undo, another item let hang) ends the session, but gravity.set: with a new direction the item goes on hanging, awake, its gravity the new one and its obstacles the bodies as they are after the change (Document::hang_follow_gravity), so that a panel can turn gravity while the item hangs; gravity.clear lets it go. No simulation ever runs in a recompute. flex.hang_step, flex.hang_set and flex.hang_cancel change only the session: they run without a design change’s work (no policy, failures or warnings before and after, no comments’ places, no recomputed or error in their answers), so that a step can run many times a second.
Command Fields Result
flex.hang flex (the item’s uid), pins (optional: the ids of the nodes that stay where they are; when left out, both ends and every node attached to a face, an edge, a point or a port: Pins above), damping (optional: 0 to 1, 0.5 when left out; Damping above) the hanging item (below); refused without a direction of gravity (set the direction of gravity first), for a feature that is not a Flex item, or an item without a route
flex.hang_step seconds (default 1/30, at most 10), grab (optional: {"point": [x, y, z], "target": [x, y, z]}, the point of the chain where the pointer took it and where the pointer is now) the hanging item after the step. With grab, the chain’s point nearest to point at the first step that has one is pulled to target (no faster than half the resting distance per substep, and not into a body) at this step and every step after that has a grab, whatever its point; a step without one lets it go. A pinned point that is dragged stays pinned where it is left
flex.hang_set pins (the ids of the nodes pinned; the others let go), length (the item’s length, mm), damping (0 to 1), one or more of them the hanging item: a new length spreads the chain evenly along where it is now, its pinned points where they are; a new damping holds it back from the next step on. Refused with none of them (flex.hang_set takes pins, a length, a damping or more of them) and for a damping outside 0 to 1 (the damping must be from 0 to 1, got 1.5)
flex.hang_lock as the flex.* commands (flex, nodes, length, warnings) and deviation (mm: the farthest the chain is from the route through the nodes); one undo step Edit Flex1. Refused (the item still hangs) when the kept nodes are not a valid item or the item is not made whole along them (Lock below)
flex.hang_cancel cancelled: whether an item hung; the design is not changed
Query Fields Result
flex_hang the hanging item (below), null when none hangs

The hanging item, points in the item’s component’s coordinates (as the flex query’s):

{"flex": "F7", "length": 300, "segment": 10, "at_rest": false, "time": 0.033,
 "taut": false, "grabbed": 150.0, "damping": 0.5,
 "polyline": [[0, 0, 40], …],
 "normals": [[0, 0, 1], …],
 "touching": [false, false, true, …],
 "nodes": [{"id": "n1", "index": 0, "point": [0, 0, 40], "along": 0, "pinned": true,
 "support": "port", "moved": false}, …]}
  • polyline, normals: the chain’s points and the section’s y at each (its direction and its length along the chain follow from the points: nothing is given twice, a step answers many times a second); touching: whether each point lies on a body.
  • nodes: the item’s nodes as points of the chain (index), where they are now, whether each is pinned, what it was attached to before (support, as the flex query’s) and whether it was dragged while pinned (moved).
  • grabbed: the length along the chain of the point the pointer holds, null when none; time: the seconds the step simulated (whole substeps); taut: the chain is pulled longer than its length between its pins (more than 1 %); damping: the session’s (Damping above).

Lock. The chain where it is becomes the item’s nodes: the pinned nodes as they were (their attachments kept; one dragged while pinned a free node where it is), and between them the fewest points of the chain through which the item’s route is the chain’s shape: the points where it meets and leaves a surface (so that a stretch along the surfaces runs between nodes on faces, and one through the air between others), the points that hold the chain’s polyline within the tolerance, then routed and, where the chain is farther from the route than the tolerance, the farthest point of each such stretch added, six times at most. No node is made where the item cannot lie (in a body, or nearer to one than its resting distance by more than a twentieth of it, at least 0.1 mm: a cable that hung down a bore narrower than itself) or where it only touches a face over its edge (the way from the face to the point more than 30 degrees off the face’s normal): the route finds its own way past them. No two of these points, nor one of them and a pinned node, lie nearer along the chain than twice the resting distance or the bend radius, whichever is longer (a point right beside a pinned end, which lies on what it is attached to, made the route turn back between them). The tolerance is half the section’s resting distance (at least 0.1 mm). A node at a point that lies on a face is on that face (on, at the surface below the centre line; a face of another component through the occurrence it is placed at); the others are free. Nodes that were let go are replaced by these. A fixed_length the item has becomes the session’s length when that was set (its slack then hangs as Hanging slack says; the route through the nodes is about as long as the chain, so little is left to hang). The item’s route is then worked out from its nodes as any item’s (Kernel::flex_route). The lock is refused, the item still hanging, when no route goes through the nodes, when the item cannot be made along them, when its route turns back on itself (a step of it more than a right angle from the one before: no section is swept round that), or when its route is not about as long as the chain (half of it at most, or longer than half again and twice the resting distance): never an item kept in part.

The kernel. Two methods, unsupported by default (core/model-base/src/kernel.rs, “Flex drape”): flex_drape_step (DrapeStepSpec: the obstacles, the points, their velocities and pins, the segment, the resting distance, the bend radius, gravity, the seconds, the grab, the time it has been still and the damping, to DrapeStep: the points, velocities, the section’s y, what each point lies on, and rest) and flex_drape_nodes (DrapeNodesSpec: the chain, what it lies on, the points to keep, the ends’ ports, the item as a route takes it and the tolerance, to DrapeNodes: the points that are nodes and the deviation). The mock kernel’s stand-ins: free points fall 100 mm a second and stop on the top of a box below them; the nodes are every fourth point and the ends.

CAM: setups, operations and machines

mitcad#1013 (core/model/src/cam/, document/cam.rs, api/cam.rs; the design is docs/cam.md): CAM is kept with the design, not on the timeline. A setup is one clamping of the stock: the bodies it machines, the stock, the work coordinate system, the work offset, the safe height, the machine (one of the design’s machines), the post-processor’s dialect and settings, and its operations in order. Editing CAM never recomputes the model, and the model’s recompute never computes toolpaths: the queries compute them from the design at the timeline marker through the crate mitcad-cam. Each command is one undo step that recomputes nothing (none when nothing changes).

  • Values (depths, heights, stepovers, feeds, margins, tool sizes) are JSON numbers in millimetres, mm/min, rpm or degrees, whatever the design’s units, or expressions with units that the design’s parameters evaluate: "0.25 in", "thickness + 1"; a bare number in an expression is in the design’s length (or angle) unit. A feed’s expression is a length per minute ("40 in" is 40 inches per minute). The program is written in millimetres or inches by the setup’s post.units (millimetres, inches). An expression follows a rename_parameter of a parameter it names, in the rename’s undo step (the toolpath stays up to date), and delete_parameter refuses a parameter a setup’s or an operation’s value uses, naming them (the CAM setup Setup 1, the CAM operation Pocket 1 of Setup 1); a feature’s parameter a value uses stays as a user parameter when the feature is deleted (mitcad#1830).
  • Ids: setups and operations have numbers unique in the design ("setup": 1, "operation": 4); a setup may also be named by its name. Machines have text ids ("router").
  • Work coordinates (wcs): origin {"kind": "stock", "corner": "top_front_left"} (also top_front_right, top_back_left, top_back_right, top_center, bottom_front_left, bottom_center; the default) or {"kind": "point", "at": <a point reference>}; z a planar face, plane or axis reference (Z along its outward normal or axis; the design’s Z when left out); x an axis reference (X along it). References are those of features (References to geometry).
  • Occurrences: CAM reads a reference in its component’s coordinates and places it where the occurrence it was picked in places that component: an input’s occurrence, a body’s {"body", "occurrence"} in bodies (a body alone is its id, "F2.b0"), the stock body’s and the work zero point’s occurrence, and the axes’ z_occurrence and x_occurrence in wcs. An occurrence is a path from the design’s root ("O1/O4", as joints and sections keep theirs); left out for the root’s own geometry and for a component placed once (its only placement). A component placed more than once needs it: the same face picked in each placement gives an outline at each. Refused: a path that is gone, or one whose component does not own the reference.
  • Stock (stock): {"kind": "around_bodies", "side", "top", "bottom"} (the setup’s bodies’ bounding box in the work axes grown by margins; the default with no margins) or {"kind": "body", "body", "occurrence"}. bodies empty: every body as placed in the design (a component placed twice: both placements) but the stock body.
  • Eye (visible, default true; the file writes it only when false): the setup’s toolpaths drawn in the view, the Browser’s eye, kept in the design. cam_setup_edit with {"visible"} alone is one undo step named as a body’s eye (Hide Setup 1, Show Setup 1), checks nothing else and marks no toolpath out of date; cam_setups reports it on every setup.
  • Operations: kind {"type": "facing"}, {"type": "contour", "side": "outside" | "inside" | "on"}, {"type": "pocket"}, {"type": "drill", "peck", "chip_break", "canned_cycle"}, {"type": "adaptive"}, {"type": "rest", "from_tool"}; tool the number in the setup’s machine’s library; inputs: {"kind": "stock"}, {"kind": "face", "body", "face"} (a planar face level with the work plane: its loops at its height), {"kind": "region", "sketch", "region"} (a sketch profile), {"kind": "edges", "body", "edges"}, {"kind": "curves", "sketch", "curves": ["c3"]}, {"kind": "point", "at"} (a hole: a point reference or a cylindrical face’s axis), each but the stock with its occurrence (above); depths {top, bottom, step_down}, heights {clearance, retract}, cutting {spindle_rpm, feed, plunge_feed} (the tool’s where left out), stepover, stock_to_leave, direction (climb, conventional), spindle (cw, ccw), coolant (off, flood, mist, air), entry ({"kind": "plunge"}, {"kind": "ramp", "angle"}, {"kind": "helix", "radius", "angle"}), tabs {count, width, height} (contours), lead {radius}, suppressed. Defaults: the top is the stock’s top; the bottom is the parts’ top for facing, a pocket face’s or profile’s height for the clearing operations, the stock’s bottom for contours and drilling; the step down the smaller of the tool’s flute length and diameter (drilling: the flutes, or a diameter per peck); the clearance the setup’s safe height above the stock and the retract 2 mm above the top. Arcs about the tool axis stay arcs (G2/G3).
  • Out of date: cam_generate records in each operation that computes the fingerprint of its inputs (generated: its definition and its setup’s but the setup’s eye and the values as typed, its tool, the work frame and stock, its values as evaluated now, the versions of the bodies and sketches it reads and where their occurrences place them). The queries give each operation’s state: up_to_date, out_of_date (the fingerprint differs: the model or the operation changed), not_generated or suppressed. Toolpaths are not saved.
  • Machines are copies with their tool libraries (tools), so that a design machines the same after a library changes. The machine library (owner 12.11.2026: a tool library per machine in the user’s settings, with a copy in the project) is a folder of cam/machines/<id>.json files, {"format": "mitcad-cam-machine", "version", "machine", "tools"}: the user’s (MITCAD_CAM_LIBRARY_DIR, or the one the application sets) and the project’s cam-library folder.
  • Messages say what is wrong in words; an operation’s own name leads the machine check’s findings.
Command Fields Result

Refused: an unknown machine, a body not at the marker, a reference or value that does not resolve, an occurrence that is gone or missing (a component placed twice)
cam_setup_edit setup (id or name), changes (the fields of cam_setup_add; machine, dialect and placement null to clear) {}; undo Edit CAM Setup; {"visible"} alone: undo Hide <setup> / Show <setup>, none when unchanged

cam_setup_move setup, index {}; undo Move CAM Setup

Refused: a tool the setup’s machine lacks, an input whose body or sketch is not at the marker, tabs on another than a contour, a ramp or helix on facing or drilling

Refused: a controller MitCad does not write for (“The machine Router has a controller MitCad does not write for.”), a dialect of the other kind of machine (“The machine Router is a milling machine; Fanuc (turning) writes for lathes.”, “The lathe Lathe needs a lathe controller; grbl writes for milling machines.”, mitcad#2119), two tools of one number

cam_tool_put machine, tool: {number (1-999), name, shape: {"kind": "flat" | "ball" | "bull" (corner_radius) | "drill" (point_angle) | "chamfer" (angle, tip_diameter) | "engraver" (angle, tip_diameter)}, diameter, shank_diameter, flute_length (three diameters), length (stick-out: the flutes and 5 mm), flutes, holder, cutting: {spindle_rpm, feed, plunge_feed}}, lengths as values with units {"tool"} as kept, in mm and degrees; replaces the tool of its number; undo Set CAM Tool

Query Fields Result

cam_operations setup {setup, operations} as above

Refused while an operation fails or the setup has no machine

cam_dialects dialects: [{id, label, extension}]

Adaptive clearing is the engine’s pocket with its adaptive option (phase 2), with the engine’s settings (45 degrees of engagement at most). Rest machining ({"type": "rest", "from_tool"}) cuts what the bigger tool from_tool (its number in the setup’s machine’s library) left: its diameter, and the stock to leave of the last operation before it that cut with that tool, go to the engine’s rest clean-up; it is refused without from_tool or when that tool is not in the library. Entries (entry), holding tabs (laid out by their count) and leads go to the engine’s contour, pocket and rest as they are, a helix without a radius turning at a quarter of the tool’s diameter. Drilling takes chip_break (pecks that back off instead of leaving the hole) and canned_cycle (on by default: the holes may be written as the controller’s canned cycle); whether cycles are written at all is the setup’s post.canned_cycles (off by default). Probing the work zero (probe_work_zero, MillenniumOS’ G6600) is passed to the post settings.

Code: core/model/src/cam/ (types, outlines, machine library), core/model/src/document/cam.rs, core/model-api/src/cam.rs. Tests: core/model-tests/cam, core/model/src/cam/outline.rs.

CAM: stock simulation

The stock as a setup’s program cuts it (mitcad#1013, phase 3; docs/cam.md “Stock simulation”): a height map of the stock in work coordinates (a Z per node of a grid over the stock’s box), each move swept by its tool’s cutting end (flat, ball, bull nose, drill point, V-bit), rapids as the posts write them. The grid is an eighth of the smallest tool’s diameter apart (at least 0.01 mm), coarser until it has at most max_nodes nodes (1 000 000 by default); what lies between nodes is not seen. Heights are written to the micrometre as runs: pairs of a height (µm) and a count of nodes, row by row from the grid’s origin (X first); in a snapshot a pair 0, -n is n nodes unchanged since the one before. The setup’s bodies, meshed and seen from above on the same grid, are the part: the material left over it (remaining) is the stock’s height less the part’s at each node where the part is, a gouge the part’s lowest height round a node less the stock’s, and the material beside it the stock left where the part is not.

Query Fields Result
cam_simulate setup, until ({operation (id), move (index in its toolpath)}; the end when left out), frames (moves to take snapshots after, at most 1000), resolution (mm), max_nodes, tolerance (thicknesses up to it count as none; 0.01 mm), result (heights, the default, or remaining) {setup, work, grid: {origin, step, nx, ny, bottom, top}, until (the last move cut), rapid_cuts: [{message, operation, move, leg, depth, at}], removed (mm³), lowest}; with heights: initial and heights (runs before and after), frames: [{operation, move, runs}] (each the changes since the snapshot before, the first since initial) and part (runs; with bodies); with bodies: remaining: {tolerance, max, mean, volume, area, thickest: [{at, model, thickness}], gouge, gouges, beside, beside_volume, part_nodes, beside_nodes} (the places in work coordinates and in the model, the thickest first, apart by the smallest tool’s diameter). Refused while an operation fails

The collision check of the spindle assembly (mitcad_cam::check_collisions) takes the stock as cut by the same simulation unless its options ask for the stock before the cut ("stock": "before_cut").

CAM: 3-axis operations

mitcad#1013, phase 3 (core/cam/src/ops/surface.rs, raster.rs, waterline.rs, roughing.rs; document/cam.rs; the design in docs/cam.md, “3-axis machining”): three operation kinds of a setup that machine the bodies’ surfaces from their triangle meshes (each body meshed within 0.005 mm, CAM_SURFACE_DEVIATION, in the setup’s work coordinates), added and edited with cam_operation_add and cam_operation_edit like the others.

  • Inputs: {"kind": "body", "body", "occurrence"} for each body machined (the setup’s bodies when none is given), and faces or sketch profiles (face, region) as the boundary, the area the tool’s center stays in (the stock’s outline when none: for roughing and raster finishing; waterline finishing runs round everything). Edges, curves and points are refused for them, and bodies for the other kinds.
  • Defaults: the top is the stock’s top, the bottom the stock’s bottom; stepover and stock to leave as for the others.
  • Out of date: the fingerprint covers the bodies they read, the setup’s bodies (their versions and placements) when they pick none.
Kind (kind) Fields What it does
{"type": "roughing_3d", "adaptive"} depths (step_down: the smaller of the flutes and the diameter), stepover (40 % of the diameter), stock_to_leave, direction, entry; adaptive true: each level by adaptive clearing Levels from the top down, at most the step down apart, and at each floor of the bodies raised by the stock to leave; each level a pocket of where the tool’s cylinder (grown by the stock to leave) may go, inside the boundary. A flat or bull nose end mill
{"type": "raster_finish", "angle", "slope"} angle (degrees from the work X; 0), slope (cut only where the surface is at most this steep, degrees from the horizontal; every slope), stepover (a tenth of the diameter), stock_to_leave, depths.bottom (the lowest the tool goes where nothing is under it) Parallel passes back and forth over the boundary, the tool dropped onto the surfaces (exact for flat, ball and bull nose end mills), within 0.01 mm between its points
{"type": "waterline_finish", "slope"} slope (cut only where the surface is at least this steep; every slope), depths (step_down: a tenth of the diameter), stock_to_leave, direction At each level the loops where the tool just touches the surfaces, climb milling round the bodies by default; only their stretches inside a boundary

Angles and slopes are values with units like the others ("90 deg"). Refused in words: a drill or V-bit (raster and waterline: “The operation needs a flat, ball or bull nose end mill.”), a ball for roughing, a slope outside 0 to 90 degrees, a retract height the bodies reach up to, ramp and helix entries on the finishing kinds, nothing to cut (“The raster finishing has nothing to cut within its boundary.”).
